stories.title: Shell drives spike in oil exploration bids off the coast of Newfoundland
stories.summary: ST. John's - Oil giant Shell is driving a surge in oil exploration interest off the coast of Newfoundland after several years of stagnation.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Newfoundland and Labrador’s offshore energy regulator says the London-headquartered company successfully bid on six exploration licenses off the province’s east and southeast coast.

The licenses are for six parcels of offshore area encompassing more than 15,000 square kilometres, for which Shell pledged more than $210 million in exploration work.

Article continues below

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

The company also partnered with Norwegian energy giant Equinor on two other licenses totalling 1,230 square kilometres, for a total work commitment of $30 million.

Shell recently announced it was buying a 30 per cent stake in Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord oil development off the coast of St. John’s, N.L., which would be the first deepwater oil project in the country.

The Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator says it received 10 successful bids in total, marking the first time since 2022 that companies have purchased exploration licenses in the province.

Spokesperson Alicia Curran said it was the largest number of successful bids since 2000.

OilCo, the province’s oil and gas corporation, successfully bid on two licenses, each for an offshore parcel of more than 2,700 square kilometres.

Jim Keating, OilCo’s chief executive officer, says the idea is to partner with interested oil companies on the licenses and give them an opportunity beyond the annual call for bids to dip their toes in the province’s oil industry.

“By securing our exploration rights to these parcels, we can create alternative commercial entry points for these investors,” Keating said in an interview.

Equinor is expected to make a final decision early next year about whether it will proceed with Bay du Nord, which would be about 500 kilometres off the coast of St. John’s, in the Flemish Pass Basin. Torgrim Reitan, the company’s chief financial officer, told investors last week that the $14 billion development, as it is currently proposed, only involves some of Equinor’s discoveries in the area, and there are opportunities for expansion.

As it stands, Bay du Nord is expected to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government has said it is considering buying a stake in the project of up to 10 per cent.

The province’s offshore area is currently home to four oil installations. Bay du Nord would be the fifth.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Here’s what you need to know as the Liberals prepare to table Budget 2026
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal Liberals are teeing up Thursday's budget as the government's next step toward fixing long-standing problems facing Canada's economy.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted November 5, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 5, 2026 5:15 am.

Ottawa — The federal Liberals are teeing up Thursday’s budget as the government’s next step toward fixing long-standing problems facing Canada’s economy.

Budget 2026 will be the second tabled under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Budgets detail a government’s expectations for economic growth and the projected pace of spending and borrowing. They’re also political documents that can serve as a launching pad for legislation and government policy initiatives.

In addition to new spending items, Thursday’s budget will include an update on the federal government’s immigration levels plan.

After the budget is tabled in the House of Commons on Thursday afternoon, members of Parliament will debate the legislation for weeks and could seek amendments or carve-outs from the wider document.

With a majority government, the Liberals are in a strong position to get their budget approved.

Under Carney, the Liberals have vowed to boost productivity, stoke private investment and build out infrastructure to help Canadian businesses reach new markets.

Ottawa has presented its higher spending on defence and infrastructure as a response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade aggression and other sources of geopolitical volatility.

It’s all about securing economic sovereignty, the government argues. That explains this budget’s name — “Maîtres chez nous,” or “masters of our destiny.”

Analysts are expecting the federal government will continue to borrow and chart relatively deep deficits as it tries to reduce economic dependence on the United States while offering supports to tariff-afflicted industries.

An annual deficit refers to how much additional debt a government is taking on in a given fiscal year to cover spending commitments. Over time, growing deficits without a plan for reducing that debt can affect a country’s sovereign credit rating, making it even more costly to borrow.

Already, the parliamentary budget officer predicts debt-servicing costs will be the fastest growing expenses on the government’s balance sheet.

Critics warn high debt costs, if left to grow unchecked, can crowd out other government spending priorities and limit Canada’s ability to respond to future shocks.

The Liberal government regularly cites Canada’s strong sovereign credit rating in comparison to many of its G7 peers to justify its borrowing plans.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has been a vocal critic of the government’s deficits and is calling on Carney to curb “out-of-control spending” in the budget.

The Liberals have committed to reducing spending on day-to-day government operations so that, eventually, federal borrowing goes solely toward capital investments like major projects. They’ve also pledged to shrink deficits as a share of the economy.

Most fiscal experts predict Ottawa will post slightly smaller deficits in the coming years than those projected in the spring economic update back in April. Even after a raft of spending announcements over the summer, higher global oil prices from the war in Iran have meant higher federal revenues are offsetting those expenses.

Despite near-term improvements in the bottom line, observers will be looking for evidence the government isn’t baking permanently higher costs into its fiscal horizon.

In Budget 2026, Ottawa needs to explain how a higher track for government borrowing will produce measurable economic results, analysts from the Institute of Fiscal Studies and Democracy at the University of Ottawa argued in a budget preview.

A key goal in the Liberal plan is to attract more private investment from inside and outside of Canada. Many business leaders have ramped up calls for tax reform to encourage those kinds of investments.

One of the major spending items in Thursday’s budget was already announced in September — the so-called “productivity mega deduction.” This expanded incentive encourages businesses to invest in new equipment and machinery in exchange for upfront tax writeoffs. It’s expected to cost $36 billion over five years.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne indicated in a speech to business leaders on Monday that the government is also planning to eliminate some tax pains for small- and medium-sized businesses.

Champagne said Budget 2026 is about “changing Canada’s growth model.” For more than a decade, that growth model has meant productivity levels that lag far behind the United States and other peer countries.

Much of the Liberals’ investment agenda is aimed at giving businesses the impetus to invest in better tools for their workers — a path most economists argue is a way to boost productivity.

Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers, who sounded the alarm on the nation’s productivity emergency two years ago, told MPs on Tuesday that the central bank was seeing signs of progress on the productivity front but there’s more work to do.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

By Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press

Here are some ways the change in the distribution of power in Washington could affect Canada.

When the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in January, they may introduce legislation to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada, which were a factor in races in battleground states such as Maine and Michigan.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Image 9Image 10

Even if a bill is introduced, Trump retains the power to block it by issuing a veto. The president’s veto can only be overridden by a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress.

During a live call with Politico late Tuesday, Trump he said he’s willing to work with the Democrats because he “has a right to veto everything. But (he) doesn’t want to sit there for two years vetoing everything.”

He later posted on social media a photo of a red baseball cap with the word “VETO” spelled out in bold white letters.

Americans casting votes in Michigan on Tuesday said they wanted to see the trade war end.

After trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed in August, Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.

Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.

Last month, Trump lifted some tariffs on Canadian exports while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

A U.S. food importer also filed a legal challenge of Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.

Military actions

Hope is emerging among some Canadian and American politicians that the shift in power will lead to the end of the U.S. war on Iran.

Trump has admitted the Iran war affected the midterm elections by causing gas prices to surge, frustrating voters, and Vice-President JD Vance outright blamed the war for losing control of Congress.

But the Trump administration could still escalate the war before the Democrats take control of Congress next year.

“If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday the war in Iran “must end.” When asked how the Democrats would end the war, he said Congress can use “the power of the purse” to deter a president who launches a war without the consent of the American people.

The United States conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on the eve of the midterm elections, a U.S. official said Monday. Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island.

The Canada-U.S. relationship

Politicians on both sides of the border are looking at the midterm elections results as an opportunity to rebuild the Canada-U.S. relationship.

Formal trade talks with the U.S. were stalled when Canada walked away from negotiations in Washington in August. Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday official trade discussions with the United States have been taking place in recent days.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday the Liberal government’s push to diversify trade won’t change direction in the midterms’ wake.

He also said recent talks with Trump’s administration have been productive and he looks forward to speaking more with his American counterparts in the coming days.

Beth Burke, CEO of the Canadian American Business Council, said in a media statement Wednesday that the newly elected and re-elected members of Congress will take office at a “critical moment for the U.S.-Canada relationship.”

Burke said reducing tariffs would lower costs for American and Canadian businesses and help bring down prices for consumers in both countries.

“With the elections behind us, both governments have a real opportunity to make progress on a trade agreement,” she said.

Former U.S. ambassador to Canada Bruce Heyman told CTV News on Tuesday that the U.S. must begin repairing its relationship with Canada.

“I am calling on this new Congress to begin immediately a formal reconciliation process with Canada,” he said. “That needs to begin almost the first day they come into office in January.”

Immigration policy

Trump has been roundly criticized at home and abroad for ramping up immigration raids after he returned to the White House in January 2025.

Since then, Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials and cases have emerged of Canadians being detained by U.S. immigration officials for minor infractions.

Global Affairs Canada said last month the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadian citizens in the United States jumped 60 per cent in the last fiscal year compared to the year before.

In its annual report on consular cases, it recorded 577 cases of Canadians arrested or detained in the U.S. between April 2025 and March 2026, up from 361 a year prior.

Democrats likely will look to address immigration policies when they take over Congress. In January, Senate Democrats threatened to block legislation to fund the Department of Homeland Security and several other agencies after the killings of two protesters by federal agents in Minneapolis.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone, David Baxter, Kyle Duggan and The Associated Press

stories.title: What Washington is missing about Trump’s Canada tariffs
stories.summary: Cfr’s Edward Alden explains what Washington is missing about the trade war — and why political pressure could improve the prospects for a Canada deal
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
The Council on Foreign Relations recently led a member delegation to Detroit and Toronto to examine the U.S.-Canada economic relationship.

The group examined how trade, investment, and advanced manufacturing continue to connect the two economies despite the trade tensions.

Edward Alden, a CFR senior fellow and visiting professor of U.S.-Canada economic relations at Western Washington University, accompanied the group. National Post spoke with him about what the delegation learned and what Washington is missing.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

I think several different things. I think one that they May be aware of but aren’t hearing enough is how damaging the tariff policies have been to that region.

I mean, these are industrial economies, most obvious in the auto industry, but it’s true in other sectors as well, that are so integrally tied to each other that trying to pull it apart inevitably causes a lot of damage to both countries. So I think message number one is just the very significant regional impacts that the tariffs are having.

Message number two, which surprised me a little bit, is how much goodwill remains. I mean, there’s obviously a lot of Canadian anger at the actions of the administration.

We’ve seen big declines in Canadian travel to the U.S., which has hurt Detroit, but has also hurt my community out here in Bellingham, Washington. But I really came away from the conversations in Windsor and in Toronto with a sense that there’s still a lot of will and desire on the Canadian side to try to fix this. Not to go back to the way things were — that won’t happen — but to try to build a more productive path going forward.

And I think the third thing, which if they’re not aware of it in D.C. they should be, is just that Canadians are prepared to be in this for the long haul. I didn’t hear a shred of willingness to accept a deal that’s going to permanently disadvantage the Canadian economy. I think if there’s a deal to be reached, it has to be a more balanced agreement of the sort that have been reached in the past. Obviously, there will be differences — this is a new administration, it’s a new world. But I think the extremely one-sided demands that we’ve seen out of Washington just aren’t going to fly in Canada. Those would be my big takeaways.

I think the argument doesn’t work very well in North America because as a result of free trade agreements going back three decades plus, we’ve created these regional production economies. Let’s look at this from an American perspective.

Goods manufactured in Mexico or in Canada have very high percentages of U.S. content. There are direct benefits to the American economy when we are importing products that have a “Made in Canada” label or a “Made in Mexico” label. It’s quite different when you’re looking at trade with China.

China is building supply chains … that are quite separate from the United States. China is increasingly making most of the inputs for its manufactured products in China. It’s internalized a lot of the supply chain. But where it’s not (internalized), it’s an Asian supply chain. So the products coming from China to the United States have very little U.S. content in them.

There is not very much in the way of industrial or manufacturing work that is created in the United States when we’re importing products from China. In fact, quite the opposite, because these products are often competing directly with North American-made products. So the problem with the approach this administration has taken is not tariffs per se, but not picking the targets intelligently.

The midterms are over. Will Trump still want to make a deal with Canada?

Who blinks first? 'It probably has to be Carney' to restart U.S. talks, trade analysts say

Even if you want to reshore manufacturing, the U.S. is not about to become a self-sufficient economy. We are going to rely on manufacturing inputs for the final products that we produce, and a lot of those are gonna come from Canada or Mexico.

If you’re putting tariffs on those intermediate goods, then you’re just costing your own manufacturers a great deal of money. So there’s nothing wrong in theory with wanting to reshore some manufacturing, and I certainly think there are strong arguments for working with allies to develop capacities in critical inputs, be they minerals or lithium batteries.

We could come up with a long list of things where North America doesn’t want to be wholly dependent on China. But fighting a trade war with Canada and Mexico undercuts that goal. I think the trade war is completely misguided, even if you accept that the goal is to try to encourage reshoring of manufacturing in the United States. This is not the way to go about it.

If you look at the election debates, I think the greatest costs are actually being felt in the U.S. border states. So we’ve got an economy out here in Washington State, and the same is true in places in Michigan and New York and others. You’ve got border towns that were heavily dependent on Canadian business that is way down.

You’ve got the industries in Michigan and the other border states that are hurting, a lot of it from the cost of the tariffs that those companies are being forced to pay. The competitive position of Ford and General Motors vis-à-vis international competitors is weakening as a result.

I mean, it’s a very cynical kind of strategy, and I don’t think one that behooves any U.S. president who’s behaving in a way that befits American interests. But the strategy was to harm the Canadians more and hope they will buckle, and I think, in fact, you’re seeing the opposite.

You’re seeing a lot of the harm being concentrated in the northern U.S. states and voters in those states complaining about it. And the administration is responding. You’ve seen some tariff modifications. I think that’s why there seems to be a prospect for the U.S.-Canada negotiations to be revived.

It is not at all clear that the tariffs have inflicted a level of pain on Canada that is making Canadians want to rush back to the negotiating table. In fact, it seems to have done the opposite.

It’s too soon to tell. I’ve followed trade negotiations closely for about three decades now, and the devil is always in the details. The U.S. and Canada were quite close to a deal back in August until things happened at the last minute. It seems to be mostly U.S.-led — that they just put unacceptable issues on the table. It’s certainly possible that that could happen again. But I think the Trump folks are aware that they are reaching the political limits of the tariff policy.

They’ve managed to do something rather extraordinary in the last two years, which is to take an American populace that was quite skeptical of trade. You look at polls on Nafta, Usmca, or polls on trade with China, and across the board, (there were) high levels of skepticism among the American public about the trade arrangements.

And, in the course of a year and a half as a result of tariff policy, they’ve turned Americans strongly against tariffs. Americans have come to equate tariffs with rising prices, with hits to their own pocketbook. And I think the administration is recognizing this.

Trump is always willing to do deals. He wants them to be as one-sided as possible. But I think he’d be more than happy to put this to rest. I don’t think he wants to get hammered for the next two years over the tariff policy with Canada …

We don’t like a lot of things about the tariffs, but the Canada tariffs — you’ve got to be kidding me, right? This is one of our closest allies, a trading partner that we’ve been able to work out disputes with for decades, that has largely the same labour rights we have here in the United States, that doesn’t have the challenges of trading with Mexico and some other countries. What the heck are we doing putting tariffs on Canada?

Trump’s tariffs are unpopular, but the Canada tariffs are uniquely unpopular. And you’ve really seen that come together in the midterm campaign. So I think we’re in a different political moment. That doesn’t mean that a deal is imminent.

For Canada, this is a hard team to negotiate with. They’re not well-organized. They change their mind frequently. So I’m not going to go out on a limb and predict that a deal is imminent. But I do think the political environment for a deal is considerably better than it was even two, three months ago.

I think at the national level, the signs of recovery would be efforts to modify the tariffs when and where it’s evident that harm is being caused to both countries.

I’m not naive enough to think we’re going to go back to the Usmca tariff environment, but I think you could end up in a situation where both countries are actually trying to make the trade relationship work, even if the rules are different than they were under Usmca. So that would be one.

I think number two would actually be serious engagement on the Usmca review, which has not happened yet between the United States and Canada. But a clear commitment from the U.S. side that, yes indeed, we want to extend the Usmca, and to do that, we have to reach agreements that are acceptable to both Mexico and Canada.

The U.S. talks with Mexico have broken down as well — not as publicly as they have with Canada because the Mexicans have taken a much quieter approach. But they’ve broken down over largely the same issue, which is the national security (Section 232) tariffs, particularly on autos in both Mexico and Canada’s case, not exclusively.

Steel is another big one and steel derivative products. But those negotiations are going nowhere. So I think a second sign would be that the review process that was set up in Usmca is actually being engaged with in a faithful fashion by all three countries. So those would be the two big things I would look for. Also, some effort to gain common benefit out of whatever the new set of rules are and a recommitment to the Usmca process. Possibly a third one would be even inklings of some common approaches vis-à-vis China. At the moment, I think Canadians aren’t the least bit interested in that, but I think if the situation with the U.S. stabilizes, then those discussions could begin again.

And I think there are interests in both countries in having somewhat more unified approaches towards China.

paragraphs: The Council on Foreign Relations recently led a member delegation to Detroit and Toronto to examine the U.S.-Canada economic relationship.
The group examined how trade, investment, and advanced manufacturing continue to connect the two economies despite the trade tensions.

Edward Alden, a CFR senior fellow and visiting professor of U.S.-Canada economic relations at Western Washington University, accompanied the group. National Post spoke with him about what the delegation learned and what Washington is missing.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
I think several different things. I think one that they May be aware of but aren’t hearing enough is how damaging the tariff policies have been to that region.

I mean, these are industrial economies, most obvious in the auto industry, but it’s true in other sectors as well, that are so integrally tied to each other that trying to pull it apart inevitably causes a lot of damage to both countries. So I think message number one is just the very significant regional impacts that the tariffs are having.
Message number two, which surprised me a little bit, is how much goodwill remains. I mean, there’s obviously a lot of Canadian anger at the actions of the administration.

We’ve seen big declines in Canadian travel to the U.S., which has hurt Detroit, but has also hurt my community out here in Bellingham, Washington. But I really came away from the conversations in Windsor and in Toronto with a sense that there’s still a lot of will and desire on the Canadian side to try to fix this. Not to go back to the way things were — that won’t happen — but to try to build a more productive path going forward.

And I think the third thing, which if they’re not aware of it in D.C. they should be, is just that Canadians are prepared to be in this for the long haul. I didn’t hear a shred of willingness to accept a deal that’s going to permanently disadvantage the Canadian economy. I think if there’s a deal to be reached, it has to be a more balanced agreement of the sort that have been reached in the past. Obviously, there will be differences — this is a new administration, it’s a new world. But I think the extremely one-sided demands that we’ve seen out of Washington just aren’t going to fly in Canada. Those would be my big takeaways.

I think the argument doesn’t work very well in North America because as a result of free trade agreements going back three decades plus, we’ve created these regional production economies. Let’s look at this from an American perspective.

Goods manufactured in Mexico or in Canada have very high percentages of U.S. content. There are direct benefits to the American economy when we are importing products that have a “Made in Canada” label or a “Made in Mexico” label. It’s quite different when you’re looking at trade with China.

China is building supply chains … that are quite separate from the United States. China is increasingly making most of the inputs for its manufactured products in China. It’s internalized a lot of the supply chain. But where it’s not (internalized), it’s an Asian supply chain. So the products coming from China to the United States have very little U.S. content in them.

There is not very much in the way of industrial or manufacturing work that is created in the United States when we’re importing products from China. In fact, quite the opposite, because these products are often competing directly with North American-made products. So the problem with the approach this administration has taken is not tariffs per se, but not picking the targets intelligently.

Even if you want to reshore manufacturing, the U.S. is not about to become a self-sufficient economy. We are going to rely on manufacturing inputs for the final products that we produce, and a lot of those are gonna come from Canada or Mexico.

If you’re putting tariffs on those intermediate goods, then you’re just costing your own manufacturers a great deal of money. So there’s nothing wrong in theory with wanting to reshore some manufacturing, and I certainly think there are strong arguments for working with allies to develop capacities in critical inputs, be they minerals or lithium batteries.

We could come up with a long list of things where North America doesn’t want to be wholly dependent on China. But fighting a trade war with Canada and Mexico undercuts that goal. I think the trade war is completely misguided, even if you accept that the goal is to try to encourage reshoring of manufacturing in the United States. This is not the way to go about it.

If you look at the election debates, I think the greatest costs are actually being felt in the U.S. border states. So we’ve got an economy out here in Washington State, and the same is true in places in Michigan and New York and others. You’ve got border towns that were heavily dependent on Canadian business that is way down.

You’ve got the industries in Michigan and the other border states that are hurting, a lot of it from the cost of the tariffs that those companies are being forced to pay. The competitive position of Ford and General Motors vis-à-vis international competitors is weakening as a result.

I mean, it’s a very cynical kind of strategy, and I don’t think one that behooves any U.S. president who’s behaving in a way that befits American interests. But the strategy was to harm the Canadians more and hope they will buckle, and I think, in fact, you’re seeing the opposite.

You’re seeing a lot of the harm being concentrated in the northern U.S. states and voters in those states complaining about it. And the administration is responding. You’ve seen some tariff modifications. I think that’s why there seems to be a prospect for the U.S.-Canada negotiations to be revived.
It is not at all clear that the tariffs have inflicted a level of pain on Canada that is making Canadians want to rush back to the negotiating table. In fact, it seems to have done the opposite.

It’s too soon to tell. I’ve followed trade negotiations closely for about three decades now, and the devil is always in the details. The U.S. and Canada were quite close to a deal back in August until things happened at the last minute. It seems to be mostly U.S.-led — that they just put unacceptable issues on the table. It’s certainly possible that that could happen again. But I think the Trump folks are aware that they are reaching the political limits of the tariff policy.

They’ve managed to do something rather extraordinary in the last two years, which is to take an American populace that was quite skeptical of trade. You look at polls on Nafta, Usmca, or polls on trade with China, and across the board, (there were) high levels of skepticism among the American public about the trade arrangements.

And, in the course of a year and a half as a result of tariff policy, they’ve turned Americans strongly against tariffs. Americans have come to equate tariffs with rising prices, with hits to their own pocketbook. And I think the administration is recognizing this.

Trump is always willing to do deals. He wants them to be as one-sided as possible. But I think he’d be more than happy to put this to rest. I don’t think he wants to get hammered for the next two years over the tariff policy with Canada …

We don’t like a lot of things about the tariffs, but the Canada tariffs — you’ve got to be kidding me, right? This is one of our closest allies, a trading partner that we’ve been able to work out disputes with for decades, that has largely the same labour rights we have here in the United States, that doesn’t have the challenges of trading with Mexico and some other countries. What the heck are we doing putting tariffs on Canada?

Trump’s tariffs are unpopular, but the Canada tariffs are uniquely unpopular. And you’ve really seen that come together in the midterm campaign. So I think we’re in a different political moment. That doesn’t mean that a deal is imminent.

For Canada, this is a hard team to negotiate with. They’re not well-organized. They change their mind frequently. So I’m not going to go out on a limb and predict that a deal is imminent. But I do think the political environment for a deal is considerably better than it was even two, three months ago.
I think at the national level, the signs of recovery would be efforts to modify the tariffs when and where it’s evident that harm is being caused to both countries.

I’m not naive enough to think we’re going to go back to the Usmca tariff environment, but I think you could end up in a situation where both countries are actually trying to make the trade relationship work, even if the rules are different than they were under Usmca. So that would be one.

I think number two would actually be serious engagement on the Usmca review, which has not happened yet between the United States and Canada. But a clear commitment from the U.S. side that, yes indeed, we want to extend the Usmca, and to do that, we have to reach agreements that are acceptable to both Mexico and Canada.

The U.S. talks with Mexico have broken down as well — not as publicly as they have with Canada because the Mexicans have taken a much quieter approach. But they’ve broken down over largely the same issue, which is the national security (Section 232) tariffs, particularly on autos in both Mexico and Canada’s case, not exclusively.

Steel is another big one and steel derivative products. But those negotiations are going nowhere. So I think a second sign would be that the review process that was set up in Usmca is actually being engaged with in a faithful fashion by all three countries. So those would be the two big things I would look for. Also, some effort to gain common benefit out of whatever the new set of rules are and a recommitment to the Usmca process. Possibly a third one would be even inklings of some common approaches vis-à-vis China. At the moment, I think Canadians aren’t the least bit interested in that, but I think if the situation with the U.S. stabilizes, then those discussions could begin again.
And I think there are interests in both countries in having somewhat more unified approaches towards China.

stories.title: Carney’s 2026 federal budget to show much lower deficit, new figures suggest
stories.summary: New Finance Department data suggest that Ottawa is on pace to post a deficit much lower than the $66.9-billion predicted in the spring economic update
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
The Carney government’s federal budget Thursday will include a projected deficit for this fiscal year that is significantly lower than what Ottawa had projected earlier this year, new data suggests.

The latest financial figures from the Department of Finance, up to the end of August, show that Ottawa’s deficit for the first five months of the year was a modest $5.4-billion. That’s less than half the $11.1-billlion that the federal government posted a year earlier during the first five months of the year.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the spring economic update that the government expected to post a deficit this year of $66.9-billion, down from the $78.3-billion that had been projected in Carney’s first budget last fall.

But the new data from the department’s Fiscal Monitor, which tracks monthly data, suggest that Ottawa is on pace – at least up until the end of August – to post a deficit much lower than that.

Trevor Tombe, an economics professor at the University of Calgary who closely follows federal finances, said the federal government would likely post a deficit of about $35-billion for the full fiscal year — if Ottawa did nothing from September to the end of March to affect its revenue or spending. That would be less than half what was projected a year ago in the budget.

The main reasons for the lower deficit have been an increase of 7.1 per cent in federal revenue so far this year, due largely to Ottawa sucking up more income tax. That’s despite a sluggish economy, a tariff war with the United States and a cut to the lowest federal income tax rate – to 14 per cent from 15 – that kicked in July 1, 2025.

Government coffers at both the federal and provincial levels have also been juiced by a spike in the prices of a number of natural resources, particularly oil, and higher-than-expected inflation.

But Tombe, also director of fiscal and economic policy at the School of Public Policy, emphasized that the government still has about half a year to make policy changes that affect spending and revenue.

“Political choices will affect things,” said Tombe.

And some of those choices will be unveiled Thursday in the Carney government’s second budget.

Carney budget to focus on taxes, shift from Trudeau era

Ottawa raking in billions more than expected thanks to inflation and natural resource revenue

As reported in late October in National Post, the budget will also provide a boost for Canada’s small and medium-sized businesses, including an effort to cut red tape. The government is also expected to include measures to support affordability, support housing, Canadian culture and tax reform.

As also reported last month in the Post, the budget will also include tax changes designed to spur economic growth. One possible measure, a formal review of Canada’s corporate tax policies, would meet a Liberal campaign promise.

“It’s a growth and competition budget,” said a senior government source.

The government has already made a series of moves that will affect federal finances – and the economy — in the coming months. Champagne already announced a holiday on the federal excise tax on gasoline and diesel until the end of January, while Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new mega-deduction that it hopes will spur investment, particularly in capital-intensive industries such as energy, mining, and technology.

The mega-deduction, which has not yet become law but May well be included in the budget, is expected to cut Canada’s projected tax rate on new investment, a key metric for large investors, by slightly more than half, to about 6.4 per cent from 13 per cent. The price tag for the changes is an estimated $36.5-billion over the next five years.

Unexpected changes to economic growth or natural resources prices or other surprises would also affect the government’s revenue and the deficit.

There’s also added economic uncertainty because of Canada’s unsettled trade relationship with the U.S., the Trump tariffs on dozens of countries, and wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Michael Chong, the Conservatives’ finance critic, said the deficit May be on pace to fall but the country’s debt payments, which account for one of the largest parts of the federal budget, continue to grow. Canadians can also expect the Carney government, which has yet to fully account for its hefty defence spending promises, to keep spending, Chong said.

“He’s a big-spending Liberal,” the Ontario MP said of the prime minister.

Champagne, meanwhile, continued Wednesday to give every indication that reducing or eliminating the deficit is not a top priority. While in Montreal to take part in the finance minister ritual of buying a new pair of shoes for a federal budget, Champagne repeated his mantra that Canada has the strongest fiscal landscape in the G7, which means more room to spend on its priorities.

“The market has seen we have the fiscal discipline,” the minister told a mostly business crowd in Ottawa on Monday night.

John Fragos, a spokesman for Champagne, declined to comment on what Ottawa’s revenue numbers will look like in the budget.

The big picture of federal finances, however, is that Ottawa continues to rack up more red ink. The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last six years.

Ottawa’s annual fiscal results also paint a grim landscape that seems to be darkening.

The pandemic year of 2020-21 was by far the worst deficit ($327.7-billion) in Canadian history, but each of the 10 worst deficits in Canadian history in absolute terms have occurred since 2009-10.

Seven of the eight worst years have been much more recent than that, each occurring since 2019-20. The only outlier was 2009-10 following the global financial crisis.

Last year’s $55.3-billion deficit was the fifth worst ever.

But economists have emphasized that the government shouldn’t use a windfall that May be short term to justify extra spending. Tombe said the government should focus on long-term policies to benefit the economy.

Don Drummond, a former executive at the Department of Finance and a fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute think tank, said the government needs to take a more prudent approach to spending because oil prices May not remain high, population growth has waned and productivity is weak. Carney has already promised tax cuts and extra defence spending, Drummond said.

Although reducing the deficit hasn’t so far been a government priority, the Carney government seems to have taken a more long-term approach to the economy than its predecessor, led by Justin Trudeau. Carney has focused on trying to boost the Canadian economy: infrastructure for exports and commercial transportation, trade relationships, and improving the investment climate.

Canadians can also expect the Carney government, which has yet to fully account for its hefty defence spending promises, to keep spending, Chong said.
“He’s a big-spending Liberal,” the Ontario MP said of the prime minister.

Champagne, meanwhile, continued Wednesday to give every indication that reducing or eliminating the deficit is not a top priority. While in Montreal to take part in the finance minister ritual of buying a new pair of shoes for a federal budget, Champagne repeated his mantra that Canada has the strongest fiscal landscape in the G7, which means more room to spend on its priorities.
“The market has seen we have the fiscal discipline,” the minister told a mostly business crowd in Ottawa on Monday night.
John Fragos, a spokesman for Champagne, declined to comment on what Ottawa’s revenue numbers will look like in the budget.

The big picture of federal finances, however, is that Ottawa continues to rack up more red ink. The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last six years.
Ottawa’s annual fiscal results also paint a grim landscape that seems to be darkening.
The pandemic year of 2020-21 was by far the worst deficit ($327.7-billion) in Canadian history, but each of the 10 worst deficits in Canadian history in absolute terms have occurred since 2009-10.
Seven of the eight worst years have been much more recent than that, each occurring since 2019-20. The only outlier was 2009-10 following the global financial crisis.
Last year’s $55.3-billion deficit was the fifth worst ever.

But economists have emphasized that the government shouldn’t use a windfall that May be short term to justify extra spending. Tombe said the government should focus on long-term policies to benefit the economy.

Don Drummond, a former executive at the Department of Finance and a fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute think tank, said the government needs to take a more prudent approach to spending because oil prices May not remain high, population growth has waned and productivity is weak. Carney has already promised tax cuts and extra defence spending, Drummond said.

Although reducing the deficit hasn’t so far been a government priority, the Carney government seems to have taken a more long-term approach to the economy than its predecessor, led by Justin Trudeau. Carney has focused on trying to boost the Canadian economy: infrastructure for exports and commercial transportation, trade relationships, and improving the investment climate.

content_blocks.text: The Carney government’s federal budget Thursday will include a projected deficit for this fiscal year that is significantly lower than what Ottawa had projected earlier this year, new data suggests.

The latest financial figures from the Department of Finance, up to the end of August, show that Ottawa’s deficit for the first five months of the year was a modest $5.4-billion. That’s less than half the $11.1-billlion that the federal government posted a year earlier during the first five months of the year.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the spring economic update that the government expected to post a deficit this year of $66.9-billion, down from the $78.3-billion that had been projected in Carney’s first budget last fall.
But the new data from the department’s Fiscal Monitor, which tracks monthly data, suggest that Ottawa is on pace – at least up until the end of August – to post a deficit much lower than that.

Trevor Tombe, an economics professor at the University of Calgary who closely follows federal finances, said the federal government would likely post a deficit of about $35-billion for the full fiscal year — if Ottawa did nothing from September to the end of March to affect its revenue or spending. That would be less than half what was projected a year ago in the budget.

The main reasons for the lower deficit have been an increase of 7.1 per cent in federal revenue so far this year, due largely to Ottawa sucking up more income tax. That’s despite a sluggish economy, a tariff war with the United States and a cut to the lowest federal income tax rate – to 14 per cent from 15 – that kicked in July 1, 2025.
Government coffers at both the federal and provincial levels have also been juiced by a spike in the prices of a number of natural resources, particularly oil, and higher-than-expected inflation.

But Tombe, also director of fiscal and economic policy at the School of Public Policy, emphasized that the government still has about half a year to make policy changes that affect spending and revenue.
“Political choices will affect things,” said Tombe.
And some of those choices will be unveiled Thursday in the Carney government’s second budget.

stories.title: Ex-Nasa chief economist Alexander MacDonald to lead Canadian Space Agency
stories.summary: MacDonald understands that space is crucial to Canada’s national and economic security, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nasa’s first chief economist has been named president of the Canadian Space Agency.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly on Wednesday announced that Alexander MacDonald had been appointed to the role.

A government news release says MacDonald helped establish Nasa’s Moon to Mars strategy and its Artemis program.

It says he has held several senior roles at the American agency, including senior economic adviser in the administrator’s office and founding program executive of the Emerging Space Office.

Joly says MacDonald brings leadership experience and expertise in space policy and economics, and understands that space is crucial to Canada’s national and economic security.

MacDonald takes over from Lisa Campbell, who became president in 2020.

stories.title: Talk to teen patients about dating violence, Canadian Paediatric Society says
stories.summary: Toronto - The Canadian Paediatric Society is urging doctors to talk to teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
In new guidance issued Thursday, the society said one-third of teens in Canada experience physical, psychological, sexual or technology-related abuse — including stalking — in relationships.

Dating violence among teens is not new, but technology like texting or social media can facilitate abusive behaviour, such as teens tracking their partners or forbidding them from communicating with friends, said Dr. Megan Harrison, chair of the society’s adolescent health committee, in an interview.

Article continues below

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

“Those types of behaviours happen to adults as well. So not just teens, but the difference is an adolescent is still, you know, forming their own identity,” she said.

“So it’s a more vulnerable time for things like that to be occurring.”

The guidance says health-care providers can normalize talking about healthy and unhealthy relationships by routinely bringing up the topic during adolescent patient visits.

“The more places where teens can feel comfortable to ask questions about relationships and to know that it’s something that they can bring up in a safe place ... the better we’ll be able to prevent these unhealthy situations,” said Harrison, who is a pediatrician in the division of adolescent medicine at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario in Ottawa.

Harrison emphasized that doctors don’t need to have answers if a teen patient discloses a problematic relationship, but are providing a safe, non-judgmental space and then connecting them to other resources in the community as needed.

“You can really do a whole lot of good in actually what ends up being a really short period of time,” she said.

The guidance recommends doctors talk to teen patients alone during part of their visits and assure them that their conversation is confidential, unless the physician is immediately worried for their safety or the safety of someone else.

It also says doctors should share educational resources about healthy relationships and teen dating violence that their patient can keep or share with friends. The guidance provides an example for health-care providers on how to start that conversation.

“A lot of dating relationships are great experiences. But some patients have shared that they have experienced situations in their relationships that made them feel uncomfortable or even scared,” the sample script says.

“We now talk to all our patients about their relationships because they can impact health. We also provide education on this topic because it is likely you or someone you know could use it.”

If the teen discloses problematic behaviour in a relationship, the health-care provider should support them by thanking them for their trust and connecting them with other resources in the community that can help.

In some cases, that can include taking the first step with the patient, Harrison said.

“If the youth feels comfortable at that time, maybe I make a phone call with the youth in the office. Maybe I help them make an appointment if that’s what they’d like, or I sit there with them while they make the phone call, or we open up the web page together.”

If the patient is going to access resources later on their own, the guidance advises discussing the possibility that an abusive partner May track the teen’s online activity and asking if printed materials would be a safer option.

Some teens are at increased risk for dating violence, including those who are homeless or living in poverty, gender-diverse youth, Black and Indigenous female teens, and young people living in care systems, the guidance says.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Kelowna supportive housing fire leaves tenants with terminated rental agreements
stories.summary: The City of Kelowna says it's aware of the situation and recognizes the challenges residents are facing as they navigate next steps for housing.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A Kelowna supportive housing complex remains vacant one month after a fire forced all 50 residents from their homes, with extensive smoke and water damage expected to require lengthy remediation work.

“We’re devastated. It’s a loss for Kelowna and we’re heartbroken,” said Patricia Bacon, executive director of the John Howard Society of Okanagan and Kootenay.

The Hearthstone supportive housing facility on Commerce Avenue was largely spared by the Oct. 5 fire, which was contained to one unit.

However, the resulting damage has left the building uninhabitable and prompted the John Howard Society of Okanagan and Kootenay to terminate residents’ tenancy agreements under what is known as a frustrated tenancy.

A frustrated tenancy occurs when a rental property becomes uninhabitable through circumstances beyond the control of either the landlord or tenant.

“It’s considered a frustrated tenancy, when due to no fault of the landlord or tenant, there is no habitable space to rent, usually earthquakes, fires, this kind of stuff,” Bacon explained.

The John Howard Society says it has helped residents find alternative accommodations, including shelter spaces and beds, although not everyone accepted the options offered.

“We found some shelter places, some shelter beds, etc. So nobody was put out on the street,” Bacon said. “Some people, however, did not choose the options that we made available to them. Some people actually chose to use the outdoor encampments.”

With winter approaching, questions remain about what additional supports May be available to those affected.

The City of Kelowna says it’s aware of the situation and recognizes the challenges residents are facing as they navigate next steps for housing.

“Staff are working with BC Housing outreach teams to identify and respond to the immediate needs of residents who have not yet accessed shelter or temporary housing options,” said Stephanie Martin, social development supervisor for the City of Kelowna.

Before remediation work can begin, assessments must be completed to determine the full extent of the damage. Crews must also finish collecting any belongings that can be salvaged from the building.

The cause of the fire has not been determined.

For Bacon, the closure represents a significant loss of an important resource for some of Kelowna’s most vulnerable residents.

“It’s so important to have this kind of housing available for folks who are very vulnerable, where the support staff are there to offer compassionate care and supports and navigation and stuff, healthcare. We had a food program in there,” she said. “All of that is lost.”

The facility is not expected to reopen until sometime in 2027, leaving residents and the community without an important source of supportive housing in the meantime.

content_blocks.caption: Dozens of people displaced by a fire at their Kelowna supportive housing complex last month face an uncertain future. As Klaudia Van Eemmerik reports, while some have found new living arrangements, others may be spending the winter outdoors.

content_blocks.text: A Kelowna supportive housing complex remains vacant one month after a fire forced all 50 residents from their homes, with extensive smoke and water damage expected to require lengthy remediation work.
content_blocks.html: A Kelowna supportive housing complex remains vacant one month after a fire forced all 50 residents from their homes, with extensive smoke and water damage expected to require lengthy remediation work.

content_blocks.text: “We’re devastated. It’s a loss for Kelowna and we’re heartbroken,” said Patricia Bacon, executive director of the John Howard Society of Okanagan and Kootenay.
content_blocks.html: “We’re devastated. It’s a loss for Kelowna and we’re heartbroken,” said Patricia Bacon, executive director of the John Howard Society of Okanagan and Kootenay.

content_blocks.text: The Hearthstone supportive housing facility on Commerce Avenue was largely spared by the Oct. 5 fire, which was contained to one unit.
content_blocks.html: The Hearthstone supportive housing facility on Commerce Avenue was largely spared by the Oct. 5 fire, which was contained to one unit.

content_blocks.text: However, the resulting damage has left the building uninhabitable and prompted the John Howard Society of Okanagan and Kootenay to terminate residents’ tenancy agreements under what is known as a frustrated tenancy.
A frustrated tenancy occurs when a rental property becomes uninhabitable through circumstances beyond the control of either the landlord or tenant.
“It’s considered a frustrated tenancy, when due to no fault of the landlord or tenant, there is no habitable space to rent, usually earthquakes, fires, this kind of stuff,” Bacon explained.
The John Howard Society says it has helped residents find alternative accommodations, including shelter spaces and beds, although not everyone accepted the options offered.

“We found some shelter places, some shelter beds, etc. So nobody was put out on the street,” Bacon said. “Some people, however, did not choose the options that we made available to them. Some people actually chose to use the outdoor encampments.”
With winter approaching, questions remain about what additional supports May be available to those affected.
The City of Kelowna says it’s aware of the situation and recognizes the challenges residents are facing as they navigate next steps for housing.

“Staff are working with BC Housing outreach teams to identify and respond to the immediate needs of residents who have not yet accessed shelter or temporary housing options,” said Stephanie Martin, social development supervisor for the City of Kelowna.
Before remediation work can begin, assessments must be completed to determine the full extent of the damage. Crews must also finish collecting any belongings that can be salvaged from the building.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Court orders end to Penticton encampment'

content_blocks.text: The cause of the fire has not been determined.
For Bacon, the closure represents a significant loss of an important resource for some of Kelowna’s most vulnerable residents.

“It’s so important to have this kind of housing available for folks who are very vulnerable, where the support staff are there to offer compassionate care and supports and navigation and stuff, healthcare. We had a food program in there,” she said. “All of that is lost.”
The facility is not expected to reopen until sometime in 2027, leaving residents and the community without an important source of supportive housing in the meantime.

stories.title: B.C. authorities investigate fatal Bella Coola bear attack as community imposes curfew
stories.summary: Jennifer Balcarras and her 19-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, were found dead earlier this week in the Snooka West Trail area
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
B.C. conservation officers investigating a suspected grizzly bear attack that killed a mother and daughter on the province’s central coast say they are working to determine whether it was the same animal that mauled a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year.

Inspector Jeff Tyre with the province’s Conservation Officer Service said Wednesday that it is still early in the investigation and that the bear population is large in the Bella Coola Valley, where both attacks took place.

“We do have the DNA from the last attack site and we will be working to collect DNA; that would be the only linkage we could put toward that,” Insp. Tyre told reporters. “It’s too early to draw any conclusions.”

Residents have been on edge since Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her 19-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, were found dead earlier this week in the Snooka West Trail area of the unincorporated community, with evidence suggesting a bear was responsible. Ms. Balcarras was located on Monday and Ms. Reed was found a day later about 150 metres away. The pair were minutes away from their home.

Family members reported the pair as missing on Sunday.

The Nuxalk Nation, whose traditional territories are in and around Bella Coola, has issued a recommended 8 p.m. curfew and is operating a shuttle service for 12 hours daily as safety measures. Conservation officers and RCMP will conduct night patrols.

A local school hosted a healing drumming circle on Wednesday afternoon.

Insp. Tyre said it’s not yet known whether more than one bear was involved in the attack, and that the Conservation Officer Service has received reports of grizzly bear sightings in the area.

The service brought bear-capture equipment into the region late Monday afternoon and continued installing the devices on Tuesday, Insp. Tyre said.

“We understand a fatal grizzly bear attack can generate many questions and concerns in the communities and beyond,” he said. “I can assure you, a thorough investigation is being conducted to try and find answers as to what May have led to the attack.”

On Nov. 20, 2025, a grizzly bear attacked a large group of elementary-school students and teachers on a trail south of Highway 20 in Bella Coola. Eleven people were injured, including four – a teacher and three students – who were airlifted to hospital in Vancouver.

The teachers had used bear spray and bear bangers in an effort to fend off the grizzly, which was believed to be with her two cubs.

After the attack, authorities captured and tagged eight bears, but the offending animal was never found. At that time, there had been no other record of such an attack in the area.

Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for Nuxalk Nation, estimated the two attack sites to be three or four kilometres apart.

To the Nuxalk people, the grizzly bear is a respected creature, an emblem of physical and spiritual strength. “We’ve occupied these lands for thousands of years, and there always has been a co-existence of grizzly bears and Nuxalk people,” Mr. Webber said Wednesday.

The two recent attacks, however, have raised questions about the changing dynamics of human-grizzly contact in the Bella Coola Valley.

The grizzly bear population in the region has increased in part because the province banned grizzly hunting at the end of 2017. First Nations have still been permitted to harvest the bears pursuant to treaty rights or Aboriginal rights for food, social or ceremonial purposes.

Ms. Balcarras was an art therapist who had recently moved to Bella Coola from Bella Bella, about 110 kilometres west. She had four grown children and one grandson. Ms. Reed, Ms. Balcarras’s youngest, had worked as an educational assistant, loved ballet and doted on her cat, Suga.

Matthew Balcarras, Ms. Balcarras’s brother, told The Globe and Mail that she had lived for years in remote communities in southeast Alaska and was no stranger to the wilderness. He believed the two had intended to go for a short walk when the attack occurred and May not have had bear deterrents on them.

“She was comfortable with wild animals, firearms, hunting,” Mr. Balcarras said Tuesday. “She was a brave, outdoorsy person.”

stories.title: Western brings military, industry and researchers together to advance Canada’s defence priorities
stories.summary: Western University held an event and is part of a new innovation network to connect military, industry and researchers for defence priorities.
stories.author: Western Communications
stories.content:
Western University is playing a growing role in bringing together researchers, industry and governments to develop creative solutions amid a renewed focus on national sovereignty.

From the new Southern Ontario Defence Innovation Network (Sodin) to a campus event connecting the Canadian Army with academic and industry collaborators, new opportunities are emerging for Western scholars to engage in research advancing Canada’s defence priorities .

On Oct. 19, the university hosted military leaders, government representatives, industry partners and researchers on campus to discuss emerging technology challenges and shared innovation goals.

“Western helped to facilitate new connections between our researchers, industry partners and the Canadian Army. This is an opportunity to explore research that can have a real-world impact,” said Dave Muir, associate vice-president of innovation and strategic partnerships.

“This is a concrete step toward building innovation pipelines that connect industry, armed forces and academia – all at the same table, at the same time. Universities are uniquely positioned to help advance national priorities as Canada works to safeguard its sovereignty.”

The success of the event at Western has prompted the Canadian Army to explore similar engagements with other post-secondary institutions, recognizing campuses as valuable spaces for linking military, industry and academic partners for discussion and collaboration. Western was the first institution to host this style of engagement.

The event was designed to increase awareness and participation in Canadian Army land systems procurement opportunities. Hosted in partnership with the Best Defence Conference and the Canadian Army, central themes included energy and power management, connecting command and control systems, supporting mobility and uncrewed systems, among others.

Major-General Stéphane Masson, chief of Army Force Development, highlighted the importance of collaboration across Canada’s defence ecosystem.

“Bringing together representatives from the defence industry, government and academia is a complex undertaking. The collaboration among these diverse stakeholders was instrumental in delivering a highly successful engagement and creating an event conducive to meaningful discussion.”

Senior university leaders and researchers from across disciplines joined representatives from local companies in aviation, manufacturing and defence, Canadian Army directors and Doug Guzman, Hba’88, CEO of the Defence Investment Agency , a new government arm to accelerate defense procurement and deliver better capabilities for the Canadian Armed Forces.

The event preceded the Best Defence Conference, held annually in London, Ont. to connect industry, the Canadian Armed Forces and governments. Best Defence is run by Pilot Hill Ltd. and was sponsored by Western.

The university can play a key role in bringing together the expertise needed to develop solutions to Canada’s evolving security and sovereignty challenges, Muir said.

“We have state-of-the-art research infrastructure, highly qualified research expertise and talent pipelines that have existed for many years – they are all incredibly relevant and can play an important role at this moment in time.” – Dave Muir, associate vice-president of innovation and strategic partnerships

“For example, our researchers are working on technologies ranging from autonomous systems and drones to advanced communications and satellite monitoring. Bringing researchers, industry and the Canadian military together helps turn those ideas into practical solutions,” he added.

Western is also one of five founding members of Sodin, joining McMaster and the universities of Guelph, Waterloo and Windsor to strengthen scientific partnerships, foster innovation and contribute to societal, technological and economic development for Canadian defence needs.

Sodin will support the Canadian Armed Forces and defence industry needs by providing access to talent, research environments and expertise in fields like advanced materials science, artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems, agricultural science and others.

Last week’s event and Western’s participation in Sodin build on a growing portfolio of defence-related research partnerships.

Earlier this year, the university signed an agreement with Dalhousie University focused on AI , defence and research security, strengthening its role in the Canadian Defence and Dual-Use Innovation Ecosystem (Cdde) . Led by German naval shipbuilder and defence company Tkms , the preferred bidder for the Canadian Patrol Submarine Project, Cdde brings together Western, Dalhousie, the University of British Columbia, Indigenous businesses and industry partners in Canada, Germany and Norway to advance technologies with both civilian and defence applications.

stories.title: UBC professor regrets helping colleague approve Galloway accuser’s unfinished thesis to complete degree
stories.summary: Creative-writing professor Annabel Lyon tells B.C. Supreme Court that she felt pressed by a more senior colleague to sign off on the incomplete thesis
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
A University of B.C. creative-writing professor says she regrets her role in the granting of a degree to the woman who accused bestselling author Steven Galloway of sexual harassment and sexual assault, even though the woman did not finish her mandatory graduate thesis.

Annabel Lyon told B.C. Supreme Court Wednesday that she felt pressed by a more senior colleague to sign off on the incomplete thesis.

“I regret it to this day,” she said.

Ms. Lyon was testifying in a defamation case brought by the bestselling author. She was one of two dozen defendants initially named in his lawsuit filed in 2018 alleging that his lucrative career was effectively ended by the allegations. He was never charged with a crime and has always denied the allegations.

Prof. Lyon, who is now the director of Ubc’s creative-writing program, said she agreed to be the second professor to approve the partial thesis after being asked by fellow faculty member Keith Maillard. The court heard that he deemed the incomplete novel excellent enough to merit approval.

Prof. Maillard was advising the student on her thesis and later gave her an A+ for 144 pages of a half-completed novel, which was her final requirement to graduate, according to Wednesday’s hearing.

Prof. Lyon said she recalled a phone call from Prof. Maillard, after the student submitted her incomplete draft, wherein he told his colleague: " ’She needs to be finished, she needs to complete her degree’ and he was asking me to sign off on it.”

She added that she approved the thesis after only reading a few the pages with the proviso that the former student, who can only be identified as A.B. because of a publication ban, submit her full novel to Prof. Lyon for detailed feedback. A.B. never did.

Four months later, the trial has heard, A.B. e-mailed Prof. Maillard and described feeling at risk and “unsafe.” She alleged that she had been sexually assaulted and harassed by Mr. Galloway.

In November 2015, the university announced that it was investigating “serious allegations” against him, setting off a firestorm in Canada’s literary world. Mr. Galloway was suspended and then fired in June 2016 as head of Ubc’s creative-writing program without severance because of breach of trust. News of the incident spurred a national debate over Mr. Galloway’s rights to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim.

A retired judge hired by the university to investigate the complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault, but that he had sexually harassed her and committed other misconduct.

Most of the defendants named in Mr. Galloway’s defamation suit have since settled, including Prof. Lyon and Prof. Maillard. A.B. is one four defendants remaining.

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial, her lead lawyer Arden Beddoes told the court that he was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment, but his client does not admit that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway. Mr. Beddoes has said that she had tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the case.

Prof. Lyon testified Wednesday that UBC had no policy at the time dictating what constitutes a complete graduate thesis in the creative-writing department and that, after this “one-off” incident with A.B., she crafted one herself.

“I wrote subsequent policies so that nobody could ever be in this position again,” she said.

Wednesday’s testimony provided more information about how the university treated A.B. before and after her allegations. A month before Mr. Galloway was dismissed, the court recently heard, UBC awarded A.B. a postgraduation bursary of $30,000, to which she was not entitled.

Prof. Lyon was asked Wednesday about an e-mail that she sent university administration after the 2016 publication of a letter signed by dozens of prominent writers, including Margaret Atwood, calling on UBC to afford Mr. Galloway due process.

Court heard that Prof. Lyon wanted to issue a statement saying she believed in the students that complained about Mr. Galloway.

“The university is losing a PR war here and they need someone to put a human face on their side of things,” Prof. Lyon wrote in the e-mail, which was read in court by Daniel Burnett, lead counsel for Mr. Galloway.

Prof. Lyon testified that she was trying to protect her creative-writing students who had complained and were still in the program.

“I know there was a real feeling of despondency amongst the students that they had not been heard, and I wanted to reassure them that, as a unit, we had heard them,” she said.

Also on Wednesday, Justice Neena Sharma denied The Globe and Mail’s request to access an exhibit filed earlier in the court proceedings involving a draft statement of claim that A.B. allegedly intended to file against the university for $3-million for negligence, breach of contract and other reasons. The judge said the lawsuit threat May be discussed during closing arguments in the coming days.

stories.title: Alberta’s new electoral map May not tilt the province, but it could help the UCP retain its majority
stories.summary: Redrawn boundaries would likely dilute urban voting power, where NDP support is strongest
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Dexter McMillan
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith ’s government has taken the first steps to approve Alberta’s new electoral map, unanimously voting to move forward with the redrawn boundaries emerging from a process that has faced charges of gerrymandering.

Ms. Smith’s governing United Conservative Party voted on Wednesday night to approve a motion that will result in the government creating a bill to put the map into law. The Alberta NDP voted against the motion.

The new map has added four new seats and will likely benefit Ms. Smith’s UCP – particularly owing to a slate of changes in Calgary’s northwest and in Lethbridge.

It has also ignited fierce debate over a process that’s traditionally a sleepy affair. Ms. Smith forced a redraw of the map in April, a decision she said was motivated by a desire to preserve rural voters’ electoral representation in light of massive population gains in Alberta’s two major cities, Calgary and Edmonton. But her decision has triggered questions about the process itself, with critics voicing concerns that the latest redrawing effort has not followed Alberta’s traditionally independent and transparent procedures.

Analysis by The Globe and Mail shows that under the most recent election results, the latest map would not tilt the political playing field as severely as some expected in April when Ms. Smith rejected the previously proposed map and restarted the process.

Specific changes to the map, however, would provide an advantage to the UCP while significantly diluting the power of voters in urban centres, where support for the Alberta NDP is most concentrated. Calgary, where some of those changes are centred, is expected to be the battleground where next October’s provincial election is won.

Earlier this week, Ms. Smith said she didn’t want urban representation to come at the expense of the rest of the province: “We did not want rural Alberta to be under-represented.”

The Alberta NDP has promised the map will end up in court. Ms. Smith has batted away accusations of gerrymandering and endorsed the changes. Alberta’s elections agency has warned it doesn’t have enough time to implement the new map, even without the prospect of a legal challenge.

Brian O’Ferrall, a retired judge and chair of the most recent five-person panel, wrote in the report of “unnecessary and counter-productive controversy” that dogged the five-person group as it attempted to redraw the map. He dismissed accusations of gerrymandering at several turns.

Meanwhile, the two panelists selected by the NDP – University of Alberta constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote a separate report suggesting that aspects of the new map would be “constitutionally fraught.”

“This 2025-26 Alberta redistricting process has pushed the envelope of democratic norms,” they wrote, adding that adopting the new map “will likely force the courts to enter this fray.”

It is unclear what effect the new map would have on the outcome of next October’s provincial election, as political tides continue to shift in Alberta. But applying the 2023 provincial election results to the new map, the UCP would hold on to its majority with a similar 11-seat margin over the NDP.

Some of the deepest divisions on the latest panel were over changes to Lethbridge and Calgary, where three panelists proposed to blend the cities’ suburban neighbourhoods with rural communities.

Boundaries commissioners typically aim to achieve similar populations across all ridings. But it can be impossible in certain cases to avoid creating ridings with small populations due to sparsely populated rural regions, resulting in electoral divisions with below-average populations.

Population disparities between city and rural ridings increase under the new proposed map. If approved, the average rural riding would be nearly 11-per-cent smaller than the provincewide average of 53,722 people. Calgary and Edmonton’s populations, meanwhile, would be roughly 6-per-cent greater than average.

These differences were key concerns for Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson, the minority authors, who wrote that new ridings in northwest Calgary “subtly dilute Calgarians’ votes in ways that are not necessary to achieve effective representation.”

They added that the proposed recommendations “exacerbate the underrepresentation of the four largest cities in Alberta.” Those are Calgary, Edmonton, Red Deer and Lethbridge.

Mr. O’Ferrall, meanwhile, defended the proposals while accusing Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson of unfairly criticizing the proposed hybrid ridings. The former judge wrote that changes in Lethbridge were reasonable because of “an identifiable, shared southern Alberta community of interest driven by dependency on agriculture and food processing industries.”

At several points, Mr. O’Ferrall wrote that residents in the new hybrid Calgary ridings shared similar interests.

“One’s vote is only diluted if a large number of people with whom one doesn’t share the same interests is added to his or her electoral division,” he wrote.

It is not boundaries commissioners’ job to assess the electoral implications of their work. But should the map slide past the legislature and a legal challenge, it will have electoral implications in key parts of the province.
