stories.title: X says B.C. law can’t force the platform to delete intimate image. Tribunal agrees
stories.summary: Social media platform argued that removing the image from Canadian view was sufficient
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A British Columbia Tribunal has ruled that X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter, does not need to remove an intimate image of a B.C. woman that was posted non-consensually.

The woman, referred to as TR due to a publication ban on her name, had complained last year about the image, and in March an order had been issued by Eric Regehr, vice chair of the B.C. Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT), to remove it from the platform.

“I will refer to it as the protection order decision,” he wrote in a followup decision, referring to the order to remove the image. “The applicant in that unpublished decision, who I will call TR, says X Corp. did not comply with the protection order. TR asks me to order X to pay an administrative monetary penalty for its failure to comply.”

He added: “X says that it complied with the order by restricting access to the intimate image within Canada, a practice it calls geofencing. It argues B.C. law cannot compel it to take any further steps.”

Regehr found this insufficient, and ordered X to pay the maximum $100,000 administrative penalty under the law.

However, in a new decision published on Monday, Regehr wrote that TR had asked for an additional $100,000 penalty since the image remains visible outside Canada.

“As I noted in the previous decision, X had provided very little evidence and raised only one legal issue with very brief submissions,” he wrote. “Here, X has provided considerably more detailed evidence and submissions and has raised new issues. It is unfortunate that X did not put its full case forward the first time it was before the CRT.”

He noted that, in its submission, X admitted that the image remains visible outside of Canada, but that “it is a global platform subject to many different legal regimes about what people are allowed to post.”

He continued: “X argues that it would be unreasonable to expect it to strictly comply with B.C. law by deleting the image, with global effect, when United States law would not require it to remove the image.”

He brought up “the comity of nations,” noting: “When laws could impact the sovereignty of other countries, the principle of comity affects how those laws are interpreted … In short, comity May operate to limit a law’s application outside Canada.”

“I appreciate that it May seem odd that an internet intermediary May avoid an administrative penalty despite not complying with the strict terms of a protection order,” Regehr wrote. “However, I agree with X that for the defence to have real force, it must be able to operate when there has been imperfect compliance with a protection order.”

X had requested that TR pay its legal fess, but Regehr denied that, saying it “would be contrary to the Crt’s mandate and unfair to TR to order her to pay any of X’s legal fees in these circumstances,” reported to be US$119,000

He also noted that TR had brought her case forward in good faith.

“Overall, I find that TR had a reasonable belief, backed by evidence, that the protection order required X to delete her intimate image. She therefore had a rational and good faith basis for prosecuting this application.”

X is said to have filed for a judicial review of the previous $100,000 penalty.

stories.title: Crook admits Facebook post ‘went too far’ after appearance on CTV News
stories.summary: A day after Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook defended a recent Facebook post about his experience as a candidate in the municipal election, he said the comments were a call for “political accountability, not violence.”
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A day after Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook defended a recent Facebook post about his experience as a candidate in the municipal election, he said the comments were a call for “political accountability, not violence.” Crook wrote in a follow-up post Tuesday morning: “I entered this election believing London needed change.

Now that it’s over, I believe we also need to change how we disagree. That includes me.” His original post referred to some elected politicians as sociopaths and stated, “The rope is useless unless we are prepared to use it to hang them.” Crook now says his words crossed a line.

“My language went too far, particularly the reference to using someone’s own ‘rope’ against them. I should have expressed myself differently,” he wrote. He added the post stemmed from “frustration with the hostility I witnessed during the election, including personal attacks, intimidation and vandalism experienced by me and other candidates.” In the Oct.

26, 2026, municipal election, incumbent David Ferreira received 4,308 votes, or 69.54 per cent, in Ward 13. Crook finished a distant second with 735 votes, or 11.86 per cent. His follow-up post reads: “I want to thank Daryl Newcombe and CTV News for the opportunity to address my recent Facebook comments.

“I entered this election believing London needed change. Now that it’s over, I believe we also need to change how we disagree. “That includes me. “We can start with common ground, disagree honestly, and hold people accountable without treating one another as enemies.

“The comments in question came from frustration with the hostility I witnessed during the election, including personal attacks, intimidation and vandalism experienced by me and other candidates. “My language went too far, particularly the reference to using someone’s own ‘rope’ against them.

I should have expressed myself differently. I was calling for political accountability, not violence. I do not advocate threats or physical harm against anyone. “I can stand my ground on the need for accountability while recognizing that I can do better in how I communicate it.

“The election is over. My responsibility to participate continues.”

“The comments in question came from frustration with the hostility I witnessed during the election, including personal attacks, intimidation and vandalism experienced by me and other candidates. “My language went too far, particularly the reference to using someone’s own ‘rope’ against them.

I should have expressed myself differently. I was calling for political accountability, not violence. I do not advocate threats or physical harm against anyone. “I can stand my ground on the need for accountability while recognizing that I can do better in how I communicate it.
“The election is over. My responsibility to participate continues.”

stories.title: N.B. introduces law to protect youth from misleading online business practices
stories.summary: Fredericton - The New Brunswick government has introduced legislation that it says will make the province the first in Canada to protect young consumers from unfair online business practices.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - The New Brunswick government has introduced legislation that it says will make the province the first in Canada to protect young consumers from unfair online business practices.

Justice Minister Robert McKee tabled the proposed law Tuesday. It includes the new Young Consumers in Digital Markets Act, which prohibits companies from engaging in misleading, deceptive or other unfair practices involving consumers under 16 years old.

“This includes misleading young consumers or hiding important information from them, using pressure or urgency to encourage a young consumer to make a purchase or agree to something,” McKee told a news conference.

The legislation also takes aim at business practices that make it difficult for young consumers to understand what they are agreeing to, or ads that unfairly influence young consumers’ decisions.

The minister, who is also responsible for addictions and mental health services, gave an example of a young person who might start playing a game on a free trial, only to be charged for a one-year subscription when the trial expires.

The new rules would apply to sellers of digital goods, such as ebooks and software, as well as providers of digital services including streaming, social media or artificial intelligence products.

It would also apply to digital platforms that connect users to goods and services, including TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox.

The act would be administered and enforced by the province’s Financial and Consumer Services Commission. McKee said he was confident the commission could take on this new role without any budget increase.

The minister said investigations will be complaint-based and will apply to any company, regardless of where they are based.

Proposed remedies could include cancelling an agreement without cost or penalty, cancelling future payments or ordering full refunds. In some cases, the commission could issue fines of up to $25,000 without a hearing.

In more serious cases requiring a tribunal, penalties could include fines of up to $5 million and imprisonment of almost five years for an individual. Fines of up to $5 million are also possible for a business.

“Sometimes these platforms will use tactics that, whether intentionally or not, pressure kids to spend money on an app or agree to a feature by using language they don’t understand,” said McKee.

The government says it’s the first law of its kind in Canada, but similar legislation exists in Australia and Europe.

The minister said the legislation will complement the federal government’s Bill C-34, which would force social media platforms to block access for children under 16. Introduced in June, the federal bill is making its way through Parliament.

New Brunswick is also amending legislation to codify its previously announced ban on personal electronic devices in schools across all grade levels.

That ban, which mainly applies to cellphones and tablets, went into effect in September for children in daycares and students from kindergarten to Grade 8. It will be expanded to students in grades 9 to 12 at the start of the second semester in February.

Teachers can still use electronic devices to deliver curriculum content. There are also exceptions to the policy for medical reasons, such as a diabetic student keeping track of blood sugar levels.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version reported incorrect information shared by a provincial official who stated the new rules were proposing fines of up to $20,000. In fact, the new provincial rules could allow the Consumer Services Commission to issue fines of up to $25,000.

stories.title: B.C. hockey team says it wasn’t aware new executive was under RCMP probe
stories.summary: The Nanaimo Clippers said it has parted ways with Tyler King. He was arrested Friday at a Canada-U.S. border crossing in Ontario on child sexual exploitation charges.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A junior hockey team in British Columbia says it wasn’t aware an executive it hired was under investigation by the RCMP.

The Nanaimo Clippers said in a statement it has parted ways with Tyler King , a 39-year-old who was arrested Friday at a Canada-U.S. border crossing on child sexual exploitation charges.

The team said the decision to part ways with King was not a determination of the merits of the allegations against him.

“The allegations reported do not relate to his time with the Clippers. Given the timing of his employment, King had no contact with any of our players,” the team said.

“We have not received, and are not aware of, any complaints or concerns regarding his conduct during his brief time with the Clippers.”

RCMP announced Monday it began investigating King in 2024, around the same time he left the Okotoks Oilers, a team in southern Alberta that plays in the British Columbia Hockey League.

An employee of the Okotoks Oilers told the RCMP a former staff member was soliciting and compensating players for intimate videos and pictures. The investigation identified multiple victims who were underage minor league hockey players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

After working in Okotoks, King went to the Clippers and eventually wound up teaching sports journalism at a university in New York state.

RCMP said King had worked with various teams across Alberta, B.C. and Ontario. A spokesperson for the Ahl’s Belleville Senators said King was a part-time worker on game nights. He won’t be working with the team while the investigation is ongoing, a spokesperson said.

King is facing three counts of luring a person under 18, sexual exploitation of a young person and making child pornography.

The number of potential victims remains unclear, according to police, who said the investigation remains active.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

— with files from Tavi Dhillon and The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘We’re overworked and exhausted’: Huron County paramedics without contract since January
stories.summary: Huron County’s 112 paramedics say they are frustrated as contract negotiations with the county continue.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Huron County’s 112 paramedics say they are frustrated as contract negotiations with the county continue.

“We see members of the community on their worst days. If you’re experiencing an emergency, who are the first people you see? Likely us, the paramedics. And nobody wants to be at that emergency. But we’re always there, ready to help. And we’re just asking the community to recognize that we need help, too,” said Kelsy Long, a Huron County paramedic with 14 years on the job.

A total of 110 of Huron County’s 112 paramedics voted in favour of strike action if a new contract cannot soon be reached with the County of Huron. Increased wages and mental health benefits are the main sticking points, according to the local paramedics’ union.

“In the province of Ontario, there’s been some recognition for paramedics and the work we do, and the hard days that we face. And all we’re asking for here in Huron County is for us to have those same benefits and wages,” said Long, who also serves as president of the Cupe Local 4513 paramedics’ union.

Long said Huron County’s paramedics have been without a contract since Jan. 1 and have met with county negotiators only six times this year. She said Huron County paramedics have seen just $6 in wage increases since 2016.

“It’s been dragged out a little bit. And I think the members are feeling frustrated in that sense, and they want their voices heard,” said Long.

The County of Huron provided the following statement regarding negotiations and the possibility of a paramedics’ strike:

“The County of Huron and the union representing County paramedics are currently engaged in collective bargaining. The County values the important role paramedics play in delivering essential emergency medical services to residents and visitors across Huron County and remains committed to respectful, good-faith negotiations.

Both parties continue to participate in negotiations in accordance with the established collective bargaining process. Out of respect for that process, the County will not comment on specific bargaining proposals or discuss details of negotiations while they are ongoing,” said Meighan Wark, Huron County’s chief administrative officer.

Long said paramedics do not want to strike and understand the impact a strike would have on the community. However, she said they want the public and the county to know they are growing tired of working without a contract. Long said the wage increases currently being offered by the county would leave Huron County paramedics earning less than their counterparts in neighbouring Bruce and Perth counties.

“At this time we have no deadline. We just wanted to send a message to say that our members are overworked and exhausted, and feel like they’re not being supported in the ways that they need to be. But at this point, we have no deadline. We’re going to keep coming to the table, and keep meeting the employer, and hopefully we can come to an agreement,” she said.

The next scheduled negotiation dates are Nov. 23 and 24. Cupe has already requested a conciliator if a deal is not reached during those negotiations.

stories.title: ‘Just trust us’ is a bad police communications strategy
stories.summary: The Bridle Path home invasion suspect’s departure from the hospital raises questions about whether the law failed Torontonians, or the police
stories.author: Robyn Urback
stories.content:
It may be that Toronto police did everything they could when they encountered Daijohn Richards in a hospital in the early hours of Oct. 29.

Mr. Richards has since been identified as a suspect in the home invasion that night in Toronto’s Bridle Path, which left four family members injured – three with gunshot wounds. But at 4:15 a.m., which is when he walked himself into St. Joseph’s Health Centre, he was just a man with a gunshot wound to his shoulder.

Though investigators “immediately recognized the potential connection,” according to a subsequent police statement, “recognizing a potential suspect and having enough evidence to arrest them are two different things.” So Mr. Richards left the hospital at 9:05 a.m. There is now a Canada-wide warrant out for his arrest.

It may be that, within the confines of the law, police had no choice but to wave goodbye as Mr. Richards walked out the hospital doors that morning. Police need evidence for an arrest, and a hunch is not enough to put someone in handcuffs.

It may be that there wasn’t even enough to justify an investigative detention, which requires a lower evidentiary threshold than an arrest, but allows police to detain an individual for a period that is “brief in duration,” as outlined by the Supreme Court of Canada in R v. Mann . But even that requires reasonable grounds (such as a match for a suspect’s description) and only when detention is reasonably necessary. A police spokesperson said officers “did not have those grounds based on the information available to them at the time.”

So it may be that there was “no failure” here, as Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw insisted on Monday. But the police have carefully limited the information they’ve made available to the public, citing a need to protect the integrity of the investigation.

Police have refused to say, for example, whether police were present when Mr. Richards left hospital, and if and when a surveillance team was assembled to monitor his subsequent movements. “The public’s questions will be answered in a court of law,” Mr. Demkiw said, which is a long time to make millions of residents wait and wonder whether the law failed in this case, or the police. Because most people will infer that something has gone wrong when a man now wanted in a violent home invasion is attended to by police in hospital, then permitted to go on his merry way.

Citing an “ongoing investigation” or “matter before the courts” is a handy crutch that police in Canada like to use to withhold information from the public – information that, by most objective accounts, would have zero impact on police operations. Indeed, it is unclear why or how saying “yes, we were watching him” or “no, we weren’t there when he left hospital” would affect the search for Mr. Richards, other than to make some investigators blush.

But withholding that information does have an impact on broader public trust. Toronto is experiencing a surge in home invasions – up 47 per cent as of a month ago compared to the same time last year, according to Toronto Police data. Some affluent neighbourhoods in the city have hired private security firms to patrol their communities, and installed gates and retractable bollards to act as physical deterrents. At the same time, and likely not coincidentally, applications for Possession and Acquisition Licences (PAL) for firearms is way up in the Greater Toronto Hamilton Area, according to RCMP data obtained by the CBC: up 49 per cent between 2016 and 2025. This is the effect of a breakdown of trust between the public and police: People take it upon themselves to ensure their own safety.

It is actually a very simple thing to tell the public what is going on. “Here’s our very specific plan to deal with the spate of home invasions in Toronto.” “Here’s why, in specific, legal detail, we could not arrest Mr. Richards in hospital on Oct. 29.” “Yes, we surveilled Mr. Richards, as we would any potential suspect in a violent crime.” “This is the specific policy change we need to ensure that police in this city are better equipped to do their jobs.”

“Just trust us,” is a bad police communications strategy, particularly when people are wondering if their home will be the target of the next violent break and enter, and when they can’t make sense of how a suspect in the Bridle Path invasion was allowed to walk out of hospital after interacting with police. Disclosure builds trust, and information promotes understanding. Police can insist that they’re doing everything right, but unless they actually try to make that case, the public will carry on believing otherwise.

stories.title: One injured in Vancouver neighbourhood after 25 e-bike riders disrupt Halloween
stories.summary: Vancouver - Police in Vancouver are issuing a warning to youth riding electric dirt bikes on city streets after multiple families on Halloween night reported a group of two dozen riders driving dangerously in their neighbourhood.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Police in Vancouver are issuing a warning to youth riding electric dirt bikes on city streets after multiple families on Halloween night reported a group of two dozen riders driving dangerously in their neighbourhood.

Police say Halloween in the Kerrisdale neighbourhood culminated with one youth evading an officer, going speeds of up to 60 kilometres an hour on an e-dirt bike before crashing with another vehicle.

stories.title: Carney says Russia will not be allowed to compete at world juniors in Alberta
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Russia will not be allowed to compete at next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta. Carney, speaking in Antigua at the Commonwealth Summit, said Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be permitted to represent their countries in Canada as long as the war in Ukraine continues. His comments come […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Russia will not be allowed to compete at next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

Carney, speaking in Antigua at the Commonwealth Summit, said Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be permitted to represent their countries in Canada as long as the war in Ukraine continues.

His comments come after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled Friday that Russia must be reinstated to international hockey competition, starting with the world junior tournament.

Several European hockey federations, including Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia, have said their teams will refuse to face Russia.

Hockey Canada says it has been consulting with the International Ice Hockey Federation and other stakeholders about the potential impact on the tournament.

The world juniors begin Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

stories.title: Hydro-Québec projects deficit that could force it to rely on U.S. and other provinces
stories.summary: Hydro-Québec has released a report suggesting it May need to import electricity from neighbouring provinces or the United States within the next three years.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Hydro-Québec has released a report suggesting it May need to import electricity from neighbouring provinces or the United States within the next three years.

The state-owned utility’s new supply plan for 2027—2041 projects a high increase in the demand for energy in the coming years.

The utility expects this demand could cause it to face energy deficits as early as 2029.

Hydro-Québec estimates that the demand for Quebec’s electricity will increase by over 30 per cent by 2041.

The report says the increasing demand is expected to be driven by a number of factors, including the electrification of transportation, data centres, and energy retrofits of buildings that currently rely on fossil fuels.

It also says demand from data centres is expected to grow significantly during the coming years.

stories.title: ‘Water was just spewing everywhere’: Violent watermain break in London neighbourhood puts residents in danger
stories.summary: Residents in London’s Oxford Park neighbourhood west of downtown and the Thames River are thanking their lucky stars that no one was hurt in a weekend blast on their street.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Residents in London’s Oxford Park neighbourhood west of downtown and the Thames River are thanking their lucky stars that no one was hurt in a weekend blast on their street. A watermain break erupted on Britannia Avenue overnight Saturday, sending a high-pressure gush of water sky-high, with rocks and other debris flying everywhere.

Resident Scott Bollert had arrived home late from work when a short while later he heard what he said sounded like an explosion. “About 1:30 in the morning, next thing I know it was a massive explosion and it just sounds like a whole bunch of rocks are hitting cars and houses and stuff.

I didn’t really even know what it was. It sounded almost like an ice-maker,” he said. Bollert took to social media that night to vent his frustration after calling 911 about the eruption on the residential street. “So I’m told by 911 that I’m holding up their line by calling them to tell them that this line is doing this in the middle of our street,” he exclaimed.

Making matters worse, Bollert’s car was parked next to the geyser with his work gear inside. He says he’s been informed by his insurance company that the vehicle is now considered a write-off. “My insurance company wants a thousand dollar deductible just to replace the stuff that’s in there.

And I don’t understand. I mean it would be different if it was my fault,” he said. The Dawson family, across the street from Bollert, was also victim to the powerful outflow. “The water was just spewing everywhere about a hundred feet up, just breaking apart concrete and the rest of the pavement,” said one resident who wished to remain anonymous.

Flying rocks took out a number of car windshields on the street, along with some property left outside. The Dawson family, across the street from Bollert, was also victimized by the powerful outflow. Al Dawson said his truck sustained $3,700 damage, based on a repair estimate.

“The guy I talked to in the city told me it was an act of God and they weren’t responsible, and I had to sue my insurance company. I talked to my insurance company, and they don’t value my truck as much as the cost of the repairs, so either I can fix it myself or they can give me a small amount of money and take my truck,” he lamented.

Neighbours say the street was a danger zone, with the high-pressure water gushing way up above the light standard and “basket-ball” sized rocks being strewn about the street. A number of people called 911. The London Fire Department and London Police attended within a couple of hours, and eventually, city works crews arrived to shut the water off.

Ward Councillor David Ferriera said the city does have an emergency line for situations like this, but it does not operate after-hours. “I’m not surprised that the response would be that ‘we are here for emergency response, whether that’s for police, fire or ambulance.’ So that’s just goes to the point that maybe we should look into an emergency after hours number that’s 24-7,” he suggested.

Ferriera said he’s waiting to hear from city staff what caused the watermain break. “I’ve already requested staff look into that part of the infrastructure to see if we have any plans in the works. But we’re fortunate that it did happen at that time,” he said.

“So if it was during the day I can only imagine there would have been some damages and somebody hurt for sure,” added Bollert.

stories.title: B.C. hockey team says didn't know exec it hired was being investigated for sex crimes
stories.summary: Nanaimo - A junior hockey team in British Columbia says it was not aware of sexual exploitation allegations against an executive when he was hired.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A junior hockey team in British Columbia says it wasn’t aware that an executive they hired in 2024 was facing sexual exploitation allegations from another club in the same league.

In a statement Tuesday, the Nanaimo Clippers said Tyler King was hired as the club’s vice-president of business operations in the summer of that year and left months later, before the hockey season started.

The team said it terminated his employment when it found out the RCMP was investigating him.

RCMP announced Monday that they began investigating King in 2024, around the time he left the Okotoks Oilers, a team in southern Alberta that also plays in the British Columbia Hockey League.

After working in Okotoks, King went to the Bchl’s Nanaimo team and eventually wound up teaching sports journalism at a university in New York state.

Last week, police arrested King at a U.S. border crossing in Ontario and charged him with sexual exploitation offences involving three underage junior A hockey players.

RCMP said the 39-year-old had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia.

The Nanaimo Clippers said that the allegations don’t relate to his time with the team.

“We have not received, and are not aware of, any complaints or concerns regarding his conduct during his brief time with the Clippers,” the team said.

“The safety and well-being of our players, billet families and young fans is our highest priority. We have contacted the RCMP to offer our full co-operation to the extent it is needed.”

The league confirmed in a separate statement that “upon learning of the accusations, his Bchl team immediately terminated his employment.”

The league did not immediately respond when asked whether it knew about the allegations when he left the Okotoks team and was hired in Nanaimo.

“Although he only spent a brief few months in the Bchl, we have fully supported the RCMP’s investigation of this matter,” the league said.

Mounties have said the Okotoks Oilers reported in June 2024 that a former employee had allegedly solicited and compensated players for intimate images and sexual videos.

A statement published on the team’s website around the same time announced King was leaving his job.

“The Okotoks Oilers would like to thank Tyler King for his tireless efforts during his three seasons in our organization as Assistant GM, Business Operations,” said the June 2024 statement.

The page, which has since been taken down, said King had been in charge of overseeing all off-ice operations.

It said King also served as the main play-by-play voice of the team on The Eagle 100.9 FM in Okotoks and online streaming platforms during his second and third seasons with the team.

The three complainants, all under 18 at the time of the allegations, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Alberta RCMP Cpl. Gina Slaney said in an interview Tuesday that Mounties couldn’t warn the Nanaimo team about the allegations, because King wasn’t officially facing charges when he was hired by Nanaimo.

“We cannot legally or lawfully do that if we don’t have evidence to support charges or if charges haven’t been pursued,” she said.

RCMP said King, who was arrested Friday, had been working with the State University of New York campus at Oswego in New York state. He is to return later this week to Alberta to face charges of luring, sexual exploitation and making child pornography.

The university said King joined the school in 2025 as a professor of practice with its communications studies department. Late Monday, the university’s student-run television station announced that King had been removed from his position as an adviser with the group.

“Wtop-10 TV has been made aware of serious charges made in regards to Tyler King,” it said in a social media post.

“We were unaware of the allegations while he was with our club. We fully do not condone or support the actions described in these charges.”

In southeastern Ontario, the Belleville Senators said King had been working with the team for the past two seasons as a public address announcer.

“We have been made aware of the serious allegations around him,” said the team, which is the American Hockey League affiliate of the NHL’s Ottawa Senators.

“He will not be working with us while this investigation is ongoing and we will provide any assistance required by the RCMP.”

Court records show King was also charged with choking in November 2025 at or near Calgary. He was further charged in February with failing to appear in court and failing to comply with a release order.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

A junior hockey team in British Columbia says it wasn’t aware that an executive they hired in 2024 was facing sexual exploitation allegations from another club in the same league.

In a statement Tuesday, the Nanaimo Clippers said Tyler King was hired as the club’s vice-president of business operations in the summer of that year and left months later, before the hockey season started.

The team said it terminated his employment when it found out the RCMP was investigating him.

After working in Okotoks, King went to the Bchl’s Nanaimo team and eventually wound up teaching sports journalism at a university in New York state.

Last week, police arrested King at a U.S. border crossing in Ontario and charged him with sexual exploitation offences involving three underage junior A hockey players.

RCMP said the 39-year-old had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia.

The Nanaimo Clippers said that the allegations don’t relate to his time with the team.

“We have not received, and are not aware of, any complaints or concerns regarding his conduct during his brief time with the Clippers,” the team said.

“The safety and well-being of our players, billet families and young fans is our highest priority. We have contacted the RCMP to offer our full co-operation to the extent it is needed.”

The league confirmed in a separate statement that “upon learning of the accusations, his Bchl team immediately terminated his employment.”

The league did not immediately respond when asked whether it knew about the allegations when he left the Okotoks team and was hired in Nanaimo.

“Although he only spent a brief few months in the Bchl, we have fully supported the RCMP’s investigation of this matter,” the league said.

Mounties have said the Okotoks Oilers reported in June 2024 that a former employee had allegedly solicited and compensated players for intimate images and sexual videos.

A statement published on the team’s website around the same time announced King was leaving his job.

“The Okotoks Oilers would like to thank Tyler King for his tireless efforts during his three seasons in our organization as Assistant GM, Business Operations,” said the June 2024 statement.

The page, which has since been taken down, said King had been in charge of overseeing all off-ice operations.

It said King also served as the main play-by-play voice of the team on The Eagle 100.9 FM in Okotoks and online streaming platforms during his second and third seasons with the team.

The three complainants, all under 18 at the time of the allegations, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Alberta RCMP Cpl. Gina Slaney said in an interview Tuesday that Mounties couldn’t warn the Nanaimo team about the allegations, because King wasn’t officially facing charges when he was hired by Nanaimo.

“We cannot legally or lawfully do that if we don’t have evidence to support charges or if charges haven’t been pursued,” she said.

RCMP said King, who was arrested Friday, had been working with the State University of New York campus at Oswego in New York state. He is to return later this week to Alberta to face charges of luring, sexual exploitation and making child pornography.

The university said King joined the school in 2025 as a professor of practice with its communications studies department. Late Monday, the university’s student-run television station announced that King had been removed from his position as an adviser with the group.

“Wtop-10 TV has been made aware of serious charges made in regards to Tyler King,” it said in a social media post.

“We were unaware of the allegations while he was with our club. We fully do not condone or support the actions described in these charges.”

In southeastern Ontario, the Belleville Senators said King had been working with the team for the past two seasons as a public address announcer.

“We have been made aware of the serious allegations around him,” said the team, which is the American Hockey League affiliate of the NHL’s Ottawa Senators.

“He will not be working with us while this investigation is ongoing and we will provide any assistance required by the RCMP.”

Court records show King was also charged with choking in November 2025 at or near Calgary. He was further charged in February with failing to appear in court and failing to comply with a release order.

stories.title: Report: Jose Berrios does not exercise opt-out on final 2 years of contract
stories.summary: The veteran right-hander did not exercise the opt-out clause on the final two years of his seven-year, $131-million contract.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
José Berríos will continue his return from Tommy John surgery with the Toronto Blue Jays.

The veteran right-hander did not exercise the opt-out clause on the final two years of his seven-year, $131-million contract, the Associated Press reported on Monday.

Berríos did not pitch this year and is recovering from Tommy John surgery on May 20.

The 32-year-old was a reliable rotation staple for the Minnesota Twins and Blue Jays before his first career IL stint came at the end of the 2025 season. He did not pitch in the ensuing post-season for Toronto.

In 31 games that year, including his second career relief appearance, Berríos posted a 4.17 ERA and 1.301 Whip with 138 strikeouts and 56 walks over 166 innings.

If healthy, he could join a rotation that is slated to include Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage and Jose Soriano, with Cody Ponce also aiming to return from a long-term injury. Spencer Arrighetti and Bowden Francis would also be in the rotation conversation entering spring training.

stories.title: Budget 2026 to include update on immigration levels, sources say
stories.summary: The annual immigration levels update will be included in the federal budget being released Thursday, a government source with knowledge of the plan confirmed.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
The annual immigration levels update will be included in the federal budget being released Thursday, a government source with knowledge of the plan confirmed.

This will be the second year the annual update is included in the budget document.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said immigration is back under control and he told the New York Times in September the question is now about when Canada should begin a “controlled increase” in population.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said Monday Canada previously was bringing in more people than public services could handle or communities could absorb.

“I always felt that you need to welcome people to Canada, but on a level that allows you to provide the basic services or the infrastructure that can support the people coming into our shore,” Champagne said during a pre-budget appearance at the Canadian Club of Ottawa.

“And therefore, that’s what we did. We’ve been able to bring the immigration level to a more sustainable level for now, but also for the future.”

During a Monday speech to the Canadian Club of Toronto, Champagne said Canada has relied too much on an expanding population for growth, instead of focusing on worker and business productivity.

While the current plan is to admit 380,000 permanent residents annually, there are two one-time programs aimed at giving permanent status to another 140,000 temporary residents through 2026 and 2027 that aren’t included in the broader target.

The previous Liberal government had planned to add 500,000 permanent residents annually. The Carney government has said that rapid population growth contributed to the cost of living squeeze and the housing crisis.

The government’s goal is to reduce the number of temporary residents in Canada to five per cent of the total population. Statistics Canada estimates the non-permanent resident population at 6.7 per cent of the total population as of July 1.

The annual update will be published after its legally mandated Nov. 1 deadline, even though the Immigration and Refugees Protection Act says the report must be tabled in Parliament on or before that day if the House is sitting.

stories.title: B.C. tribunal rules X can't be fined for not deleting intimate image
stories.summary: Vancouver - A British Columbia tribunal has ruled it cannot penalize social media platform X for not deleting an intimate image of a person shared online against her will, and that blocking the image in Canada instead reasonably addresses its unlawful distribution.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Out-going British Columbia Attorney General Niki Sharma says governments have to keep up the fight to protect people from online harms if social media companies like X don’t take on their own corporate responsibility.

B.C.‘s Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled on Monday that it can’t penalize X for not deleting an intimate image of a complainant shared online against her will, and that “geoblocking” the image from being seen in Canada instead reasonably addressed its unlawful distribution.

The ruling released Monday suggests international internet companies can’t be forced to delete intimate images under provincial legislation designed to protect people from having such pictures shared without their consent.

Sharma says she is appalled that X refused to take down an intimate image that is circulating without the person’s consent and that governments should be pushing for legal changes to bring accountability for the platforms.

She says X is the only company that has used geoblocking under the Intimate Images Protection Act, while the rest simply take down the images when requested.

Sharma, whose NDP government brought in the protections in 2024, says the “correct legal response” to the ruling would be to ask for a legal opinion on strengthening the law or seek legal recourse.

“We live in this world in which our laws need to adjust to meet the harms that are out there,” she says.

“What we found with platforms like X is that they will fight out everything legally before they take actual steps for safety.”

It means governments have to step in to legally enforce those standards or fight it out in court because the laws need to evolve to respond to the harms that are happening, she says.

The tribunal case stemmed from a March 2025 protection order issued under B.C.‘s protection act that X delete the intimate image shared on its platform.

The tribunal then ruled in September 2025 that X must pay a $100,000 penalty for not deleting the image, but the social media platform challenged that decision, saying the tribunal could not order it to do any more than geoblock the image, which it had done.

Tribunal vice-chair Eric Regehr says in the latest decision that he was reversing the fine, and that X had a valid defence under a section of the law that states an internet company is not liable if it “has taken reasonable steps to address the unlawful distribution.”

“X argues that geoblocking images that contravene the Iipa reasonably addresses the distribution of intimate images on its platform because it is a global platform subject to many different legal regimes about what people are allowed to post,” he says.

“Put another way, X argues that geoblocking is reasonable because globally enforcing a BC law about what is allowed to be posted online would violate the comity of nations,” he added.

Regehr says that comity — the idea of mutual respect among nations — “May operate to limit a law’s application outside Canada. ”

His ruling cited the “compelling” reasoning in an Australian case from 2024, although he said it was not a binding authority.

Regehr rejected X’s request that the complainant be ordered to pay its legal fees in excess of US$100,000. The company is owned by the Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, with a net worth estimated at $US900 billion by Forbes’ real-time billionaires list.

“I find that it would have a potential chilling effect if applicants had to accept substantial financial risk when deciding whether to try to enforce protection orders against internet intermediaries,” Regher said.

The complainant, whose name is under a publication ban, represented herself.

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal says it is Canada’s first online tribunal, which offers an accessible, affordable way to resolve many civil disputes without a lawyer, and without a courtroom.

The legislation at the heart of the case was tabled by the NDP government in 2023, partly in response to the 2012 suicide of teenager Amanda Todd, who faced cyberbullying and online sexual exploitation.

Sharma said at the time that the sharing of intimate images without consent “is a betrayal that can have devastating impacts” in promising redress.

“Victims are often too ashamed to come forward and those who do are met with limited, complex and expensive legal options,” she said. “We are building a path to justice for people to regain control of their private images and hold perpetrators to account.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said Amanda Todd died in 2013.

stories.title: Peel school board ‘deeply saddened’ after current, former students killed in crash
stories.summary: The school board in the region west of Toronto says one current and two former students were among those who died in the single-vehicle crash over the weekend.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Peel District School Board says it’s “deeply saddened” after four young people, three of whom had ties to the school district, died when the car they were travelling in fell into a ravine in Puslinch, Ont., just outside Guelph.

The school board in the region west of Toronto says one current and two former students were among those who died in the single-vehicle crash over the weekend.

Ontario Provincial Police said at a news conference Sunday they’re investigating if a lack of seatbelts contributed to the fatal crash, which also injured two others.

The OPP said six young people from the Greater Toronto Area were travelling along Watson Road South early Saturday when the car left the road, struck a guardrail and careened into a ravine.

Police said a 17-year-old girl from Mississauga, a 15-year-old girl from Milton and two 19-year-old men hailing from Mississauga and Brampton died in the crash.

Police said Sunday that a 17-year-old girl from Mississauga remained in hospital with life-altering injuries after the crash, while a 16-year-old from Mississauga sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

The school board extended its condolences to the families and friends of the deceased and says it is providing support to students, families and staff impacted by the incident.

Given the ongoing investigation, the board says it will not comment on the matter further.

Police said investigators believe the vehicle that crashed did not have enough seatbelts for all six occupants, but police were also probing if speed was a factor.

stories.title: Almost 70 charges laid in Brockton and Chatsworth searches: OPP
stories.summary: Almost 70 charges have been laid after OPP carried out a search warrants in Brockton and Chatsworth.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Almost 70 charges have been laid after OPP carried out a search warrants in Brockton and Chatsworth.

Police said an investigation was launched, looking into a series of break-and-enters at car washes and storage units in the area.

On Friday, search warrants were executed at a home on Sideroad 10 South in Brockton and Grey Bruce Line in Chatsworth. Suspected break-and-enter tools, stolen trailers, and stolen vehicles were seized.

The total value of recovered property is approximately $7,000. An additional $5,000 of offence-related property was also taken, police said.

A 38-year-old Brockton man has been charged with:

11 counts of breaking and entering

Five counts of mischief over $5,000

Seven counts of mischief under $5,000

Theft over $5,000 of a motor vehicle

Five counts of theft under $5,000

Six counts of possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000

29 counts of failure to comply with probation

Unauthorized possession of a prohibited weapon

Possession of a weapon contrary to prohibition order

stories.title: Carney calls for expanded trade with Caribbean at Commonwealth leaders meeting
stories.summary: Carney is spending one day in Antigua, with a full itinerary that includes other bilateral meetings and executive sessions
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Canada and the Caribbean have barely begun to realize what’s possible in their trading relationship, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a working breakfast of Commonwealth leaders Tuesday.

“There’s more than a million people in Canada who trace their roots back to the region,” Carney told the assembled leaders before attending the opening of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda.

“There is growing trade, $4-billion a year more broadly … It scratches the surface of what’s possible.”

Carney started the day by sitting down with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who told Carney at the start of their meeting that Canada “as a middle power is very influential in the Commonwealth globally.”

“And as we have discussions to make the Commonwealth more consequential, your contribution will be extremely valuable,” he added.

Carney saluted Browne’s leadership on the Commonwealth meeting, calling it “an extraordinarily important meeting at a crucial time.”

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand joined Carney at the working breakfast, where the prime minister gave each of the assembled Caribbean leaders a bottle of maple syrup with his own brand on it.

Heads of state and foreign ministers from Antigua, the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Trinidad and Tobago were in attendance, along with the secretary-general of Caricom, an intergovernmental organization representing Caribbean nations.

“We all know how much the world has changed. We’re all responding to it. We all know that the best response is to build out the close ties of friendship,” Carney said in his opening remarks at the breakfast.

The Prime Minister’s Office said in a background document ahead of the breakfast meeting that the leaders would discuss “expanding trade and investment opportunities, opening new markets, strengthening supply chains, and promoting sustainable economic growth.”

It said they also would talk about regional security and climate change, which it noted “remains one of the most pressing challenges facing Caribbean countries,” especially small island developing states.

Carney is spending one day in Antigua, with a full itinerary that includes other bilateral meetings and executive sessions.

Ahead of Carney’s trip, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada said he hopes that Canada’s relationship with the Caribbean, which used to be closer, can now be rebuilt.

Ronald Sanders told The Canadian Press “Canada needs to pay a little more attention to the Caribbean,” adding Carney is likely to find common ground with other leaders during his visit.

The Prime Minister’s Office said in a readout after Carney’s meeting with Browne that the two “discussed opportunities to strengthen the Canada-Antigua and Barbuda partnership and deepen co-operation on shared interests, including trade and investment, energy, climate resilience, youth, tourism, people to people ties and the priorities of small island developing states.”

Carney attended a lunch hosted by King Charles for new heads of government in the Commonwealth. This meeting is held every second year and is the first since Carney took office in March, 2025.

The Prime Minister’s Office said in a separate document the lunch was an opportunity for Carney “to engage informally with the King and fellow Commonwealth leaders.”

It said the event was also meant to “reaffirm a shared commitment to democracy, the rule of law, sustainable development, and international co-operation.”

The leaders of Gabon, Ghana, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia and the U.K. were also expected to attend the lunch, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said.

During his time in Antigua, Carney will also meet one-on-one with the leaders of Australia, Guyana and Ghana.

The Commonwealth is a voluntary coalition of 56 countries. Most of them have ties to the former British Empire.

The trip is the latest in a flurry of international trips Carney has been making since he became prime minister last year – part of an ongoing attempt to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and Commonwealth countries together represent 2.7 billion people. Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries – such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Experts say ties with Commonwealth countries can help Canada win support in multilateral forums like the United Nations, a strategy Canada has used in the past.

Ahead of the trip, government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation, and noted Canada currently has $100-billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

stories.title: Stock markets shaky ahead of U.S. midterm election as Apple faces pressure
stories.summary: North American stock markets are drifting in mixed trading on Tuesday morning, with Apple dropping sharply in early trading ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
North American stock markets are drifting in mixed trading on Tuesday morning, with Apple dropping sharply in early trading ahead of the U.S. midterm elections .

Some on Wall Street worry that a Democratic sweep of Congress this time around could lead to more regulations and restrictions on AI development. But Donald Trump would still be president and have the power to veto. And Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington, which it sees as offering less risk of transformative policies that could reshape the economy.

Tuesday’s midterm elections May also be keeping financial markets unsteady, but history suggests that they May not matter much for the broad market. Going back to 1970, the S&P 500 has had a positive return in the six months following a midterm election every time, according to Brock Weimer, an analyst at Edward Jones.

The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent in early trading, even though more stocks fell within the index than rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 232 points, or 0.4 per cent, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent higher.

On Bay Street, the TSX was down about 0.75 per cent as of 10:30 a.m. Eastern time, with shares of Shopify down nine per cent after reporting mixed earnings results.

Stock markets have been shaky recently as technology and artificial-intelligence stocks have swung on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI. Several of the most influential AI-related stocks held up better on Tuesday, which supported the market, though they flipped from gains in the morning to losses in the afternoon a day earlier.

Nvidia rose 3.1 per cent and was the strongest force pushing upward on the S&P 500 Tuesday. CoreWeave rose 2.6 per cent. The company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud has been at the center of the industry’s swings recently.

Apple was long seen on Wall Street as a Big Tech company that’s less dependent on AI. But it’s still feeling the effects of the AI boom.

Memory chips for computers have become more expensive because of the demand created by the rush to build AI data centers. Those additional expenses are hitting Apple, which said it expects to make less profit from each $1 of its revenue during the final three months of this year.

That helped send Apple’s stock down 3.4 per cent, even though the seller of iPhones and Mac computers reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Palantir Technologies fell 4.2 per cent even though it likewise reported a better profit than expected. The software company said it made more money from working with U.S. companies than from the U.S. government for the first time, as U.S. commercial revenue soared 148 per cent from a year earlier.

On the winning side of Wall Street Tuesday were stocks of several companies that reported stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected.

Celanese climbed 4.9 per cent, and DuPont added seven per cent.

Expectations are high for all kinds of companies to continue to deliver big gains in profits as the U.S. economy keeps chugging along, even with high inflation and elevated interest rates. That helped send the S&P 500 to a record high last month.

In the oil market, prices continued to swing. Brent climbed above US$107 per barrel in the morning before briefly dropping below $101 on continued uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. It was most recently down 0.9 per cent at $103.80.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6 per cent for one of the world’s sharpest moves following losses for its two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Stocks rose 0.3 per cent in Australia after the country’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate for the fifth time this year.

– with a file from Global’s Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Entrepreneurs take over beloved Vancouver Kidsbooks as it celebrates 43 years: ‘We know special when we see it’
stories.summary: Avni Patel Thompson takes inspiration from her parenting startups to add Amazon-level convenience to the beloved bookstore, while still keeping things human
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
As a tech entrepreneur, Avni Patel Thompson liked to think locally. What, she wondered as she became a mother last decade, can technology do to improve the “modern village?” She launched the startups Poppy and Milo to help reduce parents’ workloads and track down childcare, in that pursuit.

For her next venture, she’s keeping things local in a different way: She and her husband Joseph Thompson are taking over a beloved neighbourhood bookstore.

For 43 years, Vancouver Kidsbooks has been a staple of Kitsilano life, with co-owners Phyllis Simon and Kelly McKinnon making sure families get the right titles for their burgeoning readers. It has achieved legendary status in Canadian bookselling – not just for its elaborate front-window displays or for being the first shop to bring Harry Potter to the country, but for its proprietors’ willingness to tap into kids’ ever-evolving reading habits.

Simon and McKinnon couldn’t run the shop forever, though. And it so happened that Patel Thompson, a neighbour and big fan of Kidsbooks, had been happily nudging them about succession plans for seven years. The nudging worked. She and her husband took the shop over in October, and on Tuesday, they will make the official announcement at an event with Captain Underpants and Dog Man author Dav Pilkey.

“They see the value in the business, community, and team we have created over these many years,” Simon and McKinnon said in a joint e-mail. “Not only do they want to continue our quest, but they also have plans to expand it. Kidsbooks is very dear to us and to many people in our community. We will always celebrate together as we watch children of all ages grow into confident and enthusiastic readers.”

It was Simon and McKinnon that first convinced B.C.’s Raincoast Books to secure the Canadian rights to the Harry Potter franchise in the nineties, which significantly boosted the distribution and publishing company’s fortunes. Jamie Broadhurst, Raincoast’s vice-president of marketing, said that their impact is even broader: “They helped us think how we can better serve the independent market.”

A physical bookstore might seem like an anachronistic bet for a family of serial entrepreneurs – Thompson also co-founded the TSX-listed eye-care company Kits.com Technologies – but the pair see it as another bet on the modern village.

“We’ve travelled all over the world, and we know special when we see it,” Patel Thompson said of Kidsbooks. Her husband added: “Every family should have access to a fabulous neighbourhood bookstore.”

They’re interested in broadening access to that magic without losing Kidsbooks’s personal touch. That means continuing Simon and McKinnon’s efforts to build lifetime customers by following baby board-book readers through their young-adult phases and onto new generations.

They’re not in a rush, but the new owners hope to simplify Kidsbooks’s back-office processes and try to become a humanistic counterpoint to Amazon while retaining Amazon-level convenience. Two of Patel Thompson’s startups were built with text messaging at their core: Poppy helped parents book caregivers over text, while Milo, offered an artificial-intelligence agent for families to help them organize their complicated lives. Kidsbooks’s reputation was built on knowing what readers need. She sees an opportunity to bring the convenience of text communication and the wisdom of a good bookseller together for readers across B.C.’s Lower Mainland.

She offers the idea of a child coming home from school announcing they need a book on two days’ notice. A customer could text Kidsbooks with what they need, and the shop could get it ready for pickup the next morning. “The what doesn’t change,” Patel Thompson said. “It’s the how.”

Though the couple want to grow Kidsbooks, they’re not interested in franchising the business; they want to keep things within their own control. (KidsBooks does already have a second retail location in North Vancouver that they’re also taking over.)

Patel Thompson moved to Vancouver from Saskatchewan at 14, and considers herself a “hometown kid” in the city, while Thompson is from Ontario. Both worked at Procter & Gamble for many years, and Patel Thompson also worked for other consumer brands; they lived across Boston, Cincinnati, Shanghai and Seattle. Thompson even worked at Amazon itself for a while in Seattle, before the couple settled in Vancouver last decade.

Patel Thompson also spent time with the acclaimed Silicon startup accelerator Y Combinator. Her experience in startups, combined with her previous consumer-brand career, taught her valuable lessons on learning what people actually need.

“The message from my career has been to find the gnarliest, most interesting kind of consumer frictions and problems that people are facing,” she said. Then she asks: “How do you build delightful products that solve them through the lens of commerce?”

The couple and their two daughters have been regulars at Kidsbooks for a decade, and admired what they saw as community leadership from Simon and McKinnon. “I’ve always walked out feeling richer for the experience, because Kidsbooks understands that we’re not just selling books,” Patel Thompson said. “We’re selling a perspective on how books are centred on all of these different learning experiences, and it’s a perspective that is needed now more than ever.”

Raincoast’s Broadhurst said that Patel Thompson is “deeply interested in what will a bookstore look like in the mid-21st century.” He added: “There’s a place for the serendipity of discovery in physical retail and online, and I think that we’re going to see Avni and Kidsbooks be central to those conversations going forward.”

content_blocks.text: Simon and McKinnon couldn’t run the shop forever, though. And it so happened that Patel Thompson, a neighbour and big fan of Kidsbooks, had been happily nudging them about succession plans for seven years. The nudging worked. She and her husband took the shop over in October, and on Tuesday, they will make the official announcement at an event with Captain Underpants and Dog Man author Dav Pilkey.

stories.title: Man sentenced to 15 years for role in killing Naramata woman
stories.summary: More than five years after Kathleen Richardson was killed in her Naramata home, one of the two men responsible for her death has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
More than five years after Kathleen Richardson was killed in her Naramata, B.C., home, one of the two men responsible for her death has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.

With 204 days credited for time already served, 27-year-old Ekene Anigbo has 14 years and 161 days remaining on his sentence.

For Julie Robertson, who remembers Richardson as a kind, generous and deeply involved member of the community, the sentencing marks the end of a long and painful chapter.

“She was so kind, she was so giving, she was a huge member of our community,” a tearful Robertson said outside the Kelowna courthouse.

Richardson was 57 when she was killed on June 9, 2021.

Court heard that Anigbo and Jalen Falk broke into her home looking for her son, Wade Cudmore, in gang-related retaliation connected to the killings of brothers Erick and Carlo Fryer the previous month.

Richardson was confronted, restrained and bound with duct tape and zip ties before being shot twice in the face.

In sentencing Anigbo, Justice Allison Beames called Richardson’s killing senseless, describing how both men participated in confronting and confining her before wrapping multiple layers of duct tape around her head and covering her eyes.

The judge said Richardson was in an “obviously extremely vulnerable position” when she was shot twice in the face, killing her instantaneously or near instantaneously.

Anigbo was originally charged with first-degree murder. But following a lengthy trial earlier this year, he was convicted of manslaughter after the judge found the Crown had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt which of the two men fired the fatal shots.

The Crown had sought a life sentence, while the defence argued for a term of 12 to 14 years.

Anigbo’s parole eligibility will be determined by the Parole Board of Canada.

Under federal rules, most offenders become eligible to apply for full parole after serving one-third of their sentence or seven years, whichever is less.

Falk, meanwhile, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and is serving a life sentence, with no possibility of parole for 16 years.

Robertson says she had hoped the sentencing would bring some closure for those who have spent years waiting for answers.

“For me to be here today was like, this is the end. The trials are done,” Roberston said.

Robertson says she often thinks about Richardson, and believes her son, who remains behind bars for the Fryer brothers’ murders, likely does too.

“His actions caused this and that’s something that he has to live with for the rest of his life, and that has got to be heavy.”

stories.title: Two charged in Brockton disturbance
stories.summary: Two people have been charged after a disturbance in Brockton.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Two people have been charged after a disturbance in Brockton.

On Sunday just after 5 a.m., South Bruce OPP were called with a report of a disturbance at a home in the municipality.

Officers found and arrested two people, seizing guns.

A 30-year-old from Huron Kinloss has been charged with:

Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm

Mischief under $5,000

Operation while prohibited

Unauthorized possession of a firearm

Knowledge of unauthorized possession of a firearm

Breach of firearms regulation – storing firearm or restricted weapon

A 21-year-old from Huron East has been charged with:

Unlawfully in dwelling/house

Failure to comply with a release order other than to attend court

The suspects’ names are not being released in an effort to protect the victim.

stories.title: Nearly a third of Canadians skipping meals due to food insecurity: survey
stories.summary: Results from an annual national poverty survey paint a worsening picture of food affordability in Canada, especially for young people.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
Results from an annual national poverty survey paint a worsening picture of food affordability in Canada, especially for young people, as tariffs imposed by the United States continue to shake up the Canadian economy.

The Salvation Army’s 2026 Poverty and Socioeconomic Analysis, released today, polled more than 1,500 Canadians and found that 31 per cent skipped meals or reduced their meal sizes because they couldn’t afford groceries , up from 27 per cent one year ago.

The number of people who reported using community supports such as food banks was also up — 15 per cent of those surveyed this year, compared with 11 per cent last year.

Young people report an even worse situation, according to the research conducted by Edelman Data and Intelligence on behalf of the Salvation Army.

Forty-one per cent of respondents aged 18-34 said they skipped meals, 10 percentage points higher than the average, and 23 per cent said they accessed food supports.

A separate report from Daily Bread Food Bank says the number of children struggling with food insecurity in Toronto has risen, as food bank visits held steady at more than 4.1 million visits for the second year.

The survey also suggests that Canadians are more concerned about U.S. tariffs and their effect on the economy than last year, with nearly nine in 10 saying they were worried the trade war would spike prices for everyday goods.

Three in five surveyed reported their household was already feeling the pinch from U.S. tariffs.

The survey was conducted over several days in September among a nationally representative sample of Canadians, including some current and past users of Salvation Army services, who are members of the online Angus Reid Forum. Residents of Canada’s territories were not included in the survey and a margin of error cannot be calculated for a non-probability sample, the report noted.

On the housing front, half of respondents said they aren’t confident they could find another home in their area that was both affordable and met their household needs, while 24 per cent said they spend at least half their after-tax income on housing costs.

To cover basic needs, 50 per cent of Canadians polled said they dipped into savings while 40 per cent reported taking on debt or using credit.

Glenn van Gulik, a strategic engagement director for the Salvation Army, called the results “deeply concerning.”

“For many families, making ends meet is no longer about cutting back on extras. It’s about making difficult choices between food, housing and other basic necessities,” van Gulik wrote in a statement.

stories.title: Road worker dies after being hit by dump truck in Pickering
stories.summary: A road worker died Monday after being hit by a dump truck near Peter Matthews and Alexander Knox drives in Pickering, Durham Regional Police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A road worker died Monday after being hit by a dump truck in Pickering, Durham Regional Police say.

Officers were called around 2:40 p.m. on Nov. 2 for reports of a collision near Peter Matthews and Alexander Knox drives.

“During asphalt repair on Peter Matthews Drive, a dump truck was reversing southbound when it struck a 31-year-old male road worker,” police said in a news release Tuesday.

“The road worker was transported to local-area hospital where he succumbed to his injuries. The driver of the dump truck remained on scene and cooperated with police.”

Roads in the area were closed for several hours while police investigated.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Harper offered Mark Carney government role, new memoir reveals
stories.summary: The book offers Harper's perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney , then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.

In his new book “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper says he told Carney the finance position was already taken but indicated that he would be next in line for the job when it became vacant.

“Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open,” Harper writes.

Carney said in an interview on CBC during the 2025 Liberal leadership race that Harper had “asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012.” He said at the time it wouldn’t be appropriate to go directly from the Bank of Canada governorship to party politics.

In his book, released Tuesday, Harper says while Carney was “highly effective” as bank governor, his finance minister Jim Flaherty was “increasingly” worried in the wake of the 2011 election that Carney was nurturing political ambitions and might wish to seek the Liberal party leadership — something widely rumoured at the time.

“This was a serious concern for us,” Harper writes.

Harper says he brought it up with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff, who suggested a job offer would either secure Carney’s services for the government or force him to rule out a Liberal leadership bid, since he was in the non-partisan role of bank governor.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics,” he said, noting Carney left soon after for the top job at the Bank of England.

The mention of Carney is just a small aside in the nearly 650-page memoir. Harper says he felt he should address the issue since it has “occasionally cropped up in the media.”

The book offers Harper’s perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics from start to finish, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.

It also contains a rare first-person account of Harper’s final election campaign and the defeat of his government in 2015.

The former prime minister writes that he debated stepping down from the leadership in the summer of 2014 to rejuvenate the party.

Harper says after deciding to remain at the helm and lead his party into what he knew would be a tough race, he decided he would serve until just after the 150th anniversary of Confederation on July 1, 2017, then call a leadership race.

Harper also says he only learned of one of the most controversial episodes of the 2015 election — his party’s embrace of a “barbaric cultural practices hotline” — during his preparation for the French leaders’ debate in Montreal when the news “flashed across my screen.”

The announcement of the proposed tip line — which frustrated Red Tories and hindered the party’s outreach efforts with multicultural communities years after the fact — was fronted at the time by former cabinet ministers Kellie Leitch and Chris Alexander.

Harper writes he was “furious” upon learning about the policy, which he says he was not consulted on and had to defend on the campaign trail.

The book spans decades of Canadian political history. It includes Harper’s description of face-to-face standoffs with Russian President Vladimir Putin at G8 meetings, his reaction to the 2008 parliamentary crisis — when opposition parties attempted and failed to form a coalition government to oust the Conservatives — and Harper’s personal experience during the 2014 shooting on Parliament Hill, which happened when he was without his normal personal protective detail.

The former prime minister also offers up occasional reflections on current matters. While he attended the World Economic Forum in Davos twice during in his time in office, he now says he opposes it.

If he were prime minister today, Harper writes, he would end the Canadian government’s participation in the WEF, an event he describes as a once-useful forum that has become a club for advancing the “narrow interests of its globalist, elitist attendees.”

stories.title: Carney meeting with Commonwealth leaders in Antigua and Barbuda
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Antigua and Barbuda today for a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Antigua and Barbuda today for a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government.

Carney has a full itinerary for his one day in Antigua, which will kick off with a meeting with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Carney will then host a working breakfast for Caribbean leaders before the Commonwealth meeting begins.

He will participate in two executive sessions at the meeting and meet one-on-one with the leaders of Australia, Guyana and Ghana.

Carney will also attend a lunch and dinner hosted by King Charles before heading back to Ottawa tonight.

Much of the focus of the Commonwealth meeting will be on trade, though experts say it is also an opportunity to boost diplomatic ties with a variety of countries that belong to the 56-member organization.
