paragraphs: Mayor Olivia Chow’s re-election is not yet seen as a victory among many in Toronto’s Jewish community, but Jewish groups suggest she still has an opportunity to gain trust.

“Under her leadership to date, it is simply a fact that Toronto has emerged as an unacceptable flashpoint within a global crisis of antisemitism, and it’s not only Toronto’s community that’s noticing this,” B’nai Brith Canada CEO Simon Wolle, a Toronto resident, told National Post.
“People around the world are talking about the untenable situation for Toronto’s Jews.”
On Oct. 28, Chow was re-elected , beating city councillor Brad Bradford. The following day, speaking to media, Chow said she would be “mayor for everyone,” the Canadian Press reported.
“Well, I think that there is a large segment of the Jewish community that feels that so far, the mayor has not been one for them,” said Wolle.

Another Jewish advocacy group, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said in a statement following the election that “attention now turns to the commitments made during the campaign and the work still ahead.”
Cija said Chow made promises “to build on policing investments, expand security funding for vulnerable institutions, and continue efforts to address antisemitism and hate.”
“The election May be over, but the responsibility to deliver results is just beginning. Statements condemning antisemitism and other forms of hate must be matched by concrete action.”
B’nai Brith Canada publishes an annual audit on antisemitic incidents across the country. Last year, there were a total of 6,800 incidents , ranging from vandalism to threats of violence.

In Toronto, synagogues have been shot at , events featuring Israeli speakers have been disrupted and Jewish-owned businesses have been targeted . Not far from Toronto, in Belleville, Ont., a gunman opened fire on a synagogue on Yom Kippur in late September, in an attempt to attack its congregants. A police officer stationed outside was severely injured.

Wolle added that there have been ongoing protests in a predominantly Jewish area of the city “with masked participants, sometimes waving flags of terrorist organizations, chanting hate, spewing division, and intimidating and harassing Jewish Torontonians.”
“(Chow’s) allowing for the incitement and division to fester here,” he said.

Chow was notably absent from a debate on antisemitism held at a synagogue in September. She also did not to attend Toronto’s March for Israel over the summer. However, she did attend events like Toronto Pride Parade and Caribana festival.

“When the mayor takes those types of calculated steps to show up for one community and not another, it sends a very clear signal to anyone who’s paying attention that one thing matters and another does not,” Wolle said.
“The inference from her choices and actions to date embolden those who would like to take a position that the Jewish community of Toronto simply does not matter.”

When asked how Chow could win over the approval of Jewish Torontonians, Wolle said all she had to do was show up.

“She needs to take the necessary and sufficient steps to protect public order,” he said. “We want the mayor to step up. We want the mayor to own any mistakes that she’s made to date, and to take the corrective measures to move this city in the right direction.”

B’nai Brith and other partners from the community are willing to help her, said Wolle. “With this election, the mayor should take a good look in the mirror and say, ‘I can do this. I can change course in the city.'”
“We look forward to addressing the challenges facing Torontonians, including the surge in antisemitism and extremism, and protecting human rights for everyone in the city,” it said.

stories.title: Montreal police to fire seven after allegations of discriminatory, racist conduct
stories.summary: Chief Fady Dagher promised action after series of scandals that led police service to suspend at least six officers in recent months
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal’s police chief said Monday that seven officers have been fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist conduct that have dogged the service in recent months.

Chief Fady Dagher told a news conference that the dismissals are unprecedented and involve allegations of “discrimination and racism” and “vulnerable people.”

Dagher confirmed that the dismissals were linked to ongoing criminal investigations into a series of scandals involving officers at two police stations that have made headlines since June.

“To the victims of unacceptable conduct by (Montreal) police officers, I promised you truth and consequences,” he said.

“You have truth, to the extent the investigation allows it, and you have consequences. In the end, we judge a police officer by the way they treat those who cannot defend themselves.”

Dagher had previously announced that six officers had been suspended as part of those probes. He did not confirm the identity of the dismissed officers, but said Monday’s announcement involved the “same individuals.”

Dagher said the force has also turned over its investigative files to the provincial Crown prosecutor’s office, which will decide whether to file criminal charges against the officers.

In the meantime, he said the force worked with the city’s lawyers to carry out what he described as an “administrative dismissal” that essentially meant revoking the officers’ security clearance and police accreditation over alleged failure to uphold the code of conduct.

“They will no longer wear the uniform or carry a weapon, and they will no longer serve the citizens of Montreal,” he said.

Montreal's police chief, Fady Dagher, has announced that seven officers are being fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist conduct that have dogged the force in recen…

The series of scandals that have rocked the force in recent months include allegations of criminal misconduct and racism by some officers, including members of a patrol unit in a multicultural neighbourhood of Montreal that police dismantled in June.

Dagher confirmed earlier this year that the allegations include claims that officers at the station in the Montréal-Nord borough cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Police also announced last week that an officer linked to the investigation could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a situation involving domestic violence in 2025. Dagher did not confirm Monday whether the officer was one of the seven who was dismissed.

Radio-Canada reported last week that an officer responding to a call in connection with conjugal violence allegedly erased evidence on a smartphone that was provided by a complainant. The report suggested the officer knew the alleged perpetrator.

The Canadian Press has not independently verified the allegations in the news report.

The seven people who are being dismissed include five from the Montréal-Nord station as well as two from a downtown station. The downtown dismissals are linked to racism and conduct towards vulnerable people, Dagher said.

Montreal news outlet La Presse has reported that one of those officers allegedly urinated on a homeless person, while the second officer allegedly posed for photos mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions. The Canadian Press has not confirmed the details that led to the suspensions.

Dagher addressed the alleged urination incident on Monday, saying that his information concerns a “dishonourable act of a similar nature, but not on a human.” He said the information in the media report was being investigated by the province’s police watchdog, the Bureau des enquêtes independantes.

The police chief couldn’t confirm Monday that there would be no more officers sanctioned, but reiterated his belief that 99 per cent of officers do their jobs well and noted that some had spoken out against their colleagues.

“I think the kind of announcement that we’re doing today, it shows that the silence is broken, the omerta is broken and we’re taking action,” said Dagher.

Montreal’s mayor said Monday that the police force had taken an “unprecedented” step toward rebuilding citizens’ trust. “Nobody is above the rules,” Soraya Martinez Ferrada said in a statement.

The executive director of a civil-rights group called the Red Coalition called for an independent public inquiry into “systemic racism, racial profiling, discriminatory policing practices and institutional accountability” within the Montreal police force.

“Seven dismissals cannot be considered a sufficient institutional response to allegations of this magnitude,” Joel DeBellefeuille wrote in a statement.

“The public is entitled to know what the (Montreal police) knew, when concerns were brought to its attention, whether warnings were disregarded and whether institutional failures allowed misconduct to persist.”

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Temperatures hit 18.3 degrees on Monday and highs of 20 and 21 are forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, according to Environment Canada.

stories.title: Expert insight: Does easier access to cannabis stores increase teen use? The answer is complicated
stories.summary: A Western-led study found that having cannabis retailers near schools was not associated with an overall increase in use among adolescents.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use. But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis?

Our study suggests the relationship is more complicated. Across more than 419,000 student survey responses collected in four Canadian provinces, we found little consistent evidence that greater access to nearby cannabis retailers was associated with whether adolescents used cannabis.

However, accessibility was associated with more frequent use among existing users during the first year of legalization.

Our research team examined this question in a study published in the Drug and Alcohol Dependence journal. Our findings offer new insight into how cannabis retail accessibility relates to adolescent use as Canada’s legal market matures.

We examined student survey data collected between 2018–19 and 2023–24 through the Compass study in Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario and Québec. We measured accessibility using the distance to the nearest retailer, the number of nearby stores and a measure that gives greater weight to closer retailers.

Overall, greater retail accessibility was not consistently associated with ever using cannabis, past-year or past-month use, or daily and almost-daily use.

Cannabis use also declined in our study sample. Past-year use fell from 22.2 per cent in 2018 to 10.0 per cent in 2023. Past-month use declined from 13.0 per cent to 6.4 per cent, while almost-daily use fell from 4.2 per cent to 2.4 per cent. These figures describe students in participating schools, not a nationally representative sample.

For national context, Health Canada’s Canadian Student Alcohol and Drugs Survey reported that 18.3 per cent of students in Grades 7 to 12 used cannabis in 2023–24. This estimate comes from a separate survey and should not be directly equated with our findings.

One important exception emerged among students who had already used cannabis. In 2018, greater retail accessibility was associated with more frequent use. This association weakened and was no longer statistically significant in subsequent years. Proximity May have mattered for frequency of use early after legalization, but it did not remain a consistent predictor.

Adolescents do not necessarily obtain cannabis directly from legal retailers. They May access it through friends, family members or other social connections, so the distance between a school and a store May not reflect how easily young people can obtain cannabis.

Research on American high school students has identified friends as an important source of cannabis, whether through sharing or purchasing it. This research helps explain why the distance between a student’s school and the nearest cannabis retailer May not reflect how easily they can obtain cannabis. However, our study did not examine where students obtained cannabis, so access through friends is one possible explanation for our findings, not something we directly tested.

Other factors, including peer influences and perceptions of risk, May also affect use. Our study cannot establish which factors explain the findings.

Our findings do not mean adolescent cannabis use is harmless or that governments should abandon safeguards. Research has linked adolescent cannabis use with health and educational concerns. A meta-analysis found associations with depression and suicidal ideation, while other research examined associations between cannabis use and poorer academic outcomes.

A 2024 systematic review also examined cannabis retail availability and health outcomes, underscoring the need to consider different populations and outcomes rather than assume store proximity affects everyone in the same way.

Restrictions on how close cannabis stores can operate to schools May still serve important purposes. However, our findings suggest that store proximity alone May be insufficient to understand or prevent adolescent use. Prevention efforts May also need to address social access, peer influences and factors associated with frequent consumption.

Our study has limitations. Cannabis use was self-reported, and we surveyed students across successive years rather than following the same people over time. We measured retail access around schools, which May not reflect where students live or spend their time. The COVID-19 pandemic also disrupted school and social environments during the study period.

The number of cannabis stores near a school is easy to measure, but it is only one part of a larger picture. Understanding adolescent cannabis use requires looking beyond store locations to consider how young people obtain cannabis, why they use it and how to prevent harmful patterns of consumption.Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: When did kids’ sports become so serious?
stories.summary: Competition has invaded what I thought was the spirit of rec leagues. The days of healthy exploration and dabbling are gone
stories.author: Janna Harowitz
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Where is the beer league for the kids?

I am a geriatric parent. I had kids “late.” I was 39 years old when I had my first child and 41 with my second. The doctors, seemingly fresh out of puberty, called my twilight pregnancy “high risk.”

There are a few of us older moms in the school yard. We reminisce about the days when after-school activities were meant for filling our free time with no end game. We’d make up games from discarded juice boxes, toss hockey cards down the hallway and create loud sounds with our armpits. All healthy alternatives to prank calling.

There was competitive play and there were year-end dance shows when I was growing up, but no one thought we would amount to anything in our respective activity. We were there for the fun, the connection and the park nights with kids from next door. Tap dancing one month and soccer the next. Each activity – one afternoon a week. A select few danced or played “competitively” – but they were in a separate stream. There were no after-school play dates for them.

These days are over. I have found no true “recreational stream” for kids. Rec leagues exist in name only. Competitive serious tendencies have invaded what I thought was the spirit of rec leagues. The days of healthy exploration and dabbling are gone. Kids must commit and do so early. With dedication. Rec hockey? Three times a week. Missing dance? Verbal reprimand from the teacher. Soccer is tiered into divisions. League-facilitated video calls are permeated by parent hopefuls desperate for tips to secure spots in coveted tiers. Me? I asked about how I could ensure my kid entered the lowest-division one-day-a-week team. I made no friends on the call.

The issue came to a head in our house in spring 2025. My then-eight-year-old’s little league baseball practice (three hours!) conflicted with his hip-hop class. It was a “crisis.” I had been confident that this would not be a problem. We’ll just switch teams. Nope. I pleaded my case to the league. Surely, in the days of celebrating diversity, we would accommodate a boy who wants to go to dance class? Again, no. My boy is sweet, curious and hilarious. Top athlete? No. He prefers the locker-room banter to the field.

In the serious iron-man-recreational-sport world we were living in, I was told that moving him would disrupt the delicate balance of the league teams. There is no way that such a move was going to disrupt anything. He’s not that bad and he’s definitely not that good. No amount of convincing could change the decision. This really was the Big Leagues.

The kids had been drafted by coaches based on 45-minute assessments that had occurred in the months prior to equalize the teams. Each group needed just the right amount of “apples” and “oranges” (my code names for athletic aptitude or lack thereof). Team rosters were locked in and we had to make a choice. There was no moving or trading. We said goodbye to hip hop. My son took the news well − not quite appreciating the absurdity of the situation. After all, he’s grown up observing parents who think their children are being scouted on the playground.

And for what? My son, like the other oranges, was relegated to what some parents might consider inconsequential positions on the field. I get it, him playing first base all the time would not have helped the final score. Yes, we all want our kids to experience the jubilation in winning. But are we capital “W” winning if we are taking this too seriously? In a time when we see mental-health issues rising in our kids, and difficulties with retention rates in sport, isn’t decreasing the intensity in favour of playing just for fun, in fact, winning?

Last spring, my son, again, went through the league’s assessment. At this stage, he was now eligible for two different levels – I’ll call it the “A” and “B” grade. About a month later we received an e-mail from the league. It read like a sympathy card or my doctor e-mailing to tell me I was dying. A league representative was reaching out “personally” to inform us of the terrible news – our child was a B.

We were elated. I don’t criticize the representative. She was being kind and I’m sure there were other parents that were distraught when they received the death notice. Therein lies the problem. Why should it matter?

Let’s reclaim the beer league spirit for our kids. No tequila shooters though, let’s just let them play. And have fun. So that they keep playing. And stay happy.

Janna Harowitz lives in Vancouver.

stories.title: How U.S. border state midterm races are shaping up amid ‘insane tariffs’
stories.summary: Nowhere has the trade war with Canada occupied the election cycle narrative than in the seven border states electing new senators on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Americans will head to the polls on Tuesday for the midterms , with U.S. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and trade war with Canada looming large in the election cycle.

Many of the 33 out of 100 U.S. Senate seats are being fiercely contested between Democrats and Trump’s Republican Party.

The trade war with Canada has occupied a large part of the narrative this election cycle in the seven border states electing senators on Tuesday.

The Wolverine State is seeing a heated election campaign between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed, a Muslim, has been the subject of several Islamophobic and racists attacks, including from Trump who called the Democrat a “jihadist” and said he should have to use a metal detector to enter the U.S. Senate.

On his part, El-Sayed has kept a focus on affordability and the high price of gas from the Iran war. When asked about the attacks against his name and faith, El-Sayed turned the conversation towards the high cost of the trade war with Canada.

“My name is not the reason you can’t afford your gas or groceries or to go see a doctor. Their war in Iran is the reason why. Their insane tariffs on Canada is the reason why,” he told reporters last month.

“If you’re picking a fight with Canada, you’re the asshole,” he said.

Michigan and Ontario have deeply integrated auto and steel manufacturing supply chains, with Trump’s trade war causing economic pain on both sides of the border. Canada has become a sticking point in the Michigan Senate election, with even Rogers distancing himself from Trump’s trade policy.

“Canada is not our enemy,” Rogers said in a campaign ad, in which he called for an end to the trade war despite supporting it months earlier.

El-Sayed appears to have the lead, although polls diverge on how sizeable his lead is.

A Beacon Research and Shaw & Company poll conducted for Fox News in September found he had a slight one-point lead, and a Marist University poll found him ahead by a thin two-point margin.

However, more recent polls suggest he May have surged. A CNN/Ssrs poll conducted between Oct. 20 and 27 giving him a seven-point lead, while the latest New York Times/Siena Poll released on Sunday put him ahead by 11 points.

The Democratic campaign in Michigan, though, has had its share of hiccups with Congresswoman Haley Stevens’s shock decision to endorse Rogers, who she once said was a “fraud” and a “rubber stamp” for Trump.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed in August, broke with El-Sayed after asking him to disavow an ad from an outside group that was critical of American aid to Israel. El-Sayed said he had nothing to do with the ad.

Appearing at a campaign event with Rogers, Stevens said her endorsement was “about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country.”

The Democratic establishment rallied around El-Sayed, with Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer calling Stevens’s move a “despicable betrayal.”

During the Senate candidates’ debate last month, Republican incumbent Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson sparred in a heated exchange over Canada.

“I was successful in getting road salt removed from the tariff list,” Collins said, referring to Trump’s decision to exempt certain Canadian goods from his sweeping 50 per cent tariffs.

“What about everything else? We can’t eat road salt,” Jackson hit back, arguing that Trump’s tariffs have not only hit Maine’s lumber and fishing industries, but also put a dent in the tourism sector with visits from Canadians taking a nosedive.

Collins, who has been the senator from Maine since she was first elected in January 1997, has distanced herself from the Trump administration’s trade policies.

In a letter to U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in August, Collins warned that Trump’s trade war against Canada would mean “higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine families, small and large businesses and our communities.”

Jackson appears to have a slight edge in the polls, with the latest New York Times/Sienna poll putting him six points ahead. The same poll in September had Collins ahead with three points in September.

The latest University of New Hampshire Poll said he was nine points ahead while the CNN/Ssrs poll gave him a narrow four-point lead.

Collins, however, is known to be a bit of a political survivor who has proven the polls wrong before. In 2020, some polls had Collins trailing by as much as 12 points when she came back from behind to win the seat.

The race for traditionally ruby-red Alaska looks to be in contention this year.

Democrat Mary Peltola still leads Republican Dan Sullivan in the polls, but her lead in the New York Times/Sienna poll has narrowed from seven points in September to a single point in the latest poll released on Sunday.

The state’s Senate election is in Trump’s crosshairs after the New York Times reported a secret effort to stack the ballot to favour Peltola. It was reported that the Peltola campaign allegedly recruited another candidate called Dan J. Sullivan Jr., who has a similar name to the Republican nominee Dan S. Sullivan, to run to deliberately confuse voters.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said this was “Voter Fraud at the Highest Level” and called for Peltola to be “removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.”

Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an inquiry into what he called “an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”

There is no Democrat on the ballot for the Senate in Idaho, where the Democratic nominee withdrew in July. Instead, three-term Republican senator Jim Risch is facing independent candidate and U.S. Army veteran Todd Achilles, who has previously served as a Democrat in the Idaho House of Representatives.

Despite a spirited campaign that has focused on the anger around affordability and data centre development in the state, Achilles is trailing in the polls. Even a Nexus poll commissioned by his own campaign has him down six points, while a Republican-sponsored poll puts Risch ahead by 27 points.

Montana is seeing a three-horse race, with Republican Kurt Alme facing Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead and independent candidate Seth Bodnar.

While Bankhead won the primary, polls show she has been trailing in third place with Alme the favourite to win the race. This has prompted several prominent Democrats, including former Transport Secretary Pete Butteigeg to endorse Bodnar over the official party nominee.

Democrat Chris Pappas, who became the first openly gay member to represent New Hampshire in 2018, is heavily favoured in the polls win the race for senate.

The most recent New York Times/Sienna poll had Pappas up by 12 points over Republican John Sununu, who has Trump’s endorsement, while the most recent UMass Lowell poll had him up by seven.

Polls are divided on how wide Democrat Peggy Flannigan’s lead is in Minnesota, with the New York Times/Sienna poll putting her ahead by 14 points.

On the other hand, a Mason-Dixon poll conducted for the Minnesota Star Tribune in October had Flannigan, the state’s Lt. Gov., leading Republican conservative commentator and Republican candidate Michele Tafoya by four points.

stories.title: ‘No amendment was done’: Ridesharing issue back in St. Thomas, two years after council asked staff to amend 2013 taxi bylaw
stories.summary: After seven months driving the citizens of St. Thomas for a flat rate of $12, Bob Pate is being told he’s no longer allowed to do so.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
After seven months driving the citizens of St. Thomas for a flat rate of $12, Bob Pate is being told he’s no longer allowed to do so.

“I got a phone call on Friday from the bylaw officer, and he said I have to stop everything by Friday, Nov. 6,” said Pate – the owner of Easy Ride – who created a ridesharing app, bought a Cadillac, and has multiple drivers.

The city received a complaint about his service and is now threatening to shut him down.

“All rideshare services right now would fall under the current taxi bylaw,” said Thomas Thayer, St. Thomas’ city clerk.

“Any vehicle participating in rideshare would fall under the definition of a taxicab.”

This issue came up two years ago in November 2024.

At the request of rideshare driver Malachi Male, St. Thomas City Council asked staff to amend their 2013 Taxi bylaw to include ride shares .

It was never done.

“They didn’t pass any law or anything and no amendment was done,” said Pate.

“It is still lingering from last two years.”

Thayer said the city is looking at options.

“But as I understand it, the provincial government is looking to potentially upload rideshare enforcement and authorization regulation to their level, which would take it away from the municipalities,” said Thayer.

“To put staff effort right now into developing and amending our taxi bylaw for rideshare services, we’re going to wait until the province determines what they ultimately want to do. We’re taking a similar stance to what other medium-sized cities are currently doing.”

Pate has been told he needs to comply by either obtaining a taxi licence or be shut down.

“This is not a taxi, this is a ride sharing business,” said Pate.

“The same as Uber, Lyft, and other platforms.”

Pate says he has all the safety precautions in place to be a rideshare driver and business owner.

“I have to get the venerable sector check from the police,” said Pate.

“We get that report and after that I will hire them as a driver. I am driving [a], like, $100,000 worth car and all the cars we are having a proper insurance and plus I have additional insurance for my passengers.”

Pate has started a petition asking for “Fair Recognition, Regulation, and Support of Easy Ride.”

He is hoping to get the issue before council on Nov. 9.

“You can make it official for every ride share and apply the rules and regulations,” said Pate.

“What kind of license do you need? What kind of other stuff do we need to get? We will get it done and we will get legalized and we will get everything running.”

“We get that report and after that I will hire them as a driver. I am driving [a], like, $100,000 worth car and all the cars we are having a proper insurance and plus I have additional insurance for my passengers.”
Pate has started a petition asking for “Fair Recognition, Regulation, and Support of Easy Ride.”
He is hoping to get the issue before council on Nov. 9.
“You can make it official for every ride share and apply the rules and regulations,” said Pate.
“What kind of license do you need? What kind of other stuff do we need to get? We will get it done and we will get legalized and we will get everything running.”

stories.title: Prenatal program expands in London thanks to funding from London Food Bank
stories.summary: Multiple agencies, including the London Food Bank (LFB) and the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU), have expanded services for expecting people in London.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Multiple agencies, including the London Food Bank (LFB) and the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU), have expanded services for expecting people in London.

The partners hope the growth of the Smart Start for Babies program will go a long way towards reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition.

The program, which already operates in six locations around London, is being expanded to the Boys and Girls Club of London and the Highbury and Huron location of London Intercommunity Health Centre.

Melina Rimtebaye, a mother of a six-month-old son, has already been helped through SSB services.

“Even just changing a diaper, trying to know what the baby needs, helps,” she said during an interview with CTV News.

The program offers insight and information to pregnant people facing social or economic barriers. Programs include classes on a range of topics, including preparing for labour and cooking affordable snacks to keep themselves and their baby healthy.

“While they’re here, they’ll be preparing food together and learning about healthy nutrition and also receiving supports like grocery cards,” said Jennifer Proulx, the director of family and community health at MLHU.

The expansion of the Smart Start program was made possible by a $180,000 donation from the LFB.

Thanks to cash donations, the agency has expanded its footprint beyond traditional food donations.

“We often don’t know the people we serve, so we wanted to work with groups like the resource centers as well, that work with people on the deeper issues and in the causes of food insecurity”, said Jane Roy of the London Food Bank.

Melina says the help has given her a chance to care for her son while preparing to enter the workforce with a nearly acquired business law degree.

More information on the Smart Start for Babies program can be found here: Prenatal Health – Middlesex-London Health Unit

stories.title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he warns of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - The British Columbia Conservative caucus of 63 newly elected legislators is united to lead the province, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said Monday, but he warned there would be difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.

Doerkson made the comments as Conservative legislators gathered for their first caucus meeting in Victoria, where he said their job now would be to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.

He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.

“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”

He said B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every time.

Doerkson said people would be watching to see if his caucus would splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

“I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can hold it together,” he said.

“So, let me save everyone the suspense: this caucus is unified,” Doerkson said to cheers from the crowd.

Jaime Stein, the Conservative just elected in the riding of Vancouver-Langara, was asked about caucus unity Monday and said in an interview that his main concern was getting things done for B.C. residents.

“We left the caucus meeting this morning with a message, which is one team, and that is what we are going forward with as a team,” Stein said.

UBC political science lecturer Stewart Prest said the caucus is united for now.

“But I don’t know that it will be true for the duration,” he said. “We have in many ways a deeply divided caucus here, two parties present within the single B.C. Conservative caucus.”

Prest said the party still has a populist faction.

“On the other side, we know there are a number of MLAs, who had left to join CentreBC, who were looking for a moderate version of conservatism.”

While the caucus is united through the “promise of power,” decisions around cabinet appointments and the legislative agenda May lead to disharmony, Prest said.

Several Conservative members quit or were fired from the caucus just months into Findlay’s leadership before she resigned two days before the NDP under David Eby set off an election.

The members came back after Doerkson was appointed and he led the party to the election win.

Prest said the large size of the caucus gives Doerkson more of a cushion.

“He can afford to alienate a couple of individual MLAs,” he said. “If anyone is in a mood to be completely uncompromising, they May find themselves left in the cold.”

He said if there was a perception that one side of the party was not being listened to, then a number of members — particularly if they are left out of cabinet — were free to speak their minds, becoming like a minor opposition from the backbench.

Doerkson said Monday that B.C. residents could count on the Conservatives to stay focused on what they were elected to do.

He said a Conservative government would deliver a better economy, health care system and public safety.

“That is what we are going to do, and it is absolutely my intention to do it as quickly as possible,” he said.

The incoming premier says legislators are to be sworn in Nov. 19 and the new cabinet would be announced Nov. 20.

Former Conservative leader John Rustad said the toughest job of any premier is to build a cabinet.

No matter how many people Doerkson appoints to cabinet, he will disappoint others, he said.

“So, does he go with 12 people in cabinet, and have 50 people not in cabinet?” Rustad said in an interview last week.

Claire Rattee, who previously served as critic for mental health and addictions, said nobody has heard anything about cabinet.

“I have every confidence and faith in his ability to choose an excellent cabinet,” she said. “I’m just happy to be here to serve (the riding of) Skeena and the residents I represent and anywhere that he would see fit for me or for any of my colleagues.”

Doerkson did not say whether he would recall the legislature for a fall session, but repeated previous promises made on the campaign trail.

“That means putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working British Columbians,” he said. “It means treating taxpayers with respect and saying no to new taxes. It means giving small businesses room to grow with a (provincial sales tax) exemption that will help them to invest, hire and succeed.”

Doerkson also said his government would repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, while continuing to “build strong relationships” with First Nations in the province.

“I am committed that we will do that also as soon as we can,” he said.

B.C. First Nations chiefs have warned against repealing the legislation, urging instead to use it as a framework for reconciliation.

Doerkson also signalled a change in housing legislation.

“We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version misspelled the first name of Jaime Stein.

stories.title: Survivor of Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting cites need for extensive security
stories.summary: The vice-president of the Belleville synagogue that was attacked by a gunman in September says costly, enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — One of the leaders of the Belleville, Ont., synagogue that was targeted by a gunman in September says costly enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.

Police have described the Sept. 20 attack as a thwarted attempt at a mass killing of Jewish worshippers at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Police say the shooter had multiple guns, large amounts of ammunition and gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack when he opened fire on an officer stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

Shima Vigodda, vice-president of the synagogue, told a news conference on Parliament Hill on Monday that before the shooting, the institution’s security priorities were things like replacing windows broken in acts of vandalism and installing burglar alarms.

An existing federal program that helps places of worship make security improvements was adequate for such modest expenses, he indicated.

But Vigodda, who survived the gunman’s assault, said it has become clear that more expensive measures are necessary — improvements the Canada Community Security Program would not fully cover.

He said those measures include things like installing bullet-resistant glass, replacing inner and outer doors, building a safe room, installing fencing to slow or halt a would-be attacker, and having security personnel or armed police on site.

“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical security, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable enough to return to the synagogue.”

Approved proposals under the federal security program are eligible for funding to cover up to 70 per cent of project costs, with a maximum Public Safety Canada contribution of $5 million per project.

Vigodda said that even with the program, smaller communities struggling to ensure adequate security while trying to cover other expenses face “an agonizing and sometimes impossible choice.”

Noah Shack, chief executive of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told the news conference the federal budget, being tabled Thursday, is an opportunity for the Liberal government to build on its new national security strategy by investing in counter-radicalization, intelligence and counterterrorism.

He said the centre is working closely with Public Safety Canada to strengthen the Canada Community Security Program, “so that every institution can access the support it needs, and that the program is intended to provide, regardless of its financial circumstances.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Experts suggest Canada lock in gains with EU amid rise in far-right movements
stories.summary: Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks as right-wing movements gain ground on the continent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks as right-wing movements gain ground on the continent.

Academics studying EU relations are testifying to the House foreign-affairs committee after a Montreal summit last week which officials praised as a historic partnership.

Carleton University professor Achim Hurrelmann says that recent talk of Canada becoming an EU “associate member” attracts symbolic attention but officials could easily drop that language.

He says Canada should focus on getting wins encoded into European law, and consider restructuring the EU trade deal to increase economic gains.

University of Toronto professor Mark Manger says there are few concrete outcomes from last week’s summit and that many of the agreements match what Mexico already has with the EU.

He suggested Ottawa could allow European mobile networks to set up shop in Canada in exchange for European countries dropping restrictions on importing Canadian food.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

By Owen Schuller Nov 2, 2026 | 2:14 PM

Conflicting messages from Washington and Ottawa are raising questions about the state of Canada-U.S. trade talks, with U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting a deal is near while Canadian officials say little progress has been made.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has acknowledged that trade talks with the U.S. have become more intense. American officials have suggested a deal could be possible before the U.S. midterm elections.

A Canadian government official with knowledge of the negotiations, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said discussions have continued but that limited progress has been made.

The current dispute began in early 2025 when President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Over time, some tariffs were paused and exemptions were introduced. However, the trade dispute has continued to escalate, affecting steel, automotive, lumber and aluminum industries.

Matt Farrell, a political science professor at Fanshawe College, describes the main obstacle to reaching a trade agreement. “In short, it is the President. If Trump doesn’t like something that Canada is doing, he will add tariffs.”

Image 15 Photo credit: reuters

Farrell explained that tariffs could potentially be dropped,but only if Canada offers something in return.

To make significant progress or a trade deal, Farrell believes, “it’s just political convenience and optics. If there’s a reason where President Trump wants to make a deal, then he will. That’s it.”

Farrell said any breakthrough may ultimately depend on political priorities in Washington, leaving the timing and outcome of a potential agreement uncertain.

stories.title: Flu season hit early this year. Ask us your questions on how to stay healthy
stories.summary: Experts say rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
The influenza virus is hitting harder and earlier this year across Canada, prompting an early start to flu season.

Rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years, experts say, and some provinces are offering flu shots earlier than usual, as vulnerable populations seek to protect themselves.

In an ever-changing situation, it can be hard to know what’s best to keep you and your family safe. Health editor Caroline Alphonso and health reporter Alanna Smith answered reader questions on this year’s flu season, what infection rates and vaccination plans look like in your region and how you can prevent and manage symptoms.

Submit your questions in the box below, or send us an e-mail at audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: Cija calls for more power and resources for police to protect Jews ahead of federal budget
stories.summary: The group also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government's National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — A leading Jewish group is asking the federal government to boost police and intelligence agencies’ abilities to fight antisemitic crimes as a Liberal MP says there is still more work to be done to protect Canadian Jews.

Speaking to reporters before the Liberals table their 2026 budget on Thursday, Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs head Noah Shack called on the government to ensure proper funding for counter-radicalization programs to stem the rapid rise of antisemitism in Canada.

“The common thread among youth in particular who are susceptible to violent extremism, the common thread across all the different ideological vectors, is conspiracy theories and hate towards Jews,” Shack said Monday.

“We know that in confronting antisemitism, we are getting at the root of a larger problem, or at least a significant manifestation of a larger problem,” he added.

On Sept. 20, a gunman fired at police officers stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., while congregants met inside for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Reports state that the assailant opened fire on police constables Jeff Smith and Michael McCurdy while yelling “you are going to die for the Jews.”

The shooting was the latest in a rising number of antisemitic violent attacks against Jewish individuals or their meeting spaces across Canada.

Shack was accompanied on Parliament Hill on Monday with Douglas Lobel and Shima Vigodda, two survivors of the shooting last month at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

“For those of us at the synagogue on Yom Kippur, though we were shocked at what occurred, none of us were surprised. I hope that what occurred in Belleville is a wake-up call as to just how high the stakes are at the moment,” said Vigodda, vice-president of Sons of Jacob Congregation.

In a memo to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree on Oct. 22, Cija called on the government to further invest and expand “Charter-compliant” powers of the RCMP and Csis in order to fight antisemitism and radicalization.

Shack also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government’s National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence.

“Antisemitism has become the glue by which different extremist ideologies, from far-left radicals to neo-Nazis and Islamists come together,” Shack noted.

Liberal MP Chris Malette, who represents the riding containing Belleville and lives just two blocks from the synagogue, said there is proof that the government’s recent changes to anti-hate speech legislation are working.

“Do I agree that more needs to be done? Absolutely,” said Malette, assuring that the government was listening to the Jewish community’s concerns.

“I’m confident that that we can help adjust our security systems and our legislation to meet the changing realities and severity and the seriousness of the threats against our faith communities, because we’re seeing it at unseen levels,” he added.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

Shack was accompanied on Parliament Hill on Monday with Douglas Lobel and Shima Vigodda, two survivors of the shooting last month at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

“For those of us at the synagogue on Yom Kippur, though we were shocked at what occurred, none of us were surprised. I hope that what occurred in Belleville is a wake-up call as to just how high the stakes are at the moment,” said Vigodda, vice-president of Sons of Jacob Congregation.

In a memo to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree on Oct. 22, Cija called on the government to further invest and expand “Charter-compliant” powers of the RCMP and Csis in order to fight antisemitism and radicalization.
Shack also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government’s National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence.
“Antisemitism has become the glue by which different extremist ideologies, from far-left radicals to neo-Nazis and Islamists come together,” Shack noted.

Liberal MP Chris Malette, who represents the riding containing Belleville and lives just two blocks from the synagogue, said there is proof that the government’s recent changes to anti-hate speech legislation are working.
“Do I agree that more needs to be done? Absolutely,” said Malette, assuring that the government was listening to the Jewish community’s concerns.

“I’m confident that that we can help adjust our security systems and our legislation to meet the changing realities and severity and the seriousness of the threats against our faith communities, because we’re seeing it at unseen levels,” he added.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

Burnaby - Two family members have been charged in the death of an 11-year-old boy who was reported missing in Burnaby, B.C., more than a year ago.

Police received a report in September 2025 to check on the well-being of Kai Pavlovic, who was last known to be living with his family in Burnaby.

stories.title: Unseasonably warm temperatures expected across southern Ontario this week
stories.summary: A low-pressure system is expected to influence the region’s weather pattern, drawing moisture northward and bringing periodic chances of light showers.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southern Ontario is set to experience unseasonably warm temperatures this week, with daytime highs climbing into the upper teens and low 20s, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said mild conditions will persist through much of the week, with overnight temperatures remaining relatively warm and daytime highs ranging from 18 C to 21 C in many areas.

“We’re taking a run at some records over the next couple of days with temperatures in the upper teens and low 20s,” Atchison said.

A low-pressure system is expected to influence the region’s weather pattern, drawing moisture northward and bringing periodic chances of light showers.

Atchison said there is about a 40 per cent chance of scattered showers Monday evening into early Tuesday morning. Any rainfall that develops is expected to be light and spotty.

Cloud cover is forecast to clear Tuesday afternoon, giving way to a mix of sun and cloud.

“Tuesday is going to be gorgeous,” Atchison said, noting temperatures are expected to reach between 20 C and 21 C across much of southern Ontario, with Windsor forecast to be the warm spot at 22 C.

Another 40 per cent chance of showers is forecast for Wednesday, although temperatures are expected to remain near 21 C. Highs are expected to cool slightly to around 16 C on Thursday, which also carries a chance of showers.

The warm spell is expected to come to an end by the weekend as cooler air moves into the region. Temperatures are forecast to fall to about 8 C on Saturday, accompanied by a 40 per cent chance of rain.

Sunday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud with a high near 8 C.

stories.title: Canada on the minds of American voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections
stories.summary: As Americans are preparing to cast their ballots in their midterm election on Tuesday, their northern neighbours are in the back of their mind as Canadians are paying close attention to what the outcome could mean on this side of the border. For the Republican Party, they are looking to hold onto their slim majorities in […]
stories.author: Caryn Ceolin
stories.content:
As Americans are preparing to cast their ballots in their midterm election on Tuesday, their northern neighbours are in the back of their mind as Canadians are paying close attention to what the outcome could mean on this side of the border.

For the Republican Party, they are looking to hold onto their slim majorities in both chambers of Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and whether or not they will continue to control the legislative agenda for the last two years of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the Democrats are hoping to flip the House and Senate to attempt to restrain Trump’s unprecedented use of presidential powers.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority.

The future of the Senate is less clear. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and some polling shows that is within reach.

Trump has largely governed through executive orders in order to get around Congress to further his tariff and trade agenda.

Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed and Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a good conversation with Trump about a trade deal, but did not provide any details.

CityNews is in Washington ahead of the elections where some voters have told us that Canada will be in the back of their minds when they cast their ballots on Tuesday, many who said they were opposed to his treatment of their northern neighbour.

“It’s the closest embassy to the capital,” said one voter. When asked about what he thought of Trump’s treatment of Canada, he said, “It’s the horror story. It’s horrible. They’re our best neighbours.”

“I think it’s unfortunate that one of our biggest allies and trade partners, we’re now in this situation in which we, the American people, don’t agree with. We didn’t ask for it, and here we are having to bear the brunt of the bad news,” said another voter.

Another said they believe the former North American Free Trade Agreement hurt the manufacturing sector in the U.S.

“My perspective is that there needs to be fair trade across … I personally like our northern neighbours tremendously. But in the same sense, I’m not a fan of tariffs either way with a country as long as they’re treating each other fair,”

The top issue to most voters CityNews spoke with was the affordability and the cost of living, with some saying the economic impacts of Trump’s policies acting as major motivators in the midterms.

CityNews 24/7 will provide live coverage of the U.S. midterm elections throughout Tuesday evening. You can watch it the CityNews website here .

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Canadian dollar steadies as investors weigh officials’ trade comments
stories.summary: Bond yields fall across the curve
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar steadied near a six-week ​high against its U.S. counterpart on ‌Monday as oil prices tumbled and investors weighed positive signals on prospects of a trade deal between the U.S. and Canada.

The loonie was ⁠trading nearly ​unchanged at 1.3975 per US dollar, or 71.56 US cents, after touching on Friday its strongest intraday level since September 16 at 1.3940.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday ​that his administration has the “concept” of a ‌new trade deal with Canada while Prime Minister Mark Carney said the two leaders had a good conversation on the future of trade between their countries.

The imposition of tariffs on Canada has emerged as an issue ‌in some ​northern U.S. border ‌states like Michigan and Maine before U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

“Headlines ​have been constructive, following positive comments from ⁠both U.S. and Canadian officials on the topic of trade,” ⁠Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, FX strategists at Scotiabank, said in a ​note.

“Fundamentally, the CAD remains well supported by narrowing U.S.-Canada yield spreads which have delivered the bulk of its recent gains,” the strategists said.

The gap between Canada’s 2-year yield and the U.S. equivalent was trading at about 129 ⁠basis points in favor of the U.S. note. Last month, the gap was as wide as 161 basis points.

The Bank of Canada last week raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent, its first hike in three ⁠years, out of concern that soaring energy ​prices could drive broader inflation.

U.S. crude oil futures fell 7.8 per cent ⁠to $96.01 a barrel as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted hopes for an end to ‌the US-Israeli war with Iran and stabilization of Middle East crude supply. ​Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

Canadian bond yields fell across the curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries. The 10-year was down 5.5 basis points at 3.744 per cent, after ​earlier touching its lowest level since September 3 at 3.740 per cent.

stories.title: Toronto police didn’t know hospital patient was home invasion suspect: Demkiw
stories.summary: Investigators didn’t know a man who showed up to a Toronto hospital last Thursday with a gunshot wound was wanted in a violent home invasion, Chief Myron Demkiw says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Investigators didn’t know a man who showed up to a hospital last with a gunshot wound Thursday was wanted for a violent home invasion, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw says.

Demkiw told reporters Monday officers later learned that patient was allegedly one of three suspects involved in the break-in that sent four members of the same family to hospital .

“The home invasion happens in the middle of the night and a very short time later, an individual shows up at a hospital with a gunshot wound,” Demkiw said.

“What’s important to note is that in the home invasion investigation, there is no information that suggested to investigators an assailant had been shot.”

Police were first called to a home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:45 a.m. on Oct. 29.

Three masked men in their 20s allegedly forced their way into the home and eventually confronted the family inside, police said. The men were armed with handguns. One suspect had a hammer.

Police have not disclosed any arrests.

Daijohn Richards , 23, was identified Saturday as a suspect; police said he took himself to the hospital later that same day with a gunshot wound to his right shoulder.

Officers “responded to the hospital as they would when people walk into the hospital with a gunshot wound, which happens in the city from time to time,” Demkiw said.

“They continue to advance the investigation, gather evidence and made an announcement publicly that they’ve identified a suspect in the coming hours after that.”

Demkiw wouldn’t comment further, but said the investigators assigned to the case are “some of the best in the business.”

“Had I been a victim of this type of horrible set of circumstances, these are precisely the people I would want chasing and apprehending the offenders and bringing them to justice,” he said.

“I have complete confidence in their abilities, and we will create an opportunity for them to continue to advance their investigation, respecting the integrity of the investigative process.”

Richards is wanted on four counts of discharge of a firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault, break and enter, possession of a prohibited device and disguise with intent.

Four people were inside the home at the time: a man, his wife and their two adult daughters.

All four people were taken to hospital. Three of the victims were shot and two were struck in the head with a hammer, police said. Some have since been released from hospital.

Global News has learned the two adult daughters are Maggie and Cristina Zohil-Morton. Their parents are listed on business profiles as David Morton and Doriana Zohil.

David, CEO of Toronto-based real estate company MAC Group, said in a statement Friday the family is focused on recovery but is becoming more concerned with increasing violence associated with home invasions.

“No family should ever have to experience this,” he said.

“People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.”

— with files from Rachel Morgan and Alessia Simona Maratta

stories.title: Canada presenting itself as climate leader at COP31, despite policy rollbacks
stories.summary: Ottawa - Despite its rollbacks of climate policy, the Carney government will lead a delegation to the COP31 conference in Turkey next week presenting itself as an international climate leader.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada will present itself as an international climate leader when it sends a delegation to the annual UN climate talks next week in Turkey, despite its rollbacks of climate policy under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Government officials held a technical briefing for journalists Monday ahead of the annual two-week COP31 conference, the main forum for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the 2015 Paris climate pact.

That pact committed signatories to reducing emissions sharply to keep global warming below 2 C and as close as possible to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels by the end of this century. A UN report last month said that goal is now out of reach because emissions have not come down fast enough.

That report will be a key feature of the upcoming COP31, where discussions will address how to reduce emissions to keep warming below 2 C by 2100.

Government officials told the briefing on Monday that Canada remains a “credible international actor on climate change” that other countries are keen to engage with.

But Patrick Bonin, the Bloc Québécois environment critic who will attend COP31 as part of the Canadian delegation, said Canada’s track record of rolling back climate policy has harmed its international reputation.

“I can’t see how they can pivot over a few days during COP to have any credibility on climate change,” Bonin told The Canadian Press in French.

“We’re no longer in an era where Canada can lend itself to any credibility with its action plan on climate, since Canada is in the middle of completely halting its short-term goals and can’t meet its 2030 emission reduction goals until at least 2050.”

The government’s own numbers show Canada is nowhere close to meeting its international commitment to reduce emissions by at least 40 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030.

Since taking office Carney has rolled back a number of climate policies initiated by the former government under Justin Trudeau, including eliminating the consumer carbon price, adjusting standards for the industrial carbon price, repealing a mandate for electric vehicle sales, and cancelling a planned emissions cap on oil and gas production.

In a video released in June, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

That same month a number of Canada’s most prominent environmental groups, including the David Suzuki Foundation, Ecojustice, Greenpeace Canada, Nature Canada and Environmental Defence, pushed for meetings with Carney’s aides and MPs to discuss what they called “urgent concerns about the government’s moves to eviscerate environmental laws and procedures and to undermine Canada’s nature, climate and clean energy goals.”

Canada won the “fossil of the day” title at last year’s COP30 in Brazil. Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”

Carney will not attend the leaders’ summit at the start of the summit but Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin will be in Turkey for the first week of talks. Officials said she will convene a ministerial meeting with the European Union of the Global Methane Pledge, a group of 159 countries committed to collectively reducing global methane emissions by 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.

In June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched a global call to action on methane during an address at the London Climate Action Week.

Canadian officials on Monday said Canada will be “promoting” methane mitigation at COP31 as a “high-impact, cost-effective” way to address emissions.

In its latest annual national emissions report last month, the Canadian Climate Institute credited “fugitive methane emission reductions” as the main driver behind a lower level of emissions from Canada’s oil and gas sector in 2025, despite boosts in production.

But even on methane things have been slowed down as Canada delayed the implementation of its methane regulations.

Canada is also in the spotlight after the environment commissioner last week issued a report which found in 2024 the government abandoned work on a 2021 pledge to ban the export of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Government officials have since said the work is only “paused,” though the report said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Canada and the United Kingdom are the co-leaders of the Powering Past Coal alliance, which seeks to accelerate the transition off coal power around the world.

Government officials refused to say during Monday’s technical briefing whether Canada informed any of its international partners that its work to ban thermal coal exports had ended or was paused.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta’s Justice Minister rejects request to drop proposed electoral map, postpone vote
stories.summary: New boundaries set to be released Monday afternoon
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta’s proposed new provincial electoral boundaries would result in major changes to ridings in Calgary and Lethbridge, expanding their footprints into more rural areas, a prospect that drew accusations of gerrymandering when the maps were released publicly on Monday.

The chair of the independent panel that created the map dismissed concerns that the proposed boundaries would violate the Constitution. But Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi promised to file a legal challenge if Premier Danielle Smith’s government adopts the map, saying the new boundaries would hand an electoral edge to Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party.

Shortly after exiting Question Period, Mr. Nenshi pointed to the U.S.-style practice of manipulating electoral maps to create unfair advantages for a party.

“If the UCP has the nerve to pass this Trump-style, Maga gerrymandered map, if they have the nerve to cheat to win … we’ll see them in court,” Mr. Nenshi said at a news conference after the report containing the map was tabled in the legislature.

A redrawn electoral map has been the subject of intense debate and scrutiny since April when Ms. Smith rejected the proposed boundaries of a first independent commission.

Alberta’s political boundaries are revised every eight to 10 years by an independent panel, a process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. For decades, provincial legislatures have routinely adopted the recommendations without question.

Ms. Smith’s decision to upend tradition, however, has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering.

After rejecting the first panel’s proposed map, Ms. Smith’s government formed a UCP-dominated committee that created a new independent panel charged with making a second attempt at drawing the electoral map. It was chaired by retired Alberta judge Brian O’Ferrall, selected by the UCP, and included two members tapped by the NDP and two by the UCP.

The new report shows the five-person panel was sharply divided on how to proceed with the map, mirroring tensions among the previous group tasked with the redrawing.

The proposed map was drawn by Mr. O’Ferrall and the two members selected by the UCP: Monte Solberg, a former cabinet minister under prime minister Stephen Harper, and Darwin Durnie, who previously co-authored a submission recommending map changes that would see several ridings in Calgary blend with neighbouring rural communities.

In the report, the three jointly write that the panel’s “time and energy were taken up with responding to the indictments of the panel’s minority who suggest that the process of the advisory panel was constitutionally reckless, an abuse of process, and that the panel’s proposals infringed the Charter.”

The two remaining committee members named by the NDP – University of Alberta law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote in a separate report that some of the new recommended ridings would be “constitutionally fraught” and will likely be challenged in court.

It is unclear how long it will take for the government to pass the new map if it decides to adopt it, but it’s expected to be approved before the fall session ends on Dec. 3.

If adopted, the map would most dramatically change the boundaries of Lethbridge, which is currently split into two ridings mostly contained within the city’s borders. One is represented by the NDP, the other by the UCP.

The new map would split Lethbridge into four, with one urban riding encompassing a chunk of the city and three massive urban-rural hybrids surrounding it.

In the report, the three authors in the majority reason that hybrid ridings can “help cities receive the representation they need” and “help rural electoral divisions obtain the population they need to be relatively compact and manageable.”

Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson, meanwhile, charged the other commissioners with packing voters into the highly condensed Lethbridge riding while diluting the city’s remaining residents in rural areas that extend hundreds of kilometres beyond city limits.

“This makes it easier for the party who drew the boundaries to win additional seats,” the two wrote, adding that while they accept the panelists believe they’re improving effective representation, they are concerned the public won’t believe them.

In Calgary, the three-person majority recommended creating new boundaries that amalgamate three urban ridings in west Calgary with neighbouring rural constituencies.

Much of the Ucp’s political support is based in rural Alberta, while the Ndp’s strength lies in Calgary and Edmonton.

The panelists also disagreed on how much they should edit the proposed map recommended by the chair of the previous panel, Court of King’s Bench judge Dallas K. Miller.

The majority authors wrote that Mr. Miller’s recommendation “does not deserve deification,” while Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson argued the panel didn’t have a mandate to overhaul parts of Alberta’s boundaries.

The new map is expected to be the subject of debate in the Alberta Legislature on Tuesday. So far, Ms. Smith’s government has rejected calls to reverse course.

On Sunday, Alberta’s Justice Minister batted away Elections Alberta’s request for the government to either not approve the new electoral maps or postpone next year’s provincial election to give the agency sufficient time to prepare.

The government “has no intention” of shifting next year’s Oct. 18 fixed election date, Justice Minister Mickey Amery wrote in a statement.

Mr. Amery was responding to a letter from provincial chief electoral officer Gordon McClure, who on Friday circulated a letter to MLAs imploring them to reconsider implementing the new electoral boundaries.

Mr. McClure said Elections Alberta’s resources are strained and that the agency would need 12 to 18 months to implement the new map with 91 ridings, up from 87.

stories.title: Parts of Florida and B.C on the same time zone after Daylight saving change
stories.summary: Although they're on opposite sides of North America, some clocks in Florida and B.C. are synched for the next six months
stories.author: National Post staff
stories.content:
Parts of Canada’s westernmost province, British Columbia, and the sunshine state, Florida, now share the same time.

That means, although Pensacola, Fla. and Cranbrook, B.C. are on opposite sides of North America with vastly different climates and environments, their clocks are synched for the next five months.

That’s because B.C. decided to stick to daylight time permanently, and did not gain an hour over the weekend.

On Nov. 1, most of Canada returned to standard time.

Meanwhile, B.C., Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories have decided against it. Yukon has been on permanent daylight time since 2021 and Saskatchewan since 1966, with the exception of Lloydminster, which straddles the border with Alberta and stopped changing its time this year.

While Pensacola is a balmy 23 degrees Celsius on Monday, Cranbrook is a cool 0 degrees — so for now, it seems that time is all they have in common.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Brilliant Maps (@brilliantmaps)

Most of B.C. has adopted permanent year-round daylight time, staying on Pacific Time. The government shared information online about certain locations that would remain on Mountain Time.

Residents of parts of Southeastern B.C., including Cranbrook, Fernie and Elkford, will “remain aligned with Alberta” and use Mountain Time year round.

It said the change was “to improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”

Pensacola, located in the Florida Panhandle northwest of Miami and Tampa, switched from Central Daylight Time to Central Standard Time over the weekend, as it normally does this time of year.

There are two time zones in Florida — Eastern and Central. Nine of the state’s 67 counties operate completely on Central Time, according to the Pensacola News Journal . Pensacola is located in Escambia County, one of the nine on Central Time.

The time zones in B.C. and Florida won’t stay matched up for too long, though. In March, Pensacola and other cities within the nine counties will revert to daylight time again.

stories.title: Huron County paramedics vote in favour of strike mandate amid contract talks
stories.summary: Paramedics represented by Cupe Local 4513 have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate as contract negotiations with Huron County continue.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Paramedics represented by Cupe Local 4513 have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate as contract negotiations with Huron County continue.

The union said 99 per cent of members who cast ballots voted to authorize strike action. According to Cupe 4513, all 112 members participated in the vote.

In a news release, local president Kelsy Long said the vote reflects concerns among paramedics about wages, benefits and mental health supports.

The union said paramedics have traditionally relied on arbitration to resolve contract disputes, making the strike vote a departure from past bargaining approaches.

Cupe 4513 argues wages and benefits have fallen behind those offered by neighbouring paramedic services and says staffing levels have become a concern. The union said four paramedics have left the service since the summer and seven have left since the previous collective agreement expired.

stories.title: Gas odour prompts partial evacuation at St. Joseph’s Hospital
stories.summary: A portion of the building was evacuated Monday after a gas odour was detected during roof construction.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The “all clear” has been given after a Code Green at St. Joseph’s Hospital.

A portion of the building was evacuated Monday after a gas odour was detected during roof construction.

Hospital officials said the odour was detected in Zone D and the area was evacuated out of an abundance of caution.

As a result, appointments in several clinics had to be cancelled, including the Breast Care Program, Rheumatology, Hand and Upper Limb, Hand Therapy and the Wsib clinic.

Patients with appointments in those programs were being asked to wait for a call to reschedule.

Officials said appointments in all other programs at St. Joseph’s Hospital are proceeding as scheduled.

No injuries or additional safety concerns were immediately reported.
