stories.title: Carney to meet with King Charles and Commonwealth heads of government
stories.summary: Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries, such as Tuvalu.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries — and with King Charles III.

Much of the meetings taking place this week will focus on trade and investment. But the gathering also offers a chance for Carney to meet with representatives from a wide variety of countries he might not otherwise visit, said retired Canadian diplomat Patricia Fortier.

“Fifty-six countries, Caribbean, Europe, Africa, North America, Indo-Pacific — this is like a diplomatic feast,” she said.

Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries — such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Fortier described it as an “extraordinary gathering.”

Carney has spent much of his time in office travelling to shore up multilateral relationships as he attempts to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

Canada’s ties with the Commonwealth, especially with smaller states, could help with that effort. Multilateral organizations like the United Nations give each member country one vote, regardless of size, Fortier noted.

“If you’re trying to move things through a multilateral organization, it is very, very important that you pay attention to smaller states,” she said.

“The Caribbean and Africa and some of the Pacific Island states can make or break your initiatives.”

Michael Manulak, an associate professor of international affairs at Carleton University, said Canada has used this strategy successfully in the past, when it was an influential multilateral player under Prime Minister Lester Pearson, and in the 1980s.

“One of the kind of core constituencies that Canada often operated on was the Commonwealth,” he said.

Canada had good relations with a large number of African and Caribbean countries, which meant Ottawa could call on those leaders to support Canada’s position on international issues, he added.

Ronald Sanders, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada, said there was a time in the past when “Canada put up a candidate for a post in the UN and it knew it had 14 votes behind it automatically.”

That relationship changed as various Canadian governments moved toward closer relations with the United States and Mexico and away from those relationships in the Caribbean.

“We would hope that we can rebuild that relationship now,” he said.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and most of its members have ties to the British Empire. Together, they represent a large chunk of the world’s population — 2.7 billion people.

“It’s a legacy of British imperialism but it’s now a consensual association,” said Manulak.

He said the Commonwealth gives Canada a platform to augment bilateral relations with “a whole set of countries that we might not have a whole lot to do with on an everyday basis. And I think that can be a really valuable thing.”

Manulak said trade and investment will be the top issue at the gathering. He said it’s something Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey has been pushing for since she stepped into the role in 2025.

“There’s going to be a lot of discussion about concrete ways of reducing barriers to trade,” he said.

Carney will spend just one day at the gathering, attending a lunch hosted by the King for new leaders in the Commonwealth and a formal dinner — also hosted by the King — as well as executive sessions and other meetings.

Carney is also expected to hold bilateral meetings, but officials declined to say in advance who he will meet with.

Sanders said Carney will meet with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Browne will propose a bilateral agreement with Canada that “could see joint ventures and activities that promote economic growth and create commercial opportunities for Canadian enterprises,” Sanders said.

Canadian government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation.

They noted Canada currently has $100 billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will join Carney at the meeting. She told The Canadian Press in an interview that Canada “supports practical Commonwealth initiatives that strengthen supply chains and improve market access, that advance trade diversification.”

She added the Commonwealth has “ambitious targets” to increase trade among Commonwealth countries to $2 trillion by 2030.

The officials said in the briefing there will be a focus at the meeting on resilience and mitigation related to climate change — a major priority for states witnessing the effects of rising oceans firsthand.

“Given that many of these smaller states are islands and are most affected by climate change, I think that will also be something that will come up,” Fortier said.

Sanders noted the Commonwealth was where early discussions about climate change began. He said the Commonwealth has acted collectively on big issues in the past, such as helping to end apartheid in South Africa.

King Charles is expected to address the legacy of slavery at the meeting in Antigua. Officials did not answer directly when asked whether Carney will participate in any of those discussions.

Manulak said while the British are very reluctant to accept blame for slavery and colonialism — and the potential financial implications of that — Caribbean countries “naturally feel differently about this issue. Being in the Caribbean, this is going to be a really live issue.”

Tamanisha John, assistant professor at York University’s department of politics, predicted Canada will choose to stay quiet and, if pressed, will support the position of the U.K. government. She noted that even if King Charles apologizes, the U.K. government opposes reparations.

Before the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Carney will host a working breakfast with Caribbean leaders.

Government officials said that will be an opportunity for Carney to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

“The Caribbean and Canada have long had a kind of a special relationship, partly through the shared British colonial heritage, but also through trade with the maritime provinces going down to the Caribbean islands,” Fortier said.

John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.

“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries — and with King Charles III.

Much of the meetings taking place this week will focus on trade and investment. But the gathering also offers a chance for Carney to meet with representatives from a wide variety of countries he might not otherwise visit, said retired Canadian diplomat Patricia Fortier.
“Fifty-six countries, Caribbean, Europe, Africa, North America, Indo-Pacific — this is like a diplomatic feast,” she said.

Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries — such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.
Fortier described it as an “extraordinary gathering.”
Carney has spent much of his time in office travelling to shore up multilateral relationships as he attempts to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

Canada’s ties with the Commonwealth, especially with smaller states, could help with that effort. Multilateral organizations like the United Nations give each member country one vote, regardless of size, Fortier noted.
“If you’re trying to move things through a multilateral organization, it is very, very important that you pay attention to smaller states,” she said.
“The Caribbean and Africa and some of the Pacific Island states can make or break your initiatives.”

Michael Manulak, an associate professor of international affairs at Carleton University, said Canada has used this strategy successfully in the past, when it was an influential multilateral player under Prime Minister Lester Pearson, and in the 1980s.
“One of the kind of core constituencies that Canada often operated on was the Commonwealth,” he said.
Canada had good relations with a large number of African and Caribbean countries, which meant Ottawa could call on those leaders to support Canada’s position on international issues, he added.
Ronald Sanders, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada, said there was a time in the past when “Canada put up a candidate for a post in the UN and it knew it had 14 votes behind it automatically.”
That relationship changed as various Canadian governments moved toward closer relations with the United States and Mexico and away from those relationships in the Caribbean.
“We would hope that we can rebuild that relationship now,” he said.
The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and most of its members have ties to the British Empire. Together, they represent a large chunk of the world’s population — 2.7 billion people.
“It’s a legacy of British imperialism but it’s now a consensual association,” said Manulak.

He said the Commonwealth gives Canada a platform to augment bilateral relations with “a whole set of countries that we might not have a whole lot to do with on an everyday basis. And I think that can be a really valuable thing.”

Manulak said trade and investment will be the top issue at the gathering. He said it’s something Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey has been pushing for since she stepped into the role in 2025.
“There’s going to be a lot of discussion about concrete ways of reducing barriers to trade,” he said.

Carney will spend just one day at the gathering, attending a lunch hosted by the King for new leaders in the Commonwealth and a formal dinner — also hosted by the King — as well as executive sessions and other meetings.
Carney is also expected to hold bilateral meetings, but officials declined to say in advance who he will meet with.
Sanders said Carney will meet with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Browne will propose a bilateral agreement with Canada that “could see joint ventures and activities that promote economic growth and create commercial opportunities for Canadian enterprises,” Sanders said.
Canadian government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation.
They noted Canada currently has $100 billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will join Carney at the meeting. She told The Canadian Press in an interview that Canada “supports practical Commonwealth initiatives that strengthen supply chains and improve market access, that advance trade diversification.”
She added the Commonwealth has “ambitious targets” to increase trade among Commonwealth countries to $2 trillion by 2030.

The officials said in the briefing there will be a focus at the meeting on resilience and mitigation related to climate change — a major priority for states witnessing the effects of rising oceans firsthand.
“Given that many of these smaller states are islands and are most affected by climate change, I think that will also be something that will come up,” Fortier said.

Sanders noted the Commonwealth was where early discussions about climate change began. He said the Commonwealth has acted collectively on big issues in the past, such as helping to end apartheid in South Africa.
King Charles is expected to address the legacy of slavery at the meeting in Antigua. Officials did not answer directly when asked whether Carney will participate in any of those discussions.

Manulak said while the British are very reluctant to accept blame for slavery and colonialism — and the potential financial implications of that — Caribbean countries “naturally feel differently about this issue. Being in the Caribbean, this is going to be a really live issue.”

Tamanisha John, assistant professor at York University’s department of politics, predicted Canada will choose to stay quiet and, if pressed, will support the position of the U.K. government. She noted that even if King Charles apologizes, the U.K. government opposes reparations.
Before the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Carney will host a working breakfast with Caribbean leaders.
Government officials said that will be an opportunity for Carney to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

“The Caribbean and Canada have long had a kind of a special relationship, partly through the shared British colonial heritage, but also through trade with the maritime provinces going down to the Caribbean islands,” Fortier said.
John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.
“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.

stories.title: Canadian woman caught in Syria on trial over alleged role in Isis
stories.summary: The case against Ammara Amjad is the first terrorism prosecution of a Canadian woman accused of living under Isis.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
As Isis fighters and their families were surrounded and making their last stand in Syria in late 2018, a Canadian woman who was allegedly there with them sent a defiant text to her mother.

“Allah has written that victory is near,” Ammara Amjad wrote, according to the RCMP, which found her messages on a phone seized during a search of her parents’ home north of Toronto.

Eight years later, the 32-year-old mother of two sat in a courtroom in Brampton, Ont., last week while a jury heard evidence of her alleged involvement in the Islamic State terror group.

The Canadian government brought Amjad back from a Syrian detention camp in 2023, along with her children, both born after she allegedly left home and made her way to Isis territory.

She now faces a charge of participating in the activities of a terrorist group. It is the first prosecution of a Canadian woman accused of living under Isis as it committed untold atrocities.

To violently to impose its bleak ideology, the jihadist group massacred and enslaved Iraq’s Yazidis , executed captives on video and facilitated attacks in Western countries, including Canada.

As a result, security agencies have warned that Isis members returning to Canada following the group’s defeat in Syria are likely to pose a threat, and could either commit attacks or radicalize others.

Two other women, B.C. resident Kimberly Polman and Montreal’s Oumaima Chouay , have pleaded guilty. Canada repatriated six more Isis women from Syrian camps, but they have not been charged.

Since Amjad’s trial began on Oct. 22, much of the evidence has consisted of messages she exchanged with her mother — so many that it took the RCMP a year to translate them from Urdu, Pakistan’s national language.

In some of the estimated 10,000 texts and audio files, Amjad repeatedly pleaded with her family in Milton, Ont. to send money, and spoke of her decision to leave Canada as a religious duty.

“This is in the cause of Allah,” she wrote in an April 2018 message, according to RCMP Const. Ragiv Chaudhary, who translated most of the messages.

“You deceived us all, left us in tears,” her mother countered.

“I did not deceive,” Amjad responded. “Everyone should have taken this step.”

The Canadian courts have convicted a growing number of men who fought with Isis or plotted attacks, most recently in Ontario and B.C. But Amjad’s case is a test of whether Canada can bring to justice the women who were also part of Isis.

The trial focused initially on the role of women in the Islamic State, with an expert testifying they were mainly housewives and mothers to the next generation of jihadist fighters.

Prof. Guido Steinberg said some foreign Isis women were also given weapons training, and an all-female fighting unit was later established, but added that those caught trying to flee were often punished.

The trial also turns on the reliability of “battlefield evidence,” also called Collected Exploitable Material, which is the information taken from documents and electronic devices found in Syria.

But the Crown’s case appears to hinge largely on Amjad’s own statements in the text messages and voice recordings she sent to her mother from Syria, while the defence is challenging the accuracy of RCMP translations.

Read aloud in court by the multilingual RCMP officer who translated most of them, they allegedly chronicle Amjad’s journey through the rise and fall of Isis.

They also show how Amjad’s exasperated mother tried again and again to appeal to her headstrong daughter to get out of Syria after her first child was born.

“You are not using your brain,” her mother wrote at one point, according to the messages read into the court record by the RCMP officer. “Parents come before anyone else.”

“Parents do not come before Allah,” Amjad replied.

Like many of the dozens of radicalized Canadians who flew to Turkey and crossed into Syria to live under Isis, Amjad had a privileged upbringing, the messages suggest.

“You were living in peace and joy, you had everything,” her mother wrote to her in August 2018.

“You guys don’t understand,” Amjad wrote. “This was very important work for me and all the Muslims. But not everyone will do it. Not everyone will support the right.”

“We are here for the law to apply.”

Amjad’s messages suggest she followed her first husband to Syria. In the texts, she named him as Bilal. The Canadian military has confirmed that a former reservist by that name joined Isis.

Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.

Despite his military training, he did not last long in Syria, dying within months of arriving in Isis-controlled territory. Amjad appears to have then married another Isis fighter named Hamza.

The court heard testimony that Hamza Parvez was a British-Pakistani Isis member who, according to the terror group’s own extensive paperwork, entered Isis territory from Turkey in 2014.

Calling himself Abu Hamza al-Britani, he posted anti-Western screeds on social media. His online posts about missing junk food made him fodder for the British tabloids, which dubbed him “Hungry Hamza.”

The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed Isis fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”

“I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an Isis fighter, he reportedly smiled.

In her messages to her mother, Amjad said Hamza liked cooking in the clay oven in their backyard. “He’s a wonderful husband, exactly the kind I wanted. Intelligent, funny and caring,” she wrote.

But he was apparently upset by talk of Amjad’s first husband. “You shouldn’t mention Bilal over and over again,” Amjad told her mother. “Hamza and I always listen to all the voice messages together, and he doesn’t like it.”

Many of Amjad’s messages to her mother were requests for money, which she framed in religious terms, suggesting that if her family didn’t pay now, they would pay in the afterlife.

“Please send me dollars,” she wrote in one message, explaining that she needed a new phone and wanted to get internet service installed in her home.

“You have savings, you have been spending money on shopping for a long time. Father has savings, where else will he spend it?” she wrote.

She said she deserved it because her parents didn’t have to pay for her wedding. But her mother responded that it was risky to send money and “everyone is worried about getting caught.”

“How long will this go on,” her mother wrote in a response to one of Amjad’s pleas for cash. “You have to keep asking for money again and again.”

“This is the last time.”

Amjad wanted her family to send the money through South Africa, and spoke about going to Pakistan. She rejected returning to Canada, writing that authorities would put her son into foster care with “white people.”

Her mother encouraged her to contact Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, whom she said was a “kind person” who might give her asylum. “Tell him what you have done wrong.”

But even as Isis was headed for certain defeat in late 2018, Amjad stuck to the far-fetched belief that victory was assured, writing that the challenges they were enduring were only a test from God and that only “hypocrites” fled.

She said they were surrounded but that God was protecting them and had created a sandstorm that had forced the U.S.-backed anti-Isis Kurdish forces to temporarily pause their offensive.

“Allah turned around everything,” she wrote.

In early 2019, U.S.-backed Syrian Kurdish fighters pinned the remnants of Isis against the Iraqi border, an offensive known as the Battle of Baghuz. Routed, the surviving Isis fighters and their families were captured.

Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for Isis women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.

“I have arrived in the camp now,” she wrote to her mother on March 28, 2019. “I’m in the Al Hol camp and Hamza is somewhere else.”

When the British tabloids found out Parvez had been imprisoned, the headline in the Mirror read, “Brit Isis fanatic Hungry Hamza who moaned about missing KFC captured in Syria.”

Amjad had spent more than four years in the crowded detention camps when a Global Affairs Canada delegation finally travelled to northeast Syria to secure her release.

She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense .

Released on bail, Amjad was ordered to obey a list of conditions that included house arrest at her parents’ home. She was also banned from contacting Hamza Parvez and five other Canadian Isis women.

Her trial resumes on Monday.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

content_blocks.text: The Canadian courts have convicted a growing number of men who fought with Isis or plotted attacks, most recently in Ontario and B.C. But Amjad’s case is a test of whether Canada can bring to justice the women who were also part of Isis.
content_blocks.html: The Canadian courts have convicted a growing number of men who fought with ISIS or plotted attacks, most recently in Ontario and B.C. But Amjad’s case is a test of whether Canada can bring to justice the women who were also part of ISIS.

content_blocks.text: The trial focused initially on the role of women in the Islamic State, with an expert testifying they were mainly housewives and mothers to the next generation of jihadist fighters.

Prof. Guido Steinberg said some foreign Isis women were also given weapons training, and an all-female fighting unit was later established, but added that those caught trying to flee were often punished.
The trial also turns on the reliability of “battlefield evidence,” also called Collected Exploitable Material, which is the information taken from documents and electronic devices found in Syria.
content_blocks.html: The trial also turns on the reliability of “battlefield evidence,” also called Collected Exploitable Material, which is the information taken from documents and electronic devices found in Syria.

content_blocks.text: But the Crown’s case appears to hinge largely on Amjad’s own statements in the text messages and voice recordings she sent to her mother from Syria, while the defence is challenging the accuracy of RCMP translations.
Read aloud in court by the multilingual RCMP officer who translated most of them, they allegedly chronicle Amjad’s journey through the rise and fall of Isis.
They also show how Amjad’s exasperated mother tried again and again to appeal to her headstrong daughter to get out of Syria after her first child was born.
“You are not using your brain,” her mother wrote at one point, according to the messages read into the court record by the RCMP officer. “Parents come before anyone else.”
“Parents do not come before Allah,” Amjad replied.
Married two Isis fighters

content_blocks.alt: Screenshot from ISIS propaganda video.
content_blocks.caption: Screenshot from ISIS propaganda video.

content_blocks.text: Like many of the dozens of radicalized Canadians who flew to Turkey and crossed into Syria to live under Isis, Amjad had a privileged upbringing, the messages suggest.
“You were living in peace and joy, you had everything,” her mother wrote to her in August 2018.
“You guys don’t understand,” Amjad wrote. “This was very important work for me and all the Muslims. But not everyone will do it. Not everyone will support the right.”
“We are here for the law to apply.”
Amjad’s messages suggest she followed her first husband to Syria. In the texts, she named him as Bilal. The Canadian military has confirmed that a former reservist by that name joined Isis.
Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.
content_blocks.html: Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.

content_blocks.text: Despite his military training, he did not last long in Syria, dying within months of arriving in Isis-controlled territory. Amjad appears to have then married another Isis fighter named Hamza.
The court heard testimony that Hamza Parvez was a British-Pakistani Isis member who, according to the terror group’s own extensive paperwork, entered Isis territory from Turkey in 2014.

Calling himself Abu Hamza al-Britani, he posted anti-Western screeds on social media. His online posts about missing junk food made him fodder for the British tabloids, which dubbed him “Hungry Hamza.”

The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed Isis fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”
content_blocks.html: The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed ISIS fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”

content_blocks.text: “I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an Isis fighter, he reportedly smiled.
content_blocks.html: “I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an ISIS fighter, he reportedly smiled.

content_blocks.text: In her messages to her mother, Amjad said Hamza liked cooking in the clay oven in their backyard. “He’s a wonderful husband, exactly the kind I wanted. Intelligent, funny and caring,” she wrote.

But he was apparently upset by talk of Amjad’s first husband. “You shouldn’t mention Bilal over and over again,” Amjad told her mother. “Hamza and I always listen to all the voice messages together, and he doesn’t like it.”
‘Send me dollars’

content_blocks.alt: British ISIS member Hamza Parvez, left, in Mosul, Iraq, 2014.
content_blocks.caption: British ISIS member Hamza Parvez, left, in Mosul, Iraq, 2014.

content_blocks.text: Many of Amjad’s messages to her mother were requests for money, which she framed in religious terms, suggesting that if her family didn’t pay now, they would pay in the afterlife.
“Please send me dollars,” she wrote in one message, explaining that she needed a new phone and wanted to get internet service installed in her home.
“You have savings, you have been spending money on shopping for a long time. Father has savings, where else will he spend it?” she wrote.
She said she deserved it because her parents didn’t have to pay for her wedding. But her mother responded that it was risky to send money and “everyone is worried about getting caught.”
“How long will this go on,” her mother wrote in a response to one of Amjad’s pleas for cash. “You have to keep asking for money again and again.”
“This is the last time.”

Amjad wanted her family to send the money through South Africa, and spoke about going to Pakistan. She rejected returning to Canada, writing that authorities would put her son into foster care with “white people.”
Her mother encouraged her to contact Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, whom she said was a “kind person” who might give her asylum. “Tell him what you have done wrong.”

But even as Isis was headed for certain defeat in late 2018, Amjad stuck to the far-fetched belief that victory was assured, writing that the challenges they were enduring were only a test from God and that only “hypocrites” fled.
She said they were surrounded but that God was protecting them and had created a sandstorm that had forced the U.S.-backed anti-Isis Kurdish forces to temporarily pause their offensive.
“Allah turned around everything,” she wrote.
'Everything is finished

content_blocks.text: In early 2019, U.S.-backed Syrian Kurdish fighters pinned the remnants of Isis against the Iraqi border, an offensive known as the Battle of Baghuz. Routed, the surviving Isis fighters and their families were captured.
Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for Isis women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.
content_blocks.html: Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for ISIS women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.

content_blocks.text: “I have arrived in the camp now,” she wrote to her mother on March 28, 2019. “I’m in the Al Hol camp and Hamza is somewhere else.”
When the British tabloids found out Parvez had been imprisoned, the headline in the Mirror read, “Brit Isis fanatic Hungry Hamza who moaned about missing KFC captured in Syria.”
Amjad had spent more than four years in the crowded detention camps when a Global Affairs Canada delegation finally travelled to northeast Syria to secure her release.
She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense .
content_blocks.html: She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense.

content_blocks.text: Released on bail, Amjad was ordered to obey a list of conditions that included house arrest at her parents’ home. She was also banned from contacting Hamza Parvez and five other Canadian Isis women.
Her trial resumes on Monday.

stories.title: Blackstone, Canadian pension funds invest $3.1-billion for minority interest in Mitsubishi’s LNG Canada stake
stories.summary: Acquired stake valued at $1.6-billion; total investment includes planned capital expenditures for phase 2 expansion project
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Blackstone Inc. BX-N and four major Canadian pension funds are paying US$1.6-billion to buy a minority stake in a Mitsubishi Corp. subsidiary that owns a share of LNG Canada’s liquefaction business, and investing a further US$1.5-billion to help fund expansion plans as part of the deal.

Mitsubishi owns a 15-per-cent stake in LNG Canada through a subsidiary and will stay the controlling partner of that entity. The investor group is acquiring a 49.9-per-cent interest in the Mitsubishi subsidiary, and committing to $3.1-billion in total investment.

Blackstone is leading the investor group that includes Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, Investment Management Corp. of Ontario and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

LNG Canada operates the country’s first natural-gas export terminal, an $18-billion facility in Kitimat, B.C., that opened in June, 2025. Under the deal announced Monday, Mitsubishi will continue its agreement to offtake 2.1 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas annually from LNG Canada.

Earlier this year, both Mitsubishi and LNG Canada’s largest shareholder, Shell PLC, considered reducing their stakes to raise funds for expansion plans.

Mitsubishi hired Royal Bank of Canada’s capital markets arm to pursue a deal and both shareholders were reportedly fielding bids as early as this summer from U.S.-based asset managers such as Blackstone and Apollo Global Management Inc.

However, Shell is no longer pursuing a similar transaction, at least in the near term, three sources with knowledge of the process said.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources because they are not authorized to discuss confidential discussions.

Shell declined to comment.

The transaction marks the first investment by Canadian funds in LNG Canada. In addition to Mitsubishi’s 15-per-cent interest, Shell owns a 40-per-cent stake, Malaysia’s state-owned Petronas has 25 per cent, PetroChina owns 15 per cent and the Korea Gas Corp. (Kogas) holds 5 per cent.

It is also a sign of heightened interest among Canada’s largest pension funds and global investors such as Blackstone to invest in Canadian infrastructure and energy projects.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a target to attract $500-billion in new private-sector investment over five years, and some of the largest Canadian pension plans have made multibillion-dollar commitments to boost their domestic investments over the next few years .

“We see this as a compelling opportunity to invest at scale here in Canada,” Geoff Souter, Cppib’s head of real assets credit, said in a statement.

At the Canada Investment Summit, held in Toronto in mid-September, Blackstone president and chief operating officer Jon Gray called Canada “a bit of a sleeping giant, economically.”

An expansion plan to build a second phase of the LNG Canada terminal, confirmed in late September, would double the terminal’s annual output to 28 million tonnes from 14 million, making it one of the largest LNG facilities in the world.

The second phase was one of the first five projects referred to Canada’s Major Projects Office as a national priority.

LNG Canada’s shareholders announced a final investment decision on the expansion plan in September, reaching a key milestone that gave investors greater confidence in the project’s viability. Institutional investors have shown interest in LNG Canada because it is a large asset that can ship low-cost gas to Asia, where demand is increasing, and is capable of producing stable, long-term cash flows that produce steady returns.

The stake in Mitsubishi’s subsidiary that Blackstone and the pension funds are acquiring is valued at US$1.6-billion. The total $3.1-billion investment includes the new investors’ proportional share of planned capital expenditures for the phase 2 expansion project.

Though the Blackstone-led group is buying an equity stake in Mitsubishi’s subsidiary, the deal is being financed by the participating investors’ credit divisions.

It is an example of a type of transaction that has been gaining in popularity, often called “capital solutions” or “corporate solutions.” Using a mix of equity and debt, it provides provide large corporations a way to unlock cash from assets they own, and offers investors relatively predictable returns.

Blackstone has led similarly structured investments in Canada such as a $7-billion deal to acquire a portion of Rogers Communications Inc.’s wireless infrastructure, and a $2.5-billion investment in the Aeroplan loyalty program.

“This announcement builds on our deep conviction in Canada, our partnership with the country’s leading institutional investors and our ability to provide large corporates with flexible solutions to unlock value from their most critical assets,” said Zachary Rubenstein, managing director for Blackstone Credit & Insurance, in a statement.

Blackstone manages US$1.3-trillion, while Cppib, PSP, Omers and Imco collectively manage a total of more than $1.4-trillion in pension assets for Canadian workers and retirees.

Two climate-focused advocacy groups – Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, as well as Stand.Earth – released statements on Monday opposing the Canadian pension funds’ decision to invest in LNG Canada with Blackstone, citing risks to the environment and to pension savings.

“We are digging ourselves deeper into an incredibly risky project,” Shift Action director Adam Scott said in a statement.

LNG Canada will remain a strategic priority for Mitsubishi, which sells gas from the project into Asia, mostly in Japan, and allows it to secure a reliable supply of a key energy source. Disruptions to global energy flows from the United States war in Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine have prompted governments and companies around the world to look to diversify their access to energy.

RBC advised Mitsubishi on the transaction, while Goldman Sachs and Scotiabank advised Blackstone. Kirkland & Ellis and Stikeman Elliott served as legal counsel to Blackstone.

With a report from Andrew Willis

stories.title: Parents cheer, businesses brace as Western Canada ditches the time change
stories.summary: Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round
stories.author: Ashley Joannou and Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

“(Children) show up a little bit irritable, as we all do when we’re tired,” she said. “Nap times get thrown out of whack.”

She’s hopeful things will be a little bit easier this year.

Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round rather than have clocks fall back one hour.

Saskatchewan already doesn’t adjust its clocks.

At a recreation centre in Edmonton’s south end on Sunday, some parents said not having to adjust their children’s sleep schedule felt refreshing.

“I’m going to be honest, I do kind of like it,” said Amanda Petrie after her seven-year-old son’s hockey game. “It’s just easier with kids when you don’t have to adjust their schedule.”

Siva Sivabalan, another resident, said he felt the Alberta government had made the right call by not changing the time.

“I rather have more daylight in the evening time rather than the morning,” he said as his daughter played nearby.

“Especially the November time change, I just didn’t like it at all.”

In Calgary, hairstylist Jordan Janovcik said he feels anxious about the work week ahead.

He said he spent the entire summer double- and sometimes triple-checking with clients to make sure they knew Alberta was not falling back.

Hairstylists like him have busy but by-the-book schedules, and missed appointments or delays could mean lost time and money.

“I am really concerned for this week,” he said in a phone interview.

“I think this is going to be really hard for a lot of businesses.”

Technology experts have said the change could cause problems for scheduling systems and older computer software.

Online, some Canadians reported Sunday that their cellphones displayed the incorrect time.

A statement from Telus says the issue is related to how some phones update their time zone information, rather than the service provider.

“Customers experiencing this issue can check their phone’s settings to ensure that ‘set time zone automatically’ is selected, then restart their phone to help apply any available time zone updates,” the company says.

A Rogers spokesperson said the company experienced no issues with its network, and referred questions to an industry group that posted instructions for updating phones and tablets.

In the skies, Air Canada said Sunday its operations were normal, noting that all flights use the internationally recognized time standard and that time changes are managed using established industry data sources.

Tech giant Google responded to an inquiry about how new time zones are affecting its services by linking to a blog post with instructions on how to make sure devices and services stay on schedule.

“From morning alarms to critical calendar invites, we know how much you rely on your devices to stay organized and on time,” the post said.

“Our teams are working to ensure these updates reach all Canadian users as quickly as possible.”

Back in Edmonton, Irwin-Greer said she’s curious how no time change might affect life on the Prairies.

She noted darker mornings in the months ahead and whether they would affect commutes for students and workers.

“I don’t love that it’s going to be darker for longer when the kids are going to school,” she said. “My teenage son is not overly worried about it, but it is a little bit concerning when they’re trying to travel.

“Crossing the street and it’s hard enough for traffic to see, so hopefully there are not more accidents.”

stories.title: Thousands of Osap applications came from a single IP address, ministry alleges
stories.summary: In completing its final decision to deny the schools Osap eligibility this year, the ministry appears to have taken a closer look at IP address activity.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
At two career colleges now under the Ontario government’s microscope, more than half of the thousands of student financial aid applications last year came from a single IP address, officials allege in documents filed in court.

The government has also received more than 200 tips about that network of schools, including allegations that certain recruiters were submitting students’ Ontario Student Assistance Program applications at those schools, which is not allowed, and completing their coursework, those same documents show.

The Academy of Learning did not provide comment on the new court filings in response to a request from The Canadian Press, but has previously denied allegations of wrongdoing. They say the schools have implemented a long list of corrective actions, including cutting ties with some recruiters and bolstering admissions practices. The ministry’s allegations have not been proven in court.

The newly filed allegations against the schools come as Premier Doug Ford’s government is under increasing fire for its handling of Osap. Critics say alleged misuse of the system was allowed to fester under lax oversight, then when it was brought to light Ford left innocent students paying the price.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn says his government acted on tips and conducted in-depth inspections that ultimately led to barring the schools from Osap eligibility and launching a broader probe.

Quinn earlier this year drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs.

Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges. Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year.

The Academy of Learning operates as franchises but the three schools barred from Osap share a parent company, Opulence Education Group. Its campuses in Toronto on Bay Street and in North York, and one in Brampton East, accounted for one-fifth of that spending.

The three schools were among six that in May the province made ineligible for Osap, citing an “inability to reliably determine bona fide studies,” a decision the schools are challenging in court. As part of that case, the province issued a final decision in August and added that to the court record this month.

“The ministry is not satisfied that the institutions have adequate processes in place to ensure that its records and processes can be relied on for the proper administration and disbursement of Osap funding to eligible students,” the decision says.

Ministry officials who last year inspected the campuses at issue looked at a sampling of student accounts and found evidence of shared IP address activity across students referred by the same recruiter, the government alleges.

In completing its final decision to deny the schools Osap eligibility this year, the ministry appears to have taken a closer look at IP address activity.

There were 6,001 Osap applications from students at the Brampton East campus for the 2025-26 year and 3,136 of them — 52 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. There were five more IP addresses responsible for 100 or more applications, they allege.

At the North York campus, 3,460 out of 6,070 Osap applications for that year — 57 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Two other IP addresses were responsible for another 255 applications, they allege.

The Bay campus saw 6,966 Osap applications that year, with 1,736 — 25 per cent — coming from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Five other IP addresses submitted 100 or more applications, they allege.

The Academy of Learning argued in an earlier letter to the ministry that shared IP addresses May be due to multiple people living at the same address, but the ministry is calling that into question.

“While patterns of shared IP addresses among students attending the same physical school campus space accessing their student accounts May be expected, patterns of shared IP address activity among the institution’s asynchronous learners referred to the institution by the same recruiter is significant and renders the institution’s proposed explanation unlikely in this case,” the ministry wrote in the court filing.

In its letter to the province to rebut any nefarious assumptions about students’ logins, the Academy of Learning also wrote, “the presence of the same IP address among different users does not, by itself, establish misconduct, misrepresentation, or unauthorized activity.”

Quinn has tasked Kpmg with an audit of Osap payments to career colleges and earlier this month referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, while pausing such payments to all private post-secondary institutions. It is not known if the referral contains specific allegations relating to the Academy of Learning.

It comes after warnings from Career Colleges Ontario, the federal government, and hundreds of tips and complaints about possible misuse of the Osap system.

The new ministry court filings reveal that since Jan. 1, 2024 it has received more than 220 tips, complaints, referrals and investigations relating to the three Academy of Learning campuses, with the volume and consistency of the concerns “significant,” the government alleges.

“The ministry received related third-party complaints and tips alleging that certain recruiters were acting on behalf of students, including in submitting Osap applications, in uploading supporting documentation on students’ Osap accounts, and in completing coursework on behalf of students, and that recruiters were using Osap funding as a recruitment or marketing tool,” the ministry wrote.

The schools have since cut off ties with some recruiters, they have said.

Academy of Learning did not directly respond to a request for comment by The Canadian Press on the allegation that recruiters were completing students’ coursework, but has noted in a corrective action plan last year that it added enhanced IP tracking to identify possible third-party access and added two-factor authentication “to safeguard against third-party completion of assignments.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said given all the information that is now public about what the government knew or should have known about the skyrocketing Osap usage at some career colleges, it is shocking they did not act with more urgency.

“I think the more details that we learn through these court proceedings, the clearer it is that the minister was completely incompetent at doing his job,” she said. “It is stunning that these five-alarm fires were being ignored by the government.”

Liberal critic Tyler Watt also said the new revelations reflect poorly on Quinn.

“Minister Nolan Quinn keeps insisting he’s taken this scandal seriously, but every new revelation raises more questions about what his ministry knew, when they knew it, and why they failed to act,” he wrote in a statement.

Quinn’s office said when serious concerns are identified, they do not hesitate to cut an institution off from Osap entirely, as was done with the Academy of Learning locations in this court case.

“Any misuse of Osap is unacceptable,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement. “We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system.”

Quinn has indicated he will introduce further legislation this fall to enhance accountability in the system.

This semi-detached house near Chorley Park was listed for $2,649,000 in September, hoping to round up buyers before the seasonal slowdown at end of the year. Agent Nigel Denham said getting about half a dozen visitors over a few weeks was a good sign. Securing an offer from one guest, and negotiating it to $2.5-million, was a relief.

“Gone are the days of selling in ten days or less,” said Mr. Denham. “Everything takes three or four weeks, assuming it’s priced right.

“The market is so unpredictable, but we figured it would be well received based on the merits of the property.”

The nearly 50-year-old house has numerous assets, including a private driveway with space for three cars and a garage accessed through the finished basement.

“There were a few other houses for sale, in and around that price point, but they were either lacking parking, kissing the railroad tracks, or needed complete gut jobs,” Mr. Denham said.

“This home was well removed from the tracks, and it had best-in-class parking - better than you can find at most properties two or three times the price. And it’s a fairly turnkey proposition; a totally move-in ready house from top to bottom.”

This two-storey house has 1,816 square feet of living space, including three bedrooms, four bathrooms and an eat-in kitchen.

The dining room is next to a living room with a fireplace and has direct access to the patio on the 23-by 130-foot lot.

“It’s at the northern end of Rosedale, and that comes with conveniences,” Mr. Denham said.

“It’s down the street from Chorley Park, which is popular. Also, down the street, you have the Summerhill strip and market, which is a huge draw for the area.”

stories.title: Brookfield Asset Management, Cppib close purchase of LXP Industrial Trust
stories.summary: Deal valued LXP at about $5.2-billion
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Brookfield Asset Management BAM-T and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board say they have closed their purchase of LXP Industrial Trust.

Lxp’s portfolio includes 107 industrial properties in the United States.

Sophie van Oosterom, head of real estate at CPP Investments, says the deal adds a portfolio of modern logistics properties to the fund’s diversified portfolio of U.S. real estate investments.

The assets will be integrated into Brookfield’s global logistics platform, which includes over 850 properties in 20 countries.

The deal valued LXP at about US$5.2-billion , including net debt and preferred equity.

Under the terms of the agreement, LXP shareholders received US$61.20 per share in cash.

stories.title: Why repealing the Indian Act isn’t so simple
stories.summary: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called for the Indian Act to be abolished, which was met with echoes from Prime Minister Mark Carney who agreed that it should be scrapped.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called for the Indian Act to be abolished, which was met with echoes from Prime Minister Mark Carney who agreed that it should be scrapped.

The act was passed in 1876 with aims of assimilating Indigenous populations into Eurocentric ways of living through legislation that governs where they live, where their kids go to school, and who they are. Host Maria Kestane speaks to John Borrows, the Loveland Chair in Indigenous Law at the University of Toronto’s faculty of law. They discuss the different approaches that could help repeal and replace the act, and why other Indigenous leaders believe Ottawa should keep it right where it is.

John Borrows is a leading voice in Indigenous governance across Canada. Read his latest book here: The Seven Cycles of Life by John Borrows | Penguin Random House Canada

stories.title: Trump covets the Keystone XL pipeline because its path runs through key U.S. midterm election races
stories.summary: Donald Trump touted a resurrected pipeline and a “concept” of a trade deal with Canada as Republicans brace for potential losses in key states.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
It’s no great surprise that Donald Trump is talking now about the “concept” of a trade deal with Canada and the rebirth of the cross-border Keystone XL pipeline.

Even though Prime Minister Mark Carney has confirmed he had a ” good conversation ” with his American counterpart, it’s no indication that we’re any closer to an agreement over tariffs, automobile production and dueling liquor bans. Nor does it signal an imminent increase in the southbound flow of Alberta oil.

It’s more a reminder that we are just hours away from the all-important midterm elections in the United States.

In Tuesday’s vote, Trump’s Republican party is in grave danger of losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. If the Democrats win control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, the next two years of Trump’s presidency promise to be even more chaotic than the first two have been.

Those are the electoral stakes, but to understand the political logic in Trump’s bullish comments on a trade deal with Canada, you need to overlay the proposed route of the Keystone XL pipeline and the American electoral map.

Barring a late Republican surge before Tuesday’s elections, America could finally be turning a page on a decade-long Trump epoch in American

Do this, and you’ll see that the oil pipeline that Carney has promoted — and that Trump clearly covets — runs right through key election races in Montana, Nebraska, Kansas and Texas.

On Sunday, just ahead of a stop in Kansas for a midterm rally, Trump confirmed he had spoken to Carney about “the concept of a very good deal with Canada” — one that he said would resurrect a Keystone XL project.

The pipeline proposal has a long and turbulent history. It was launched in 2008 by TransCanada, shut down by president Barack Obama in 2015, resurrected by Trump in 2019 and shut down once again by president Joe Biden in 2021.

“They’re going to pay for all of it. We’re going to give them the route that’s largely been determined, but they’ll build the Keystone pipeline,” he told reporters.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, a former governor of North Dakota, added that the pipeline was politically popular in states throughout the American Midwest.

“Canada exports over four million barrels of oil to the United States and that’s a great thing for American farmers, ranchers, for diesel prices,” he said. “Nobody’s done more for ranchers and farmers in this country than President Trump.”

The northern segment of the proposed pipeline runs from the Alberta town of Hardisty and into Montana, where the Republican candidate for the Senate, Kurt Alme, is leading in polls over Independent candidate Seth Bodnar and Democrat Alani Bankhead.

From there, the Keystone pipeline runs south to Steele City, Nebraska, where another Independent candidate, Dan Osborn, is trying to unseat the incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.

When he stopped at Sunday’s election rally in Kansas, Trump said the trade dispute with Canada would be “settled pretty soon” and would include the removal of tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports.

The Kansas Senate race pits Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Christian megachurch pastor and author, against the incumbent Republican, Roger Marshall.

Marshall has been a strong proponent of the Keystone XL project and argued that its cancellation would increase fuel prices, cost jobs and make the U.S. reliant “on foreign oil.”

Numerous polls and election trackers have classified the race as a “toss up” or handed a small statistical lead to Hamilton, who has campaigned on the need to reduce energy costs and eliminate “self-destructive tariffs.”

Trump urged Kansas voters on Sunday to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

“Every time I was on the ballot, we won everything,” he said. “(In) the midterms, when I’m not on the ballot, we don’t do so well.”

The Keystone XL pipeline’s ultimate destination is Texas refineries located on the Gulf Coast.

Canada makes the perfect suspect. For two years, Americans have heard that Canada is “ripping us off.” Ripping off an election is a short step. In

There, one of the most heated Senate battles is being waged between Democrat James Talarico, a teacher and four-term state senator, and Republican Ken Paxton, Texas’s attorney general.

Paxton led a lawsuit against the Biden administration in 2021 over its rejection of the Keystone XL pipeline, arguing that the power to approve or reject the energy project lay with the U.S. Congress, not the White House. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit a year later.

As a Texas senator, Talarico pledged in 2022 not to accept campaign donations from organizations and individuals promoting fossil fuel use.

He is now running on what he calls an “ all of the above strategy ” that proposes protecting the existing oil-and-gas industry in Texas while pushing for a transition to renewable and low-emission energy sources.

In Tuesday’s election, polls have predicted a narrow lead for Talarico.

Trump attended two Texas midterm rallies last week — one at the port of Corpus Christi where he referred to Talarico as a “communist,” nicknamed him “Talafreako” and falsely accused him of being a vegan.

“He doesn’t want meat, oil or guns,” Trump said.

And he also drew the attention of the crowd to a ship in the water that he said was carrying one million barrels of crude oil that had been sent from Venezuela — a sign if ever there was of the importance and value that Trump attaches to energy in the midterm vote.

But there was one small-yet-noteworthy change to Trump’s usual script — a change that would resonate with beleaguered Canadian ears.

Speaking of Venezuela, Trump said the U.S. was securing “a lot of oil for ourselves” and the country was on the road to becoming “prosperous.”

“Maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state,” he mused. “Let’s make it the 51st state. And instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor. How about that?”

The response from the crowd? It was tepid, at best.

stories.title: New U.S. rules on flight delays May affect Canadian travellers. Here’s how
stories.summary: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
stories.author: Christl Dabu
stories.content:
New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), which published the new rules on the Federal Register daily journal in September, is reclassifying 10 types of events that cause flight delays and cancellations as outside the airline’s control. These events include a passenger’s death, unscheduled mechanical issues, severe weather, cybersecurity attacks and potential tech outages.

The rule was supposed to take effect Oct. 19 but was postponed until Feb. 1, 2027.

The department acknowledged in the notice that “the total value of amenities and compensation currently provided by air carriers to consumers will be reduced under this final rule.”

Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said the new rules May mean travellers won’t be entitled to the same type of protections they used to have.

“So basically, it’s taking some of what was the responsibility of the airlines and recategorizing them … outside of the airline’s control,” Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said in a video interview with CTVNews.CA on Friday. “And very simply, for travellers, that means you May not be entitled to the same type of protections that you are now.”

“Now, when this new rule goes into effect, you as a passenger, if you are impacted due to an unscheduled maintenance event, this is outside of the airline’s control, meaning that they’re not now forced, or really obliged, to provide a hotel voucher or a meal voucher,” she added.

Airline passenger advocacy group FlyersRights is suing the U.S. Department of Transportation over the rules, which they say shift the costs from airline delays to passengers.

“A change in reporting classifications is not permission to reduce passenger rights,” Paul Hudson, president of FlyersRights, said in a news release Friday. “... The rule sneakily transfers costs from airlines back to passengers for delays involving mechanical problems that are the responsibility and fault of the airlines.”

Nastro, a correspondent with the Flighty flight-tracker app, said the change will affect anyone “travelling within the U.S., to the U.S., or from the U.S.,” regardless of their nationality or the airline, if their flight experiences certain types of disruptions that are now outside the airline’s control.

“In certain circumstances, it does grey the disruption category for consumers,” Nastro said. “This new regulation … just makes it even more confusing for travellers when they’re trying to navigate what exactly they’re entitled to in terms of disruption protections.”

Under the current DOT regulations, Nastro said disrupted flights May allow travellers to get hotel or meal vouchers, rebook flights or get refunds.

Gábor Lukács, president of Air Passenger Rights, said he believes the new rules May have a “minimal” impact on Canadian travellers flying to or from the U.S. because they would have some rights under the Canadian Air Passenger Protection Regulations .

However, he said Canada’s passenger protection regulations are “weak” with rules that are “unnecessarily complex” and “very difficult to enforce.”

He said the U.S. rule change’s effect is “primarily administrative,” because it involves how flight disruptions are being reported and passengers aren’t compensated in cash for flight disruptions in the U.S.

Lukács said the main issue with the new rules will be unexpected maintenance issues, which he said is “completely unreasonable.”

stories.title: Can gene editing stop ALS? Toronto’s Specific Biologics advances therapy that could help some with fatal disease
stories.summary: Western University spinout raises $35-million after generating promising pre-clinical results
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
David Edgell’s childhood love of science fiction and Lego inspired him to pursue cutting-edge science when he grew up. Starting in the 2000s, the Western University biochemistry professor developed a gene-editing technique that could treat people with devastating hereditary diseases.

Now a Toronto company putting his technology to work is emerging as a budding star of Canada’s biotechnology sector.

Specific Biologics Inc. is seeking to treat people with dozens of neurological and neuromuscular diseases known as repeat expansion disorders, which are caused by a similar genetic defect. Its first target is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the fatal condition known as Lou Gehrig’s disease.

If the treatment works in humans, as it has in petri dishes and mice, Specific believes it could stop the progression of ALS in the one in 10 patients whose condition is caused by the defect. (About 1,000 people are diagnosed with ALS in Canada annually.) The ultimate goal is to treat people with the disorder early enough “so they never become symptomatic,” said Specific chief executive officer Brent Stead, who studied in the same lab as Dr. Edgell at Western and later convinced him to let the company commercialize his technology.

If successful, the technology, called Dualase, could be applied to other repeat conditions, such as a variant of Huntington’s disease, and more broadly to genetic diseases including cystic fibrosis, Mr. Stead said.

Specific has pulled in a who’s who from Canada’s biotech sector to help. Its board includes industry heavyweights Paul Hastings, former CEO of B.C. biotech pioneer QLT Inc., and serial entrepreneur Richard Glickman. It has recruited U.S.-based Canadian gene-editing veterans Brad Geddes and Paul Alloway to its senior management team. “This technology could revolutionize the way people are treated with these disorders,” said Mr. Hastings. “The reward, if it works here, will be spectacular.”

On Monday, Specific will announce it has closed a US$35-million venture capital round led by North Carolina-based Hatteras Venture Partners. But Canadians still own a vast majority of the company, including early backers Lumira Ventures and adMare BioInnovations, plus Genesys Capital, BDC Life Sciences Venture Fund and Seido Capital. That degree of Canadian ownership is rare at this stage for a promising domestic biotech company, said Lumira partner Nikhil Thatte.

Dr. Edgell grew up in Victoria, obsessed with Star Trek and the novels of science-fiction writers William Gibson and Philip K. Dick. He decided to study ancient history before changing his mind and enrolling in a kinesiology program at the University of Victoria. It wasn’t scientific enough for him, so he switched to molecular biology. That brought him closer to the scientific vanguard that had long intrigued him.

As his academic career progressed, he studied so-called “junk DNA,” parts of deoxyribonucleic acid – the hereditary, twisted ladder-shaped biological blueprints inside the cells of life forms – that appeared to serve no purpose. He eventually focused on gene editing after arriving at Western in London, Ont., in 2003. (Genes are sequences of subunits within DNA that instruct cells to make proteins.)

The field of genetic editing, in which scientists change targeted genetic material within DNA, dates back decades. Scientists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier transformed the space in 2012 by demonstrating a new process called Crispr/Cas9, later winning the Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Crispr is a molecular, scissors-like tool that destroys a single mutated gene on strands of DNA, then instructs the body’s cells to fix it. It was simpler, faster and cheaper than prior technologies and led to some clinical successes, including sickle-cell anemia treatment Casgevy. Health Canada in 2024 approved the sale of the gene therapy, which was developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals Inc. and Crispr Therapeutics AG.

But Crispr technology has its limits. Many treatments can have “off-target” effects, destroying the wrong part of the DNA, causing serious consequences. That has irked investors. “Gene editing is virtually unfundable in the U.S.,” Lumira’s Mr. Thatte said. But “Specific has delivered every time” on its scientific milestones, he added.

Unlike other gene editors, Specific goes after problems that can’t be fixed by a single gene cut. DNA contains sections of repeated sequences which serve genetic functions. But in people with repeat expansion disorders, those sequences repeat and repeat out of control. That creates increasingly long strands within DNA, which cause toxic effects. Fixing the problem requires not one edit, but two.

Its solution is to deploy the molecular equivalent of two pairs of scissors coded into a protein. Specific packages the technology into the shell of a non-toxic virus that will be injected into the spine, travel to the brain and target neuron cells where the problem lies.

The treatment is programmed to latch onto the specific point in the DNA where the trouble starts, as well as the other end of the out-of-control repeated sequence. It slices both ends, removes the problematic section, then fuses together the cut ends of the DNA – “like molecular Lego,” Dr. Edgell said. That leaves healthy DNA with normal repeat sequences.

The solution will require a single injection and has had no off-target effects, Specific has confirmed in preclinical studies of human cell samples and mice. It hopes to launch its first human studies in ALS patients in 2028. “There’s a straightforward, cost-effective path to demonstrating feasibility of whether or not this platform can work,” said Hatteras partner Ben Scruggs. Specific is also in talks with a pharmaceutical giant on a development partnership deal, Mr. Stead said.

For the 56-year-old Dr. Edgell, Specific’s progress and fundraising success offer some satisfaction as his family struggles with its own health struggles. He has a child with an autoimmune condition called Anca vasculitis where the body attacks its own blood vessels. While there are treatments, they haven’t worked on his child, who was recently hospitalized with related complications.

Dr. Edgell, a scientific adviser to Specific, admits that if his child had a monogenic disorder – a condition caused by a mutation in a single gene – he’d be pushing for the company to look into the condition. “But cell gene therapy isn’t going to work here, at least not now,” he said.

stories.title: Law society fails to police members amid rampant real estate fraud allegations
stories.summary: As with many industries, self-regulation and voluntary codes of conduct just don’t do enough
stories.author: John Turley-Ewart
stories.content:
John Turley-Ewart is a contributing columnist for The Globe and Mail, a regulatory compliance consultant and a Canadian banking historian.

“I shall neglect no one’s interest and shall faithfully serve and diligently represent the best interests of my client,” so goes the Barrister and Solicitor Oath in Ontario. Every lawyer recites it when called to the Ontario bar.

Yet the pledge falls flat given the Law Society of Ontario’s response to requests from Ontario Superior Court Justice Sean Dunphy to protect the public interest. The Globe and Mail reported last week that Justice Dunphy believes he is “shouting into the wind” when asking the LSO to swiftly investigate accusations of fraud against a handful of real estate lawyers in the Greater Toronto Area.

In an Oct. 19 decision , he pointed to the “extraordinary circumstances” of the allegations that have been “occurring with distressing regularity in the recent past” and that “a decisive reaction is called for and without delay.”

He is asking too much of the LSO. With distressing regularity, industry self-regulation and voluntary codes of conduct fail to meet public expectations.

The sums involved are large. In one case, a lawyer is accused of fraud exceeding $17-million and having failed to pay $200-million in loans. In another, more than $18-million was advanced by clients to a lawyer to discharge multiple mortgages – “Not one in fact was discharged,” wrote Justice Dunphy.

These cases represent, in Justice Dunphy’s words , “an exceptionally grave attack on the profession of law at large and the integrity of our civil legal system.”

The LSO is charged with regulating the legal professions in the public interest by Ontario’s government under the Law Society Act. Through this legislation, it investigates allegations of misconduct by legal professionals and metes out professional punishment when misconduct is proven.

The theory sounds good, but the practical reality is found wanting. Governments too often hand off regulatory responsibilities to politically influential industry groups that later suffer the fallout from regulatory failures while the public bears the cost.

Consider the case of the Real Estate Council of British Columbia. It was charged with supervising real estate trading practices, ethics and licensing in 2005 and was run by licensed real estate agents.

A decade later, it was accused , among other issues, of failing to prevent real estate agents from colluding with foreign buyers in a tax avoidance scheme that had foreign buyers use the B.C. addresses of real estate agents to appear domiciled in the province.

B.C.’s provincial government stripped the organization of its regulatory authority in 2016 and appointed a Superintendent of Real Estate that in 2021 was integrated into the B.C. Financial Services Authority.

In 2014 and again in 2018, Visa and Mastercard, subjected to loud calls for lower merchant payment fees from small and medium-sized businesses, agreed to a voluntary pricing code that would cap merchant charges for SMEs. The federal government relied on an honour system for compliance from the card companies.

By 2023, Ottawa had little choice but to give up voluntary codes in the wake of continued complaints from small business and impose hard caps on merchant fees charged to SMEs using negotiated agreements.

Recall too the sad saga of Ontario’s Tarion Warranty Corporation, a self-regulatory organization for new-home builders. It was dominated by developers who used Tarion to protect shoddy builders from public scrutiny and made warranty claims an arduous process to limit payouts.

Typical self-regulatory bodies are reactive supervisors that investigate complaints rather than proactively seeking to prevent them through continuing oversight, spot audits and inspection processes.

Importantly, such organizations are conflicted between serving the public interest and serving the interest of their members. Those that propose voluntary conduct codes suffer similar dilemmas.

Solving the problem of better regulation and oversight for the legal profession doesn’t require breaking new ground. Independent statutory authorities are used in England and Wales as well as some Australian states to better protect the public and keep lawyers honest.

In England and Wales, the Legal Services Board operates as the independent body appointed by the government. It is required to have a majority of lay board members and oversees front-line regulators that conduct proactive supervision.

If nothing else, the LSB offers a system better able to respond quickly to reports of misconduct and assure the public that its interests take priority.

As officers of the court, lawyers are rightly held to a higher standard in society. That does not mean they should be afforded a lesser standard of oversight. The Lso’s conduct, as Justice Dunphy has witnessed, makes this clear.

stories.title: 4 Americans and 1 Canadian among the 69 dead in Spain’s train collision
stories.summary: Madrid (AP) — Four Americans and one Canadian were among the 69 people killed in last week's high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Madrid (AP) — Four Americans and one Canadian were among the 69 people killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.

So far, 66 of the dead have been identified, authorities said late Sunday.

Most of those killed — 54 of the 69 victims — were Spanish nationals. The crash took place last Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks.

Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include one each from France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.

Authorities said they have three bodies still to identify and three people reported missing — two Australians and one Japanese.

The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The collisions have shaken confidence in the Spanish rail network that has long been hailed for its speed and safety.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the system that carried some 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.

The crash happened one month before a Nov. 29 general election in which Sánchez is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership. He is now facing questions about the safety of the railways and investments under his governments in Spanish infrastructure.

The Associated Press
