stories.title: Growing evidence shows potential harms of screens on young children
stories.summary: Experts are increasingly urging policymakers to treat screens as a public health issue
stories.author: Ann Hui
stories.content:
A few years ago, the daycare where Dana Infald was working sent out a survey to parents asking about their children’s screen use.

Even before the results came in, Ms. Infald, an early childhood educator in Toronto, knew what to expect. It was already obvious to her which kids had screens and which were screen-free.

The latter group, she said, had stronger language development and longer attention spans.

“They would make more eye contact with the educators,” she said. “There was more serve-and-return with their language. You could just see it.”

With the toddlers who had an excessive amount of screen time, “you could see there was this need for constant stimulation.”

In recent years, much of the conversation around digital technology and kids has focused on school-aged children – on limiting social media among teenagers and restricting phone use in classrooms. But a growing body of evidence shows that the potential harms can begin much earlier, with experts increasingly urging policy-makers to treat screens as a public health issue.

Last week, researchers at Western University published a study focused on toddlers that found a connection between excessive screen time and poor language development. This followed a widespread study in Britain warning of a “baby blind spot” among policy-makers around screen time for children under the age of 5.

The Canadian Paediatric Society currently recommends no screen time (with the exception of video calling) for children under 2. And for children between ages 2 and 5, the recommendation is to limit screens to less than one hour a day.

But according to an earlier report from ParticipACTION, fewer than half of children in Canada are currently meeting these recommendations.

In the case of the Western University study, researchers conducted MRI scans on the brains of two-year-olds. They found that the children who spent more time with screens each day (including televisions, tablets and iPhones) had reduced volumes in the area of the brain associated with language development, and poorer language skills.

“They weren’t expressing themselves as clearly as other two-year-olds,” said Emma Duerden, one of the co-authors of the study, and a professor of child psychology and neuroscience at Western.

What’s more, the study showed that children who had more screen time at the age of 2 were also likely to have more screen time at the age of 3.

“It just becomes habit,” Dr. Duerden said. ”We just fall into routines and patterns very easily that can become hard to break.”

When Ms. Infald had her own child, it was because of her experience at that daycare that she decided to parent without screens. Her daughter is now 16 months old and has never watched television or movies. She doesn’t use a tablet and only occasionally uses her mother’s phone to video chat with relatives.

So far, it feels like it’s been beneficial to her daughter’s development.

“She can tell us exactly what she wants. Her vocabulary is through the roof. Every day, she’s saying something new.”

Compared with other toddlers, Ms. Infald said, “she just has this attention span and imagination that seems to not get bored.”

Dr. Duerden acknowledged that limiting screens can become more challenging as kids grow older. Digital technologies have become ubiquitous everywhere – including in schools, with the use of Chromebooks and tablets.

But while many teachers use these as teaching tools in classrooms, she said, others rely on them for classroom management, including to occupy kids during lunch hour or breaks.

And in her conversations with teachers and educators, even they are sometimes unaware of the recommendations around screen limits. They’re often surprised to learn that the time children spend with screens at school goes toward their daily screen limit.

“I do think it’s a public health issue because it involves so many different individuals at so many different levels. We have governments. We have provincial public health. Schools. Parents. And the students.”

Ms. Infald acknowledges that we need technology as a tool. “But at the same time, it can be harmful.”

Toronto parent Caroline Dönni’s biggest concern is the time that screens take away from everything else.

Instead of screens, Ms. Dönni said that her two kids, ages 5 and 8, read books and listen to audiobooks. They play with their toys and spend time outside with their friends.

“There’s so much in childhood to do – to play and explore. I feel like they’re so busy doing their own things that I wouldn’t even know when to incorporate TV,” she said.

Ms. Infald recognizes that parenting screen-free might feel like additional labour for already overburdened parents. She’s currently a stay-at-home parent and understands that not all families are in the same position.

“No shame to other parents who do use screens,” she said. But she does have some advice for those who want to limit them in their households.

“You really just have to give them things to do,” she said. She makes a schedule for each day at home with her daughter, breaking the days into chunks. “So you’re not thinking, ‘Oh my God, I have 12 hours. What are we going to do?’”

It’s a lot of work, but worth it. “I really feel like it’s going to help her down the road with everything.”

stories.title: Ottawa and provinces losing billions from illegal cigarettes, study finds
stories.summary: The EY report said legal cigarette sales have fallen 46 per cent in Ontario since 2019 and 59 per cent in B.C.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — Cash-strapped governments are losing billions in revenue because almost half of all cigarettes in Canada are now sold on the black market, a new report by the accounting firm EY Canada has found.

The report, to be released Monday, found that Ottawa, British Columbia and Ontario have already lost between $1.7-billion and $2.75-billion in taxes from illegal cigarette sales over the last three years, a period of strong growth in the contraband tobacco market.

Commissioned by the Convenience Industry Council of Canada (Cicc), the EY study said the fast-growing illegal cigarette market has now almost caught up to the size of the legal market. In Ontario, contraband makes up between 42 and 53 per cent of the cigarette market, compared to an estimated range of 34-46 per cent just three years ago.

In B.C., the report estimates that the illegal market has grown from between 21 and 36 per cent in 2023 to between 33 and 46 per cent in 2025.

Those illegal sales, much of which is controlled by organized crime, are denying convenience stores and other retailers an important source of revenue, not to mention the public purse.

“It’s a major underground economy operating in plain sight,” said Anne Kothawala, the Cicc’s president.

The motivation for smokers to buy illegal cigarettes is simple: price. A carton of 200 legal cigarettes, usually 10 packs of 20 smokes, costs about $160 in Ontario and $190 in B.C., depending on the brand, with federal and provincial taxes comprising more than 60 per cent of the price. An illegal carton often costs less than $50.

The RCMP has identified southeastern Ontario and southwestern Quebec, particularly on First Nations reserves near the Canada-U.S. border, as key manufacturing sites for illegal cigarettes. Some illegal tobacco products are also smuggled into Canada from the U.S. and elsewhere and then distributed throughout the country by truck, sometimes with guns, drugs and other contraband, or through the mail.

Governments in Canada, meanwhile, while fighting intense fiscal battles, are losing out on an important revenue stream.

Ontario announced Thursday that the province expects to post a deficit of $16.9-billion for this fiscal year, one of the province’s highest ever. B.C.’s deficit for this year is now expected to reach $13.8-billion, the highest in the province’s history. The deficit was a key issue in this month’s provincial election that saw incumbent NDP premier David Eby tossed out of office.

The EY report says Ontario and B.C., which served as test cases for the study, lost an estimated $1.1-billion and $400-million in revenue respectively over the last three years because of illegal tobacco sales.

The Carney government is scheduled to unveil its second budget on Thursday and is expected to post another massive deficit. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has forecast a budget deficit of $63.3-billion for this fiscal year, one of the largest in history. Ottawa lost between $788-million and $1.3-billion over the three-year period due to black market tobacco, EY found.

The EY report said legal cigarette sales have fallen 46 per cent in Ontario since 2019 and 59 per cent in B.C. That’s a function of the growth of the black market, the increase in the number of people who have quit smoking, and by the growth of potential substitute products such as vapes and legal cannabis.

The convenience store council is calling on governments to crack down on illegal sales by:

instructing the new Financial Crimes Agency to go after the revenue from the illegal tobacco trade

increase resources for the RCMP’s Contraband Tobacco Task Force

require banks, search engines and social media platforms to block illegal sellers, and

allow adults to buy legal nicotine pouches from authorized stores

Ottawa lost between $788-million and $1.3-billion over the three-year period due to black market tobacco, EY found.

The EY report said legal cigarette sales have fallen 46 per cent in Ontario since 2019 and 59 per cent in B.C. That’s a function of the growth of the black market, the increase in the number of people who have quit smoking, and by the growth of potential substitute products such as vapes and legal cannabis.
The convenience store council is calling on governments to crack down on illegal sales by:

items: instructing the new Financial Crimes Agency to go after the revenue from the illegal tobacco trade
increase resources for the RCMP’s Contraband Tobacco Task Force
require banks, search engines and social media platforms to block illegal sellers, and
allow adults to buy legal nicotine pouches from authorized stores

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada set for busy November with major hearings, pending judgments ahead
stories.summary: Landmark ruling expected in Quebec secularism case on limits of Charter of Rights and Freedoms
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
November is shaping up to be a particularly busy month at the Supreme Court of Canada , with major hearings scheduled and a pile of pending judgments, including the landmark ruling in the Quebec secularism case on the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

A number of those expected judgments are complicated by the retirement earlier this year of justice Sheilah Martin. She left the court at the end of May but is allowed to participate in published judgments on cases on which she sat for six months thereafter – until the end of November.

On rulings issued from the start of December onward, she wouldn’t be counted in the votes of a decision in cases on which she sat. Her name would be marked with an asterisk, with a note that states: “Took no part in the judgment.”

In past retirements from the top court, some judges have been marked with an asterisk on a handful of cases. Right now, however, there are 19 pending rulings on which retired justice Martin was part of the hearings, according to a tally from Supreme Advocacy, a law firm in Ottawa that specializes in Supreme Court work.

The most anticipated ruling is the Quebec secularism case, which was heard over four days in March , one of the longest hearings in the court’s history. The case revolves around the Charter of Rights and the notwithstanding clause. It began in 2019 when Quebec passed Bill 21 and shielded the law against Charter challenges with the notwithstanding clause. Bill 21 prohibits many public-sector workers including teachers, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or cross, ON the job.

In June at his annual press conference, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the judges were working to get the Bill 21 ruling out within retired justice Martin’s six-month window.

“I would like to ensure that she is part of the decision,” Chief Justice Wagner said in remarks translated from French. “That’s a deadline we’re taking into account.”

While Bill 21 will be the most significant judgment from the court in recent years, there are a number of other important rulings pending. The absence of former justice Martin wouldn’t always matter, if the judges are unanimous or near unanimous in their rulings, but it could make a big difference if there’s a split in the court.

“I can’t see them all being released,” said Supreme Advocacy’s Thomas Slade in a LinkedIn post, of the 19 pending judgments on which former justice Martin sat. “I would imagine the focus would be on those where there’s a split decision. We’ve already had a few close splits this fall.”

Among the pending judgments are cases on overlapping Aboriginal title , police powers to randomly stop drivers in the name of road safety, and a major privacy case against Facebook.

There are also two important sexual assault cases, including one called Bilinski. It was heard May 22, the final case on which justice Martin sat during her 8½ years on the Supreme Court. Among her specialties is criminal law, including sexual assault.

“There are some significant cases in the mix,” said Michael Plaxton, a law professor at the University of Saskatchewan, in a Substack post.

Beyond the pending judgments, the biggest hearing of the fall at the Supreme Court is set for Nov. 9 and 10. There are four appeals on the same issue: the federal government’s 2020 firearms regulations. Those rules effectively prohibited more than 1,500 types of firearms that had previously been legal for licensed ownership and use. Ottawa has described the banned guns as assault weapons that have been used in mass shootings.

Legal challenges against the gun prohibitions have twice failed, first at the Federal Court in 2023 and then again at the Federal Court of Appeal last year.

Another important hearing is set for Nov. 6, a heavily redacted case called “Named Persons.”

It involves negligent disclosure by the government related to the identity of a confidential informer. The trial court in British Columbia concluded there was a breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms’ Section 7, the security of the person, and awarded damages to Named Persons. The federal government won at the B.C. Court of Appeal and the award of Charter damages was set aside.

stories.title: Carney seeks to boost trade and ties at Commonwealth meeting
stories.summary: Prime Minister will meet with King Charles and hold bilateral meetings with countries seeking to increase investments
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries – and with King Charles.

Much of the meetings taking place this week will focus on trade and investment. But the gathering also offers a chance for Carney to meet with representatives from a wide variety of countries he might not otherwise visit, said retired Canadian diplomat Patricia Fortier.

“Fifty-six countries, Caribbean, Europe, Africa, North America, Indo-Pacific – this is like a diplomatic feast,” she said.

Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries – such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Fortier described it as an “extraordinary gathering.”

Carney has spent much of his time in office travelling to shore up multilateral relationships as he attempts to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

Canada’s ties with the Commonwealth, especially with smaller states, could help with that effort. Multilateral organizations like the United Nations give each member country one vote, regardless of size, Fortier noted.

“If you’re trying to move things through a multilateral organization, it is very, very important that you pay attention to smaller states,” she said.

“The Caribbean and Africa and some of the Pacific Island states can make or break your initiatives.”

Michael Manulak, an associate professor of international affairs at Carleton University, said Canada has used this strategy successfully in the past, when it was an influential multilateral player under Prime Minister Lester Pearson, and in the 1980s.

“One of the kind of core constituencies that Canada often operated on was the Commonwealth,” he said.

Canada had good relations with a large number of African and Caribbean countries, which meant Ottawa could call on those leaders to support Canada’s position on international issues, he added.

Ronald Sanders, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada, said there was a time in the past when “Canada put up a candidate for a post in the UN and it knew it had 14 votes behind it automatically.”

That relationship changed as various Canadian governments moved toward closer relations with the United States and Mexico and away from those relationships in the Caribbean.

“We would hope that we can rebuild that relationship now,” he said.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and most of its members have ties to the British Empire. Together, they represent a large chunk of the world’s population – 2.7 billion people.

“It’s a legacy of British imperialism but it’s now a consensual association,” said Manulak.

He said the Commonwealth gives Canada a platform to augment bilateral relations with “a whole set of countries that we might not have a whole lot to do with on an everyday basis. And I think that can be a really valuable thing.”

Manulak said trade and investment will be the top issue at the gathering. He said it’s something Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey has been pushing for since she stepped into the role in 2025.

“There’s going to be a lot of discussion about concrete ways of reducing barriers to trade,” he said.

Carney will spend just one day at the gathering, attending a lunch hosted by the King for new leaders in the Commonwealth and a formal dinner – also hosted by the King – as well as executive sessions and other meetings.

Carney is also expected to hold bilateral meetings, but officials declined to say in advance who he will meet with.

Sanders said Carney will meet with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Browne will propose a bilateral agreement with Canada that “could see joint ventures and activities that promote economic growth and create commercial opportunities for Canadian enterprises,” Sanders said.

Canadian government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation.

They noted Canada currently has $100-billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will join Carney at the meeting. She told The Canadian Press in an interview that Canada “supports practical Commonwealth initiatives that strengthen supply chains and improve market access, that advance trade diversification.”

She added the Commonwealth has “ambitious targets” to increase trade among Commonwealth countries to $2-trillion by 2030.

The officials said in the briefing there will be a focus at the meeting on resilience and mitigation related to climate change – a major priority for states witnessing the effects of rising oceans firsthand.

“Given that many of these smaller states are islands and are most affected by climate change, I think that will also be something that will come up,” Fortier said.

Sanders noted the Commonwealth was where early discussions about climate change began. He said the Commonwealth has acted collectively on big issues in the past, such as helping to end apartheid in South Africa.

King Charles is expected to address the legacy of slavery at the meeting in Antigua. Officials did not answer directly when asked whether Carney will participate in any of those discussions.

Manulak said while the British are very reluctant to accept blame for slavery and colonialism – and the potential financial implications of that – Caribbean countries “naturally feel differently about this issue. Being in the Caribbean, this is going to be a really live issue.”

Tamanisha John, assistant professor at York University’s department of politics, predicted Canada will choose to stay quiet and, if pressed, will support the position of the U.K. government. She noted that even if King Charles apologizes, the U.K. government opposes reparations.

Before the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Carney will host a working breakfast with Caribbean leaders.

Government officials said that will be an opportunity for Carney to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

“The Caribbean and Canada have long had a kind of a special relationship, partly through the shared British colonial heritage, but also through trade with the maritime provinces going down to the Caribbean islands,” Fortier said.

John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.

“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.

stories.title: U.S. government has new rules on flight delays. Will it affect Canadian travellers?
stories.summary: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
stories.author: Christl Dabu
stories.content:
New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), which published the new rules on the Federal Register daily journal in September, is reclassifying 10 types of events that cause flight delays and cancellations as outside the airline’s control. These events include a passenger’s death, unscheduled mechanical issues, severe weather, cybersecurity attacks and potential tech outages.

The rule was supposed to take effect Oct. 19 but was postponed until Feb. 1, 2027.

The department acknowledged in the notice that “the total value of amenities and compensation currently provided by air carriers to consumers will be reduced under this final rule.”

Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said the new rules May mean travellers won’t be entitled to the same type of protections they used to have.

“So basically, it’s taking some of what was the responsibility of the airlines and recategorizing them … outside of the airline’s control,” Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said in a video interview with CTVNews.CA on Friday. “And very simply, for travellers, that means you May not be entitled to the same type of protections that you are now.”

“Now, when this new rule goes into effect, you as a passenger, if you are impacted due to an unscheduled maintenance event, this is outside of the airline’s control, meaning that they’re not now forced, or really obliged, to provide a hotel voucher or a meal voucher,” she added.

Airline passenger advocacy group FlyersRights is suing the U.S. Department of Transportation over the rules, which they say shift the costs from airline delays to passengers.

“A change in reporting classifications is not permission to reduce passenger rights,” Paul Hudson, president of FlyersRights, said in a news release Friday. “... The rule sneakily transfers costs from airlines back to passengers for delays involving mechanical problems that are the responsibility and fault of the airlines.”

Nastro, a correspondent with the Flighty flight-tracker app, said the change will affect anyone “travelling within the U.S., to the U.S., or from the U.S.,” regardless of their nationality or the airline, if their flight experiences certain types of disruptions that are now outside the airline’s control.

“In certain circumstances, it does grey the disruption category for consumers,” Nastro said. “This new regulation … just makes it even more confusing for travellers when they’re trying to navigate what exactly they’re entitled to in terms of disruption protections.”

Under the current DOT regulations, Nastro said disrupted flights May allow travellers to get hotel or meal vouchers, rebook flights or get refunds.

Gábor Lukács, president of Air Passenger Rights, said he believes the new rules May have a “minimal” impact on Canadian travellers flying to or from the U.S. because they would have some rights under the Canadian Air Passenger Protection Regulations .

However, he said Canada’s passenger protection regulations are “weak” with rules that are “unnecessarily complex” and “very difficult to enforce.”

He said the U.S. rule change’s effect is “primarily administrative,” because it involves how flight disruptions are being reported and passengers aren’t compensated in cash for flight disruptions in the U.S.

Lukács said the main issue with the new rules will be unexpected maintenance issues, which he said is “completely unreasonable.”

stories.title: This Ontario hospital locked Jake Gordon up alone for five years. It transferred him just after the Star told his story
stories.summary: Jake Gordon has been transferred closer to family just weeks after the Star published footage of his life kept locked in isolation at Waypoint Centre.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
This story is part of 20 Years in Isolation , the Star’s ongoing investigation into the use of psychiatric seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. The Star’s reporting has been met with calls for an independent review of Ontario’s mental health system .

Diane Worden was happy but in shock when she got a call a few weeks ago from Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care about her son, Jake Gordon.

After more than five years detained in Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital in Penetanguishene — almost entirely spent locked in isolation in his room — the 31-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia was being transferred immediately to a less secure hospital just a 15-minute drive from the family home.

The move to Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby came just a month after a Star profile on Gordon’s case , featuring six-and-a-half hours of video surveillance footage provided by Worden showing her son pacing alone while in seclusion in his tiny room at Waypoint last year. Worden had requested the video from Waypoint in the hopes of finding out how her son was able to cause a serious injury to his eye, but the incident was not captured in the footage.

At the time of his transfer, Gordon had been out of seclusion for just over two months, having been released amid the Star’s ongoing investigation into Waypoint’s use of the practice.

“It’s shocking how fast they made this happen,” Worden said.

Jake with his mother, Diane Worden.

Seclusion is meant to be the option of last resort, to be used for as brief a time as possible, to deal with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others. The Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint has been keeping seriously mentally ill patients in seclusion for years, and in the case of Camelott Hamblett , 20 years and counting. An independent assessment concluded in August that Waypoint is holding patients in conditions the United Nations has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.

Medication alone had failed to improve her son’s condition, Worden noted, as he had a poor response to many different drugs. But on the heels of the Star’s coverage this spring , Worden said her son started spending an increasing amount of time out of seclusion and out of restraints; he was being taken to the canteen and into the courtyard; he was seen by a dentist and an optometrist; he was being given access to music more often; and he was showering again.

He then improved to the point that he was released from seclusion in August, and is now well enough that he can be managed in a less secure facility.

She said Gordon — who had trouble walking and talking and would drool when Worden visited him at Waypoint — is doing significantly better. On a recent visit to Ontario Shores, Worden noted that he’s communicative and “very happy” to be there.

“He talked about the hope of getting out one day, getting a job, a nice place to live and seeing his family more often now that he is closer to home,” she said.

Everything that has happened for her son in such a short period of time is no coincidence, Worden said. She attributed the increased focus on her son's care this year to the Star’s investigation, the multiple experts who have come forward with their concerns, and the work of Gordon’s new lawyer, Anita Szigeti, who specializes in mental health law and represents a number of other men in seclusion at Waypoint.

“It’s 100 per cent because of the public scrutiny,” Worden said. “You don’t go from five-and-a-half years in seclusion to all of a sudden you’re out and making cupcakes and two months later you’re being transferred to Ontario Shores.”

For years, Worden made the drive to Waypoint — about five hours round trip — to visit her son as much as she could, when he would be permitted to briefly leave his room. While she did have her concerns about his care and would voice them to the hospital, she said she ultimately trusted that they were doing the right thing for Gordon.

The exterior of Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

Worden, who also serves as her son’s substitute decision-maker, worries about the damage that five years in isolation will have caused. She also continues to question whether seclusion for such a lengthy period of time was even necessary, pointing to Gordon’s voluminous medical records, which she said do not indicate risk or aggression from Gordon on a daily basis that would warrant him remaining locked up.

“They always told me it was because he was a harm to himself or to others,” she said. “Well, where is the harm?”

It was only when she came across the initial stories from the Star’s investigation in the spring, profiling the cases of Hamblett and other patients who’ve been kept in locked seclusion at Waypoint, that she became alarmed.

“Obviously that trust was misguided,” she said.

Unlike most of the other men in long-term seclusion at Waypoint, Gordon was not a forensic patient, meaning he hadn’t committed any crime. Rather, he was a civil patient, involuntarily detained under the Mental Health Act because he’s been found to pose a serious risk of bodily harm to himself and others.

Worden is under no illusions: she does believe her son should remain in a hospital. But his case calls into question the independent oversight of the detention of civil patients, and whether there was a missed opportunity to get Gordon out of seclusion sooner.

The Consent and Capacity Board (CCB) — whose three-member panels are made up of a medical professional, lawyer and layperson — is required to hold a review of a civil patient’s case after six months, and then every year afterward, to determine whether their involuntary status should be upheld; the patient can also ask for orders such as a transfer to another facility.

It’s unknown whether the board was ever presented with any evidence about Gordon’s seclusion status and whether any panel members expressed concern. That’s because while the board must provide its decision within a day of the hearing, it isn’t required under Ontario law to produce written reasons for that decision unless one of the parties — Gordon, his psychiatrist and the hospital — asks for them within 30 days of the hearing. No one ever did.

That’s in stark contrast to the Ontario Review Board, the independent body with oversight of forensic patients , which is required to produce written reasons after every hearing.

The chair of the CCB, Philip Squire, said in an email the board’s practices accord with the legislation: “The CCB is unable to comment on the practices of other administrative tribunals or their governing legislation.”

Gordon was represented by five different lawyers at six CCB hearings; it’s unclear how they came on board, though one possibility is they were arranged by legal aid after an order from the board.

Jake Gordon as a child.

When Szigeti was contacted by Gordon’s family and recently retained to be his lawyer, she found it “shocking and really disconcerting” that there were no records she could access to determine if his seclusion had been reviewed by the CCB. Notwithstanding what the law says, Szigeti has long been raising the need for the CCB to adopt a policy requiring the board to always produce written reasons for the mandatory hearings reviewing an individual’s involuntary status.

“There has to be some documentation somewhere as to what is happening with someone who is locked in a facility, and in this case locked in seclusion for more than five years,” Szigeti said.

“What is the purpose of having an oversight body tasked with mandatory hearings when there’s no record of what they did and why?”

Worden never went to her son’s hearings, which are held on Zoom, because she says his Waypoint social workers told her it was just to decide whether his involuntary status should be upheld — something she wasn’t looking to challenge anyway. She had no idea that the board would have had the power to transfer her son out of Waypoint.

She can’t help but think of other families who still don’t know.

“There are all these patients like Jake who are locked in there, and nobody can do anything about it because we don’t know the system,” Worden said. “They lock us out.”

The campus of the Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby.

Now that Gordon is back at Ontario Shores, his mother will be able to visit him daily. When he was at Waypoint, months would pass by before she could see him because she wasn’t comfortable driving the long distance in winter weather.

And for the first time in over five years, Gordon will be able to see his father, who has multiple sclerosis and is mostly bedridden. Given the proximity of Ontario Shores, Worden plans to find a way to transport her husband there to see their son.

“The hardest part of having him at Waypoint was either his dad would pass away or something bad would happen to Jake, and he would never be able to see his dad again,” Worden said. “Jake is always worried about him. The first thing he always says is: ‘How is Dad?’”

While seclusion is used for various lengths of time in practically all hospitals, including Ontario Shores, none have been known to keep patients locked up for years like Waypoint. At Ontario Shores, Gordon’s room has a big window with a view of Lake Ontario, as well as a bed with a pillow and blankets; at Waypoint, as seen on the surveillance footage, he only had a mat on the floor.

Overall, Worden is still taken aback by just how much progress has been made since her son was released from isolation, and she hopes to see that progress continue.

“He’s lost weight, he’s talkative, he’s smiling,” she said. “He’s just the old Jake that was there before he went to Waypoint.”

It was only when she came across the initial stories from the Star’s investigation in the spring, profiling the cases of Hamblett and other patients who’ve been kept in locked seclusion at Waypoint, that she became alarmed.
“Obviously that trust was misguided,” she said.

Unlike most of the other men in long-term seclusion at Waypoint, Gordon was not a forensic patient, meaning he hadn’t committed any crime. Rather, he was a civil patient, involuntarily detained under the Mental Health Act because he’s been found to pose a serious risk of bodily harm to himself and others.

Worden is under no illusions: she does believe her son should remain in a hospital. But his case calls into question the independent oversight of the detention of civil patients, and whether there was a missed opportunity to get Gordon out of seclusion sooner.

The Consent and Capacity Board (CCB) — whose three-member panels are made up of a medical professional, lawyer and layperson — is required to hold a review of a civil patient’s case after six months, and then every year afterward, to determine whether their involuntary status should be upheld; the patient can also ask for orders such as a transfer to another facility.

It’s unknown whether the board was ever presented with any evidence about Gordon’s seclusion status and whether any panel members expressed concern. That’s because while the board must provide its decision within a day of the hearing, it isn’t required under Ontario law to produce written reasons for that decision unless one of the parties — Gordon, his psychiatrist and the hospital — asks for them within 30 days of the hearing. No one ever did.
That’s in stark contrast to the Ontario Review Board, the independent body with oversight of forensic patients , which is required to produce written reasons after every hearing.

The chair of the CCB, Philip Squire, said in an email the board’s practices accord with the legislation: “The CCB is unable to comment on the practices of other administrative tribunals or their governing legislation.”
Gordon was represented by five different lawyers at six CCB hearings; it’s unclear how they came on board, though one possibility is they were arranged by legal aid after an order from the board.
Jake Gordon as a child.

When Szigeti was contacted by Gordon’s family and recently retained to be his lawyer, she found it “shocking and really disconcerting” that there were no records she could access to determine if his seclusion had been reviewed by the CCB. Notwithstanding what the law says, Szigeti has long been raising the need for the CCB to adopt a policy requiring the board to always produce written reasons for the mandatory hearings reviewing an individual’s involuntary status.
“There has to be some documentation somewhere as to what is happening with someone who is locked in a facility, and in this case locked in seclusion for more than five years,” Szigeti said.
“What is the purpose of having an oversight body tasked with mandatory hearings when there’s no record of what they did and why?”

Worden never went to her son’s hearings, which are held on Zoom, because she says his Waypoint social workers told her it was just to decide whether his involuntary status should be upheld — something she wasn’t looking to challenge anyway. She had no idea that the board would have had the power to transfer her son out of Waypoint.
She can’t help but think of other families who still don’t know.
“There are all these patients like Jake who are locked in there, and nobody can do anything about it because we don’t know the system,” Worden said. “They lock us out.”
The campus of the Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby.

Now that Gordon is back at Ontario Shores, his mother will be able to visit him daily. When he was at Waypoint, months would pass by before she could see him because she wasn’t comfortable driving the long distance in winter weather.

And for the first time in over five years, Gordon will be able to see his father, who has multiple sclerosis and is mostly bedridden. Given the proximity of Ontario Shores, Worden plans to find a way to transport her husband there to see their son.

“The hardest part of having him at Waypoint was either his dad would pass away or something bad would happen to Jake, and he would never be able to see his dad again,” Worden said. “Jake is always worried about him. The first thing he always says is: ‘How is Dad?’”

While seclusion is used for various lengths of time in practically all hospitals, including Ontario Shores, none have been known to keep patients locked up for years like Waypoint. At Ontario Shores, Gordon’s room has a big window with a view of Lake Ontario, as well as a bed with a pillow and blankets; at Waypoint, as seen on the surveillance footage, he only had a mat on the floor.
Overall, Worden is still taken aback by just how much progress has been made since her son was released from isolation, and she hopes to see that progress continue.
“He’s lost weight, he’s talkative, he’s smiling,” she said. “He’s just the old Jake that was there before he went to Waypoint.”

stories.title: Political betrayal, Canada trade war: Why Michigan is a Senate race to watch
stories.summary: Detroit - Michelle Taylor gasped and shook her head in disbelief.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Detroit - Michelle Taylor gasped and shook her head in disbelief.

Outside a church where she was waiting to hear Democrat Abdul El-Sayed speak on Sunday, the longtime Detroit resident watched an unimaginable party fracture in a race that could ultimately decide who controls power on Capitol Hill.

El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers with just less than 48 hours to go before election day.

“It’s all about being bigger than your ego,” Taylor said shaking her head, looking at Stevens’ social media endorsement minutes after it was posted. “And for her to do that is really a slap in the face to the Democrats.”

Stevens was quickly rebuked by Michigan and national Democrats after the remarkable show of support for the candidate backed by President Donald Trump.

Barring a late Republican surge before Tuesday’s elections, America could finally be turning a page on a decade-long Trump epoch in American

It’s unclear how Stevens’ endorsement May impact the outcome of the closely-watched contest, whose outcome could determine whether Democrats can rein in Trump’s unwieldy use of executive power for the remainder of his term.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear, where some polling shows a Democrat net gain of four seats is within reach.

The Michigan seat is crucial for Democrats to get a Senate majority. It’s also a race where Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a ballot box issue.

The economies of Michigan and Canada have long been integrated and Trump’s tariffs have had a significant impact on the state. The auto industry on both sides of the border has been struggling with the 25 per cent auto tariffs for vehicles finished in Canada — which Trump has threatened to increase to 50 per cent next year.

The Detroit Regional Chamber has repeatedly said the tariff battle causes economic pain on both sides of the border. Multiple polls have shown most Michiganders — no matter their political affiliation — disapprove of Trump’s tariff attack on Canada.

The president’s decision to hold up the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge has also been a high-profile issue in the campaign — along with the drop in Canadian visitors driven by Trump’s anti-Canada rhetoric.

The blowback over the trade war was bad enough that Rogers put some distance between himself and Trump. In a campaign ad released last month, Rogers is seen drinking a Labatt’s beer and telling voters “Canada is not our enemy.” El-Sayed has long said the trade war with Canada is nonsensical.

Both candidates have spent weeks releasing sharp attack ads criticizing the other.

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said El-Sayed is facing an “othering” — where Rogers is trying to tie the Democrat to foreign parents and previous controversial comments.

El-Sayed has condemned Rogers for his corporate ties and legislative records, connecting the Republican to Trump’s unpopular policies, including his trade war with Canada.

Michigan, considered a battleground state, has historically seen Democrat support linked to unions. But Trump was able to win the state in 2024, making gains in unexpected areas like those with large Arab-American populations.

It’s unclear how the Republican attacks on El-Sayed’s religion will impact those areas of support.

Chris Vitale said he feels “cautious optimism” that Rogers is in a good place to win the race. The longtime Trump supporter hopes the Democrats’ eleventh-hour blow-up will bring even more voters to the Republican ballot.

Supporters of Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed pushed for their party in a tight race for a Michigan Senate seat in Tuesday's midterm elections. (Nov. 2, 2026)

“A lot of the things over the last few days have only gone Mike’s way,” said Vitale, a council member for the City of St. Clair Shores in Michigan. “So maybe that optimism is even a little more increased.”

As a retired autoworker, Vitale sees value in some of the president’s tariffs. He’s more hesitant about the duties targeting of Canada.

Canada makes the perfect suspect. For two years, Americans have heard that Canada is “ripping us off.” Ripping off an election is a short step. In

Vitale said he wants to see a strong Canadian automobile industry but argues the Trump administration needs stronger trade policy around Mexico and China.

”(The Trump administration) should understand that Canada is different than all those other countries I named,” he said. “And it’s very frustrating because you want to get behind this guy but there’s that one little asterisk that it’s like, that’s not Canada.”

Despite trade tensions making Michigan Republicans more wary, Vitale said they still want to send someone “normal” to the Senate and Rogers “checks the boxes.”

Donald Trump touted a resurrected pipeline and a ‘concept’ of a trade deal with Canada as Republicans brace for potential losses in key states.

Meanwhile in downtown Detroit, Kenneth Ware was preparing a get-out-the-vote effort for Democrats in Michigan. He said it’s important for people to come together to make sure the right person gets the job — and for him that’s El-Sayed.

There was a lot of noise among Democrats over the weekend but Ware said it’s like running a marathon. Now is the time to come out and participate to make sure the race is finished, he said.

“I do feel that we can take a stand now,” he said. “I believe our stand is stronger when we all come together than just being alone.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear, where some polling shows a Democrat net gain of four seats is within reach.
The Michigan seat is crucial for Democrats to get a Senate majority. It’s also a race where Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a ballot box issue.

The economies of Michigan and Canada have long been integrated and Trump’s tariffs have had a significant impact on the state. The auto industry on both sides of the border has been struggling with the 25 per cent auto tariffs for vehicles finished in Canada — which Trump has threatened to increase to 50 per cent next year.

The Detroit Regional Chamber has repeatedly said the tariff battle causes economic pain on both sides of the border. Multiple polls have shown most Michiganders — no matter their political affiliation — disapprove of Trump’s tariff attack on Canada.

The president’s decision to hold up the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge has also been a high-profile issue in the campaign — along with the drop in Canadian visitors driven by Trump’s anti-Canada rhetoric.

The blowback over the trade war was bad enough that Rogers put some distance between himself and Trump. In a campaign ad released last month, Rogers is seen drinking a Labatt’s beer and telling voters “Canada is not our enemy.” El-Sayed has long said the trade war with Canada is nonsensical.
Both candidates have spent weeks releasing sharp attack ads criticizing the other.

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said El-Sayed is facing an “othering” — where Rogers is trying to tie the Democrat to foreign parents and previous controversial comments.
El-Sayed has condemned Rogers for his corporate ties and legislative records, connecting the Republican to Trump’s unpopular policies, including his trade war with Canada.

Michigan, considered a battleground state, has historically seen Democrat support linked to unions. But Trump was able to win the state in 2024, making gains in unexpected areas like those with large Arab-American populations.
It’s unclear how the Republican attacks on El-Sayed’s religion will impact those areas of support.

Chris Vitale said he feels “cautious optimism” that Rogers is in a good place to win the race. The longtime Trump supporter hopes the Democrats’ eleventh-hour blow-up will bring even more voters to the Republican ballot.

“A lot of the things over the last few days have only gone Mike’s way,” said Vitale, a council member for the City of St. Clair Shores in Michigan. “So maybe that optimism is even a little more increased.”
As a retired autoworker, Vitale sees value in some of the president’s tariffs. He’s more hesitant about the duties targeting of Canada.
Canada makes the perfect suspect. For two years, Americans have heard that Canada is “ripping us off.” Ripping off an election is a short step. In
Vitale said he wants to see a strong Canadian automobile industry but argues the Trump administration needs stronger trade policy around Mexico and China.

”(The Trump administration) should understand that Canada is different than all those other countries I named,” he said. “And it’s very frustrating because you want to get behind this guy but there’s that one little asterisk that it’s like, that’s not Canada.”
Despite trade tensions making Michigan Republicans more wary, Vitale said they still want to send someone “normal” to the Senate and Rogers “checks the boxes.”

Meanwhile in downtown Detroit, Kenneth Ware was preparing a get-out-the-vote effort for Democrats in Michigan. He said it’s important for people to come together to make sure the right person gets the job — and for him that’s El-Sayed.
There was a lot of noise among Democrats over the weekend but Ware said it’s like running a marathon. Now is the time to come out and participate to make sure the race is finished, he said.
“I do feel that we can take a stand now,” he said. “I believe our stand is stronger when we all come together than just being alone.”

stories.title: Commonwealth meeting offers Carney a chance to boost diplomatic ties, experts say
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries — and with King Charles.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries — and with King Charles.

Much of the meetings taking place this week will focus on trade and investment. But the gathering also offers a chance for Carney to meet with representatives from a wide variety of countries he might not otherwise visit, said retired Canadian diplomat Patricia Fortier.

“Fifty-six countries, Caribbean, Europe, Africa, North America, Indo-Pacific — this is like a diplomatic feast,” she said.

Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries — such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Fortier described it as an “extraordinary gathering.”

Carney has spent much of his time in office travelling to shore up multilateral relationships as he attempts to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

Canada’s ties with the Commonwealth, especially with smaller states, could help with that effort. Multilateral organizations like the United Nations give each member country one vote, regardless of size, Fortier noted.

“If you’re trying to move things through a multilateral organization, it is very, very important that you pay attention to smaller states,” she said.

“The Caribbean and Africa and some of the Pacific Island states can make or break your initiatives.”

Michael Manulak, an associate professor of international affairs at Carleton University, said Canada has used this strategy successfully in the past, when it was an influential multilateral player under Prime Minister Lester Pearson, and in the 1980s.

“One of the kind of core constituencies that Canada often operated on was the Commonwealth,” he said.

Canada had good relations with a large number of African and Caribbean countries, which meant Ottawa could call on those leaders to support Canada’s position on international issues, he added.

Ronald Sanders, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada, said there was a time in the past when “Canada put up a candidate for a post in the UN and it knew it had 14 votes behind it automatically.”

That relationship changed as various Canadian governments moved toward closer relations with the United States and Mexico and away from those relationships in the Caribbean.

“We would hope that we can rebuild that relationship now,” he said.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and most of its members have ties to the British Empire. Together, they represent a large chunk of the world’s population — 2.7 billion people.

“It’s a legacy of British imperialism but it’s now a consensual association,” said Manulak.

He said the Commonwealth gives Canada a platform to augment bilateral relations with “a whole set of countries that we might not have a whole lot to do with on an everyday basis. And I think that can be a really valuable thing.”

Manulak said trade and investment will be the top issue at the gathering. He said it’s something Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey has been pushing for since she stepped into the role in 2025.

“There’s going to be a lot of discussion about concrete ways of reducing barriers to trade,” he said.

Carney will spend just one day at the gathering, attending a lunch hosted by the King for new leaders in the Commonwealth and a formal dinner — also hosted by the King — as well as executive sessions and other meetings.

Carney is also expected to hold bilateral meetings, but officials declined to say in advance who he will meet with.

Sanders said Carney will meet with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Browne will propose a bilateral agreement with Canada that “could see joint ventures and activities that promote economic growth and create commercial opportunities for Canadian enterprises,” Sanders said.

Canadian government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation.

They noted Canada currently has $100 billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will join Carney at the meeting. She told The Canadian Press in an interview that Canada “supports practical Commonwealth initiatives that strengthen supply chains and improve market access, that advance trade diversification.”

She added the Commonwealth has “ambitious targets” to increase trade among Commonwealth countries to $2 trillion by 2030.

The officials said in the briefing there will be a focus at the meeting on resilience and mitigation related to climate change — a major priority for states witnessing the effects of rising oceans firsthand.

“Given that many of these smaller states are islands and are most affected by climate change, I think that will also be something that will come up,” Fortier said.

Sanders noted the Commonwealth was where early discussions about climate change began. He said the Commonwealth has acted collectively on big issues in the past, such as helping to end apartheid in South Africa.

King Charles is expected to address the legacy of slavery at the meeting in Antigua. Officials did not answer directly when asked whether Carney will participate in any of those discussions.

Manulak said while the British are very reluctant to accept blame for slavery and colonialism — and the potential financial implications of that — Caribbean countries “naturally feel differently about this issue. Being in the Caribbean, this is going to be a really live issue.”

Tamanisha John, assistant professor at York University’s department of politics, predicted Canada will choose to stay quiet and, if pressed, will support the position of the U.K. government. She noted that even if King Charles apologizes, the U.K. government opposes reparations.

Before the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Carney will host a working breakfast with Caribbean leaders.

Government officials said that will be an opportunity for Carney to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

“The Caribbean and Canada have long had a kind of a special relationship, partly through the shared British colonial heritage, but also through trade with the maritime provinces going down to the Caribbean islands,” Fortier said.

John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.

“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published on Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bob Aaron: B.C. and Alberta protect homebuyers from rogue builders. Why won’t Ontario?
stories.summary: Illegal builders continue to exploit a loophole, obtaining municipal building permits without proving they are licensed or legitimately exempt.
stories.author: Bob Aaron
stories.content:
Ontario was warned about illegal homebuilding nearly a decade ago, but consumers remain vulnerable to bad actors in the construction industry. Ontario homebuyers deserve protection before a shovel goes into the ground or a sale agreement is signed.

In his 2017 report on the Ontario New Home Warranties Plan Act and the Tarion Warranty Corporation, Justice J. Douglas Cunningham examined illegal building and owner-built homes. He identified two categories:

• unregistered builders, who are individuals or companies constructing homes for resale without the registration then required by Tarion, and

• disguised builders, who are individuals claiming to build homes for their own occupation, thereby avoiding registration and warranty-enrolment requirements, when their actual intention is resale.

Illegal building is a long-standing and serious problem in Ontario. As a member of the Home Construction Regulatory Authority Consumer Advisory Council, I have seen firsthand how seriously this issue is taken — and how little government action has followed. Cunningham flagged it in 2017, and subsequent enforcement proceedings and prosecutions demonstrate that it continues.

The true scale of illegal building is unknown — no published estimate exists of how many new homes are built or sold illegally each year.

Cunningham concluded that additional measures were necessary to protect purchasers. He also identified the possibility of requiring proof of warranty registration or a valid exemption before a municipality issues a building permit.

That suggestion anticipated the same regulatory weakness identified by the auditor general eight years later.

The Home Construction Regulatory Authority (Hcra) 2024-25 annual report logged more than 300 complaints about illegal building. One builder was convicted of offences involving 39 homes built without the required licences and Tarion enrolment, with fines exceeding $1 million.

In May 2025, Hcra laid charges over the allegedly illegal sale of 453 homes.

To support proposed legislative changes and demonstrate that illegal builders were obtaining building permits, Hcra conducted an ad hoc analysis of publicly available building permit data from Kitchener, Ont., in November 2023. The analysis revealed that:

• of 91 builders issued new homebuilding permits by the city, 23 (25 per cent) were not licensed by Hcra;

• the 23 unlicensed builders held 44 building permits for single-family homes — an average of nearly two each;

• some of these builders were likely operating illegally.

An illegally built home does not necessarily violate the Building Code. But a purchaser May encounter construction deficiencies, disputes about warranty entitlement, or difficulties obtaining repairs and compensation if an unlicensed builder becomes insolvent.

The solution seems straightforward: Ontario could enact legislation requiring that no building permit be issued for a single-family home unless the builder is licensed with Hcra or provides satisfactory evidence of competence to build for personal use.

This is hardly a revolutionary proposal. British Columbia and Alberta already require municipalities to verify builder licensing or owner-builder authorization before issuing building permits.

British Columbia goes further. Anyone wishing to build personally without a builder’s licence must obtain government authorization and pass a 100-question examination covering construction knowledge and legal responsibilities.

If British Columbia and Alberta can make builder licensing a condition of obtaining a building permit, why can’t Ontario?

On Oct. 20, I emailed Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack, Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement Stephen Crawford, and their media relations staff.

I noted that I was writing in my personal capacity and not as a member of the Home Construction Regulatory Authority Consumer Advisory Council.

I pointed out that Ontario’s regulatory system allows building permits to be issued without verifying whether the applicant holds an Hcra licence to construct a new home.

I asked the ministers why the government has not acted to protect consumers from illegal builders and why regulations have not been enacted to prohibit municipalities from issuing permits for new homes without evidence of Hcra licence or satisfactory proof that the builder is competent and committed to build their own home for personal use.

I also asked whether the government has any plans in the near term to take such action to protect the public.

Neither minister responded in time for publication.

Illegal builders continue to exploit a loophole, obtaining municipal building permits without proving they are licensed or legitimately exempt. Ontario homebuyers deserve more than warnings, investigations and prosecutions after the damage is done.

stories.title: Carney’s government tilts policy toward business as critics question who benefits
stories.summary: A $36-billion tax break, faster project approvals and less red tape win praise from industry leaders, while labour and economists say their priorities are being overlooked
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa—Ensconced in the exclusive company of corporate investors and big money bankers, Prime Minister Mark Carney was in a safe place. And he had an announcement to make.

Canada, his Canada, wants to haul in capital from leading institutions of finance, both public and private, domestic and far-flung. The cash should flow to oil and gas infrastructure, ports, mining projects, new homes, airports run by pension funds — all to “build Canada strong” as it faces a trade crisis, a capricious United States, and a warping world order.

So, at September’s global investment summit , Carney unveiled his government's "mega deduction." At an anticipated cost of $36 billion over five years, the newly generous tax break is the most expensive policy Ottawa has proposed since last spring, according to Parliament’s budget watchdog. It is designed to spur businesses, from fossil fuel companies to heavy manufacturers, to put money into expanding their operations now, thereby juicing economic activity and the almighty GDP.

After Carney spoke, the VIP-only room at a downtown Toronto hotel broke into applause.

A short time later, Goldy Hyder’s inbox pinged with a new message. The head of the Business Council of Canada, a lobby group made up of executives from more than 170 major corporations, checked to see what it said.

It was from his counterpart at Australia’s business council.

“It said, ‘Do you even need to work anymore?’” Hyder recalled this week with a laugh.

It’s funny because, with Carney in the Prime Minister’s Office, that’s basically how it feels.

Days ahead of the second federal budget since Carney took office, his ambition for Canada’s economy is clear.

Donald Trump touted a resurrected pipeline and a ‘concept’ of a trade deal with Canada as Republicans brace for potential losses in key states.

Through a series of reforms, his government has tilted Canadian policy in favour of business. Oil and gas companies have welcomed the rollback of climate policies imposed when Justin Trudeau was in power. Billions of dollars in tax deductions are on the table to make private investment more profitable. New authorities are written into federal law and legislation to shepherd development projects to completion faster, and the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline from Alberta to the British Columbia coast is the first to get the special treatment.

It doesn’t stop there. A rolling review of “red tape” inside the federal government is lifting hundreds of millions of dollars in expected compliance costs for businesses, according to federal officials. Regulatory “sandboxes” have been created and proposed , so companies can be exempt from government rules to test new products. And taxes Ottawa planned or implemented under the Trudeau administration, from the consumer carbon price to a levy on the revenues of online giants , now lie in the policy scrap heap.

Much of this has been met with approbation, especially from those who saw in the previous Liberal government muted enthusiasm — or even antipathy — to the interests and desires of business. Yet it is also proving controversial , with environmentalists, Indigenous nations and union leaders decrying how they believe the government is trampling their priorities in the name of speed and economic growth.

But those are undoubtedly the priorities of this Carney government, and by all accounts the Nov. 5 budget will press on in that direction. The question, both for Canadians and the staying power of the prime minister’s popularity, is whether this agenda is truly — or sufficiently — to the benefit of the broad public.

“We have got the perfect business playbook, written to the letter just the way it was in the 1980s,” said Armine Yalnizyan, an economist and fellow at the Atkinson Foundation, referring to the prominence of a “more market, less government” philosophy during the heyday of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan.

“When you want more money, this is what you have to do,” she said.

For Hyder, the changes are like a cool and refreshing breeze from Parliament Hill — especially after the “challenging” decade of the Trudeau government.

“You have at the top someone who understands how investment works,” Hyder said. “He’s sort of become Canada’s best salesman to bring capital into our country, to build the infrastructure and create the jobs that are necessary.

“This is a win-win situation,” he added. “It’s not happening at the expense of anybody. It’s happening because we should have been doing this a long time ago.”

Yet to economists like Katherine Scott, a senior researcher with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, Carney appears to be marching in lockstep with a way of thinking she argues is discredited: that gearing public policy to the benefit of big business will also benefit everyone else.

What’s more, the focus on economic growth appears to put social policies lower down the ladder of federal priorities, Scott said. She pointed to lingering questions about the future of federal pharmacare coverage that the Carney government has not yet expanded, and a recent stopgap decision to extend money for mental health and long-term care for one year while provinces raise concerns about a coming “fiscal cliff” in health care funding.

“I think the central banker has really turned up to govern,” Scott said, referring to Carney’s past as the head of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England.

That economy-first outlook isn’t just decipherable in the big announcements. Quiet changes, published online without fanfare, have also been made in favour of businesses.

One example is a proposal to ditch federal requirements on cannabis retailers to track and report shifts in their inventories, which the government says could save the sector more than $110 million in compliance costs over 10 years. A bill tabled Oct. 7 could save businesses another roughly $250 million over that time span through a range of proposed “red tape” changes, like making it easier for railroads to renew existing exemptions to federal regulations, and recognizing foreign assessments for seeds and animal health products.

Dan Kelly, head of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, said the push to remove red tape is helpful, and that, taken together, can be a big lift for small- and medium-sized firms.

But Kelly said there is still a sense that Ottawa is preoccupied mostly with bigger businesses, with policies like the mega deduction and the fast-tracking of major projects. Data from his own agency has found several quarters running now where more businesses are closing than new ones are opening, he said, suggesting an “entrepreneurial drought” that is still dragging the economy.

“The Carney government has certainly been focused more on the economy and more on business than the Trudeau government was on its best day. But that has been, to this point, focused on the large, corporate side,” Kelly said.

The overall economy also has challenges. Citing inflation driven largely by the spike in energy prices with war in the Middle East, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates this week, and expects prices to keep rising at an annual rate of 3 per cent for much of the next year. The ongoing trade war with the U.S., with Trump threatening to double tariffs on Canadian autos on Jan. 1, is also a source of uncertainty that the Bank of Canada says could “weigh on growth” if businesses decide to delay expansion plans or hiring decisions.

On Friday, Statistics Canada reported economic growth flatlined in August, the second straight month when GDP was “essentially unchanged.”

For David Pierce, vice president of government relations with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, it is clear that Canada must make changes so that it can beat out other countries in the competition for investment in which Carney is playing.

He sees hope in Carney’s major project push, as well as legislation like Bill C-39, which seeks to create new powers to more rapidly approve other development projects while creating rules for the use of a controversial legal provision that allows Ottawa to force striking workers back to talks with employers.

“The paradigm has shifted,” Pierce said, describing the global contest for investment as trade flows are roiled by Trump’s tariffs and jurisdictions jockeying to be the most attractive to private money.

“If we’re not competitive, we aren’t even in the conversation,” he said.

A recent survey of 346 businesses by Kpmg found almost half of businesses will make capital investments larger or sooner because of the government’s mega deduction, but there are still questions about whether Ottawa must go further, possibly with corporate income tax cuts, said Brian Ernewein, a senior adviser and tax expert with Kpmg Canada.

“Under the previous government … taxation was a stick,” Ernewein said, pointing to policies like the carbon tax designed to drive down emissions that cause climate change.

“It did not seem very pro-business. And then I think the current government is really attempting to signal a change in that direction.”

For Bea Bruske, head of the Canadian Labour Congress, that change risks overlooking needs she sees as urgent in a stuttering economy — like increasing jobless benefits and making them more widely available to people without work.

But she also believes that decisions of recent months reveal the character of the current administration. Bill C-39, which is meant to transform federal project assessments to make them faster, also reduces the “leverage” of workers in seeking better wages and job conditions by enshrining Section 107 of the labour code with new rules around its use, Bruske said.

The provision — which the Conservatives, NDP and Bloc Québécois recently voted to remove — allows the federal government to intervene to stop labour disputes.

“They don’t want any speed bumps to getting their agenda through,” Bruske said. “And workers are seen to be speed bumps in exercising their right to strike.”

Scott, from the Ccpa, said the public mood now May favour Carney’s direction. But significant changes are afoot, she said, and the outlook could easily change if concerns like the cost of living, health funding and the climate crisis sharpen before the government takes them more seriously.

That’s especially the case if policies to boost business, like the $36-billion mega deduction, mean other federal programs will take a back seat.

“Do Canadians know what’s coming?” Scott asked. “I don’t think the enormity of what that means has come into focus yet.”
paragraphs: Ottawa—Ensconced in the exclusive company of corporate investors and big money bankers, Prime Minister Mark Carney was in a safe place. And he had an announcement to make.

Canada, his Canada, wants to haul in capital from leading institutions of finance, both public and private, domestic and far-flung. The cash should flow to oil and gas infrastructure, ports, mining projects, new homes, airports run by pension funds — all to “build Canada strong” as it faces a trade crisis, a capricious United States, and a warping world order.

So, at September’s global investment summit , Carney unveiled his government's "mega deduction." At an anticipated cost of $36 billion over five years, the newly generous tax break is the most expensive policy Ottawa has proposed since last spring, according to Parliament’s budget watchdog. It is designed to spur businesses, from fossil fuel companies to heavy manufacturers, to put money into expanding their operations now, thereby juicing economic activity and the almighty GDP.
After Carney spoke, the VIP-only room at a downtown Toronto hotel broke into applause.

A short time later, Goldy Hyder’s inbox pinged with a new message. The head of the Business Council of Canada, a lobby group made up of executives from more than 170 major corporations, checked to see what it said.
It was from his counterpart at Australia’s business council.
“It said, ‘Do you even need to work anymore?’” Hyder recalled this week with a laugh.
It’s funny because, with Carney in the Prime Minister’s Office, that’s basically how it feels.
Days ahead of the second federal budget since Carney took office, his ambition for Canada’s economy is clear.
Donald Trump touted a resurrected pipeline and a ‘concept’ of a trade deal with Canada as Republicans brace for potential losses in key states.

Through a series of reforms, his government has tilted Canadian policy in favour of business. Oil and gas companies have welcomed the rollback of climate policies imposed when Justin Trudeau was in power. Billions of dollars in tax deductions are on the table to make private investment more profitable. New authorities are written into federal law and legislation to shepherd development projects to completion faster, and the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline from Alberta to the British Columbia coast is the first to get the special treatment.

It doesn’t stop there. A rolling review of “red tape” inside the federal government is lifting hundreds of millions of dollars in expected compliance costs for businesses, according to federal officials. Regulatory “sandboxes” have been created and proposed , so companies can be exempt from government rules to test new products. And taxes Ottawa planned or implemented under the Trudeau administration, from the consumer carbon price to a levy on the revenues of online giants , now lie in the policy scrap heap.

Much of this has been met with approbation, especially from those who saw in the previous Liberal government muted enthusiasm — or even antipathy — to the interests and desires of business. Yet it is also proving controversial , with environmentalists, Indigenous nations and union leaders decrying how they believe the government is trampling their priorities in the name of speed and economic growth.

But those are undoubtedly the priorities of this Carney government, and by all accounts the Nov. 5 budget will press on in that direction. The question, both for Canadians and the staying power of the prime minister’s popularity, is whether this agenda is truly — or sufficiently — to the benefit of the broad public.

“We have got the perfect business playbook, written to the letter just the way it was in the 1980s,” said Armine Yalnizyan, an economist and fellow at the Atkinson Foundation, referring to the prominence of a “more market, less government” philosophy during the heyday of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan.
“When you want more money, this is what you have to do,” she said.
For Hyder, the changes are like a cool and refreshing breeze from Parliament Hill — especially after the “challenging” decade of the Trudeau government.

“You have at the top someone who understands how investment works,” Hyder said. “He’s sort of become Canada’s best salesman to bring capital into our country, to build the infrastructure and create the jobs that are necessary.

She pointed to lingering questions about the future of federal pharmacare coverage that the Carney government has not yet expanded, and a recent stopgap decision to extend money for mental health and long-term care for one year while provinces raise concerns about a coming “fiscal cliff” in health care funding.
