stories.summary: London, ON (November 2, 2026) – The London Police Service (LPS) is joining police services and community partners across Ontario to recognize Crime Prevention Week, taking place November 1-7, 2026. This year’s theme, “Protecting Ontario Together,” highlights the important role everyone plays in preventing crime and building safer communities.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 2, 2026) – The London Police Service (LPS) is joining police services and community partners across Ontario to recognize Crime Prevention Week, taking place November 1-7, 2026. This year’s theme, “Protecting Ontario Together,” highlights the important role everyone plays in preventing crime and building safer communities.

Crime prevention is most effective when police, governments, community organizations, businesses, and residents work together. Through education, awareness, reporting, and community engagement, everyone can help reduce victimization and strengthen community safety.

As part of Crime Prevention Week, members of the LPS Crime Prevention Unit will be engaging directly with the community through information displays at local shopping centres.

Residents are encouraged to stop by, speak with officers, ask questions, and learn more about crime prevention resources and community safety initiatives.

Community Displays

Tuesday, November 3, 2026 CF Masonville Place – Centre Court 12:30 p.m. to 2:00 p.m.

Thursday, November 5, 2026 White Oaks Mall – Main Court (in front of Ikea) 10:00 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.

“Community safety is strongest when everyone plays a role,” said A/Inspector Michelle Romano, Community Policing Section. “Crime Prevention Week is an opportunity to share practical safety information, build connections within our community, and encourage residents to take steps to protect themselves and others.

We invite the public to visit us at our community displays throughout the week and to follow the London Police Service on social media as we share crime prevention tips, resources, and information that can help keep our community safe.”

Residents who witness suspicious activity or become victims of crime are encouraged to report it through the appropriate reporting channels. Information shared by the public helps identify patterns, support investigations, and address emerging community safety concerns.

Crime Prevention Week is supported by the Ontario Association of Chiefs of Police (Oacp) and the Government of Ontario.

For more information about Crime Prevention Week initiatives and community safety resources, visit www.londonpolice.CA and follow the London Police Service on social media throughout the week for crime prevention tips and information.

stories.title: Partnerships and a New Funder Allow Expansion of Health Unit Program Supporting Healthy Pregnancies
stories.summary: Home |
stories.content:
Home |

News & Media |

For Immediate Release

London, ON – This morning, community leaders met outside the commercial kitchen at the Huron Street location of the London InterCommunity Health Centre. They were gathered to celebrate the expansion of a 30-year-old program operated by the Middlesex-London Health Unit called Smart Start for Babies. The Health Centre is one of two new sites for a program that supports nearly 200 participants each year.

Smart Start is a weekly prenatal education and nutrition program offered to pregnant individuals who enroll before 30 weeks of pregnancy and continue until the birth of their baby. It offers pregnancy specific nutritional guidance, hands on food preparation and skill building, social connection, and referrals to community services. Public health dietitians and nurses facilitate the programming.

A three-year commitment of more than $200,000 annually from the London Food Bank allowed the program to expand from six groups a week to eight. One is offered at the Huron Street site and welcomes clients of Lihc. The second is offered at BGC London in partnership with Type Diabeat-it and serves members of the African, Caribbean and Black communities.

“Good nutrition is foundational for healthy pregnancy and healthy newborns. For many reasons, not every pregnant individual has access to the nutrition they need during this time. Smart Start for Babies fills an important role – but we couldn’t grow to meet the diverse needs of our community without partnerships like these ones,” says Dr. Alex Summers, Medical Officer of Health at the Middlesex-London Health Unit.

“The London Food Bank firmly believes that an effective response for vulnerable infants is of highest priority in our community. Forty percent of the people we help at the food bank are kids and we believe our community would be heartened to see that we are coming together to put our efforts and resources where our policies and research are. It’s our hope to bring the public, and other groups that support us, onside in the belief that our Health Unit is pivotal to us all, and that partnering with them would present an opening response to the chances of a better and healthier live for these children and their families. The Ssfb program will be the key delivery mechanism, but what caused the coming together as organizations was our belief that our kids deserve better in such an affluent society,” says Jane Roy, Co-Executive Director, London Food Bank.

Within the context of a community in which one in three households experiences food insecurity, programs such as Smart Start for Babies are increasingly important for the reduction of pre-term births and low birth weight, improved infant health outcomes and better maternal health.

stories.title: Ancaster Jewellers was robbed 5 times, including at gunpoint. Now it is closing its Wilson Street store
stories.summary: Ancaster Jewellers will consolidate their business at its Garner Road location in 2027
stories.author: Susan Clairmont
stories.content:
And save the jewelry.

J.P. (as he is called) was quite literally staring down the barrel of a gun. Yet he knew from past experience that if he did not save the jewelry, his insurance policy may not pay and then, while he might be alive, his livelihood would be as good as dead.

So, he fought.

His son, Russell Verbunt, did too. As did a security guard.

It was Dec. 5, 2024, just before closing. A stolen pickup truck smashed through the front window of their shop, Ancaster Jewellers, on Wilson Street. Masked men sledgehammered display cases.

“We had nine people that came through the store, and a guy held a gun to my forehead,” J.P., 63, told The Spectator in a recent interview. “Four or five others were screaming ‘Shoot him. Shoot him.’”

“My dad’s life was at stake,” says Russell. “They were actively bludgeoning him. Something had to be done.”

J.P. Verbunt, owner of Ancaster Jewellers, is pictured inside his store on Wilson Street.

J.P. activated an alarm to call 911 before grabbing a mandrel — a steel rod used to make bracelets — and hurling it at the head of the armed robber.

The gun was an imitation firearm. But J.P. and Russell had no idea it wasn’t real.

Hamilton police recently interrupted a robbery at Eastgate Square, where officers were on patrol

Russell was hit in the back with a sledgehammer. J.P. was struck in the head with a hammer. No customers were in the shop at the time, according to court records.

The robbers fled in a getaway car, but didn’t get far thanks to a police officer who happened to be nearby.

Damage to the store and the stolen goods was valued at $200,000. Plus, the business had to close for the holiday season.

Windows are boarded up at the Ancaster Jewellers store on Wilson Street West following a 2024 robbery.

Recently, three young men, all from Scarborough, were each sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for that robbery.

Not quite a year after that ordeal, the store was hit again . At 3:43 a.m. on Nov. 17, 2025, four masked suspects pried off the door frame and used crowbars to smash display cases. They were in and out in two minutes, causing $40,000 damage and taking $40,000 in jewelry.

Police arrested five people , some of whom were found with stolen goods. They were allegedly tied to similar break-ins around Ontario and Quebec.

In December 2025, police arrested suspects in connection to a recent overnight robbery at Ancaster Jewellers.

Ancaster Jewellers turns 50 in November.

It was started by J.P.’s parents. He worked there during high school before going to Switzerland to become a watchmaker.

In Europe, even in the 80s, jewelry stores were fortresses with bars on their windows.

Here in Canada, protecting these shops is a newer phenomenon.

“We were naïve that it couldn’t happen here, because we are too honest and too respectful of the law,” J.P. says. “Now we’re catching up with the rest of the world.”

Over the decades, Ancaster Jewellers on Wilson Street has been robbed five times — three times at night and twice while J.P. was at the Wilson Street store. Both times a gun was aimed at him.

At 10 a.m. on Christmas Eve 1998, two masked robbers stormed in waving a gun and a hunting knife. They roughed up staff and a customer, kicking them while they lie on the floor. They held a gun to the back of J.P.’s head.

“Where’s the diamonds?” they shouted.

They got away with $250,000 worth of engagement rings, diamond bracelets and gold watches. Shoppers noted the licence plate of their getaway car and 20 minutes later it was stopped by police.

The store closed while police dusted for fingerprints, but by mid-afternoon, J.P. was again serving his customers.

Afterward, the business’s insurance company refused to cover the losses — despite the robbers being criminally convicted — because a security camera malfunctioned.

J.P. sued the insurance company. Five years after the robbery, the Court of Appeal for Ontario ordered the insurance company to pay up.

Ahmad Munir repairs a gold bracelet at Ancaster Jewellers’ Garner Road location, where the business will consolidate early next year.

Jewelry retailers must have controlled, locked doors to qualify for insurance for theft and robberies.

At Ancaster Jewellers’ Wilson Street store , a security guard has been hired to work from now until the end of the holiday season. All the robberies have happened during that time of year.

It will be the final Christmas at that location. Early next year the Wilson Street store will close and merge with the business’s second location on Garner Road. The Verbunts own the Garner Road building and therefore have more control over what security measures they put in place, they say.

At that building, customers are let in through electronic doors. Security measures incorporate hefty planters, bollards, reinforced glass and walls, cameras and a smokescreen machine that can be activated if needed to fill the store with a harmless, but thick, fog.

Russell Verbunt, co-owner of Ancaster Jewellers, says security “is always a concern.” He and his father fought off armed robbers at the Wilson Street store in 2024.

Russell, 34, says he tried other jobs before becoming the third generation of Verbunt jewellers.

“I drove a dump truck, cut grass, worked in machine shops. Nothing was feeling really satisfying for me.”

He entered the family business knowing its inherent dangers.

“Security is always a concern,” he says. “But they’re not pointing a gun at my head because they want to kill me. They’re pointing a gun at my head because they want my jewelry.”

Earlier this month, Ontario Court Justice Jason Little sentenced the men he tried and convicted for the 2024 heist.

In his reasons, he called it “a carefully planned, co-ordinated and highly organized robbery involving multiple participants, multiple vehicles, assigned roles, disguises, weapons and advanced preparation.”

The judge acknowledged daylight jewelry store robberies have become too common. Locally, criminals have targeted stores at Eastgate Square, Mapleview Mall, Burlington Centre Mall and Lime Ridge Mall. In some cases, police have said, the robbers are kids hired by crime rings.

“These offences create understandable fear among business owners, employees and members of the public,” the judge wrote. “Hamilton deserves better.”

Vishaal Suthagar held the gun to J.P.’s head, according to the sentencing decision. He was 20 and a first-time offender. He was born and raised in Scarborough and is the eldest of five children. Vishaal made the honour roll in high school and was the first in his family to attend university, financing it through student loans and part-time jobs. He was in his second year of the criminology program at Toronto Metropolitan University when he was arrested. Vishaal was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm in the commission of the robbery. He will serve six years and eight months in prison.

Arun Thavalingam was 19 and the getaway driver. He had no prior adult criminal record. His parents separated while he was a child in Sri Lanka, then his father disappeared. He and his mother fled to Thailand before coming to Canada in 2017. He graduated high school and completed two years of a university business management program while working part-time. He was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm in the commission of the robbery. He will do six years and 35 days behind bars.

Khapil Suthagar was 18 when he helped plan and carry out the robbery. He had no prior criminal record. He was born in Scarborough and raised by his mother, who relied on government assistance and various jobs to care for her family. He completed high school and was accepted into an accounting program at a post-secondary institution. He wanted a career in banking. Khapil was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm. He must serve six years and four months.

“In a matter of moments, these accused shattered not only the storefront and display cases,” the judge wrote, “but also shattered the sense of safety and security that the complainants were entitled to enjoy while earning their livelihood. The impact of these offences extends well beyond the value of the jewelry stolen.”

J.P. sued the insurance company. Five years after the robbery, the Court of Appeal for Ontario ordered the insurance company to pay up.
Ahmad Munir repairs a gold bracelet at Ancaster Jewellers’ Garner Road location, where the business will consolidate early next year.
Jewelry retailers must have controlled, locked doors to qualify for insurance for theft and robberies.
At Ancaster Jewellers’ Wilson Street store , a security guard has been hired to work from now until the end of the holiday season. All the robberies have happened during that time of year.

It will be the final Christmas at that location. Early next year the Wilson Street store will close and merge with the business’s second location on Garner Road. The Verbunts own the Garner Road building and therefore have more control over what security measures they put in place, they say.

At that building, customers are let in through electronic doors. Security measures incorporate hefty planters, bollards, reinforced glass and walls, cameras and a smokescreen machine that can be activated if needed to fill the store with a harmless, but thick, fog.
Russell Verbunt, co-owner of Ancaster Jewellers, says security “is always a concern.” He and his father fought off armed robbers at the Wilson Street store in 2024.
Russell, 34, says he tried other jobs before becoming the third generation of Verbunt jewellers.
“I drove a dump truck, cut grass, worked in machine shops. Nothing was feeling really satisfying for me.”
He entered the family business knowing its inherent dangers.
“Security is always a concern,” he says. “But they’re not pointing a gun at my head because they want to kill me. They’re pointing a gun at my head because they want my jewelry.”
Earlier this month, Ontario Court Justice Jason Little sentenced the men he tried and convicted for the 2024 heist.

In his reasons, he called it “a carefully planned, co-ordinated and highly organized robbery involving multiple participants, multiple vehicles, assigned roles, disguises, weapons and advanced preparation.”

The judge acknowledged daylight jewelry store robberies have become too common. Locally, criminals have targeted stores at Eastgate Square, Mapleview Mall, Burlington Centre Mall and Lime Ridge Mall. In some cases, police have said, the robbers are kids hired by crime rings.
“These offences create understandable fear among business owners, employees and members of the public,” the judge wrote. “Hamilton deserves better.”

Vishaal Suthagar held the gun to J.P.’s head, according to the sentencing decision. He was 20 and a first-time offender. He was born and raised in Scarborough and is the eldest of five children. Vishaal made the honour roll in high school and was the first in his family to attend university, financing it through student loans and part-time jobs. He was in his second year of the criminology program at Toronto Metropolitan University when he was arrested. Vishaal was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm in the commission of the robbery. He will serve six years and eight months in prison.

Arun Thavalingam was 19 and the getaway driver. He had no prior adult criminal record. His parents separated while he was a child in Sri Lanka, then his father disappeared. He and his mother fled to Thailand before coming to Canada in 2017. He graduated high school and completed two years of a university business management program while working part-time. He was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm in the commission of the robbery. He will do six years and 35 days behind bars.

Khapil Suthagar was 18 when he helped plan and carry out the robbery. He had no prior criminal record. He was born in Scarborough and raised by his mother, who relied on government assistance and various jobs to care for her family. He completed high school and was accepted into an accounting program at a post-secondary institution. He wanted a career in banking. Khapil was convicted of robbery and using an imitation firearm. He must serve six years and four months.

“In a matter of moments, these accused shattered not only the storefront and display cases,” the judge wrote, “but also shattered the sense of safety and security that the complainants were entitled to enjoy while earning their livelihood. The impact of these offences extends well beyond the value of the jewelry stolen.”

stories.title: Lung cancer screening available at LHSC and in the southwest region
stories.summary: November 2, 2026
stories.content:
Photo from left: Dr. Richard Malthaner,Thoracic Surgery Lead, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Division Head of Thoracic Surgery, LHSC; Caroline Rothwell, Clinical Navigator, OLSP; Dr. Narinder Paul, Lead Physician, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Department Head of Medical Imaging, LHSC standing with one of the CT scanners used for lung cancer screening.

November 2, 2026

Since April 2025, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has been the primary southwestern Ontario screening site for the Ontario Lung Screening Program (OLSP). This provincial screening program, overseen by Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario), began with pilots across the province before rolling out in two phases. People across southwestern Ontario who are at increased risk of lung cancer now have greater access to organized lung cancer screening, with screening locations available across the region. The first scans in the southwest region were completed in June 2025, and more than 1,400 participants have since completed screening.

The South West Regional Cancer Program (SWRCP) developed a hub and spoke model when implementing the program in our region with LHSC as the main hub and the following regional partners as the current spokes – St. Joseph’s Health Care London, Strathroy Middlesex General Hospital, St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital, and Listowel Wingham Hospitals Alliance. The hub serves as the main centre in London with the spokes serving as alternate centres to make screening more accessible across southwestern Ontario so eligible participants can have their scan closer to home.

The OLSP clinic operates virtually, with eligibility assessments, education, and navigation provided by phone. Participants attend an OLSP screening location in person for their low-dose CT scan.

To connect with OLSP:

If you have a primary care provider: Talk to them about whether lung cancer screening may be right for you and ask about a referral to the OLSP. If you do not have a primary care provider: Connect with the Thames Valley Family Health Team to connect with a care provider through their centralized intake team. This provider can help you access an assessment for this program. Once referred, you will connect by phone with an OLSP clinical navigator who completes an eligibility assessment. If eligible, the navigator helps arrange a low-dose CT scan at a regional screening location and supports you through the screening process.

2. The clinical navigator helps schedule eligible participants for a low-dose CT scan at an OLSP screening location of their choice. The navigator provides education and support to help participants understand the program, the screening process, and what to expect during a low-dose CT scan if they have not had one before.

Caroline Rothwell, Clinical Navigator, OLSP, shares that she also helps point participants in the direction of smoking cessation opportunities. “We offer education, guidance, and referrals to available community resources to help patients quit smoking, as they progress through the lung screening process.”

There are different pathways a person may find themselves on, depending on the results of the scan, whether they require more imaging, or monitoring, but the program’s navigator will help patients move through the program in the way they need to, making the process as smooth as possible.

You may be eligible for the OLSP if you:

Are between the ages of 55 and 80

Have a smoking history of any amount of commercial tobacco (e.g., cigarettes, cigars, loose tobacco, pipes, or bidi/beedi) daily for 20 years (does not have to be consecutive)

Have Ontario health card (OHIP) coverage

People who meet these initial criteria complete an assessment with the OLSP team to determine whether they are eligible for lung cancer screening and if it is appropriate for them.

As a navigator, Rothwell has seen that many people are hesitant to share their smoking history. “We commonly have patients express feelings of embarrassment, frustration, or a sense that they ‘should know better.’ My goal is to create a supportive, non-judgemental environment where patients feel comfortable discussing their experiences. As healthcare providers, our role is not to pass judgement but to provide patients with the tools, resources, and support they need to improve their health and achieve their goals.”

Many participants experience anxiety related to screening and receiving those results, which is why Rothwell takes additional time to provide reassurance, education, and strategies to make the process as comfortable as possible because screening when eligible is so important.

“Earlier detection increases the chances of curative treatment, including surgery,” says Dr. Narinder Paul, Lead Physician, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Department Head of Medical Imaging, LHSC. “Multiple international trials have demonstrated that lung cancer screening with low dose CT saves lives through earlier disease detection.”

Dr. Richard Malthaner, Thoracic Surgery Lead, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Division Head of Thoracic Surgery, LHSC expands on that noting the role of lung cancer screening is to identify a suspicious lung nodule or possible cancer and move patients quickly from detection to diagnosis and treatment.

“For patients who require surgery, our goal is to provide timely, minimally invasive treatment whenever possible. Just as importantly, we try to guide patients through what can be a very stressful period with clear information and a coordinated plan,” explains Dr. Malthaner.

As a result of this screening program, Dr. Malthaner has seen cancers detected earlier when patients may not have had symptoms and when the cancer was still potentially curable with surgery.

“Ontario data supports what we are seeing clinically in the program – about 78 percent of lung cancers detected through OLSP have been early stage, compared to about 35 per cent diagnosed in the age group from age 55 to 80,” shares Dr. Malthaner. “That represents a major shift. Instead of first meeting some patients after their cancer has already become advanced, screening gives us an opportunity to intervene when the tumour is smaller, localized, and potentially curable.”

Dr. Paul summarizes noting that “earlier detection increases the chances of curative treatment, including surgery.”

Stage of diagnosis is one of the strongest predictors of survival for cancers, including lung cancer.

Dr. Malthaner says “Canadian data demonstrates how important early detection is. For Stage I lung cancer, the five-year survival is about 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent for Stage II, 16 per cent for Stage III, and only three per cent for Stage IV. This is why screening matters – the earlier we find lung cancer; the more options we have to treat it effectively and potentially cure it.”

Access to OLSP is particularly important for the southwest region of Ontario because we serve a large geographic region, including many rural communities, and with the hub and spoke model, this program brings the opportunity to screen for lung cancer closer to home and provides a direct pathway from screening, to diagnosis, to treatment, and to survivorship.

“I want to emphasize this message,” says Dr. Malthaner, “Lung cancer screening saves lives by changing when we find the disease. Finding lung cancer early can transform it from an advanced illness into one that we may be able to cure.”

To learn more about the OLSP, visit the Cancer Care Ontario website .

If eligible, the navigator helps arrange a low-dose CT scan at a regional screening location and supports you through the screening process.

2. The clinical navigator helps schedule eligible participants for a low-dose CT scan at an OLSP screening location of their choice. The navigator provides education and support to help participants understand the program, the screening process, and what to expect during a low-dose CT scan if they have not had one before.

Caroline Rothwell, Clinical Navigator, OLSP, shares that she also helps point participants in the direction of smoking cessation opportunities. “We offer education, guidance, and referrals to available community resources to help patients quit smoking, as they progress through the lung screening process.”

There are different pathways a person may find themselves on, depending on the results of the scan, whether they require more imaging, or monitoring, but the program’s navigator will help patients move through the program in the way they need to, making the process as smooth as possible.
You may be eligible for the OLSP if you:
Are between the ages of 55 and 80
Have a smoking history of any amount of commercial tobacco (e.g., cigarettes, cigars, loose tobacco, pipes, or bidi/beedi) daily for 20 years (does not have to be consecutive)
Have Ontario health card (OHIP) coverage
People who meet these initial criteria complete an assessment with the OLSP team to determine whether they are eligible for lung cancer screening and if it is appropriate for them.

As a navigator, Rothwell has seen that many people are hesitant to share their smoking history. “We commonly have patients express feelings of embarrassment, frustration, or a sense that they ‘should know better.’ My goal is to create a supportive, non-judgemental environment where patients feel comfortable discussing their experiences. As healthcare providers, our role is not to pass judgement but to provide patients with the tools, resources, and support they need to improve their health and achieve their goals.”

Many participants experience anxiety related to screening and receiving those results, which is why Rothwell takes additional time to provide reassurance, education, and strategies to make the process as comfortable as possible because screening when eligible is so important.

“Earlier detection increases the chances of curative treatment, including surgery,” says Dr. Narinder Paul, Lead Physician, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Department Head of Medical Imaging, LHSC. “Multiple international trials have demonstrated that lung cancer screening with low dose CT saves lives through earlier disease detection.”

Dr. Richard Malthaner, Thoracic Surgery Lead, OLSP, SWRCP and Chair/Division Head of Thoracic Surgery, LHSC expands on that noting the role of lung cancer screening is to identify a suspicious lung nodule or possible cancer and move patients quickly from detection to diagnosis and treatment.

“For patients who require surgery, our goal is to provide timely, minimally invasive treatment whenever possible. Just as importantly, we try to guide patients through what can be a very stressful period with clear information and a coordinated plan,” explains Dr. Malthaner.
As a result of this screening program, Dr. Malthaner has seen cancers detected earlier when patients may not have had symptoms and when the cancer was still potentially curable with surgery.

“Ontario data supports what we are seeing clinically in the program – about 78 percent of lung cancers detected through OLSP have been early stage, compared to about 35 per cent diagnosed in the age group from age 55 to 80,” shares Dr. Malthaner. “That represents a major shift. Instead of first meeting some patients after their cancer has already become advanced, screening gives us an opportunity to intervene when the tumour is smaller, localized, and potentially curable.”
Dr. Paul summarizes noting that “earlier detection increases the chances of curative treatment, including surgery.”
Stage of diagnosis is one of the strongest predictors of survival for cancers, including lung cancer.

Dr. Malthaner says “Canadian data demonstrates how important early detection is. For Stage I lung cancer, the five-year survival is about 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent for Stage II, 16 per cent for Stage III, and only three per cent for Stage IV. This is why screening matters – the earlier we find lung cancer; the more options we have to treat it effectively and potentially cure it.”

Access to OLSP is particularly important for the southwest region of Ontario because we serve a large geographic region, including many rural communities, and with the hub and spoke model, this program brings the opportunity to screen for lung cancer closer to home and provides a direct pathway from screening, to diagnosis, to treatment, and to survivorship.

“I want to emphasize this message,” says Dr. Malthaner, “Lung cancer screening saves lives by changing when we find the disease. Finding lung cancer early can transform it from an advanced illness into one that we may be able to cure.”
To learn more about the OLSP, visit the Cancer Care Ontario website .

stories.title: Canada seeks full participation in the EU’s Erasmus+ program
stories.summary: As Ottawa and the EU explore ways of working closer together, negotiations are now underway to make Canada a full participant in the Erasmus+ program.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
Ottawa – For first year student Riley Alliman, the possibility of studying in Europe one day is an exciting proposition.

“I think I would gain better connections in the world and advance my career,” she said.

Alliman is a student of biopharmaceutical science at the University of Ottawa, and she said her hope is to become a medical researcher.

Adding that the opportunity to conduct some of her studies in a European Union country would allow her to broaden her expertise and learn how scientists elsewhere approach the same challenges.

“It allows us to further our knowledge in how other places are doing things, versus how maybe here we have different ideas of how we might do research in things like Parkinson’s, because that’s what I’m really into,” she said.

It’s that kind of enthusiasm that officials hope will fuel interest in the EU’s student scholarship program known as Erasmus+, in which Canada already participates. But as Ottawa and the EU explore ways of working closer together, negotiations are now underway to make Canada a full participant in the program.

If that happened, it would mean Canadian students would have access to grants and scholarships that would allow them to study in an EU country. It could also facilitate more transatlantic co-operation and research partnerships. That in turn could lead to economic growth, which is one reason why Canada and the EU are coming together in the first place.

“Ultimately, students gain from those experiences, and that certainly will influence perhaps their own trajectories in the future,” said Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Studies. “But we’re also talking about strengthening Canada’s talent pipeline while building lasting connections with Europe that support research, innovation, and ultimately economic growth.”

Jeremy Kinsman, a former Canadian ambassador to the EU, says the exchange is also a useful tool for bringing citizens of Canada and the European bloc closer together.

“It was always at the foundation of the European political project that if you get people to work together,” he said, “Then you’ll forge a sense of functional achievement much more easily. You’re not strangers anymore. You’re partners.”

Partners that work together in research, technology and industry, but also share values that are increasingly challenged around the world.

“I think when they’re talking about values, people think of democracy and civil rule by law,” said Kinsman. “But it’s much more than that. It’s internationalist values of co-operation, which Canada has been committed to since the end of the Second World War. The building of an international system that’s institutional, that enables countries to come together to do what they have to do.”

“No one country can do that alone, and they do much better in concert,” he added.

Still, there are questions about cost, and how much Canada would have to pay to participate in the Erasmus+ program.

Talks are now underway, as Canadian and EU officials also explore a potential “associate EU membership” for Canada.

stories.title: Yukon seeks federal funding to shore up aging power grid
stories.summary: Territory’s ratepayers cannot afford to shoulder costs of upgrades and repairs, Energy Minister says
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Yukon ’s government is urging Ottawa to help pay for urgent upgrades to the territory’s aging power grid, warning that residents face massive rate hikes absent federal intervention.

Ted Laking, the territory’s Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has asked the federal government to pay three-quarters of the cost of upgrading Yukon’s grid, a scheme dubbed the Arctic Sovereignty Grid Plan; his government would cover the rest.

“We cannot afford to make these investments on our own, and neither can our ratepayers,” Mr. Laking testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs last week.

“It would be unreasonable to expect a small northern population that’s half the size of Sault Ste. Marie to shoulder those full costs on their own.”

Earlier this year, the Yukon Energy Board approved rate increases of 34 per cent over a three-year period. Mr. Laking estimates rates must rise an additional 53 per cent to pay for urgent repairs and upgrades.

Mr. Laking told The Globe and Mail he submitted a collection of energy projects dubbed the Arctic Sovereignty Grid Plan to the federal government for consideration as a project of national interest. But whereas other project proponents hope the Major Projects Office can speed up regulatory approvals, he’s more interested in accessing funding across disparate federal sources.

“We’ve received, I would say, encouraging feedback.”

But it’s just one of a deluge of power projects vying for federal support, from nuclear power plants in Saskatchewan and offshore wind farms around Nova Scotia.

The list of needed repairs and upgrades for Yukon’s power grid is lengthy and growing. Mr. Laking noted that the territory bears responsibility for not intervening sooner, and vowed to change how the government plans work on existing and future assets.

“If you know something was built in the 1950s, you shouldn’t be surprised that in 2026 it’s getting to the end of its life,” he said.

“If these costs had been addressed a decade ago, or planned more appropriately, we wouldn’t be dealing with as urgent a situation.”

Yukon’s generation capacity is only about 160 megawatts, smaller than single power plants found in many provinces. Three hydroelectric dams account for most of it: Whitehorse, Aishihik and Mayo. Yukon Energy also has 65 megawatts of diesel generators in Whitehorse, Faro, Mayo and Dawson, some of them rented.

All this faces rising stress. The territory’s population grew by more than one-quarter between 2014 and 2024. Demand is rising further as electricity replaces fossil fuels for heating and transportation, a trend Yukon Energy, the Crown generation and transmission utility, expects will continue. Its grid is isolated from the rest of the continent, meaning it cannot import electricity during shortfalls.

Yukon’s power demand is nearly three times higher in winter than summer. It reached a record high during a December, 2025, cold snap, rising above 90 per cent of generating capacity. Rolling blackouts were averted after standby diesel generators kicked in, and residents and mining operations shifted power consumption to off-peak periods.

The Mayo hydro facility, commissioned in 1952, is in dire condition. According to filings from Yukon Energy, its spillway has deteriorated beyond repair; engineering studies have found that it’s at risk of imminent failure, which could cause serious, potentially life-threatening flooding in nearby Mayo, a village of about 200 residents. Mr. Laking estimates the total repair bill at $400-million.

Prime Minister Mark Carney outlines his government's plan to double electricity generation by 2050, a plan that includes linking provincial grids to meet increasing electricity deman…

Yukon Energy planned to connect a $35-million Whitehorse battery-storage system to the grid this year, describing it as “crucial” for improving grid stability. But the batteries froze during last December’s cold snap after generators that had been keeping them warm failed. In early October, Yukon Energy reported that the manufacturer, LG Energy Solution, was testing the batteries to assess the damage.

“We believe that there is something that’s salvageable there, but of course this is not ideal,” Mr. Laking said.

It’s a reminder that technologies designed for lower latitudes can struggle in extreme northern environments.

Energy think tanks, such as the Pembina Institute, promote adoption of renewable generation throughout the North to replace diesel generators. But the Yukon government says it has already reached the limits of its ability to incorporate renewables.

Mr. Laking said the territory’s solar facilities actually drew more power than they generated during the cold snap, owing to the energy used to heat them. Wind generation “works fine in the cold,” he added, but Yukon can’t rely on it because it’s not necessarily generating power when power is most needed.

Yukon’s immediate plans include building more diesel generators in Whitehorse, with the first expected to enter service in 2028. All told, its plan would add 150 megawatts of fossil fuel capacity, at an estimated cost of $560-million.

Yukon also wants to hook up to the North American grid. The government’s preferred solution: a high-voltage transmission line running roughly 800 kilometers from Bob Quinn Lake, B.C., north into the Yukon. The government estimates the cost of the Yukon-B.C. Grid Connect at $4-billion.

Earlier this year, Ottawa unveiled a national electricity strategy that emphasized connecting provinces and territories through new and expanded transmission lines. In June, the government identified the Yukon-B.C. Grid Connect among five prioritized intertie projects.

But Mr. Laking said the intertie would likely take at least a decade to construct, in part because Yukon’s antiquated grid does not meet continental standards.

“It doesn’t get us out of these short- and medium-term challenges that we have right now,” he said.
paragraphs: Yukon ’s government is urging Ottawa to help pay for urgent upgrades to the territory’s aging power grid, warning that residents face massive rate hikes absent federal intervention.

Ted Laking, the territory’s Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has asked the federal government to pay three-quarters of the cost of upgrading Yukon’s grid, a scheme dubbed the Arctic Sovereignty Grid Plan; his government would cover the rest.

“We cannot afford to make these investments on our own, and neither can our ratepayers,” Mr. Laking testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs last week.
“It would be unreasonable to expect a small northern population that’s half the size of Sault Ste. Marie to shoulder those full costs on their own.”

Earlier this year, the Yukon Energy Board approved rate increases of 34 per cent over a three-year period. Mr. Laking estimates rates must rise an additional 53 per cent to pay for urgent repairs and upgrades.

Mr. Laking told The Globe and Mail he submitted a collection of energy projects dubbed the Arctic Sovereignty Grid Plan to the federal government for consideration as a project of national interest. But whereas other project proponents hope the Major Projects Office can speed up regulatory approvals, he’s more interested in accessing funding across disparate federal sources.
“We’ve received, I would say, encouraging feedback.”
But it’s just one of a deluge of power projects vying for federal support, from nuclear power plants in Saskatchewan and offshore wind farms around Nova Scotia.

The list of needed repairs and upgrades for Yukon’s power grid is lengthy and growing. Mr. Laking noted that the territory bears responsibility for not intervening sooner, and vowed to change how the government plans work on existing and future assets.
“If you know something was built in the 1950s, you shouldn’t be surprised that in 2026 it’s getting to the end of its life,” he said.
“If these costs had been addressed a decade ago, or planned more appropriately, we wouldn’t be dealing with as urgent a situation.”

Yukon’s generation capacity is only about 160 megawatts, smaller than single power plants found in many provinces. Three hydroelectric dams account for most of it: Whitehorse, Aishihik and Mayo. Yukon Energy also has 65 megawatts of diesel generators in Whitehorse, Faro, Mayo and Dawson, some of them rented.

All this faces rising stress. The territory’s population grew by more than one-quarter between 2014 and 2024. Demand is rising further as electricity replaces fossil fuels for heating and transportation, a trend Yukon Energy, the Crown generation and transmission utility, expects will continue. Its grid is isolated from the rest of the continent, meaning it cannot import electricity during shortfalls.

Yukon’s power demand is nearly three times higher in winter than summer. It reached a record high during a December, 2025, cold snap, rising above 90 per cent of generating capacity. Rolling blackouts were averted after standby diesel generators kicked in, and residents and mining operations shifted power consumption to off-peak periods.

The Mayo hydro facility, commissioned in 1952, is in dire condition. According to filings from Yukon Energy, its spillway has deteriorated beyond repair; engineering studies have found that it’s at risk of imminent failure, which could cause serious, potentially life-threatening flooding in nearby Mayo, a village of about 200 residents. Mr. Laking estimates the total repair bill at $400-million.

But the batteries froze during last December’s cold snap after generators that had been keeping them warm failed. “We believe that there is something that’s salvageable there, but of course this is not ideal,” Mr. Laking said.

But Mr. Laking said the intertie would likely take at least a decade to construct, in part because Yukon’s antiquated grid does not meet continental standards.
“It doesn’t get us out of these short- and medium-term challenges that we have right now,” he said.

stories.title: Minister backs 2027 fixed election date as Elections Alberta suggests change
stories.summary: A contentious report is set to be released this week on new electoral boundaries that the NDP previously said gerrymanders ridings in two cities.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Alberta’s justice minister is pouring cold water on Elections Alberta’s request to delay the next provincial election as concerns over changes to electoral boundaries continue.

In a letter to Elections Alberta, Justice Minister Mickey Amery said the government has “no intention of changing” the date of the provincial election, which is legislated to take place on or before Oct. 18, 2027.

“Alberta’s fixed election date is established by law and provides Albertans with certainty and predictability concerning the democratic process,” wrote Amery.

His letter was in response to Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure, who wrote to Speaker Ric McIver suggesting the election either be held with the current electoral boundaries or be postponed.

McClure said in a letter, shared by the Opposition NDP, that either option would give the elections body sufficient time to hold the vote with integrity and safeguards in place.

A contentious report is set to be released this week on new electoral boundaries that the NDP previously said amount to gerrymandering in two cities in southern Alberta – Lethbridge and Calgary.

Gerrymandering, a practice more often seen in the U.S. than in Canada, involves designing voting districts not to reflect geography or population patterns, but to concentrate or fragment voters to benefit a political party.

Though the report has yet to be released, Opposition Leader Naheed Nenshi made the gerrymandering allegation after he was briefed on the report.

Two members of the committee that wrote the report also said the suggested ridings draw a line between rural and urban voters.

The report has been put before an all-party legislative committee and is set to be tabled Monday in the legislature. But McClure cautioned that disagreements could create delays.

A typical provincial vote, McClure said, requires up to 18 months of preparations. He added his agency has been stretched thin.

Amery argued in his letter that the legislature will consider the full report and determine the final electoral boundaries before the end of the fall sitting.

“That timetable will provide your office with approximately 320 days (about 11 full months) to prepare for and administer the next provincial election,” Amery wrote.

He added Alberta law doesn’t guarantee Elections Alberta “lengthy advance notice” of a general election.

In 2024, Smith’s government moved the fixed election date every four years from May to October to avoid clashing with major natural disasters like wildfires or floods which are more common in the spring in Alberta.

stories.title: DNA test leads Toronto performer to 35 half-siblings
stories.summary: A DNA test purchased on sale led Toronto performer Noam Tomaschoff to discover he was donor-conceived and had at least 35 half-siblings. He has turned the unexpected family discovery into a new musical, Our Little Secret, running Nov. 3 to 22 in Toronto.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
A DNA test bought on sale led to a discovery that would change one Toronto performer’s understanding of his family and eventually inspire a musical.

At 31, Noam Tomaschoff learned that the man he had grown up calling his father was not his biological father and that he had been conceived using a sperm donor. But that was only the beginning of the surprises.

After taking a consumer DNA test, Tomaschoff discovered he had at least 35 half-siblings around the world, a revelation that has since become the inspiration for Our Little Secret: A True New Musical .

Speaking on CTV’s Your Morning on Wednesday, Tomaschoff said the decision to take the test was not driven by any particular suspicion.

“Absolutely nothing other than the fact that it was on sale.”

A family secret comes to light

Tomaschoff said his parents initially questioned why he wanted to take the test. Realizing they would have to explain the circumstances of his birth before the results arrived, they decided to tell him the truth.

“They sat me down together, and we were on the table, and we all held hands, and this is when I knew something was wrong,” he recalled.

The conversation was an emotional surprise, particularly because his parents had never intended to reveal the secret, Tomaschoff added.

He said his immediate reaction was one of complete disbelief.

“The reaction was total surprise. I was shocked,” he said.

Tomaschoff said his parents had followed the general clinical guidance of the time, which encouraged some families not to disclose donor conception to their children. They were also concerned about preserving his sense of connection to them and the family.

“My first instinct, once I could gather the words, was to tell my friends about it,” he said.

From 35 siblings to the stage

The DNA results initially connected Tomaschoff with 15 close relatives. That number eventually grew as he found more siblings through other platforms.

Although he has not connected with all of them, many are part of a Facebook group, and one lives close enough that they regularly spend time together.

For someone who grew up as an only child, discovering such a large extended family was an unexpected turn.

The revelation left Tomaschoff with a story he felt compelled to share, even if he wasn’t initially sure how to tell it.

“I need to tell somebody. I need to tell this story.”

He eventually began discussing the idea with two of his high school friends, Ryan Peters and Russell Citron, who would become his collaborators on the project.

Rather than simply recounting the experience on stage, the trio decided to turn it into something more theatrical.

“This should be a musical,” Citron told Tomaschoff.

The idea made sense for the longtime friends, who shared a love of musicals and a history of singing together. Their unusual story would eventually become Our Little Secret, A True New Musical.

An opportunity to perform at the Toronto Fringe Festival, secured through a lottery, gave them a deadline to bring the production to life.

They secured a spot through the festival’s lottery, giving them a July 2023 performance date to work toward. What had started as conversations between three longtime friends was now something they had to write, develop and bring to the stage.

Our Little Secret: A True New Musical runs from Nov. 3 to 22 at Toronto’s CAA Theatre.

At 31, Noam Tomaschoff learned that the man he had grown up calling his father was not his biological father and that he had been conceived using a sperm donor. But that was only the beginning of the surprises.

After taking a consumer DNA test, Tomaschoff discovered he had at least 35 half-siblings around the world, a revelation that has since become the inspiration for Our Little Secret: A True New Musical .

content_blocks.alt: Noam Tomaschoff
content_blocks.caption: Noam Tomaschoff's Our Little Secret: A True New Musical poster. Source mirvish.com

content_blocks.text: Speaking on CTV’s Your Morning on Wednesday, Tomaschoff said the decision to take the test was not driven by any particular suspicion.
“Absolutely nothing other than the fact that it was on sale.”
A family secret comes to light

Tomaschoff said his parents initially questioned why he wanted to take the test. Realizing they would have to explain the circumstances of his birth before the results arrived, they decided to tell him the truth.
“They sat me down together, and we were on the table, and we all held hands, and this is when I knew something was wrong,” he recalled.
The conversation was an emotional surprise, particularly because his parents had never intended to reveal the secret, Tomaschoff added.

content_blocks.alt: Noam Tomaschoff
content_blocks.caption: Noam Tomaschoff performing Our Little Secret: A True New Musical. Photo courtesy of mirvish.com and Amanda Chieco

content_blocks.text: He said his immediate reaction was one of complete disbelief.
“The reaction was total surprise. I was shocked,” he said.

Tomaschoff said his parents had followed the general clinical guidance of the time, which encouraged some families not to disclose donor conception to their children. They were also concerned about preserving his sense of connection to them and the family.

content_blocks.alt: Noam Tomaschoff and his father Gideon
content_blocks.caption: Noam Tomaschoff and his father Gideon

content_blocks.text: “My first instinct, once I could gather the words, was to tell my friends about it,” he said.
From 35 siblings to the stage
The DNA results initially connected Tomaschoff with 15 close relatives. That number eventually grew as he found more siblings through other platforms.
Although he has not connected with all of them, many are part of a Facebook group, and one lives close enough that they regularly spend time together.
For someone who grew up as an only child, discovering such a large extended family was an unexpected turn.

content_blocks.alt: Noam Tomaschoff
content_blocks.caption: Noam Tomaschoff and his siblings

content_blocks.text: The revelation left Tomaschoff with a story he felt compelled to share, even if he wasn’t initially sure how to tell it.
“I need to tell somebody. I need to tell this story.”
He eventually began discussing the idea with two of his high school friends, Ryan Peters and Russell Citron, who would become his collaborators on the project.
Rather than simply recounting the experience on stage, the trio decided to turn it into something more theatrical.
“This should be a musical,” Citron told Tomaschoff.
The idea made sense for the longtime friends, who shared a love of musicals and a history of singing together. Their unusual story would eventually become Our Little Secret, A True New Musical.
An opportunity to perform at the Toronto Fringe Festival, secured through a lottery, gave them a deadline to bring the production to life.

They secured a spot through the festival’s lottery, giving them a July 2023 performance date to work toward. What had started as conversations between three longtime friends was now something they had to write, develop and bring to the stage.
Our Little Secret: A True New Musical runs from Nov. 3 to 22 at Toronto’s CAA Theatre.

stories.title: Brault-Guillard helps Supra du Quebec past Cavalry 2-1; Atletico Ottawa, Forge draw
stories.summary: Laval - An own goal by Cavalry midfielder Eryk Kobza was costly as Supra du Quebec held on for a 2-1 win over the Calgary-based side on Sunday in the first leg of their Canadian Premier League semifinal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Laval - An own goal by Cavalry midfielder Eryk Kobza was costly as Supra du Quebec held on for a 2-1 win over the Calgary-based side on Sunday in the first leg of their Canadian Premier League semifinal.

Zachary Brault-Guillard opened scoring for Supra du Quebec in the fourth minute before Kobza’s error gave them a 2-0 lead in the ninth minute.

Tobias Warschewski replied for Cavalry in injury time before intermission.

In the other semifinal, Ballou Tabla’s goal in the 43rd minute tied the game up as Atletico Ottawa earned a 2-2 draw with Hamilton’s Forge FC.

Diego Guitterez had the other Ottawa goal in the 23rd minute.

Anthony Aromatario scored in the 15th minute for the early Forge lead and then defender Marko Jevremovic gave the Hamilton club another lead at the 35th minute.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta emergency physician and health care advocate seeks NDP nomination
stories.summary: Dr. Paul Parks wants to represent the reliably conservative riding of Cypress-Medicine Hat, a seat currently held by Justin Wright, Minister of Primary and Preventative Health Services
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Alberta emergency physician Paul Parks, a long-time health care advocate and prominent critic of the UCP government, never imagined himself entering politics. But now he’s doing just that.

On Sunday, Dr. Parks announced that he is seeking the Alberta New Democratic Party nomination for the riding of Cypress-Medicine Hat, a reliably conservative electoral district in southeast Alberta. The seat is currently held by the United Conservative Party’s Justin Wright, who serves as Minister of Primary and Preventative Health Services.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, in a statement, said Dr. Parks is an “extraordinary candidate” and would help, if elected, drive the party’s health care policy. Dr. Parks, however, May have to fight for the party position should others put their name forward.

Dr. Parks has spent the past two decades pushing for a better health care system for workers and patients, including as the past president of the Alberta Medical Association. He said he’s frustrated with the provincial government ignoring the voices of front-line workers while the state of emergency departments (EDs) continues to crumble.

“Advocating within the normal channels and through the AMA and through my roles as a physician are broken,” said Dr. Parks. “I don’t want to be a politician, but I think the only way to afford meaningful change now, in the current environment, is to run for politics.”

Dr. Parks has been a staunch critic of Premier Danielle Smith and her government’s handling of the health care file, opposing, for example, the Ucp’s venture into private health care delivery and its dismantlement of Alberta Health Services as the single health authority.

One of his chief criticisms has been the Ucp’s inaction to address severe overcrowding in provincial EDs. In January, he led a call to action from doctors working in Edmonton’s major hospitals for Alberta to declare a formal emergency after the death of Prashant Sreekumar. He died on Dec. 22 after spending eight hours in one of the city’s EDs.

Also in January, Dr. Parks collected a list of at least six preventable deaths and more than 30 “near-misses” that occurred in Alberta emergency rooms, which he said underscored how precarious the situation had grown for health care professionals and patients.

“I think we can change the path we’re on,” Dr. Parks said. “I want to try to improve day-to-day life. I don’t want to be just sitting in the back trying to advocate and be critical. I want to roll up my sleeves and try to make it better.”

The UCP government has strongly pushed back against his critiques, arguing that improvements have been made in health care delivery, while acknowledging that there is still work to do. Last week, Ms. Smith said the health system is “better prepared than ever” to handle respiratory virus season, which tests hospital capacity each year.

Dr. Parks said, in addition to his frustrations growing over what he said is government inaction to fix the health system, the Ucp’s use of the Canadian Constitution’s notwithstanding clause pushed him to enter the political ring. He disagrees with the Ucp’s “top-down approach.”

The clause – historically viewed to be a last resort – allows governments to override certain sections of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms for up to five years. The UCP used it to shield its trio of laws affecting transgender youth from court challenges and to order teachers back to work last year.

Alberta’s NDP has been gaining political momentum in recent months after capitalizing on opposition to the recent referendum on separatism. One sign of growth came in September when the NDP flipped a conservative stronghold riding with a win in the Calgary-Shaw by-election .

But in areas like Cypress-Medicine Hat, the NDP will face a steep challenge winning local support. In the referendum, electors in the area voted yes to all nine of Ms. Smith’s proposals to challenge the federal government on immigration and constitutional issues.

The NDP strongly rejected the referendum and advocated for Albertans to say No to all nine questions, underscoring a stark division of opinions.

Dr. Parks, who describes himself as “fiscally conservative and socially progressive,” acknowledged that it would be a difficult task to rally support for the NDP in his community but said his deep connections in the region give him a leg up. He said his values on health care and beyond align with the NDP.

“You don’t join the battle when you know the war is won. You jump in and join when you think you can help win the battle,” he said.

Dr. Parks moved to Medicine Hat from Edmonton in 2009 with his wife and two kids and has, since then, cared for patients at the Medicine Hat Regional Hospital. He also co-founded the city’s first craft brewery, Hell’s Basement Brewery, in 2016 and is an active member of Medicine Hat’s local theatre community.

He said his neighbours are more concerned about the daily pressures of everyday life – the cost of groceries, health care access and school funding – than the contentious issues outlined in the referendum.

“They want government that works to make their community better,” he said. “They want to be able to have a family physician in their community. They want ambulances, when they call, to respond in time so loved ones don’t die waiting.”

Mr. Nenshi said the NDP has a “real plan” for health care focused on reducing waiting lists and ED congestion and hiring more family doctors.

Alberta’s next general election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.

stories.title: Next mayor of Niagara Falls calls for community consultations on Ford’s casino plan
stories.summary: The Premier is seeking up to three new casino operators for the region as Ontario aims to spur tourism
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford should consult with Niagara Falls residents about his plan to bring more casinos to the region, the city’s incoming mayor says, citing some community concerns about the viability of expanding the gambling industry.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail, Lori Lococo, who was elected mayor in the Oct. 26 municipal election, said she supports increasing tourism but added that the community should have a chance to give feedback about the province’s plans to spur development in Niagara.

Ms. Lococo, a 56-year-old two-term city councillor who focused her campaign on affordability, beat 16-year incumbent Jim Diodati. She is to be sworn into office on Nov. 16.

Ms. Lococo said voters wanted to see change in the city of about 100,000, known for its spectacular waterfalls and tourist attractions. Niagara Falls currently has two casinos, but the region has also struggled with changing visitor habits in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Mr. Ford has made boosting tourism in the region one of his priorities, releasing a multi-billion dollar “Destination Niagara” strategy last December with the goal of attracting 25 million annual visitors and doubling the region’s tourism to generate an additional $3-billion for Ontario’s GDP each year.

The government said the plan – which includes additional “world-class gaming,” culinary experiences, and arts and culture, as well as an expanded airport – will lead to billions of dollars in growth for the provincial economy, as well as tens of thousands of jobs.

But the focus on gambling, including more Las Vegas-style casinos, has also raised questions about the government’s priorities and added to general concerns around the proliferation of online gambling, as well as the need for community consultation.

Last week, the Ontario government announced it would be slashing the gambling tax rate in Niagara as it issued a call for investors for up to three new casino operators.

Ms. Lococo said the province has heard from the tourism industry, experts and investors on it Destination Niagara strategy.

“Now, I think we need input from our residents. It’s really important that the residents feel heard,” she said, noting that before the first casino opened in Niagara Falls in 1996, there was a local referendum.

“I’m not saying that we need a referendum. But what I’m saying is, that the residents want to be heard, and they’re wondering why they haven’t been asked yet about their feelings and how it’s going to impact them.”

She said she will be reaching out to Mr. Ford’s office to ask how residents can offer feedback, either through open houses, surveys or other means. The province has given casino operators until Dec. 3 to show interest in the region, and will then choose shortlisted proponents who will be able to enter a competitive process to submit detailed proposals for new casino developments.

Ms. Lococo said the Premier called her after her win last week to congratulate her, but they did not discuss substantial issues.

She said among residents’ concerns are falling revenues for traditional casinos and job losses.

“A lot of casino cities are seeing the same decreases,” she said.

“It changes their city when a lot of people lose their jobs. So people are concerned about, if we bring more casinos here, how is that going to work itself out when there’s already a decrease in spending.”

Addictiveness of online gambling is also an issue she wants to see addressed.

“A lot of young people are getting so in debt because of this online gaming, it wrecks their financial future,” she said.

In addition, there are questions about infrastructure needs and traffic if tourism increases substantially, she said.

Scott Clark, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Tourism, Culture and Gaming Minister Zee Hamid, said the government is championing the region as a premier tourist destination, including by making the “gaming environment more competitive.”

“We will continue to engage with municipal leaders, including Mayor-elect Lori Lococo, as well as Indigenous communities, industry partners and community members as we deliver on our plan to double the number of annual visitors to more than 25 million, generate $3 billion annually for Ontario’s GDP and create 46,500 new jobs across the region,” he said in a statement.

Born and raised in Niagara Falls, Ms. Lococo worked for more than 25 years in the legal field as an administrator and clerk before running for council in 2018.

Ms. Lococo said she agrees with the province that the tourism sector is incredibly important. She said plans for the area should strike a balance between attractions, natural beauty, gambling, restaurants and entertainment.

“I don’t think that people really want to be considered a gaming city. It could be part of a bigger picture,” she said. “But it’s also people’s homes.”

stories.title: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon to meet with Mark Carney after Canada-EU summit tension
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has agreed to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney before the Francophonie Summit in November.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has agreed to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney before the Francophonie Summit in November.

St-Pierre Plamondon made the announcement in a social media post, and it comes after days of tension between the two leaders.

St-Pierre Plamondon did not attend the Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal last week after Ottawa refused to grant him official speaking rights.

Carney told daily newspaper La Presse in an interview published Saturday that he wanted to meet St-Pierre Plamondon to set common goals and ensure good relations between Ottawa and Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon, who became premier after his Parti Québécois won a minority government in last month’s provincial election, thanked Carney for what he called his change of tone.

He said he was accepting the invitation as long as the meeting took place in Quebec City.

Quebec’s separatist movement knows exactly what it’s doing. It won’t pass up a single chance to turn a slight from Ottawa into something that

“Unsurprisingly, I simply ask that this meeting be held in accordance with Quebec law, specifically the Act Respecting the National Capital Commission, which stipulates that meetings of this nature must take place in Quebec City,” wrote St-Pierre Plamondon.

The Canada-EU summit, which took place on Thursday and Friday, brought together Canadian and European leaders including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The federal government said that St-Pierre Plamondon had been invited to dinner with EU representatives, but had not been given a speaking role at the summit.

St-Pierre Plamondon accused Ottawa of muzzling him.

“The federal government would have us believe that giving the Quebec premier permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence in representing Quebec’s interests,” he wrote on social media on Tuesday.

He later announced he would not be attending the summit, sending newly-appointed chief diplomat Pascal Paradis in his place.

“He was invited to the dinner and he refused,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa, also on Tuesday. “It’s his decision to leave the chair empty.”

In his post on Sunday, St-Pierre Plamandon looked back on the summit, writing that Quebec was “relegated to the status of an extra” and that the federal government had not recognized the province’s “existence and right to be at the discussion table.”

St-Pierre Plamondon also did not attend the First Nations-First Ministers meeting in Ottawa early last week, saying he wanted to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples.

The Francophonie Summit, scheduled for Nov. 14–16, will take place in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. St-Pierre Plamondon is set to lead the Quebec delegation there.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Veteran whose daughter died in military training exercise named Silver Cross Mother
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks’ family has a long history of military service and she served in the Canadian Armed Forces for 29 years.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A veteran whose daughter died during a military training exercise in 2002 has been named the 2026 National Silver Cross Mother.

The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks will place a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Nov. 11, an annual tradition on behalf of Canadian mothers who have lost a child serving in the Canadian military.

Hicks’ daughter Mariebeth Short died on Sept. 23, 2002 during a training exercise in Petawawa, Ont., when the light armoured vehicle she was training in rolled over.

The Royal Canadian Legion says Hicks’ family has a long history of military service and she served in the Canadian Armed Forces for 29 years, working in supply and logistics.

This year’s Remembrance Day ceremony comes just weeks after four Canadian soldiers were killed and dozens more were injured during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed in a grass fire last month.

Strong, sudden winds propelled the nearby fire toward 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry who were conducting two exercises in the military base’s training area, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy with support from the RCMP.

Hicks says she has much in common with all mothers who have lost a child serving in the military.

“We all share the same sorrow, we all share the same bravery, and same love and respect for our children as we do for any other child who has passed,” she said in a statement.

stories.title: Amid criticism, Toronto police say they couldn’t arrest Bridle Path suspect at the hospital
stories.summary: Police say evidence to arrest Daijohn Richards came the day after he was discharged
stories.author: National Post staff
stories.content:
Toronto Police are moving to address what they call “confusion” about why a suspect in the violent Bridle Path home invasion that injured a family of four was allowed to leave the hospital after being treated for a gunshot wound himself.

Police are asking the public for help in finding Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto. The other two suspects were described as being in their 20s but have not been identified. Richards is believed to have been shot accidentally by one of the attackers.

Toronto police inspector Kristy Smith told reporters Saturday morning that police had spoken to Richards prior to him being discharged from hospital late Thursday morning. She added that police gathered evidence to arrest him by evening on Friday.

Amid social media criticism of the decision not to detain him, Toronto police issued a statement late Saturday afternoon.

“We want to address some confusion surrounding the investigation into the home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood,” police said in the statement.

“Investigators immediately recognized the potential connection between the home invasion and the individual who showed up at hospital with a gunshot wound. But recognizing a potential suspect and having enough evidence to arrest them are two different things.”

“Police need reasonable grounds, supported by evidence, to make an arrest,” it added.

The statement, which was posted on X with replies turned off, was nevertheless flooded with fierce opposition among users.

“There is no realm of the universe in which this is an acceptable thing for law-enforcement to say and do (or more specifically, not do),” wrote @thevivafrei, who identified themselves as a former litigator, in a quote tweet.

“There’s a lot of ground between ‘arrest’ and ‘do nothing,’” wrote user @pdrobertson.

Richards is wanted for four counts of discharge firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault and three other charges. Police have released his image and said he May show signs of a shoulder injury.

“We will continue to gather evidence and will go where the evidence takes us. We are grateful for the professionalism, tenacity and commitment of our investigators who continue this work,” Toronto police said in the Saturday afternoon statement.

“Let’s keep the focus where it belongs: finding the outstanding suspects and holding those responsible for this violent home invasion accountable.”

At 3 a.m. on Thursday, three attackers armed with guns and a hammer broke into a home in Toronto affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood. The suspects, each armed with a gun, located the residents on the second floor and demanded valuables, police said.

The victims, David Morton, a 75-year-old real-estate executive, his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and two adult daughters Maggie and Cristina, were all injured. Three family members were shot, and two were struck in the head with a hammer.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton said in a statement released Friday.

“While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto,” he added.
