stories.title: New evidence challenges military’s account of deadly Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Weather records, satellite observations and expert analysis suggest the deadly CFB Wainwright fire was growing for hours before it overran soldiers.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
In its account of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright , the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) describes an extraordinary chain of events on Oct. 17.

The base, it says, was monitoring a common grass fire that erupted in “uncommonly strong winds,” with flames soon devouring a kilometre in just 30 to 60 seconds.

The military called the event “entirely anomalous.”

A Global News analysis of satellite imagery and weather records, reviewed by seven Canadian wildfire experts, paints a different picture.

As soldiers continued their training on that day, satellites showed the fire had already spread. But the day before, Environment Canada forecast a cold front bringing powerful winds and later issued wind warnings for the area.

And experts say the flames were unlikely to travel at the speed the military suggests, although estimates made during a traumatic event May understandably be imprecise.

More importantly, however, experts say base leadership should have known the dangers posed by the incoming weather, even if they couldn’t predict the precise timing or consequences.

“This was not unexpected given the forecast cold front, the actively spreading fire and the wind warnings that were issued earlier in the day,” says Jen Beverly, an associate professor of wildland fire at the University of Alberta.

According to the military, four soldiers were killed and 39 injured, including 19 critically, when the fire swept through the military training grounds.

It said the fire rapidly intensified and overran soldiers around 4 p.m.

But satellite imagery and weather records show a two-kilometre stretch of fire at noon was likely spreading as winds picked up and a violent cold front approached.

Nearly two weeks after the disaster, crucial questions remain unanswered: What did commanders know about the growing fire and approaching weather? What warnings were passed on? And why were soldiers still training nearby?

The military says its Board of Inquiry, which will answer those questions, could take more than a year.

But weather records, satellite observations and decades of wildfire research already offer important clues about how the tragedy unfolded.

Global examined the evidence and had seven leading wildfire experts review its findings, reconstructing the hours before the disaster to better understand what happened — and whether the fire behaved as unexpectedly as the military has suggested.

The reconstruction traces how the fire May have spread throughout the day, what warnings were issued, and how a forecast wind shift changed the danger. It also raises questions about how quickly the flames advanced — and why soldiers remained in their path.

Long before it became a military training ground, CFB Wainwright was known as Buffalo National Park, established in 1909 to help save plains bison from extinction. Dozens of the once-overhunted beasts still graze on the base today as a commemorative herd.

Those vast, open grasslands face powerful winds, with few natural barriers to interrupt them as they sweep across the prairie.

While the precise combination of weather and fire conditions on Oct. 17 May have been exceptional, the area has seen destructive winds before.

Exactly nine years earlier, ON Oct. 17, 2017, gusts exceeding 100 kilometres per hour derailed 13 railway cars at a trestle bridge west of town.

Local Wainwright residents told Global News the area is known for being windy, but the day’s gusts were extraordinary.

However, forecasts predicted those winds.

Since the previous morning, Environment Canada had forecast strong winds, with gusts expected to rise from 60 to 80 kilometres per hour by Oct. 17. The forecast also predicted a shift in wind direction, from southwest to west, that afternoon.

Two hours before the soldiers were reportedly overrun, at 2:14 p.m., Environment Canada extended a yellow wind warning to Wainwright, indicating “hazardous” winds, and forecast gusts up to 100 kilometres per hour.

The base has its own weather station to monitor conditions, while CFB Wainwright’s standing orders , which set out safety rules, require Range Control to receive forecasts twice daily, at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.

But it remains unclear who was monitoring the weather on Oct. 17.

In a tense exchange with a reporter days after the disaster, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, speaking on behalf of the military, repeatedly declined to say whether Wainwright had a meteorologist or wildfire-behaviour expert, citing the ongoing investigation. Environment Canada provides meteorologists at some military bases, but confirmed none was stationed at Wainwright that day, adding that the base instead received remote forecasting support from CFB Gagetown in New Brunswick.

“Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction,” Rutland said on Oct. 18, speaking on behalf of the military.

While much remains unknown about that day, wildfire experts consulted by Global News said the forecasts and warnings should have raised serious concerns, particularly with an established grass fire already burning on the base. The approaching front threatened to intensify the blaze and abruptly change its direction.

“It was a classic setup,” said Mike Flannigan, a wildfire researcher at Thompson Rivers University.

“You don’t want to be out in the field on a day like Saturday.”

A grass fire ignited on the automatic grenade launcher range that Saturday, although the military has declined to say precisely when it began. At the time, the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System categorized the wildfire danger in Wainwright as “extreme.”

The military’s account of the blaze’s timing has changed. The morning after the tragedy, officials put the ignition time at around 4 p.m. Later that day, Rutland told a briefing that the fire started “several hours earlier,” adding that officials believed it was “contained.”

Asked how big the fire had grown, he declined to say: “I wouldn’t say it was small nor large.”

Four days later, military officials provided more detail, saying the fire was burning inside an area known as Permanent Danger Area 2, a restricted section of the base where live ammunition is fired, and unexploded munitions pose a hazard.

This “restricted the firefighters’ ability to conduct direct suppressive operations,” they said.

However, the base’s standing orders explicitly exempt firefighting and emergency vehicles from certain restrictions on entering the area, including the grenade range impact zone, although the danger posed by unexploded munitions could still prevent firefighters from entering.

They also give Range Control authority to halt dangerous training and coordinate emergency responses. Units must also report changes in a fire’s intensity, direction and speed.

The military has declined to say whether those procedures were followed on Oct. 17, citing the ongoing investigation.

Military officials said Range Control and the base’s fire department monitored the blaze while soldiers continued training nearby.

But high above the Alberta prairie, satellites captured images of a fire far larger than a small patch of burning grass as early as noon.

U.S. Earth-observation satellite Landsat 8 showed active fire at 12:17 p.m., stretching roughly two kilometres in length across the grasslands, with scorched ground already visible behind the flames.

Using the co-ordinates of satellite-detected hotspots recorded in Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (Firms), Beverly estimates the blaze covered roughly 48 hectares — equivalent to about 50 football stadiums, including their surrounding grounds.

The military did not respond to questions about whether it agreed with that estimate.

“A one hectare fire is getting to be problematic… so imagine 50 of those,” Beverly said.

“I was quite surprised that anybody would have been working within several kilometres of an active fire knowing that a cold front was coming and there were wind warnings.”

And those winds were already gathering strength.

The military has described a fire that suddenly intensified as powerful winds swept through the base, overtaking soldiers around 4 p.m. An internal memo obtained by Global News later attributed the rapid spread to an “unexpected and sudden wind change.”

But satellite and weather records suggest the conditions were deteriorating well before then.

At the base airfield, about 15 kilometres from the fire, sustained winds doubled from 15 to 30 kilometres per hour between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m., according to Environment Canada records.

At 2:49 p.m., the U.S. weather satellite Noaa-20 passed overhead and detected heat beyond the earlier fire locations, suggesting the blaze May have been spreading outward.

Based on satellite hotspot data, Beverly estimates the fire had nearly tripled in size, to about 140 hectares, describing it as a “problem fire growing in size.”

Flannigan agrees, noting low humidity and dry grass: “I’d say it was quite active. By two o’clock that fire was running.”

By 3 p.m., temperatures had climbed above 23 C and humidity had fallen below the temperature – a term in fire science known as “crossover” fire conditions. Within an hour, temperatures plunged more than 10 degrees, according to Environment Canada records.

Then the weather began to turn.

At 3:10 p.m., another U.S. weather satellite, Goes-18, which monitors Western North America at 10-minute intervals, recorded about 76 megawatts of fire radiative power — a measure of the energy emitted by the blaze. Twenty minutes later, satellite readings showed the fire’s radiative power had surged almost sixteenfold to 1,215 megawatts — before falling sharply over the next 10 minutes.

The readings indicate a major escalation in fire activity as a cold front reached the training grounds, Flannigan said, about 30 minutes before the military said the fire reached soldiers.

As the cold front swept through, Environment Canada recorded an 82-kilometre-per-hour wind gust at the CFB Wainwright airfield at 3:16 p.m. Temperatures plunged more than 10 degrees within the hour.

Beverly described the sudden change in fire behaviour as a textbook example of what happens when a cold front moves across an established blaze.

“This is a well-known pattern,” she said, adding that she teaches it to the students in her undergraduate course.

For soldiers caught in its path, the speed and intensity of the flames could have left little time to escape.

Both the military and Prime Minister Mark Carney have described the fire travelling roughly a kilometre in under a minute, from where it had been burning on the training grounds to soldiers conducting exercises.

Rutland put the time at 30 to 60 seconds, citing a commander on the ground — equivalent to 60 to 120 kilometres per hour if the flames travelled the full distance. However, he acknowledged the fire May have already spread unseen through the terrain, something the investigation would seek to establish.

Three wildfire experts cautioned that estimates made in the chaos of a rapidly advancing fire, particularly one involving serious injuries and loss of life, May understandably be imprecise.

But they also said the reported speed would be extraordinary.

Marty Alexander, one of Canada’s most experienced wildfire researchers, developed a widely used rule of thumb suggesting spread rates of roughly 20 per cent of sustained wind speed under critical burning conditions. His research documented a fire in New South Wales, Australia, that spread at 27 kilometres per hour — the fastest he was aware of.

“A grass fire rate of spread of more than 60 kilometres per hour is very highly improbable,” he told Global.

Researcher Cordy Tymstra said the fastest documented Canadian grass fire he knew of, a fire in Granum, southern Alberta in 1997, averaged 14.7 to 16.8 kilometres per hour — far below the military’s Wainwright estimate.

However, three experts Global spoke to said spotting could have driven the rapid spread, as wind-blown embers ignite new fires ahead of the main blaze.

But they also said whether the fire travelled a kilometre in one minute or several, soldiers caught in its path would have had little chance of escape.

The greater danger, they said, was the forecast wind shift, which could turn the long flank of an established fire into a rapidly advancing front, sending flames racing in a different direction.

All the experts whom Global consulted said it was well understood that a wind shift can intensify an established fire.

“If a two-kilometre fire turns into a two-kilometre fire front, you can’t go sideways,” says Flannigan.

“You can only go directly away from it. But given the speed it was travelling and the terrain, most people couldn’t outrun it.”

The base’s standing orders identify August through October as a high-risk fire period and advise units to plan live-fire exercises in the early morning, when fire danger is generally lower.

The orders also prohibit tracer ammunition, pyrotechnics and white phosphorus during extreme fire danger, but do not specifically list automatic grenade launchers or high-explosive grenades in those fire-hazard restrictions.

Asked about the orders, Rutland described them as a “guideline,” saying commanders must assess multiple factors before deciding whether to proceed with shooting and that soldiers train in all conditions.

It’s commonly known that fires are a recurring hazard at CFB Wainwright, as they are at military bases where live ammunition can ignite dry vegetation. The military also conducts controlled fires in spring to reduce the grass and other material that could fuel future outbreaks. But these too can escape in strong winds.

A 2026 scientific study, in collaboration with the Department of National Defence (DND) and CFB Wainwright, examined an April 2024 prescribed burn at Wainwright that escaped its intended boundaries under strong winds and eventually burned approximately 600 hectares.

In 2017, another military grass fire at CFB Suffield burned approximately 36,000 hectares during strong winds, prompting the military to pledge improvements to its fire-prevention procedures.

It found that half of hazardous incidents at the sites examined had not been investigated and warned that safety risks could be accepted without appropriate authorization or senior management awareness.

The audit did not establish whether those failures occurred specifically at Wainwright.

But two weeks after the disaster, lingering questions remain.

DND did confirm, however, that it has made no changes to safety measures since the tragedy and that its Board of Inquiry has yet to be formally convened, although it expects that to happen “in the near future.”

Other agencies have also been reluctant to release information. Environment Canada initially declined to confirm the timing of weather warnings and recorded wind gusts in response to media questions, but later answered after repeated questions.

Wildfire researchers say the tragedy should prompt a closer examination of how the military assesses fire risks, communicates warnings and trains personnel to respond to changing conditions.

“From a fire science perspective it was predictable, and there should have been information flows and procedures in place to ensure that the fire behaviour was understood by those interacting with fire or working near fire on the base,” said Beverly.

Rutland has said the military’s investigation will be made public, with changes to follow where necessary.

“Where they find our procedures, our training, our equipment, or our policies must change, they will change,” he said.

And experts say the flames were unlikely to travel at the speed the military suggests, although estimates made during a traumatic event May understandably be imprecise.
More importantly, however, experts say base leadership should have known the dangers posed by the incoming weather, even if they couldn’t predict the precise timing or consequences.

“This was not unexpected given the forecast cold front, the actively spreading fire and the wind warnings that were issued earlier in the day,” says Jen Beverly, an associate professor of wildland fire at the University of Alberta.
According to the military, four soldiers were killed and 39 injured, including 19 critically, when the fire swept through the military training grounds.
It said the fire rapidly intensified and overran soldiers around 4 p.m.
But satellite imagery and weather records show a two-kilometre stretch of fire at noon was likely spreading as winds picked up and a violent cold front approached.

Nearly two weeks after the disaster, crucial questions remain unanswered: What did commanders know about the growing fire and approaching weather? What warnings were passed on? And why were soldiers still training nearby?
The military says its Board of Inquiry, which will answer those questions, could take more than a year.
But weather records, satellite observations and decades of wildfire research already offer important clues about how the tragedy unfolded.

Global examined the evidence and had seven leading wildfire experts review its findings, reconstructing the hours before the disaster to better understand what happened — and whether the fire behaved as unexpectedly as the military has suggested.

The reconstruction traces how the fire May have spread throughout the day, what warnings were issued, and how a forecast wind shift changed the danger. It also raises questions about how quickly the flames advanced — and why soldiers remained in their path.

Long before it became a military training ground, CFB Wainwright was known as Buffalo National Park, established in 1909 to help save plains bison from extinction. Dozens of the once-overhunted beasts still graze on the base today as a commemorative herd.
Those vast, open grasslands face powerful winds, with few natural barriers to interrupt them as they sweep across the prairie.
While the precise combination of weather and fire conditions on Oct. 17 May have been exceptional, the area has seen destructive winds before.
Exactly nine years earlier, ON Oct. 17, 2017, gusts exceeding 100 kilometres per hour derailed 13 railway cars at a trestle bridge west of town.
Local Wainwright residents told Global News the area is known for being windy, but the day’s gusts were extraordinary.
However, forecasts predicted those winds.

Since the previous morning, Environment Canada had forecast strong winds, with gusts expected to rise from 60 to 80 kilometres per hour by Oct. 17. The forecast also predicted a shift in wind direction, from southwest to west, that afternoon.

Two hours before the soldiers were reportedly overrun, at 2:14 p.m., Environment Canada extended a yellow wind warning to Wainwright, indicating “hazardous” winds, and forecast gusts up to 100 kilometres per hour.

The base has its own weather station to monitor conditions, while CFB Wainwright’s standing orders , which set out safety rules, require Range Control to receive forecasts twice daily, at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.
But it remains unclear who was monitoring the weather on Oct. 17.

In a tense exchange with a reporter days after the disaster, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, speaking on behalf of the military, repeatedly declined to say whether Wainwright had a meteorologist or wildfire-behaviour expert, citing the ongoing investigation. Environment Canada provides meteorologists at some military bases, but confirmed none was stationed at Wainwright that day, adding that the base instead received remote forecasting support from CFB Gagetown in New Brunswick.
“Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction,” Rutland said on Oct. 18, speaking on behalf of the military.

While much remains unknown about that day, wildfire experts consulted by Global News said the forecasts and warnings should have raised serious concerns, particularly with an established grass fire already burning on the base. The approaching front threatened to intensify the blaze and abruptly change its direction.
“It was a classic setup,” said Mike Flannigan, a wildfire researcher at Thompson Rivers University.
“You don’t want to be out in the field on a day like Saturday.”

A grass fire ignited on the automatic grenade launcher range that Saturday, although the military has declined to say precisely when it began. At the time, the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System categorized the wildfire danger in Wainwright as “extreme.”

The military’s account of the blaze’s timing has changed. The morning after the tragedy, officials put the ignition time at around 4 p.m. Later that day, Rutland told a briefing that the fire started “several hours earlier,” adding that officials believed it was “contained.”
Asked how big the fire had grown, he declined to say: “I wouldn’t say it was small nor large.”

Four days later, military officials provided more detail, saying the fire was burning inside an area known as Permanent Danger Area 2, a restricted section of the base where live ammunition is fired, and unexploded munitions pose a hazard.
This “restricted the firefighters’ ability to conduct direct suppressive operations,” they said.

However, the base’s standing orders explicitly exempt firefighting and emergency vehicles from certain restrictions on entering the area, including the grenade range impact zone, although the danger posed by unexploded munitions could still prevent firefighters from entering.
They also give Range Control authority to halt dangerous training and coordinate emergency responses. Units must also report changes in a fire’s intensity, direction and speed.
The military has declined to say whether those procedures were followed on Oct. 17, citing the ongoing investigation.
Military officials said Range Control and the base’s fire department monitored the blaze while soldiers continued training nearby.
But high above the Alberta prairie, satellites captured images of a fire far larger than a small patch of burning grass as early as noon.
U.S. Earth-observation satellite Landsat 8 showed active fire at 12:17 p.m., stretching roughly two kilometres in length across the grasslands, with scorched ground already visible behind the flames.

Using the co-ordinates of satellite-detected hotspots recorded in Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (Firms), Beverly estimates the blaze covered roughly 48 hectares — equivalent to about 50 football stadiums, including their surrounding grounds.
The military did not respond to questions about whether it agreed with that estimate.
“A one hectare fire is getting to be problematic… so imagine 50 of those,” Beverly said.
“I was quite surprised that anybody would have been working within several kilometres of an active fire knowing that a cold front was coming and there were wind warnings.”
And those winds were already gathering strength.

The military has described a fire that suddenly intensified as powerful winds swept through the base, overtaking soldiers around 4 p.m. An internal memo obtained by Global News later attributed the rapid spread to an “unexpected and sudden wind change.”
But satellite and weather records suggest the conditions were deteriorating well before then.
At the base airfield, about 15 kilometres from the fire, sustained winds doubled from 15 to 30 kilometres per hour between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m., according to Environment Canada records.
At 2:49 p.m., the U.S. weather satellite Noaa-20 passed overhead and detected heat beyond the earlier fire locations, suggesting the blaze May have been spreading outward.
Based on satellite hotspot data, Beverly estimates the fire had nearly tripled in size, to about 140 hectares, describing it as a “problem fire growing in size.”
Flannigan agrees, noting low humidity and dry grass: “I’d say it was quite active. By two o’clock that fire was running.”

By 3 p.m., temperatures had climbed above 23 C and humidity had fallen below the temperature – a term in fire science known as “crossover” fire conditions. Within an hour, temperatures plunged more than 10 degrees, according to Environment Canada records.
Then the weather began to turn.

At 3:10 p.m., another U.S. weather satellite, Goes-18, which monitors Western North America at 10-minute intervals, recorded about 76 megawatts of fire radiative power — a measure of the energy emitted by the blaze. Twenty minutes later, satellite readings showed the fire’s radiative power had surged almost sixteenfold to 1,215 megawatts — before falling sharply over the next 10 minutes.
The readings indicate a major escalation in fire activity as a cold front reached the training grounds, Flannigan said, about 30 minutes before the military said the fire reached soldiers.
As the cold front swept through, Environment Canada recorded an 82-kilometre-per-hour wind gust at the CFB Wainwright airfield at 3:16 p.m. Temperatures plunged more than 10 degrees within the hour.
Beverly described the sudden change in fire behaviour as a textbook example of what happens when a cold front moves across an established blaze.
“This is a well-known pattern,” she said, adding that she teaches it to the students in her undergraduate course.
For soldiers caught in its path, the speed and intensity of the flames could have left little time to escape.

Both the military and Prime Minister Mark Carney have described the fire travelling roughly a kilometre in under a minute, from where it had been burning on the training grounds to soldiers conducting exercises.

Rutland put the time at 30 to 60 seconds, citing a commander on the ground — equivalent to 60 to 120 kilometres per hour if the flames travelled the full distance. However, he acknowledged the fire May have already spread unseen through the terrain, something the investigation would seek to establish.
Three wildfire experts cautioned that estimates made in the chaos of a rapidly advancing fire, particularly one involving serious injuries and loss of life, May understandably be imprecise.
But they also said the reported speed would be extraordinary.

Marty Alexander, one of Canada’s most experienced wildfire researchers, developed a widely used rule of thumb suggesting spread rates of roughly 20 per cent of sustained wind speed under critical burning conditions. His research documented a fire in New South Wales, Australia, that spread at 27 kilometres per hour — the fastest he was aware of.
“A grass fire rate of spread of more than 60 kilometres per hour is very highly improbable,” he told Global.

Researcher Cordy Tymstra said the fastest documented Canadian grass fire he knew of, a fire in Granum, southern Alberta in 1997, averaged 14.7 to 16.8 kilometres per hour — far below the military’s Wainwright estimate.
However, three experts Global spoke to said spotting could have driven the rapid spread, as wind-blown embers ignite new fires ahead of the main blaze.
But they also said whether the fire travelled a kilometre in one minute or several, soldiers caught in its path would have had little chance of escape.
The greater danger, they said, was the forecast wind shift, which could turn the long flank of an established fire into a rapidly advancing front, sending flames racing in a different direction.
All the experts whom Global consulted said it was well understood that a wind shift can intensify an established fire.
“If a two-kilometre fire turns into a two-kilometre fire front, you can’t go sideways,” says Flannigan.
“You can only go directly away from it. But given the speed it was travelling and the terrain, most people couldn’t outrun it.”
The base’s standing orders identify August through October as a high-risk fire period and advise units to plan live-fire exercises in the early morning, when fire danger is generally lower.

The orders also prohibit tracer ammunition, pyrotechnics and white phosphorus during extreme fire danger, but do not specifically list automatic grenade launchers or high-explosive grenades in those fire-hazard restrictions.

Asked about the orders, Rutland described them as a “guideline,” saying commanders must assess multiple factors before deciding whether to proceed with shooting and that soldiers train in all conditions.

It’s commonly known that fires are a recurring hazard at CFB Wainwright, as they are at military bases where live ammunition can ignite dry vegetation. The military also conducts controlled fires in spring to reduce the grass and other material that could fuel future outbreaks. But these too can escape in strong winds.

A 2026 scientific study, in collaboration with the Department of National Defence (DND) and CFB Wainwright, examined an April 2024 prescribed burn at Wainwright that escaped its intended boundaries under strong winds and eventually burned approximately 600 hectares.
In 2017, another military grass fire at CFB Suffield burned approximately 36,000 hectares during strong winds, prompting the military to pledge improvements to its fire-prevention procedures.

It found that half of hazardous incidents at the sites examined had not been investigated and warned that safety risks could be accepted without appropriate authorization or senior management awareness.
The audit did not establish whether those failures occurred specifically at Wainwright.
But two weeks after the disaster, lingering questions remain.

DND did confirm, however, that it has made no changes to safety measures since the tragedy and that its Board of Inquiry has yet to be formally convened, although it expects that to happen “in the near future.”

Other agencies have also been reluctant to release information. Environment Canada initially declined to confirm the timing of weather warnings and recorded wind gusts in response to media questions, but later answered after repeated questions.
Wildfire researchers say the tragedy should prompt a closer examination of how the military assesses fire risks, communicates warnings and trains personnel to respond to changing conditions.

“From a fire science perspective it was predictable, and there should have been information flows and procedures in place to ensure that the fire behaviour was understood by those interacting with fire or working near fire on the base,” said Beverly.
Rutland has said the military’s investigation will be made public, with changes to follow where necessary.
“Where they find our procedures, our training, our equipment, or our policies must change, they will change,” he said.

stories.title: Food Banks of Saskatchewan loses charity status, director points to accounting error
stories.summary: The head of the organization that supports 36 Saskatchewan food banks says it’s “business as usual” as they seek to regain its charity status.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
The director of an organization supporting dozens of food banks across Saskatchewan says its accounting firm is to blame for the loss of its charitable status.

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) revoked Food Banks of Saskatchewan’s registration on Sept. 12, 2026, for failing to file its annual return, according to a statement from the agency to Global News.

Executive director Michael Kincade says the accounting firm never submitted the necessary paperwork, even though it was completed and signed.

“This wasn’t an administrative issue on our behalf,” Kincade told Global News in an interview. “We were told it was done.”

The organization then received a notification from the CRA in February that it hadn’t received the return, Kincade said, adding the firm assured him it would be handled.

“I trusted that it was submitted and entered and then in September we got a notice from the CRA that they revoked our charitable status,” he said.

“We did everything we were supposed to do and even follow-ups and so it was not our fault at all.”

All registered charities are required under the Income Tax Act to file annual return information, attachments and financial statements no later than six months after the end of their fiscal year, said the CRA.

Organizations with a revoked status can continue their operations, according to the CRA, but can no longer issue donation receipts or accept gifts from registered charities.

The tax agency says that while it cannot discuss specific cases due to the “confidentiality provisions” of the Act, any organization whose charitable status has been revoked can apply to regain it.

Kincade says his organization is seeking to reinstate its charity status and that all required documents have been filed, adding that it is “business as usual” as it continues to accept donations and work with its 36 member food banks.

But with no timeline for when the organization will regain its status, Kincade says he is worried about how it will impact them as they gear up for the busiest time of the year.

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) revoked Food Banks of Saskatchewan’s registration on Sept. 12, 2026, for failing to file its annual return, according to a statement from the agency to Global News.
Executive director Michael Kincade says the accounting firm never submitted the necessary paperwork, even though it was completed and signed.
“This wasn’t an administrative issue on our behalf,” Kincade told Global News in an interview. “We were told it was done.”
The organization then received a notification from the CRA in February that it hadn’t received the return, Kincade said, adding the firm assured him it would be handled.
“I trusted that it was submitted and entered and then in September we got a notice from the CRA that they revoked our charitable status,” he said.
“We did everything we were supposed to do and even follow-ups and so it was not our fault at all.”

All registered charities are required under the Income Tax Act to file annual return information, attachments and financial statements no later than six months after the end of their fiscal year, said the CRA.
Organizations with a revoked status can continue their operations, according to the CRA, but can no longer issue donation receipts or accept gifts from registered charities.

Member food banks keep their own charitable status so they are not affected, said Kincade.

stories.title: Why Toronto's municipal election turnout beat the provincial average
stories.summary: Toronto - What appeared to be a neck-and-neck race between two top contenders for the mayor's seat helped draw more people to the polls in Toronto, leading to the city's highest turnout in more than a decade, some experts say.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - What appeared to be a neck-and-neck race between two top contenders for the mayor’s seat helped draw more people to the polls in Toronto, leading to the city’s highest turnout in more than a decade, some experts say.

Nearly one million people in the city cast a ballot in this week’s municipal election, and unofficial results collected by the Association of Municipalities of Ontario show 46 per cent of those eligible to vote in Toronto did so.

Meanwhile, the average turnout across the province was around 36 per cent, according to the association’s data.

Some political scientists say a competitive race, increased civic engagement, a stronger political culture and greater media coverage all contributed to the higher turnout in Toronto.

The top driver for Toronto’s increased voter participation was the apparent close contest between mayoral front-runners Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford, as well as tight races for council positions in several wards, said Cristine de Clercy, a political scientist who teaches at Trent University.

“It attracted attention, and it seems to me an important effect that that contest, which seemed to become closer as the campaign wore on ... certainly had a large effect on turnout.”

Polls placing the two so close, including one that put Bradford ahead just days before the election, motivated voters and campaign volunteers because they felt their efforts and votes could make a difference, she said.

“So that certainly got some other people out to the polls who normally might not have voted if they thought either the incumbent was going to win in a landslide, or her opponent was going to win a landslide,” she said.

Community organizations also played an important role in getting people to vote in Toronto during this municipal election cycle, she said.

While the competitive race between Chow and Bradford was the main draw, Myer Siemiatycki, a professor emeritus of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University, said that alone couldn’t explain why Toronto’s turnout eclipsed that of other municipalities with hard-fought elections.

In nearby Mississauga, where both the incumbent Carolyn Parrish and her predecessor Bonnie Crombie lost a close three-way race to Alvin Tedjo, 34 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots. While that represents a 12-point surge from 2022, it’s still significantly lower than in Toronto, Siemiatycki said.

“I think the difference in Toronto is number one, there’s a much stronger political culture of participation in the city than in Mississauga,” which many still consider a suburb, he said. “Generally, central cities have a stronger history and pattern of political participation than suburban areas do.”

Robust media coverage in Toronto, along with a wide range of issues that people cared about, such as bike lanes, school nutrition programs and traffic gridlock, could also have fuelled higher turnout, he said.

Chow’s army of volunteers also made a difference, he said.

“She has a lot of very dedicated supporters who, ON election day, canvass and knock on doors and encourage people to go out and vote, and that certainly played out to drive up the vote,” he said.

Meanwhile, the declining media landscape in smaller communities has created an information gap, Siemiatycki said.

“Whereas in Toronto, of course, there’s such a rich and multifaceted, diverse media ecosystem, there’s just a lot more information, a lot of reminders and focus on the municipal election race,” he said.

Despite being higher than the rest of the province, the turnout in Toronto is “still too low and is a problem and we need to think about how to increase it,” he added.

The Association of Municipalities of Ontario’s data show more than four million Ontarians voted across the province, including Toronto, where the city said 989,990 ballots were cast. Chow secured victory with 532,201 certified votes compared to Bradford’s 404,013.

In London, Ont., where the incumbent Josh Morgan was re-elected, the turnout was 31 per cent, an increase of around six percentage points from 2022. Morgan got over 45 per cent of the total votes, while his closest competitor received a little over 26 per cent.

Cameron D. Anderson, a professor of political science at the University of Western Ontario, said the city’s voter turnout has historically been behind Toronto’s, but the lack of tough opposition for Morgan further dampened participation.

“Generally speaking ... it was assumed that he would win again,” Anderson said. “Whereas in Chow’s case, there was a sense that, oh no, look, the challenger is getting really, really close and maybe could beat her,” which increases the motivation to vote, he said.

The Association of Municipalities of Ontario said unofficial results show that voter turnout varied considerably across municipalities with populations of over 100,000.

Chatham-Kent and Greater Sudbury, for example, were at 41 per cent while Kitchener had the lowest turnout at 22 per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: University of Guelph scientist leads project to recover butterfly species in Ontario
stories.summary: The last time the frosted elfin butterfly, known for its brown hue and delicate wings, was spotted in Ontario was in 1988.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The last time the frosted elfin butterfly, known for its brown hue and delicate wings, was spotted in Ontario was in 1988.

Several surveys, including one in 2019, have turned up no sightings of the small, non-migratory butterfly in nearly 40 years, according to the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada.

A group of Canadian scientists is now working to bring the extirpated species back to the northern shores of Lake Erie in Norfolk County it once inhabited. Extirpation refers to a species’ disappearance from a specific geographic region or habitat.

Ryan Norris, who teaches at the University of Guelph’s department of integrative biology, said the team is planning to import frosted elfin butterflies and their eggs from New York to breed them at the Cambridge Butterfly Conservatory before releasing them into the wild next spring in Port Rowan, southeast of London, Ont.

“And some of those habitats, many of them are restored. They’re old tobacco fields and now they’re really thriving kind of oak savanna habitats that allow us to reintroduce species like frosted elfin,” he said.

Norris attributed the butterfly’s extirpation to the loss of habitat due to urban development and creation of farmland.

“We’ve destroyed things in the past, and in some cases we have, for some habitat types, … very little left of it, and it used to be much more abundant in places like southern Ontario,” he said in an interview.

He said the team is making sure there are enough wild sundial lupins, the frosted elfin’s host plant, before breeding could begin.

The project is part of larger cross-country efforts involving universities, conservation organizations and government agencies to save three endangered species of butterflies that also include the mottled duskywing and curiously isolated hairstreak, the University of Guelph said in a statement.

“By co-ordinating the recovery of three at-risk butterfly species at once, the team will develop what researchers believe is Canada’s first multi-species framework for insect conservation,” it said.

The federal government has provided $2.4 million in funding, the school said.

As part of the project, the mottled duskywing, a medium-sized butterfly that is dark grey and brown in colour, was reintroduced at Pinery Provincial Park in Grand Bend, Ont., and some other protected areas in Norfolk County five years ago.

The results have been remarkable, Norris said.

The butterfly’s population has reached several hundred at the Pinery site and close to 100 at a second location. At Pinery, the population could be even bigger, he added.

“They’re spilling over into campsites … We have seen them at other sites that we’re not monitoring. So, we’re really happy about that,” he said.

“So, I think (with) mottled duskywing, we’re kind of, we’re giving it a foothold. We’re giving it a chance for long-term persistence already in Ontario.”

The project also aims to strengthen the population of a rare species of butterfly known as the curiously isolated hairstreak that inhabits Waterton Lakes National Park in southern Alberta.

“So now what we have is a species with a single population … that we are obligated to protect and understand a little bit more about,” he said, adding that scientists are exploring to see if they can reintroduce the species in other locations, or supplement their population at their current location.

Restoring the habitat is key to secure the viability of all three species, he said.

The concentration of the butterfly’s population at one site is risky and makes them vulnerable as it could cause the insect to go extinct if a natural disaster strikes the area, experts say.

“I think our hope is if you kind of introduce it into an area that has suitable habitats surrounding it, that they’ll colonize those areas themselves,” he said. “That’s when you start to get into long-term stability.”

Norris said butterflies are pollinators, and they serve as a vital food source for other animals, making them a key player in a healthy ecosystem.

But bringing them back is a much more meaningful task, he said.

“By us assisting them, we’re restoring, rewilding places in Canada. I think that’s quite symbolic.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version mistakenly referred to the frosted elfin as the frosted dolphin in a direct quote.

As part of the project, the mottled duskywing, a medium-sized butterfly that is dark grey and brown in colour, was reintroduced at Pinery Provincial Park in Grand Bend, Ont., and some other protected areas in Norfolk County five years ago.
The results have been remarkable, Norris said.
The butterfly’s population has reached several hundred at the Pinery site and close to 100 at a second location. At Pinery, the population could be even bigger, he added.
“They’re spilling over into campsites … We have seen them at other sites that we’re not monitoring. So, we’re really happy about that,” he said.
“So, I think (with) mottled duskywing, we’re kind of, we’re giving it a foothold. We’re giving it a chance for long-term persistence already in Ontario.”
The project also aims to strengthen the population of a rare species of butterfly known as the curiously isolated hairstreak that inhabits Waterton Lakes National Park in southern Alberta.

“So now what we have is a species with a single population … that we are obligated to protect and understand a little bit more about,” he said, adding that scientists are exploring to see if they can reintroduce the species in other locations, or supplement their population at their current location.
Restoring the habitat is key to secure the viability of all three species, he said.
The concentration of the butterfly’s population at one site is risky and makes them vulnerable as it could cause the insect to go extinct if a natural disaster strikes the area, experts say.

“I think our hope is if you kind of introduce it into an area that has suitable habitats surrounding it, that they’ll colonize those areas themselves,” he said. “That’s when you start to get into long-term stability.”
Norris said butterflies are pollinators, and they serve as a vital food source for other animals, making them a key player in a healthy ecosystem.
But bringing them back is a much more meaningful task, he said.
“By us assisting them, we’re restoring, rewilding places in Canada. I think that’s quite symbolic.”

stories.title: No matter what happens in the midterms, Canada-U.S. tensions are likely to remain
stories.summary: Detroit - Democrats are hoping Tuesday's midterm elections will give them the power to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump — but Canadians hoping for an outcome that stabilizes the rocky bilateral relationship May be disappointed.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Detroit - Democrats are hoping Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them the power to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump — but Canadians hoping for an outcome that stabilizes the rocky bilateral relationship May be disappointed.

Once-safe Republican seats are now in peril and control of Congress could flip. Trump’s poll numbers are plummeting thanks to his unpopular war in Iran, rising energy prices and inflation.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority.

Amelia Cunningham and Gwyneth Love are ready for the midterm elections to be over. Like many Michiganders, they have been inundated with political advertisements from the tight race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for a key Senate seat. (Oct. 31, 2026)

The future of the Senate is less clear. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and some polling shows that is within reach.

Even if Democrats gain control of both chambers, Trump will still be president, said Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont.

Presidents have a lot of power over foreign policy and Trump — unhappy with being seen as a lame duck in the final stretch of his term — May be even more motivated to use it.

Lebo said that could make Trump more “erratic” and “dangerous.”

“It’s not clear how much the Democratic Senate will push back on him or can push back,” Lebo said.

The size of the expected Democrat win will be an important factor, Lebo added. Numerous reports suggest Republicans are worried about bleeding seats as contests in places Trump dominated in 2024, like Kansas and Ohio, become competitive.

Congress has control over tariffs and taxes but Republican lawmakers have largely given Trump a free hand to deploy tariffs worldwide. If the midterms demonstrate that the president has lost his hold over loyal voters, GOP members May be more inclined to break with Trump, Lebo said.

But a large number of Republicans would have to join with Democrats to secure the supermajority needed to bypass presidential veto power and overturn Trump’s tariffs.

And many observers question whether Democrats are looking to return to a pre-Trump era in trade policy.

Trump’s first administration demonstrated how vulnerable Canada is to American whims when the president scrapped the North American Free Trade Agreement.

It was replaced with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as Cusma. Former Democrat vice-president Kamala Harris and current Democrat Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer were among the Democrats who voted against the trilateral agreement.

President Joe Biden brought more stability to the Canada-U.S. relationship but not much change. He kept many of Trump’s first term tariffs in place, despite promises to reverse them, and expanded other protectionist policies.

“What Canadians have learned in the last few years is we don’t trust Americans to correct course when they can in terms of the presidency,” Lebo said.

While Trump’s first term rattled the bilateral relationship, his second term blew it up. Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed. Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The trade war is deeply unpopular in states like Michigan and Maine, where tight Senate races ultimately could decide which party gains congressional control.

But even if Democrats emerge triumphant next week, or win the White House in 2028, it’s not clear that Trump’s tariff wall would suddenly drop.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is considering a run for president, told CTV in August that he couldn’t guarantee Trump’s tariff policies would be reversed under Democratic leadership.

One factor Democrats likely are considering is how to deal with the United States’ $40-trillion debt problem. Trump has argued tariffs bring in much-needed revenue — although they have yet to make much of a dent in the U.S. balance sheet. Democrats have not said how they plan to deal with the problem.

Vermont Democrat Sen. Peter Welch, who was in Montreal this week, vowed to repeal the tariffs on Canada.

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said Democrats traditionally have been more protectionist than Republicans and he could see the party maintaining a baseline tariff wall.

What that means for the future of Cusma is not clear. The Trump administration did not renew the trilateral agreement earlier this year, triggering an annual rolling review for up to 10 years. Once that period ends, and if the partners haven’t agreed to an extension at that point, the agreement would expire.

Sands said as long as the United States doesn’t walk away from Cusma, there’s still room to negotiate.

“You just want to hang on to that and hope that in a different environment, you can have a conversation about keeping it,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Royal Conservatory of Music names New Yorker Nicholas Russotto as artistic director
stories.summary: The 36-year-old Connecticut native will share a leadership role with the conservatory’s Aida Aydinyan
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
The Royal Conservatory of Music has landed its new concert programmer. Nicholas Russotto, hired away from New York’s 92nd Street Y, will be artistic director of the Toronto institution’s performing arts division.

In the newly created position, the 36-year-old Connecticut native shares a leadership role in the division with the conservatory’s Aida Aydinyan, who is promoted to executive director. Together, they replace Mervon Mehta , the popular impresario who stepped down this summer after 17 years of programming music at the conservatory’s three venues, including the 1,135-seat Koerner Hall.

Mr. Russotto cited the flagship venue as one of the new job’s chief attractions. “It’s judged to be one of the greatest concert halls in the world,” Mr. Russotto told The Globe and Mail this week, referring to the space actress Meryl Streep once said had “the most lustrous sound, the warmest embrace of any room I’ve been in.”

He will focus on artistic vision and programming, while Ms. Aydinyan will lead operations and strategic development. In accepting the position at the conservatory, he departs one of New York’s iconic performing arts venues and cultural centres after more than nine years there. Most recently, he was executive director of the organization’s Tisch Music division.

‘It was thrilling’: Looking back at 75 years of the National Ballet of Canada

“I don’t feel in any way sad about leaving New York,” he said. “The 92nd Street Y was one of the greatest musical programs I could ever hope to run in my life. But, as Stephen Sondheim said in Company , there’s a time to come to New York and a time to leave.”

The search to replace Mr. Mehta was international in scope, conducted by members of the conservatory’s board of directors. Ultimately, 10 candidates were interviewed for the position.

Like the conservatory, the 92nd Street Y is more than simply a music presenter. Among the eight programming components are the Bronfman Center for Jewish Life, the May Center for Health & Fitness and the Tisch Center for the Arts.

“Nicholas has been able to navigate a really interesting and complex institution,” said Alexander Brose, the conservatory’s president and chief executive officer since 2024. “That experience will lend itself coming into the school and Koerner Hall here.”

Mr. Russotto will work in tandem with new executive director Ms. Aydinyan, previously general manager of the conservatory’s performing arts division.

“Aida knows the institution so incredibly well,” Mr. Brose said. “She and Nick will raise all ships within the department, all halls within the school and certainly the school itself.”

Mr. Russotto majored in business (arts administration) and music (organ performance) at American University in Washington. Prior to joining 92nd Street Y, he was executive director of Sympho, a New York-based orchestral collective focused on large-scale experiential projects.

It’s scary out there. Live theatre is trying to make the most of it

In New York, Mr. Russotto built relationships with such Canadian virtuosos as violinist James Ehnes and pianists Angela Hewitt, Marc-André Hamelin and Stewart Goodyear. He mentioned Canadian-American singer-songwriter Rufus Wainwright, Montreal post-rockers Godspeed You! Black Emperor and members of the Toronto indie-rock collective Broken Social Scene as Canadian artists he hopes to program at Koerner Hall.

He also wants to integrate the conservatory’s school with the performing arts division.

“There’s a great symbiosis there we can explore a little further,” he said. “It’s a unique dyad in the cultural presentation landscape.”

stories.title: Nova Scotia photographer’s new book explores how Canada and Europe honour Canadian war dead
stories.summary: For more than 30 years photographer Len Wagg has captured touching images from European war cemeteries and monuments.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
For more than 30 years photographer Len Wagg has captured touching images from European war cemeteries and monuments.

“When you walk through them, you feel like you are on hallowed ground,” said Wagg, who has written a new book. “At Home and Beyond, Honouring Canada’s War Dead”. In the book Wagg examined the bravery and sacrifice by Canadians during the First and Second World Wars through pictures and short summaries.

Throughout the book Wagg also highlighted the continued expressions of gratitude shown by Europeans toward Canadians to this day because of the efforts and sacrifices made by Canadians during both wars.

According to Veterans Affairs Canada , 66,000 Canadians died in the First World War, while more than 42,000 lost their lives in the Second World War.

“What they left behind overseas was a lot of respect from a lot of the world,” said Wagg.

That respect is felt especially at the Menin Gate Memorial in Ypres, Belgium, which was officially unveiled in 1927, to honour the more than 55,000 Commonwealth soldiers who went missing.

“Seven thousand of those missing are Canadians, and every single day the Last Post is played there,” said Wagg, who also used the book as an opportunity to delve into war stories that some Canadians might not know about.

For example, the death of Pte. George Lawrence Price who was the last Commonwealth soldier killed in the First World War. Price was a Canadian who died on November 11, 1918, and was laid to rest in St. Symphorien Cemetery near Mons, Belgium.

“About 10 metres way there is a Pte. Parr from the British Expeditionary Force who is buried there and he was the first one killed in the war,” said Wagg. “And between those two graves you could say there were 20-million others killed.”

Wagg also focussed on some historic moments closer to home, like five-year-old Warren “Whitey” Bernard reaching for his father Jack, as he marched off to war from New Westminster, B.C., in 1940. The picture of the two, called “Wait for me Daddy” captured by photographer Claude P. Dettloff, was shown around the world and used to rally support for the war effort both in Canada and abroad.

“That picture showed us the tragedy of a little boy,” said Wagg, who updated the Bernard family history with a picture of Whitey’s post-war reunion with his father.

“Whitey said it was the happiest day of his life and that’s why I chose to have that photo of the day when he came home,” said Wagg.

The book also has a Halifax-focused chapter on The Last Steps Memorial Arch, which honours the more than 350,000 Canadian military men and women who left for Europe from Halifax Harbour, during the First World War.

“It was such a significant place in our nation’s history,” said Corinne MacLellan, who helped lead a volunteer campaign to get the arch rebuilt and unveiled in 2025.

“It was to remind myself, and my family and everyone about the importance that Canada had,” said Keating.

Wagg wants all the pictures and stories in the book to serve as a commemoration of the contributions made by Canadians and how those sacrifices are remembered today at home and beyond.

“These people gave their lives for our country,” said Wagg.

stories.title: How fraudsters got a slice of Canada’s bread price-fixing settlement
stories.summary: A landmark payout was meant to compensate Canadians who paid too much for groceries. Now, it illustrates why class-action scams are a growing problem
stories.author: Susan Krashinsky Robertson, Chen Wang, Tim Kiladze
stories.content:
Ken Wu was on his phone this past spring, scrolling through the popular Chinese social-media app RedNote, when a stranger messaged him with a proposition.

The stranger explained how Mr. Wu could make some easy money off a landmark class-action settlement. Canada’s largest grocer, Loblaw Cos. Ltd. L-T , and its parent company had agreed to pay $500-million in compensation for their role in a high-profile scheme to fix bread prices.

The settlement was the first to come out of lawsuits that were launched after the companies reported an alleged industry-wide conspiracy to the Competition Bureau in 2015, in exchange for immunity from criminal prosecution. (Other grocers have denied involvement.)

The person reaching out to Mr. Wu was among millions of people who had registered on the official website, Canadianbreadsettlement.ca, to receive recompense. For most recipients, that added up to $49.11 sent in the form of an e-transfer via digital-payments giant Interac.

There was much more up for grabs than that paltry sum, the RedNote user explained to Mr. Wu. The stranger had registered for multiple payments using different e-mail addresses, and had received not just one Interac link, but many. The links could be forwarded, and anyone who clicked on them would be able to deposit the money.

But there was a snag: Claimants needed a Canadian bank account to accept the e-transfer, something the stranger didn’t have.

If Mr. Wu, a Vancouver resident, would agree to use his account to make the deposit, the user would ask for an upfront payment for the links, a price lower than the payout that would land in his account – effectively meaning they would split the proceeds.

As a newcomer to Canada who had not purchased bread at Loblaw -owned stores during the time covered by the lawsuit, Mr. Wu knew he wasn’t eligible for a payment.

“I don’t have that right,” he said.

He refused the offer. And several others. But he wasn’t the only person being solicited.

Loblaw Cos. Ltd. and its parent company agreed to a $500-million payout for their role in an alleged industry-wide scheme to fix the price of bread.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

As soon as the bread settlement was distributed in May, a market for the e-transfer links emerged on RedNote – and not just in private messages.

When people began posting that they’d received bread payments, the comments on those posts were wall-to-wall with other people hawking links, some offering generous terms to anyone with a Canadian bank account willing to make, in some cases, hundreds of deposits.

As with any questionable offers made in online forums, it’s impossible to say how many of those posts were selling working e-transfer links, versus looking for a mark who would hand over money and receive nothing.

But around the same time, warning signs began flaring inside Canadian banks. Three small institutions reported unusual account activity to the settlement administrator, Verita Global LLC, and its banking partner that helped make the payments, the Bank of Nova Scotia.

Multiple deposits of the bread money were being funnelled into the same accounts. In one case, a single bank customer deposited roughly 1,000 such e-transfers.

Suddenly, one of the country’s biggest-ever class-action settlements had a big problem.
