Class actions are designed to deliver justice to people who have been wronged. But when bad actors succeed at faking claims, legitimate claimants get a smaller slice of the pie.

The highly publicized bread settlement attracted a large number of applications for the funds, many of which were bogus. Official estimates of suspicious deposits that flowed into Canadian banks have grown.

Court records from June show that, at the request of administrators, Interac provided an estimate that roughly $3.7-million in payments were suspicious, and possibly fraudulent. Within a month, that had been revised to $8.5-million, a figure that has not been previously reported.

But it’s still just an estimate. There has been no official, transparent accounting of how many people received multiple suspicious deposits of $49.11 over the 14-day payment period.

While Canada’s largest grocer paid the settlement money, it did not manage the distribution. The apparatus that oversaw the process involved the court, lawyers, administrators and payment distributors – and it is difficult to determine who is ultimately accountable for the losses.

It’s not clear that any of these actors have a complete picture of how much was taken.

The three small financial institutions that first raised the red flag account for only a tiny fraction of Canada’s banking sector.

Other banks were asked to return bread settlement payments from accounts their own internal systems identified as suspicious. But some are still reviewing the amounts, and others confirmed they had no funds to return, a class-action lawyer told The Globe and Mail.

The Big Six banks, which hold about 90 per cent of Canadian personal deposits, declined to answer questions from The Globe about what their fraud-detection practices found in this case, and whether they froze any accounts related to suspicious payments or returned any funds.

But a fraud specialist from one of the banks told The Globe the number of suspicious transactions discovered in its system pushes the total higher than has been publicly disclosed. The Globe is not identifying the source because they are not authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

Two years after the settlement was first announced, it is clear that fraudsters exploited the system.

And two questions remain unanswered: How much money did they siphon off, and could they have been stopped?

Applying for the Canadian bread settlement was a model of ease and simplicity: Only a handful of basic details were needed, including your name, date of birth, contact information and an attestation of where you bought bread between 2001 and 2021. But more proof was not required.

Huge consumer lawsuits, where a large number of people are eligible to claim compensation, are “a constant battle between accessibility and fraud,” said Suzanne Chiodo, an assistant professor at York University’s Osgoode Hall Law School and author of The Class Actions Controversy , a book about the origins and development of Ontario’s class-action law.

When a class action is resolved, lawyers and settlement administrators have an obligation to ensure as many eligible people as possible receive their payouts. (In the industry, this is known as the “take-up rate.”)

Historically, take-up rates have been very low: Many people simply couldn’t be bothered filling out the forms, particularly when their share of a settlement was relatively small. To combat the problem, lawyers in a case like this are reluctant to set up a process that asks for too much verification – such as proof of purchases that may have occurred years in the past, or banking information to process payments.

As people become more aware of online scams, they are reasonably hesitant to hand over detailed personal information. So while security measures are needed in these cases, ideally the process will avoid scaring off legitimate claimants.

The problem is, the easier a claim is to make, the easier it is to scam. “The wider you open the gates, the more likely you are to get some bad actors,” Prof. Chiodo said.

Grocery receipts were not required from people applying for the bread settlement, only an attestation that they bought bread between 2001 and 2021.Paul Daly/The Canadian Press

The lawyers involved in the bread settlement said they tried to strike an appropriate balance at the outset.

“If the payments process has too much friction, the number of paid claims shrinks. That is contrary to the objective of the class action,” said David Wingfield of Strosberg Wingfield Sasso LLP, a lawyer for the plaintiffs in the Ontario class-action suit over the bread scheme, which covered claimants across most of the country. (A different class-action suit covered Quebec consumers. The settlement resolved Loblaw’s involvement in both.)

Because of the structure of this settlement – and many more like it – fraud is, to some extent, baked in. Administrators in this case were fending it off from the beginning.

On behalf of the class, lawyers hired Verita, which did not respond to questions from The Globe, to oversee the distribution of the settlement outside Quebec. The legal and fiduciary services company screened the applications looking for nefarious actors.

Verita’s firewall blocked 40 million attempted claims before they were filed, for example by rejecting requests to the website where bot activity was detected. Many of those fraudulent attempts came from outside Canada.

Then, an initial screening process looked for people who had filed multiple applications using the same home address or e-mail. That led to millions more claims being rejected.

Another layer of screening examined the digital attributes of each device used to make a claim. Nearly 14 million more suspicious claims were rejected as a result.

But some fraudulent attempts still sneaked through.

All told, Verita approved nearly 3.6 million claims for payment, totalling roughly $174-million – the amount reserved for customers outside Quebec, after factoring in $136-million in legal, administrative and other costs, as well as a chunk of money already paid out in gift cards and payments to businesses that were affected by the scheme.

Once the settlement was divvied up, each successful individual applicant received an e-transfer for $49.11. (For those who registered for and accepted a $25 gift card Loblaw distributed in 2018 as an apology for the scheme, the payout was $24.11.)

But once those payments were sent out, Verita had no line of sight into where the money was flowing. Because of confidentiality rules, neither Interac nor the receiving banks could provide Verita with any confirmation that the names or e-mail addresses on the settlement claims were linked to the accounts where the money was deposited, according to court documents filed in June after allegations of possible fraud were brought forward.

A Verita executive explained in an affidavit, filed in Ontario Superior Court, how someone could enter an e-mail address on the settlement website, then simply forward their Interac e-mail payment to someone else.

“That e-mail may be forwarded on to another e-mail address without impacting the functionality of the deposit link,” Ivan Bobanovic, Verita’s vice-president of settlement administration in Canada, stated. “A person who clicks the Interac deposit link may choose to deposit funds into any Canadian bank account.”

A post from a user on Chinese social-media app RedNote advertises links for sale that would allow buyers to claim $49.11 payments issued in the bread settlement.

An analysis of posts on RedNote from May, translated from Chinese, shows how that feature made it possible for people without Canadian bank accounts to get in on the action. They could offer to share those links with other users who had ties to Canada – for a price.

The analysis does not suggest that fraudulent activity was limited to RedNote. The Globe focused on the app because a high volume of solicitation was taking place out in the open. RedNote did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

In one RedNote thread, a user posted a screenshot of a successful deposit of $49.11 into an unidentified TD Canada Trust account, along with the reference number, as proof of the legitimacy of the links they had for sale. They touted a “large shipment just in,” with 500 links available.

Other users went as far as to post prices that were advertised in cryptic shorthand. Comments such as “2.8” or “3.3” communicated that payment for the links would be settled in Chinese yuan, at multiples of the $49.11 settlement payout. For example, a price of 2.8 meant a buyer would multiply 49.11 by that number, and as a result pay roughly 138 yuan for each Interac link, which they could then deposit into their Canadian bank account.

Because the currency exchange rate at the time was just under five yuan per Canadian dollar, each link at that 2.8 rate would net a buyer roughly $21 in profit. Because sellers were offering links in bulk, that margin quickly added up. In this scenario, a person who bought 200 links would net a profit of roughly $4,200 after paying the fraudster nearly $5,600.

The ‘2.8’ in the first RedNote exchange refers to a price for links, communicated as a multiple of the $49.11 settlement that buyers would pay in Chinese currency.

In some cases, the more links people were willing to buy, the lower the price.

But people also used RedNote to warn each other away from such schemes. Not long after the payments went out last spring, users began posting about accounts being frozen after multiple payments were deposited.

One user identified themselves as a bank employee who had dealt with customers whose accounts were locked for “over-claiming” bread money.

“Because the eligibility bar is so low, bad actors quickly smelled a ‘business opportunity’ and started spreading offers widely on WeChat groups, RedNote, and similar platforms: ‘Help us collect settlement payments, easy commission,’ ‘Buying settlement eligibility at a high price,’ ‘Help receive e-Transfers, we’ll give you a better exchange rate,’” wrote another user, Montreal financial adviser Tim Wen, in a post warning his clients and the broader RedNote community.

“What you stand to gain is only a few dozen or a couple hundred dollars, but what you risk is having your account frozen, your credit damaged, and getting pulled into an anti-money-laundering investigation – it’s simply not worth it,” the same post stated. “If it’s not your money, seriously, don’t touch it.”

Ken Wu said his decision to reject the offers to buy links had nothing to do with avoiding such consequences.

“For me, it’s simply a matter of right and wrong,” he said. “You shouldn’t do something that’s wrong.”

Asked for comment on The Globe’s reporting, Loblaw’s senior vice-president of corporate affairs and communication, Scott Bonikowsky, noted that Loblaw and its parent company were not involved in this year’s settlement distribution process.

“We support efforts to protect the integrity of the claims settlement process as any attempt to exploit that process and divert funds intended for eligible Canadians is concerning,” he wrote in a statement on behalf of Loblaw and George Weston.

The people overseeing the bread settlement payments may never have known about any of this without the tip in late May from three banks identified in court filings as “smaller” financial institutions.

They alerted Verita and Scotiabank that multiple e-transfers were being “aggregated” and channelled through the same accounts, court documents show. Verita then tried to find out if other banks had made similar reports, and why some accounts would be receiving multiple payments.

“Given the receiving banks’ confidentiality obligations, after numerous discussions, the only meaningful insight available was from Interac,” Verita’s Mr. Bobanovic stated in an affidavit sworn in early June. (Seeking a formal court order to compel information from the banks would be a lengthy, expensive and unrealistic process, class-action lawyers explained.)

Scotiabank communicated with financial institutions – including the major banks – requesting that they return any settlement funds that had been deposited to accounts that appeared suspicious.

“Canadian banks have robust monitoring in place to flag suspected fraudulent transactions,” Ethan Teclu, a spokesperson for the Canadian Bankers Association, wrote in an e-mail to The Globe. “When transactions are deemed fraudulent, banks work to return the funds wherever possible when requested by another financial institution.”

The Big Six banks – Scotiabank, Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, National Bank of Canada, Royal Bank of Canada and Toronto-Dominion Bank – did not answer The Globe’s questions about frozen accounts, suspicious payments and returned funds.

Canada's major banks and Interac were limited in how much they could tell Verita about where settlement money was deposited because of confidentiality rules.Ryan Remiorz and Joe O'Connal/CP

Meanwhile, Verita asked Interac to investigate how many more potentially fraudulent payments were made. Interac’s $8.5-million estimate, which was provided to The Globe in July by Mr. Wingfield, the class-action lawyer, would equal just under 5 per cent of the payout.

Interac spokesperson Cillian Murphy declined to explain how the company arrived at the updated estimate and why it grew.

Bryan Heller, co-founder and chief operating officer of Covalynt – a technology provider that specializes in fraud detection and prevention in class-action settlements – told The Globe that judging by his own experience in similar cases, such a low percentage is almost certainly not a complete picture of the fraud in the bread case.

“I’ve frankly never done a settlement with that few claims having fraud,” Mr. Heller said. “It’s significantly higher percentages than that, on 100 per cent of the cases that we do.”

By his guess, “a lot more than 5 per cent of these claims are fraudulent.”

Just a tiny fraction of the money has been reclaimed so far.

As of the end of September, just $14,831.22 had been returned as requested; another $376,176.78 in frozen payments was in the process of being returned, according to information provided by Mr. Wingfield that has not previously been reported. The amount of funds that had been frozen and were being investigated was still to be determined, he said.

The court approved a protocol for returning funds in cases where banks determined that accounts were used improperly, Mr. Wingfield said. “Recipient banks must make these decisions.”

Returned funds could eventually be added to future settlements in the bread price-fixing case, which involves other corporate defendants.

Lawyers in Quebec have said such problems were not present in their separate class-action case, though Quebec applicants were asked to provide similar information. The lawyers declined to answer questions about how they were able to verify that all payments went to legitimate claimants.

Whatever the scale of loss in this case, this kind of fraud is not unique to Canada’s bread settlement.

Another example of alleged large-scale fraud came to light in New York just a week before the first reports of suspicious payments in the Canadian case.

In May, police raided a home in Greece, a suburban town in upstate New York a short drive from the shores of Lake Ontario. As they swept the premises, law enforcement found photoshopped documents sporting fake names; electronic devices with records of class-action lawsuit filings; and multiple paper cheques from settlements.

A 38-year-old named Phillip Digennaro was arrested and charged with conspiracy, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. He stands accused of gathering more than 27,000 payments from various settlements, totalling roughly US$1.3-million, which he deposited into 480 bank accounts. None of the allegations have been proven in court.

While fraud has always been a risk in class-action settlements, the rise of digital payments has reshaped the landscape.

In 2020, only 16 settlements in the U.S. used digital payments over the course of the year, according to a report published by Western Alliance Bank; by 2024, the number of settlements paying out digitally had skyrocketed to 426.

The reason is clear: The courts prioritize forms of payment that are most successful in reaching the people who are entitled to the compensation. The report, published in April last year, found cheques are deposited much less frequently than digital payments, which are cashed 98 per cent of the time in class actions and mass torts, another type of legal proceeding with multiple plaintiffs.

It also costs less to send a digital payment than to mail a cheque, an important consideration for settlement administrators tasked with keeping costs down to ensure more of the settlement money goes to class members.

The digitization of class-action settlements has given rise to a cottage industry of fraud. In the U.S. alone, “significant” indications of fraud in class actions and mass torts ballooned by more than 19,000 per cent between 2021 and 2023, according to the Western Alliance report.

“There’s big money in this,” said Prof. Chiodo of Osgoode Hall.

“The level of sophistication is insane,” Mr. Heller of Covalynt said.

Playing sleight of hand with IP addresses is one way for fraudsters to get through the defences of class-action settlement administrators.Lisi Niesner/Reuters

He has seen fraudsters that seem to test how many applications they can send from a single IP address before being rejected, and then consistently file claims under that threshold before moving on to another IP address.

He said fraudsters will sometimes use “phone farms,” essentially a server stack filled with cellphones controlled by a computer that can reconfigure a device’s fingerprint – telltale signs such as the IP address, the operating system, the text-size setting, the track record of applications, the security permissions it allows, and other details that can identify it – to make it appear as a new, unique device to get around bot detection.

“I deal with a lot of settlement administrators that think they have it figured out, and they do not,” Mr. Heller said, speaking generally about the class-action landscape.

“If you just use these bot-detection tools, somewhere in the ballpark of 35 to 80 per cent of ‘valid’ claims are actually fraudulent,” he added. And with the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, further advances in fraud technology are inevitable.

The Western Alliance Bank report identified three types of fraud that are most commonly involved in such cases: fake-identity fraud, which uses made-up identities to make claims; synthetic-identity fraud that makes claims using real people’s stolen information; and duplication fraud that uses one person’s information to make multiple claims.

Experts say that for those looking to steal compensation from legitimate class members, this kind of scam can be perpetrated on a mass scale, is seen as relatively low-risk and can be extremely lucrative.

“About two years ago, I would say, all of a sudden the level of the fraud increased and the sophistication of the fraud increased,” said Linda Visser, a class-action lawyer at Siskinds LLP with broad experience in price-fixing and consumer-protection cases. It’s “a widespread problem” in Canada and the U.S., she said.

Jean-Marc Leclerc, a Toronto-based partner at Sotos LLP, has had a front-row seat for the explosion of fraud in recent years.

“They were slamming the website, filing claims every second,” Mr. Leclerc said of bot activity in the auto-parts case. He’d never seen anything like it.

It created a mountain of work for the settlement administrator, which in this case was Verita. Along with class-action lawyers, they sifted through the claims, knocking out those they deemed fraudulent. The lawyers also used ClaimScore, Covalynt’s fraud-detection software, to do a second analysis.

After that, Verita made “significant investment to strengthen its security framework” to identify and reduce bot attacks, the company’s operations director, Brett Parker, stated in an affidavit filed with the court in July, 2025, related to that case.

Just months after Mr. Parker detailed his company’s efforts to combat fraud, Verita ran into the problem again – in the bread settlement.

This case is not over.

When Loblaw and its parent company, George Weston, first admitted to price fixing in 2015, they alleged the conspiracy was “industry-wide,” implicating other companies and shattering many Canadians’ trust in the multibillion-dollar grocery sector.

The lawsuits triggered by that admission also name other grocers and a bread manufacturer as defendants. All have denied participating in the alleged scheme, except for Canada Bread.

Under a new owner, Grupo Bimbo, which acquired the company in 2014, Canada Bread pleaded guilty in a Competition Bureau investigation in 2023, and agreed to pay a $50-million fine. (Maple Leaf Foods, which owned a majority stake in Canada Bread at the time of the alleged price fixing, has denied unlawful behaviour at Canada Bread while it was a shareholder.)

The question is, as lawyers continue to press for further settlements in the bread case, how can more theft be prevented?

“In the future, it may be necessary to accept much more friction in class action payment protocols to minimize fraudulent activity, such as by using physical cheques for payment,” Mr. Wingfield, the lawyer in the bread case, told The Globe.

“But this will also reduce the number of legitimate claims paid and increase distribution costs. This is a difficult balance to achieve.”

When lawyers ask courts for approval for a settlement process, it is largely expected that they do their best to combat fraud. But they are also expected not to be profligate with whatever money remains to be paid out to the class – after lawyers’ fees, which can be significant.

“If you have a possible $25 claim, which many of the claims were in this bread case, you don’t want to spend $10 trying to reduce the fraud on a $25 claim, per claim. You want it to be proportionate,” said Pujan Modi, a class-action lawyer at Silver Tree LLP.

Ultimately, the banks have the most visibility. It’s why smaller institutions were able to flag the wrongdoing in this case. Mr. Teclu of the Canadian Bankers Association suggested banks are aware of the role they can play in combatting fraud into the future.

“The banking sector shares information, as appropriate and in compliance with applicable laws, related to a range of ever-evolving fraud and scams and works closely with law enforcement nationwide to help prevent and minimize the impact of fraud and theft,” he wrote.

The fear is that if fraud runs rampant, it could jeopardize trust in the system.

“People are jaded enough about class actions,” said Mr. Leclerc from Sotos, adding that the public is aware of how much lawyers make on successful cases while individual payments may be relatively small, as they were in the bread settlement.

In addition, lawyers have to be able to tell judges they can ensure the money goes into the pockets of the people who actually deserve it.

“So it’s a question of credibility with the public. It’s a question of credibility with the courts,” he said.

Class actions were designed to compensate people who were wronged, and to deter misconduct, said Prof. Chiodo of Osgoode Hall. Instead, when fraud occurs, some of that money is rewarding bad actors.

“The whole point of class actions is access to justice,” she said. “And you’re not going to get access to justice if money is hemorrhaging to fraudsters.”

“I don’t have that right,” he said.

Meanwhile, Verita asked Interac to investigate how many more potentially fraudulent payments were made. Interac’s $8.5-million estimate, which was provided to The Globe in July by Mr. Wingfield, the class-action lawyer, would equal just under 5 per cent of the payout.
Interac spokesperson Cillian Murphy declined to explain how the company arrived at the updated estimate and why it grew.

Bryan Heller, co-founder and chief operating officer of Covalynt – a technology provider that specializes in fraud detection and prevention in class-action settlements – told The Globe that judging by his own experience in similar cases, such a low percentage is almost certainly not a complete picture of the fraud in the bread case.
“I’ve frankly never done a settlement with that few claims having fraud,” Mr. Heller said. “It’s significantly higher percentages than that, on 100 per cent of the cases that we do.”
By his guess, “a lot more than 5 per cent of these claims are fraudulent.”
Just a tiny fraction of the money has been reclaimed so far.

As of the end of September, just $14,831.22 had been returned as requested; another $376,176.78 in frozen payments was in the process of being returned, according to information provided by Mr. Wingfield that has not previously been reported. The amount of funds that had been frozen and were being investigated was still to be determined, he said.
The court approved a protocol for returning funds in cases where banks determined that accounts were used improperly, Mr. Wingfield said. “Recipient banks must make these decisions.”
Returned funds could eventually be added to future settlements in the bread price-fixing case, which involves other corporate defendants.

Lawyers in Quebec have said such problems were not present in their separate class-action case, though Quebec applicants were asked to provide similar information. The lawyers declined to answer questions about how they were able to verify that all payments went to legitimate claimants.
Whatever the scale of loss in this case, this kind of fraud is not unique to Canada’s bread settlement.
Another example of alleged large-scale fraud came to light in New York just a week before the first reports of suspicious payments in the Canadian case.

In May, police raided a home in Greece, a suburban town in upstate New York a short drive from the shores of Lake Ontario. As they swept the premises, law enforcement found photoshopped documents sporting fake names; electronic devices with records of class-action lawsuit filings; and multiple paper cheques from settlements.

A 38-year-old named Phillip Digennaro was arrested and charged with conspiracy, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. He stands accused of gathering more than 27,000 payments from various settlements, totalling roughly US$1.3-million, which he deposited into 480 bank accounts. None of the allegations have been proven in court.
While fraud has always been a risk in class-action settlements, the rise of digital payments has reshaped the landscape.

In 2020, only 16 settlements in the U.S. used digital payments over the course of the year, according to a report published by Western Alliance Bank; by 2024, the number of settlements paying out digitally had skyrocketed to 426.

The reason is clear: The courts prioritize forms of payment that are most successful in reaching the people who are entitled to the compensation. The report, published in April last year, found cheques are deposited much less frequently than digital payments, which are cashed 98 per cent of the time in class actions and mass torts, another type of legal proceeding with multiple plaintiffs.

It also costs less to send a digital payment than to mail a cheque, an important consideration for settlement administrators tasked with keeping costs down to ensure more of the settlement money goes to class members.

The digitization of class-action settlements has given rise to a cottage industry of fraud. In the U.S. alone, “significant” indications of fraud in class actions and mass torts ballooned by more than 19,000 per cent between 2021 and 2023, according to the Western Alliance report.
“There’s big money in this,” said Prof. Chiodo of Osgoode Hall.

Settlement administrators have upped their security measures in response. But while it is possible to weed out rudimentary bot attacks, as technology develops, it’s becoming easier to file more of these fraudulent claims at scale.
“The level of sophistication is insane,” Mr. Heller of Covalynt said.
Playing sleight of hand with IP addresses is one way for fraudsters to get through the defences of class-action settlement administrators.Lisi Niesner/Reuters

He has seen fraudsters that seem to test how many applications they can send from a single IP address before being rejected, and then consistently file claims under that threshold before moving on to another IP address.

He said fraudsters will sometimes use “phone farms,” essentially a server stack filled with cellphones controlled by a computer that can reconfigure a device’s fingerprint – telltale signs such as the IP address, the operating system, the text-size setting, the track record of applications, the security permissions it allows, and other details that can identify it – to make it appear as a new, unique device to get around bot detection.
“I deal with a lot of settlement administrators that think they have it figured out, and they do not,” Mr. Heller said, speaking generally about the class-action landscape.

“If you just use these bot-detection tools, somewhere in the ballpark of 35 to 80 per cent of ‘valid’ claims are actually fraudulent,” he added. And with the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, further advances in fraud technology are inevitable.

The Western Alliance Bank report identified three types of fraud that are most commonly involved in such cases: fake-identity fraud, which uses made-up identities to make claims; synthetic-identity fraud that makes claims using real people’s stolen information; and duplication fraud that uses one person’s information to make multiple claims.

Experts say that for those looking to steal compensation from legitimate class members, this kind of scam can be perpetrated on a mass scale, is seen as relatively low-risk and can be extremely lucrative.

“About two years ago, I would say, all of a sudden the level of the fraud increased and the sophistication of the fraud increased,” said Linda Visser, a class-action lawyer at Siskinds LLP with broad experience in price-fixing and consumer-protection cases. It’s “a widespread problem” in Canada and the U.S., she said.
Jean-Marc Leclerc, a Toronto-based partner at Sotos LLP, has had a front-row seat for the explosion of fraud in recent years.

Mr. Leclerc represented the plaintiffs in a series of class actions over allegations of price fixing against companies that supply parts to automobile manufacturers. The cases resulted in tens of millions of dollars in settlement payments.
In the first round of applications, in 2020, more than 120,000 people made claims to the funds. In the second round, in 2023, “it was in the millions,” he recalled.
“They were slamming the website, filing claims every second,” Mr. Leclerc said of bot activity in the auto-parts case. He’d never seen anything like it.

It created a mountain of work for the settlement administrator, which in this case was Verita. Along with class-action lawyers, they sifted through the claims, knocking out those they deemed fraudulent. The lawyers also used ClaimScore, Covalynt’s fraud-detection software, to do a second analysis.
“There were an overwhelming number of fraudulent claims compared to valid claims,” Mr. Leclerc said.

After that, Verita made “significant investment to strengthen its security framework” to identify and reduce bot attacks, the company’s operations director, Brett Parker, stated in an affidavit filed with the court in July, 2025, related to that case.
Just months after Mr. Parker detailed his company’s efforts to combat fraud, Verita ran into the problem again – in the bread settlement.
This case is not over.

When Loblaw and its parent company, George Weston, first admitted to price fixing in 2015, they alleged the conspiracy was “industry-wide,” implicating other companies and shattering many Canadians’ trust in the multibillion-dollar grocery sector.
The lawsuits triggered by that admission also name other grocers and a bread manufacturer as defendants. All have denied participating in the alleged scheme, except for Canada Bread.

Under a new owner, Grupo Bimbo, which acquired the company in 2014, Canada Bread pleaded guilty in a Competition Bureau investigation in 2023, and agreed to pay a $50-million fine. (Maple Leaf Foods, which owned a majority stake in Canada Bread at the time of the alleged price fixing, has denied unlawful behaviour at Canada Bread while it was a shareholder.)
The question is, as lawyers continue to press for further settlements in the bread case, how can more theft be prevented?

“In the future, it may be necessary to accept much more friction in class action payment protocols to minimize fraudulent activity, such as by using physical cheques for payment,” Mr. Wingfield, the lawyer in the bread case, told The Globe.
“But this will also reduce the number of legitimate claims paid and increase distribution costs. This is a difficult balance to achieve.”

When lawyers ask courts for approval for a settlement process, it is largely expected that they do their best to combat fraud. But they are also expected not to be profligate with whatever money remains to be paid out to the class – after lawyers’ fees, which can be significant.

“If you have a possible $25 claim, which many of the claims were in this bread case, you don’t want to spend $10 trying to reduce the fraud on a $25 claim, per claim. You want it to be proportionate,” said Pujan Modi, a class-action lawyer at Silver Tree LLP.
From their headquarters in Toronto, Canada's major banks have a big role to play in combatting fraud.Adrien Veczan/The Canadian Press

Ultimately, the banks have the most visibility. It’s why smaller institutions were able to flag the wrongdoing in this case. Mr. Teclu of the Canadian Bankers Association suggested banks are aware of the role they can play in combatting fraud into the future.

“The banking sector shares information, as appropriate and in compliance with applicable laws, related to a range of ever-evolving fraud and scams and works closely with law enforcement nationwide to help prevent and minimize the impact of fraud and theft,” he wrote.
The fear is that if fraud runs rampant, it could jeopardize trust in the system.

“People are jaded enough about class actions,” said Mr. Leclerc from Sotos, adding that the public is aware of how much lawyers make on successful cases while individual payments may be relatively small, as they were in the bread settlement.
In addition, lawyers have to be able to tell judges they can ensure the money goes into the pockets of the people who actually deserve it.
“So it’s a question of credibility with the public. It’s a question of credibility with the courts,” he said.
Class actions were designed to compensate people who were wronged, and to deter misconduct, said Prof. Chiodo of Osgoode Hall. Instead, when fraud occurs, some of that money is rewarding bad actors.
“The whole point of class actions is access to justice,” she said. “And you’re not going to get access to justice if money is hemorrhaging to fraudsters.”
With a report from Stefanie Marotta

stories.title: With a labour board ruling expected soon, Ontario teacher talks set for November
stories.summary: Talks are set to start after a labour board ruling, which is expected mid-month.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
Two teachers unions will start bargaining with the provincial government in late November, now that a ruling from the labour board is expected in the next couple of weeks to clear up what issues can be discussed.

Talks are scheduled for the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation on Nov. 24, Dec. 2 and Dec. 15 for the permanent and occasional teachers it represents. Negotiators for education workers represented by the federation will start talking with the province on Nov. 20, with additional dates set for Dec. 9 and 10.

The Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association told members it will be bargaining Nov. 24 and Dec. 7 and 8, according to a memo obtained by the Star.

Other education unions are expected to announce bargaining dates in the coming days.

All education contracts expired at the end of August, but talks have been in limbo while the sides wait for the Ontario Labour Relations Board to decide what items should be hammered out with the provincial government or with local boards under the province’s two-tiered bargaining system.

Typically, costly items such as salary and benefits are discussed provincially, while more administrative issues are handled locally.

Union leader representing custodians, educational assistants and office staff says work-to-rule hasn’t been effective in the past.

The unions have said the province wants to add a number of issues to the central talks — such as salary grid progression, short-term paid and unpaid time off, scheduling/student supervision and contracting out — that in the past have been handled locally.

Labour board hearings were held in recent weeks for all unions and “we are hopeful a decision will be available in early November,” said a memo from Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions to members.

In the meantime, the labour relations board will bring the education unions and government together on Nov. 2 to try last-ditch mediation to resolve the central-local divide, but said that won’t delay its decision.

“Mediation is a normal part of the process, and (the secondary school teachers’ federation) remains committed to moving bargaining forward,” president Martha Hradowy said in a statement to the Star.

“We continue to pursue all options available to us as we work toward fair collective agreements that protect the interests of our members and the students they support.”

All education unions have scheduled strikes votes in November, though there are a number of legal steps they must take before calling any job action such as a work-to-rule or full work stoppage.

Emma Testani, press secretary to Education Minister Paul Calandra, has previously said the province respects the unions’ rights to take their case to the labour board, “but this process has delayed the start of bargaining. Once the process has concluded, we will be ready and willing to negotiate whenever the unions are ready to begin.”

stories.title: Elections Alberta urges MLAs to hold off on approving new electoral map or postpone 2027 vote
stories.summary: In a letter sent to MLAs, the agency says it lacks the resources to implement new riding boundaries before the election
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta’s chief electoral officer is urging members of the provincial legislature to either not approve the new electoral maps scheduled to be released Monday or delay next year’s provincial election, saying Elections Alberta doesn’t have the time or resources to implement the changes by next year’s fixed election date.

Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure, in a Friday letter sent to each of the province’s 87 MLAs, and circulated by the Alberta NDP, warned that the flurry of electoral activity in the province over the past year has severely constrained the agency’s ability to prepare for the next provincial election.

Elections Alberta typically requires 12 to 18 months to plan and prepare for a provincial election, and establishing the boundaries is only the first step in the process, he wrote.

As a consequence, Mr. McClure urged MLAs to consider one of two options: hold the Oct. 18, 2027 provincial election using the already established electoral map, or accept the new map and extend the fixed-election date “where legally authorized and necessary.”

“I urge all Members to consider the time required for implementation as deliberations concerning electoral boundaries proceed,” Mr. McClure wrote.

“A timely and definitive resolution, together with an appropriate contingency plan should additional time be required, is essential to protecting the readiness and successful delivery of Alberta’s next provincial general election.”

Alberta’s electoral boundaries are expected to be tabled in the provincial legislature on Monday and, if approved, would be used for next year’s election.

The redrawing process, mandated by Alberta law, has been clouded by allegations of gerrymandering, the U.S.-style tactic of manipulating electoral maps to create an artificial advantage, since Premier Danielle Smith in April rejected a independent commission’s proposed boundaries.

Her government then formed a UCP-dominated committee that created a new independent panel charged with taking a second attempt at drawing the electoral map. The panel consisted of two members tapped by the NDP, two by the UCP, and was chaired by retired Alberta judge Brian O’Ferrall.

It delivered that map to the committee of MLAs last week.

The report remains confidential, but on Wednesday Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi and two fellow New Democrat MLAs detailed extensive concerns about the new proposed boundaries.

Mr. Nenshi called the map “illegal,” saying Ms. Smith’s government had “engineered the single worst case of gerrymandering in Alberta history” – though he stopped short of saying whether the NDP planned to launch a legal challenge.

The Premier has said she will withhold judgment on the map until it is publicly released.

But with the prospect of a bitter political fight and potential court challenge over the boundaries, Mr. McClure wrote that compressing the timeline ahead of next year’s election would stretch Elections Alberta even further.

“While Elections Alberta takes no position on the merits of any potential legal proceedings, the prospect of a court challenge introduces additional uncertainty into an already compressed implementation schedule,” he wrote.

He continued that Elections Alberta is already the leanest electoral agency in Canada on a per-voter-served basis.

Mr. McClure has issued several warnings this year about Elections Alberta’s ability to manage the recent referendum and next year’s provincial election, in addition to the wave of citizen-initiated and recall petitions launched over the past year.

He reiterated those concerns in his letter, saying resources normally dedicated to the general election were diverted for the referendum.

“In the last 24 months we have been increasingly required to do more, with less resources,” he wrote.

Mr. McClure’s recommendations give Ms. Smith’s government the option of pushing back the next general election.

The Premier’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party government was elected on May 29, 2023, giving the province the option of holding the next election in spring, 2028, at the latest.

Her government in 2024 pushed back the fixed election date from May to October to reduce the risk of elections being impacted by natural disasters, which tend to occur more often in the spring. Wildfires during the 2023 vote forced the evacuation of nearly 30,000 people as parties jostled on the campaign trail.

Under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, provincial legislatures have a maximum legal lifespan of five years.

Mr. Nenshi, in a statement, called on Ms. Smith to adopt the electoral map proposed by the previous independent panel.

“Danielle Smith and the UCP should have implemented the independent commission’s report six months ago and they could still do it now,” he wrote.

“Albertans deserve to vote in free, fair and timely elections.”

Elections Alberta did not respond to a request for comment.

stories.title: Eviction day at contentious homeless encampment in Penticton
stories.summary: RCMP officers were on scene to ensure everyone's safety as outreach workers helped roughly a dozen residents vacate the property.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Residents of Penticton’s Fairview homeless encampment were forced to pack up and leave Friday, as a court-ordered injunction cleared the site following months of safety concerns.

RCMP officers were on scene to ensure everyone’s safety as outreach workers helped roughly a dozen residents vacate the property.

For John Tanghe, the eviction came with little time to figure out what comes next.

“They decided on Monday that we had to go, and then Friday we got to get out of here,” Tanghe said.

With residents packing up and no resistance reported, authorities allowed people to remain beyond the noon deadline as they worked to clear the site.

But the displacement drew criticism from some Penticton residents, who questioned the timing of the eviction as temperatures drop heading into November.

“This is not going to solve the problem. It’s not very humane. It’s not a humane approach,” said concerned citizen Danielle Savage.

Savage, along with two others, stood near the encampment Friday to draw attention to the impact on those being displaced.

“It’s going on November. It’s freezing out, and people have very modest means to stay warm, and that’s being destroyed today,” she said.

The eviction follows growing safety concerns surrounding the encampment, including several fires. One fire last year spread onto the neighbouring Leisureland RV Centre property, destroying two recreational vehicles.

For Leisureland owner Yvonne Marsden, the removal of the encampment was a long time coming.

“It’s been a very long time coming,” Marsden said.

While she welcomed the move from a business perspective, Marsden also expressed concern for the people being forced to leave.

“As a business owner, happy to see it happen. Personally, though, the support for them — where are they going to go? And I feel for them in that way,” she said.

Questions also remain about what additional supports will be available to those displaced. With shelter space already at capacity, the province would not say whether more resources would be provided, citing its post-election caretaker status.

The latest eviction is reminiscent of efforts to clear the same encampment in June 2025. Despite those efforts, not everyone left, and the camp eventually grew again.

This time, however, the court-ordered injunction gives authorities the ability to enforce the removal of residents from the property.

For some Penticton residents, the focus remains on whether removing the encampment will address the broader challenges facing people experiencing homelessness.

Concerned resident Jeff Andrew says more than simply clearing the site is needed.

“I just don’t see how tearing it down right now will make things better,” Andrew said.

He says the community needs a wider range of services, including shelter options and treatment facilities.

“We need dry shelters, wet shelters, we need detox centres, we need places for people to go during the day and set up during the night,” he said.

For Tanghe, the immediate concern is finding somewhere to go.

“We really don’t know, so I’m gonna start at City Hall. Yeah, that’s where I’m gonna go,” he said.

stories.title: From mess to majority: how the BC Conservatives won the election
stories.summary: The party was in turmoil leading up to the snap election call, with a brand-new interim leader and a wave of departures. How did it turn the ship around?
stories.author: Mike Hager, Andrea Woo, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
In the months leading up to David Eby’s snap election call, chaos reigned in the BC Conservative Party.

It was plagued by staff dismissals, MLA defections, damaging leaks of internal conversations, separate probes by the RCMP and the elections watchdog into alleged political inducements , and – amid the mayhem – a leader unable to calm her dwindling caucus as it sought answers.

Peter Milobar was the first domino to fall, quitting the Conservative caucus to sit as an independent in mid-August.

“You could tell that this was going to just keep spiralling out of control,” Mr. Milobar, who was re-elected last weekend as Kamloops Centre MLA, told The Globe at the time.

Andrew Coyne: Did the B.C. Conservatives’ election win run against the federal tide, or with it?

Over the next month, a dozen other MLAs either quit or were expelled by the new leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, fuelling speculation that Mr. Eby, then the NDP leader and B.C. premier, would call an election to capitalize on his ravaged rivals.

As the pressure on her mounted to right the Conservative ship, it became increasingly clear that was unlikely.

Ms. Findlay’s resignation on Sept. 20 capped months of turmoil that threatened to squander the party’s hard-fought gains in popularity. Her departure cleared the path for new leader Lorne Doerkson and catalyzed a remarkable reversal of fortunes that would carry the Conservatives all the way to victory and a majority government.

The Globe and Mail spoke with more than a dozen Conservative politicians, staffers and strategists to piece together the days leading up to the Sept. 22 election call and ensuing campaign.

In mid-September, delegates at the annual Union of BC Municipalities convention, rankled by the prospect of overlapping provincial and municipal elections, passed an emergency resolution urging Mr. Eby to hold off. Mr. Eby said he would “take the resolution under advisement.”

That same Wednesday, Sept. 16, the Conservative caucus held an emergency meeting.

MLA Claire Rattée said the next day she was one of 10 signatories on a letter urging Ms. Findlay to step down. A defiant Ms. Findlay told the municipalities convention that she was “not going anywhere,” and on Sept. 18 expelled Ms. Rattée, Trevor Halford and John Rustad, the long-time Northern B.C. MLA who led the Conservatives to within three seats of forming government in the 2024 election.

“There’s no room for internal power struggles or vanity projects. If your priority is building the movement, and supporting the Conservative Party of B.C., you are welcome,” Ms. Findlay wrote in a post on X.

But behind the scenes, Ms. Findlay was already negotiating severance pay with the party before she would agree to leave, according to a member of the campaign team. The Globe is not naming the person, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

Ms. Findlay did not respond to The Globe’s requests for comment this week.

When Ms. Findlay’s inevitable resignation did happen, strategists and the caucus immediately began floating names for her potential replacement: MLA Harman Bhangu; Mr. Halford, the party’s former interim leader; Conservative MP Aaron Gunn; and former provincial leadership hopeful Iain Black.

Caroline Elliott, who had narrowly lost the leadership race to Ms. Findlay four months earlier, said she received calls from people “just assuming she’d be jumping in.” But she thought Mr. Doerkson was the perfect candidate, in part because, as a past supporter of Mr. Milobar’s failed leadership bid, he had the best chance at bringing the Conservative defectors back into the fold. Mr. Milobar had since become leader of the nascent CentreBC party, bringing with him seven former Conservative MLAs.

That afternoon, long-time conservative pollster Dimitri Pantazopoulos arrived home to Vancouver and immediately called Mr. Milobar to discuss how CentreBC might capitalize on the chaos to become the viable option for right-wing voters in the province. A merger with the Conservatives wasn’t ruled out either, Mr. Pantazopoulos told The Globe this week.

A marathon caucus meeting was held that night and resulted in a letter to the board supporting Mr. Doerkson as interim leader, signed by more than half the party’s 29 MLAs at the time. According to Conservative caucus chair and MLA Jody Toor, this included Brent Chapman, then the MLA for Surrey South, and also the husband of Ms. Findlay.

Kiel Giddens, who was re-elected as Prince George-Mackenzie MLA last weekend, said Mr. Doerkson had long been “a leader in the caucus room” and didn’t have the baggage of past leadership hopefuls.

Mr. Doerkson, meanwhile, learned of the developments on a layover in Amsterdam while returning from a conference in South Africa. He accepted the position , recognizing the stakes of the imminent election, and began making calls the moment he stepped off the plane in Vancouver.

The next day, Sept. 21, Mr. Doerkson met with Mr. Milobar and Mr. Pantazopoulos in Vancouver. They crafted a reunification proposal that the two leaders would present to their respective caucuses the next morning.

“It’s important to recognize that when people left the caucus, myself and others, it wasn’t because there was this big rift between people within the caucus room,” Mr. Milobar said in an interview this week. “It was really around leadership, leadership decisions and electoral viability.”

Mr. Doerkson also met with Katy Merrifield, a political operative who had served as communications director to former B.C. premier Christy Clark, former Alberta premier Jason Kenney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. As well, she had managed leadership campaigns for both Mr. Poilievre and former BC Liberal leader Andrew Wilkinson.

Conservative Party members approached Ms. Merrifield about managing the campaign, but she was hesitant, with a new private-sector job just days away. As well, polling then had the Conservatives at least seven points behind, and internal morale was low.

That night, she sought advice, including from Ms. Clark, who encouraged her to serve as campaign director.

“She said, ‘Look, you guys have a chance here. Folks are coming together. I think you should do this,’” Ms. Merrifield said in an interview.

Mr. Eby called the snap election the next morning, Sept. 22, saying his party needed a stronger mandate to meet the “existential moment” brought by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

For Mr. Doerkson’s first news conference as leader, held in Vancouver’s Crab Park, the campaign team crafted a script that introduced him to British Columbians and emphasized party unity and credibility. They illustrated the point with a backdrop of former defectors, including Mr. Milobar, who stood smiling behind their new leader.

Asked by a reporter about Mr. Trump, Mr. Doerkson called the U.S. President a bully. Conservative insiders said the response neutralized a central tenet of the Ndp’s campaign: that the Conservatives were “Maple Maga” and only the New Democrats would fight back.

Standing out of frame was the party’s former executive director, Angelo Isidorou, who was still hesitant to formally rejoin the group. A week and a half earlier, news broke that he was one of several members allegedly surveilled by a private eye hired by his successor in an ill-fated attempt to root out Conservatives leaking incriminating audio recordings.

But Mr. Isidorou was impressed by Mr. Doerkson, and joined the campaign “war room.”

Ms. Merrifield said her team scrambled to recruit people to manage tour logistics, communications and fundraising, scaling up an operation of more than 70 people in a matter of days.

Ben Woodfinden, a former director of communications for Mr. Poilievre, was brought on. He said Mr. Doerkson’s performance at that first news conference proved to the team that the relative newcomer was “not a weakness; he’s an immense asset.”

Internal polling also showed that the Ndp’s attacks on the Conservatives were failing to slow the party’s rising popularity. This included the revelation of Mr. Doerkson’s letter to trial lawyers and insurance executives, promising to repeal the province’s no-fault auto insurance system.

The Globe’s Andrea Woo explains what led to the B.C. Ndp’s defeat. Andrea Woo and Alex Migdal/The Globe and Mail

Mr. Giddens was appointed chair of the party’s election readiness committee, which – with no time for traditional nomination contests – relied on trusted networks and past contenders to quickly assemble a full slate of 93 candidates. Those selected received phone calls and information packages from campaign headquarters each morning and were directed to stay on message: affordability, safety, “supercharging” the economy.

Candidates were vetted as quickly as possible, through criminal-record checks, social-media scans and other research, party insiders said. Two approved candidates were later turfed after the NDP surfaced their social-media posts – one calling for the murder of pro-Palestinian protesters, the other minimizing the Holocaust. Mr. Doerkson immediately denounced their views.

The party faced a more difficult decision when the NDP brought to light an anti-Islamic post by Ms. Merrifield from June.

Ms. Merrifield, who had deleted the post within hours, said it was made in response to accounts of sexual abuse by grooming gangs in Britain, which she found deeply upsetting as a survivor of sexual violence. Her anger was directed at extremism, not Muslims or their faith, she said.

Mr. Doerkson publicly defended Ms. Merrifield and kept her on as campaign director. But the issue spooked some operatives, who felt she should go.

Ms. Merrifield said she checked internal data multiple times a day to see whether the issue was hurting their campaign. It wasn’t.

“If there was ever a chance that I would have ruined our chances, I would have resigned on the spot,” she said.

Brad Zubyk, a senior strategist with the Conservatives, said the weakness of the Ndp’s campaign surprised him.

“The fatal flaw was them thinking that they were actually popular or the Conservatives were unpopular, as opposed to KLF [Ms. Findlay] was unpopular, but that didn’t necessarily extend to the Conservatives,” Mr. Zubyk said.

By election night, internal polling had the Conservatives winning more than 60 seats. Mr. Doerkson watched the results come in from a green room at the party’s headquarters, surrounded by family and members of his team. Ultimately, the Conservatives took 63 seats, enough to give them a healthy majority.

Mr. Isidorou said he is so cynical he had a hard time imagining a major victory, despite the very positive polling numbers Mr. Pantazopoulos delivered daily throughout the campaign.

“All that happened is that we did a good enough job of walking and chewing gum at the same time,” said the strategist credited with helping resurrect the party from the political wilderness just three years ago. “What I mean is that we kept our base – we kept our coalition that we had – but we also expanded it.”

But Mr. Isidorou was impressed by Mr. Doerkson, and joined the campaign “war room.”
Ms. Merrifield said her team scrambled to recruit people to manage tour logistics, communications and fundraising, scaling up an operation of more than 70 people in a matter of days.

Ben Woodfinden, a former director of communications for Mr. Poilievre, was brought on. He said Mr. Doerkson’s performance at that first news conference proved to the team that the relative newcomer was “not a weakness; he’s an immense asset.”

Internal polling also showed that the Ndp’s attacks on the Conservatives were failing to slow the party’s rising popularity. This included the revelation of Mr. Doerkson’s letter to trial lawyers and insurance executives, promising to repeal the province’s no-fault auto insurance system.
The Globe’s Andrea Woo explains what led to the B.C. Ndp’s defeat. Andrea Woo and Alex Migdal/The Globe and Mail

Mr. Giddens was appointed chair of the party’s election readiness committee, which – with no time for traditional nomination contests – relied on trusted networks and past contenders to quickly assemble a full slate of 93 candidates. Those selected received phone calls and information packages from campaign headquarters each morning and were directed to stay on message: affordability, safety, “supercharging” the economy.

Candidates were vetted as quickly as possible, through criminal-record checks, social-media scans and other research, party insiders said. Two approved candidates were later turfed after the NDP surfaced their social-media posts – one calling for the murder of pro-Palestinian protesters, the other minimizing the Holocaust. Mr. Doerkson immediately denounced their views.
The party faced a more difficult decision when the NDP brought to light an anti-Islamic post by Ms. Merrifield from June.

Ms. Merrifield, who had deleted the post within hours, said it was made in response to accounts of sexual abuse by grooming gangs in Britain, which she found deeply upsetting as a survivor of sexual violence. Her anger was directed at extremism, not Muslims or their faith, she said.
Mr. Doerkson publicly defended Ms. Merrifield and kept her on as campaign director. But the issue spooked some operatives, who felt she should go.
Ms. Merrifield said she checked internal data multiple times a day to see whether the issue was hurting their campaign. It wasn’t.
“If there was ever a chance that I would have ruined our chances, I would have resigned on the spot,” she said.
Brad Zubyk, a senior strategist with the Conservatives, said the weakness of the Ndp’s campaign surprised him.

“The fatal flaw was them thinking that they were actually popular or the Conservatives were unpopular, as opposed to KLF [Ms. Findlay] was unpopular, but that didn’t necessarily extend to the Conservatives,” Mr. Zubyk said.

By election night, internal polling had the Conservatives winning more than 60 seats. Mr. Doerkson watched the results come in from a green room at the party’s headquarters, surrounded by family and members of his team. Ultimately, the Conservatives took 63 seats, enough to give them a healthy majority.
Mr. Isidorou said he is so cynical he had a hard time imagining a major victory, despite the very positive polling numbers Mr. Pantazopoulos delivered daily throughout the campaign.

“All that happened is that we did a good enough job of walking and chewing gum at the same time,” said the strategist credited with helping resurrect the party from the political wilderness just three years ago. “What I mean is that we kept our base – we kept our coalition that we had – but we also expanded it.”

stories.title: Pride flag effectively banned from being displayed at Alberta schools, Lgbtq non-profit says
stories.summary: New regulation prohibits flags that make ‘political, social or ideological statement’ on behalf of school board
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
The rainbow Pride flag will effectively be banned from being displayed at schools in Alberta beginning in the new year as part of legislation to remove what the province calls ideology from classrooms, a prominent Lgbtq organization says.

The new Flag Display Regulation prohibits flags that “constitute a political, social or ideological statement or position on the part of the school board,” according to the province.

In practice, this will remove Pride flags from Alberta schools, Pflag Canada, a non-profit organization that supports and advocates for Lgtbq individuals, said in a statement.

Student advocacy organizations and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association have also criticized the move, saying it raises concerns about freedom of expression and will harm Lgbtq students.

“It’s deeply troubling on many fronts,” said Harini Sivalingam, director of Ccla’s equality program.

The new rules do not apply to individuals or their personal items, such as clothing or pins worn by students.

School boards will be required to fly the Canadian and Alberta flags outside of school buildings during the academic year, beginning Jan. 4.

Other flags, such as the Franco-Albertan flag, civil and municipal flags and the Royal Union Flag will be permitted on specified days.

Flags that are directly related to the instruction of a course or program of study can be temporarily displayed, and First Nations, Métis Settlements General Council and Métis Settlement flags and foreign national flags May be displayed during official visits, celebrations, ceremonial occasions or on specific days.

School boards that wish to display any other flags must submit a written request to the Ministry of Education and Childcare.

The proposed flag would have to meet at least one of the following criteria: be representative of the school population and community context; be part of existing physical infrastructure; be reflective of school identity; be associated with a commemorative day or observance; or be part of a school event.

School boards hoping to display a Pride flag in June for Pride month or some other time would need to submit an exemption request to the ministry. They would have to make the case that the flag meets at least one of the above criteria while also persuading the ministry that the flag does not constitute a political, social or ideological statement or position on the part of the school board.

Earlier this year, Alberta passed Bill 25 , An Act to Remove Politics and Ideology from Classrooms, which the government said would help ensure school divisions do not take sides in politically or socially divisive causes and issues, including restrictions on the display of flags.

Implementation of the flag law was delayed to the new year to give school boards more time to provide feedback and work through issues related to the changes.

“The Canadian and Alberta flags are symbols that unite us and reflect the values we share. These changes will provide a clear and consistent approach to flag displays in schools, while keeping the focus where it belongs: on student learning and success,” Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said in a statement. His office declined a request for an interview.

The new regulation will have a chilling effect, said Christopher Longtin, board chair of Pflag Canada.

“The flag means a lot more than I think people realize,” he said. “It tells students, teachers, visitors in a school that they can be themselves and talk openly,” he said.

While the new regulation raises questions about freedom of expression and whether government should dictate what symbols of identity and inclusion are welcomed in public spaces, it fundamentally sends a message to young people about whether they belong in schools, the Ccla’s Ms. Sivalingam said.

“The message that it sends is a message of exclusion.”

Wing Li, a spokesperson for Support Our Students, a public education advocacy organization, said the flag rules are part of the government’s “culture war” on schools.

“This is not the first culture-war issue or target that the province has launched,” she said.

Last year, the province ordered schools to remove books featuring explicit sexual content , which resulted in Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale and other literary classics being pulled.

In the wake of public outcry, the government amended the rules to only focus on books that featured visual depictions of sexual acts.

“We’re moving backward to where we’re going to see more negativity and stigmatism to an already tough journey for gay, queer and trans kids,” Ms. Li said.

Alberta NDP education critic Amanda Chapman accused the government of ignoring more important issues facing schools.

“Albertans are worried about overcrowded classrooms and increasingly complex student needs, not policing flags. None of the Ucp’s culture war nonsense helps a single student or teacher,” she said in a statement.

Jason Schilling, president of the Alberta Teachers’ Federation, called the flags regulation a solution to a problem that doesn’t exist.

“What problem is the government trying to solve here? Albertans aren’t asking for more rules about flags. They’re asking for smaller classes and better supports for students,” he said in a statement.
paragraphs: The rainbow Pride flag will effectively be banned from being displayed at schools in Alberta beginning in the new year as part of legislation to remove what the province calls ideology from classrooms, a prominent Lgbtq organization says.
The new Flag Display Regulation prohibits flags that “constitute a political, social or ideological statement or position on the part of the school board,” according to the province.
In practice, this will remove Pride flags from Alberta schools, Pflag Canada, a non-profit organization that supports and advocates for Lgtbq individuals, said in a statement.
Student advocacy organizations and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association have also criticized the move, saying it raises concerns about freedom of expression and will harm Lgbtq students.
“It’s deeply troubling on many fronts,” said Harini Sivalingam, director of Ccla’s equality program.
The new rules do not apply to individuals or their personal items, such as clothing or pins worn by students.
School boards will be required to fly the Canadian and Alberta flags outside of school buildings during the academic year, beginning Jan. 4.
Other flags, such as the Franco-Albertan flag, civil and municipal flags and the Royal Union Flag will be permitted on specified days.

Flags that are directly related to the instruction of a course or program of study can be temporarily displayed, and First Nations, Métis Settlements General Council and Métis Settlement flags and foreign national flags May be displayed during official visits, celebrations, ceremonial occasions or on specific days.
School boards that wish to display any other flags must submit a written request to the Ministry of Education and Childcare.

The proposed flag would have to meet at least one of the following criteria: be representative of the school population and community context; be part of existing physical infrastructure; be reflective of school identity; be associated with a commemorative day or observance; or be part of a school event.

School boards hoping to display a Pride flag in June for Pride month or some other time would need to submit an exemption request to the ministry. They would have to make the case that the flag meets at least one of the above criteria while also persuading the ministry that the flag does not constitute a political, social or ideological statement or position on the part of the school board.

Earlier this year, Alberta passed Bill 25 , An Act to Remove Politics and Ideology from Classrooms, which the government said would help ensure school divisions do not take sides in politically or socially divisive causes and issues, including restrictions on the display of flags.
Implementation of the flag law was delayed to the new year to give school boards more time to provide feedback and work through issues related to the changes.

“The Canadian and Alberta flags are symbols that unite us and reflect the values we share. These changes will provide a clear and consistent approach to flag displays in schools, while keeping the focus where it belongs: on student learning and success,” Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said in a statement. His office declined a request for an interview.
The new regulation will have a chilling effect, said Christopher Longtin, board chair of Pflag Canada.
“The flag means a lot more than I think people realize,” he said. “It tells students, teachers, visitors in a school that they can be themselves and talk openly,” he said.

While the new regulation raises questions about freedom of expression and whether government should dictate what symbols of identity and inclusion are welcomed in public spaces, it fundamentally sends a message to young people about whether they belong in schools, the Ccla’s Ms. Sivalingam said.
“The message that it sends is a message of exclusion.”
Wing Li, a spokesperson for Support Our Students, a public education advocacy organization, said the flag rules are part of the government’s “culture war” on schools.
“This is not the first culture-war issue or target that the province has launched,” she said.
Last year, the province ordered schools to remove books featuring explicit sexual content , which resulted in Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale and other literary classics being pulled.
In the wake of public outcry, the government amended the rules to only focus on books that featured visual depictions of sexual acts.
“We’re moving backward to where we’re going to see more negativity and stigmatism to an already tough journey for gay, queer and trans kids,” Ms. Li said.
Alberta NDP education critic Amanda Chapman accused the government of ignoring more important issues facing schools.

“Albertans are worried about overcrowded classrooms and increasingly complex student needs, not policing flags. None of the Ucp’s culture war nonsense helps a single student or teacher,” she said in a statement.
Jason Schilling, president of the Alberta Teachers’ Federation, called the flags regulation a solution to a problem that doesn’t exist.
“What problem is the government trying to solve here? Albertans aren’t asking for more rules about flags. They’re asking for smaller classes and better supports for students,” he said in a statement.

stories.title: Family traumatized after violent Bridle Path home invasion, injured father says
stories.summary: Police are searching for three suspects who forced their way into the home before fleeing in an SUV
stories.author: Colin Freeze, Tavia Grant
stories.content:
A real estate executive is decrying an increase in violent robberies in Toronto after he and his family members were shot during a home invasion in the city’s upscale Bridle Path neighbourhood.

Toronto police are investigating what they described as a random home invasion by assailants early Thursday morning.

David Morton, 75, released a statement on Friday thanking the public for its support after the incident left his family traumatized, with some members still in the hospital.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Mr. Morton, chief executive of the MAC Group, said in the statement.

“It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.”

The family includes Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and the couple’s two adult daughters Cristina and Maggie Zohil-Morton.

Toronto has seen an increase in home invasions even as shootings and homicides have declined. Canada’s largest city has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year, according to police statistics.

Police said Friday they are looking for three suspects, who allegedly broke into the home, went up to the second floor and demanded valuables.

During an altercation, police said, the attackers shot the father and his two daughters, while their mother was injured with a hammer.

Mr. Morton’s statement pointed to an increase in home invasions in the city.

“While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto,” he said.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.”

The Bridle Path is one of Canada’s most exclusive neighbourhoods, where large houses are hidden behind high walls and wrought-iron gates. The family’s house on Hyde Park Circle is now surrounded by extra police security.

Years ago, the couple started the MAC Group, which rents out luxury apartments in several countries.

The company’s website has a blog by family members which speaks about their life before the attack.

Mr. Morton writes he spent decades in the hospitality industry before striking out on his own. “My career began with some of the world’s leading hotel brands, including Four Seasons and Westin Hotels, before I went on to build our family of businesses,” he says.

His wife Doriana says she is involved in running the MAC Group and also charities, including ones that help provide furniture to teenagers leaving the child-welfare system. “Relationships remain at the heart of everything I do,” she writes.

Maggie Zohil-Morton graduated from Queen’s and Dalhousie universities. “Maggie’s passion for her hometown of Toronto is evident in her work,” the posting says, adding she is “also a trusted Caribbean expert.”

Cristina Zohil-Morton graduated from the University of Birmingham in England and became a lawyer. She now “offers professional legal guidance to those seeking to relocate to Canada,” the family blog says.

On Friday, members of the Toronto Police Service’s mounted unit paraded through the neighbourhood on horseback. Officers in squad cars and on foot were nearby. Commanders of the force say that this show of law-enforcement will continue for the time being.

“Residents can expect an increased police presence in coming days,” Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said in a statement on X . He said he is ordering “additional resources to address this concerning trend of home invasions.”

With reports from Stephanie Chambers
