stories.title: Road construction horrors haunt family-run costume shop in London, Ont.
stories.summary: McCulloch’s Costume, Party Supplies, and Dancewear has served customers since 1962, but ongoing road construction continues to haunt the local Halloween destination.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
McCulloch’s Costume, Party Supplies, and Dancewear has served customers since 1962, but ongoing road construction continues to haunt the local Halloween destination.

Co-owner Rose McCulloch says repeated construction closures near Dundas Street and Nightingale Avenue is taking a toll, “Our sales this year are down about a third, so that really hurts.”

After roadwork in front of the store wrapped up, construction of the bus rapid transit (BRT) system moved just east, closing all four lanes of Dundas.

Access from the north was also temporarily closed for roadwork on Nightingale Avenue last weekend, adding to the challenge during the Halloween shopping season.

“There’s been about three times in the last few years when they have closed down Dundas Street in our busiest season,” explains McCulloch. “We know they have to do it, but some signage would help. Like Dundas is closed here, but to get past the construction, this is how you do it.”

In an emailed statement, the City of London’s Director of Construction and Infrastructure Jennie Dann acknowledged the situation.

“We recognize that McCullough’s has experienced several years of disruption from multiple construction and infrastructure projects in the area, and that the cumulative impact has been challenging, particularly during one of its busiest times of year,” Dann writes.

The statement adds, “City staff make every effort to maintain access to local businesses, provide advance information, coordinate work and find opportunities to minimize disruptions. However, some repairs are time-sensitive, and work on the critical path can have less flexibility to shift without affecting the overall project schedule. We recognize the impact this has on businesses and will continue working to maintain access wherever possible.”

McCulloch says road widening for bus rapid transit has already reduced the store’s parking lot by more than half, “They have taken away 11 parking spots out of our 19, so they left us with eight.”

She says a planned extension of the centre median along Dundas Street when BRT is completed will prevent left turns onto or from Nightingale Avenue.

McCulloch urges Londoners to support local businesses that are open year-round.

“We need the support because the pop-up stores are here for a month, month and a half,” she says. “We are here 12 months of the year. We employ four full-time employees who are supporting families and without the support from the people in London, it’s hard to survive.”

Co-owner Rose McCulloch says repeated construction closures near Dundas Street and Nightingale Avenue is taking a toll, “Our sales this year are down about a third, so that really hurts.”
After roadwork in front of the store wrapped up, construction of the bus rapid transit (BRT) system moved just east, closing all four lanes of Dundas.
Access from the north was also temporarily closed for roadwork on Nightingale Avenue last weekend, adding to the challenge during the Halloween shopping season.

“There’s been about three times in the last few years when they have closed down Dundas Street in our busiest season,” explains McCulloch. “We know they have to do it, but some signage would help. Like Dundas is closed here, but to get past the construction, this is how you do it.”
In an emailed statement, the City of London’s Director of Construction and Infrastructure Jennie Dann acknowledged the situation.

“We recognize that McCullough’s has experienced several years of disruption from multiple construction and infrastructure projects in the area, and that the cumulative impact has been challenging, particularly during one of its busiest times of year,” Dann writes.

The statement adds, “City staff make every effort to maintain access to local businesses, provide advance information, coordinate work and find opportunities to minimize disruptions. However, some repairs are time-sensitive, and work on the critical path can have less flexibility to shift without affecting the overall project schedule. We recognize the impact this has on businesses and will continue working to maintain access wherever possible.”
McCulloch says road widening for bus rapid transit has already reduced the store’s parking lot by more than half, “They have taken away 11 parking spots out of our 19, so they left us with eight.”
She says a planned extension of the centre median along Dundas Street when BRT is completed will prevent left turns onto or from Nightingale Avenue.
McCulloch urges Londoners to support local businesses that are open year-round.

“We need the support because the pop-up stores are here for a month, month and a half,” she says. “We are here 12 months of the year. We employ four full-time employees who are supporting families and without the support from the people in London, it’s hard to survive.”

stories.title: Canadian grocery billionaire fears food inflation is coming back
stories.summary: Disruptions to global oil supplies due to the Middle East war are raising costs for food producers, which could be reflected in store, says Weston
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
The owner of Canada’s largest grocery chain said he’s concerned surging energy prices are threatening to reignite food inflation.

Galen Weston, the controlling shareholder and chairman of retailer Loblaw Cos., said disruptions to global oil supplies due to war in the Middle East are raising costs for food producers’ inputs, from diesel to fertilizer, which could be reflected on store shelves.

“We’re worried about it,” he said at an event in Toronto. “Not worried that it’s going to go back to 11% like it was in 2021, but worried that all these forces out there are going to continue to put pressure on that value chain.”

Grocery prices have jumped by 33% in six years in Canada, according to recent data from the country’s statistics agency.

The Bank of Canada raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 this week to combat inflation already creeping into the economy from higher fuel prices. Pressure on food would add one more pain point for consumers.

Owing most of his $22.8 billion net worth to his Canadian grocery stores, that’s a problem for Weston too. In his speech, Weston recalled that he was labeled “the most hated person in Canada” when food inflation ran out of control during the COVID-19 supply shock, and he was called before a parliamentary committee to answer for it.

He was grilled by politicians and lampooned on comedy shows. A Reddit group called “Loblaws Is Out of Control,” where shoppers vent about food prices and post pictures taken in stores, grew to tens of thousands of users.

Weston said that vilification was based on mistaken analysis, politics and “lies.” Grocery stores have little ability to impact food prices because they’re mostly locked in during earlier steps in the supply chain — and that’s where he’s seeing pressure now, he said. “Whether it’s disruption in the Strait of Hormuz or whether it’s the cost of fertilizer, which has been peaking recently, even the disruption from El Niño,” he said. “That’s something we’re watching very carefully.”

Weston said out of every $25 spent on groceries, only $1 is profit for the store, which gives companies like his very little room to lower prices.

The parliamentary committee Weston was called before a few years ago eventually released a report that blamed the post-pandemic surge in food inflation on pressure in the supply chain as well as corporate concentration in the food sector. It went on to recommend the government take steps to boost competition among grocery retailers.

In his Friday speech, Weston argued the Canadian grocery industry is already competitive, with American stores Walmart Inc. and Costco Wholesale Corp. two of the largest players by market share in Canada.

Weston urged company executives to work harder to show their companies are investing in Canada, creating employment and helping their communities.

“Young people worry about opportunities in their future, and those of us who are in the private sector, we need to do more to show the rest of Canada that what we do genuinely contributes to prosperity across the nation,” Weston said.

Members of the Business Council of Canada, a major business organization of which Weston is a member, expect they’ll need to find 800,000 new workers over the next decade “to fulfill the ‘Build Canada’ ambition,” he said. “And yet what our young people read, what often parents read, is about how your child’s going to struggle to get a job.”

He said Loblaw does not engage in algorithmic pricing, the practice of using data to change prices based on a variety of conditions, and in some cases personalizing those prices for individual shoppers.

Weston went further by promising to never engage in the practice and cast doubt on whether it would even be possible in physical grocery stores, despite most of the price signage being digital now.

“Just think for a second what they’re alleging the grocers will do,” he said. “That you will walk down the aisle of a store, and the price tag, because it’s digital, will change as you approach the product and raise the price because you’re wearing a nice sweater. It’s total nonsense.”

stories.title: More communities offering internet voting, but not London
stories.summary: While London voters marched out to the polls this week to cast their ballots in person, many other municipalities offered the option of voting online.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
While London voters marched out to the polls this week to cast their ballots in person, many other municipalities offered the option of voting online.

In London, a total of 103,163 ballots were cast in person or by mail, for a voter turnout of 31.01 per cent.

Former London Mayor Matt Brown, now co-owner of the podcast London Ontario Online News, believes the city could do more to get people engaged.

“Well I think the community needs to first set a goal, and if that’s to increase voter turnout, which I think that it is, then I think they need to come up with a strategy. Online voting could be part of that strategy,” said Brown.

Across Ontario, 272 municipalities or two thirds used internet voting with a combination of other voting methods. That is up from 217, or just over half in 2022.

Among a small sample of southern Ontario municipalities that provided an online option:

Sarnia had 48.02 per cent voter turnout, with 73.6 percent voting online.

Woodstock had a voter turnout of 33.17 per cent, with 53.41 per cent voting online. While Burlington reported voter turnout at 35.5 per cent, with 46.5 per cent voting online.

Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) executive director Lindsay Jones says the online option gives voters more choice.

“For municipalities with fewer than 10-thousand residents the voter turnout rate was 42 per cent. Which is much higher than the provincial average at 36 per cent. And interestingly, it does tend to be the smaller municipalities who have been making that move towards internet voting. It definitely makes it more convenient for folks. It’s really more of a case by case basis,” she explained.

But when it comes to the prospect of London making the move in the future, Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis says online voting does not get his vote.

“You actually have no proof that the person on the other end of the keyboard is the registered voter. Could be their spouse voting for both of them. Could be a parent voting for a child who’s just turned 18 and is on the voters list but hasn’t voted themselves. And I think that really undermines the basic principle of one person, one vote,” he said.

Lewis says he also has concerns about cyber-security, and potential errors with the voters list.

stories.title: 100-year-old Exeter woman prepares for 100th Halloween
stories.summary: Macdonald is marking 100 years of Halloween’s, after hitting the century mark in June.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Some early trick-or-treaters stop in at Evelyn Macdonald’s Exeter home.

Macdonald is marking 100 years of Halloween’s, after hitting the century mark in June.

“I keep saying to myself, how come I’m even here. I’m five months over 100. I’m going into 2027,” said the Huron County centenarian.

Helping her mark a century of trick-or-treating is Macdonald’s granddaughter, Kyleigh Richards.

“We get really excited about it, because we always plan ahead, and we’re always talking months before. What are we going to do this year? I’m giving her ideas. I’m coming over with little things to show her and stuff. And, then I usually end up with a bunch of stuff and come over, I decorate, and then she gets to come see it all,” said Richards.

Still living in her own home at 100 years of age, Macdonald is dressing up as herself tomorrow night with a custom 100 th Halloween shirt, with pictures from previous Halloween’s created by her granddaughter.

“I look after myself, mostly. Are you proud of that? I am proud of that,” she said.

Richards is hoping to hit 100 trick-or-treaters for her granny’s 100 th Halloween. Last year, they were hoping for 99 Halloween visitors, and nearly hit 150.

“You don’t get 100 years twice, you know what I mean. So you can’t ever count the next. You always got to make it the year that counts. So, this is the biggest one we’re ever going to do. And, I’m really excited to see what’s in store,” said Richards.

Macdonald says she’s excited to see the preschooler’s make their way to her door for her 100 th Halloween.

“I like it when the little kids come. That’s my favourite,” said Macdonald, whose called Exeter home for 27 years.

stories.title: Operation Mincemeat review: A dead body takes on new life in a musical slice of the Second World War
stories.summary: The unapologetically British stage show is a trolley problem to the nth degree – and a fabulous piece of musical theatre
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: Operation Mincemeat

Book, music and lyrics by: David Cumming, Felix Hagan, Natasha Hodgson and Zoë Roberts

Directed by: Robert Hastie

Actors: Mariah Copeland, Katie Kleiger, Luke Antony Neville, Erin Ramirez, Jake Bentley Young

Company: Mirvish Productions

Venue: Royal Alexandra Theatre

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Dec. 13

Critic’s Pick

Deep in the throes of the Second World War, a homeless vagabond eats rat poison and dies. British intelligence officers, hoping to trick the Nazis into moving out of Sicily to make room for an upcoming Allied invasion, quickly seize the body – it is perfect.

The cadaver is christened Bill, and the plan plummets into place. Bill – whose actual name and biography are low-priority for the officers of MI5 – receives a Royal Marine uniform, plus a briefcase stuffed with trumped-up details about the Allied Forces’ plans for Italy.

When the Brits dump the corpse off the coast of Spain – with a tightly harmonized send-off song à la Elton John, no less – they can only hope he’ll stay intact long enough for Hitler to get wind of the phony documents floating by his side.

Operation Mincemeat , the unapologetically British musical by David Cumming, Felix Hagan, Natasha Hodgson and Zoë Roberts, doesn’t attempt to justify the real-life means Allied forces used to deceive the Nazis. Its lyrics highlight the paradox of British gentility, the barbarism baked into the country’s upper crust; its earwormy score, which ranges in genre from German techno to sea shanty, illustrates rather than obfuscates the complexity of the dilemma at hand.

When we meet lead officer Ewen Montagu (an outstanding Katie Kleiger), it’s in a haze of self-adulating showmanship. He’s charming and waggish, a Barney Stinson type used to getting his way – not once does he give even the appearance of caring if the corpse in his care had a family.

Charles Cholmondeley (Jake Bentley Young) shows a touch more compassion for Bill’s former identity, but then again, Operation Mincemeat was his concoction in the first place – Monty’s simply who packaged it for Colonel John Bevan (Mariah Copeland)’s approval. As such, Charles’ fidelity to the plan shifts between scenes, in stark contrast to Monty’s belligerent belief that all will work out.

Hester Leggatt (Luke Antony Neville, another standout in a cast of standouts), meanwhile, doesn’t seem to feel any particular way about the mission at hand. It’s simply what needs to be done. But before long, the matronly senior secretary and supervisor to young clerk Jean Leslie (Erin Ramirez) reveals a tender inner life that underscores the importance of understanding exactly who MI5 has recruited as its maritime bait. Her song Dear Bill , about the fake love letters in the body’s briefcase, brings sharply into focus the terrible – and necessary – task the team has carried out.

Indeed, Operation Mincemeat doesn’t answer the enormous questions it lobs into the air: Is life truly only for the living? Was the desecration of a helpless corpse worth the liberation of continental Europe? Does the luxury of hindsight justify the unjustifiable?

Instead, the high-energy show passes those debates to the audience, in the blazing technicolor glamour of musical theatre. Sure, Monty’s a scoundrel – but he sings like a dream and supplies the show’s best laughs. Yes, Bill’s fate is completely, indefensibly tragic – but the won war results in a glitzy finale (cheekily titled A Glitzy Finale ) that rivals any you’d see in a less morally thorny piece of theatre.

Add in the show’s highly British use of drag – each of the show’s five actors play jump-rope with gender, hopping nimbly between characters of all types in the spirit of Monty Python – and Operation Mincemeat emerges as one of the most entertaining touring musicals to play a Mirvish stage in years.

But those questions of culpability hang heavily over the confection, enriching the musical into something far deeper than K-pop-inspired Nazi dance routines. (Yes, seriously, and yes, it works.) Until Operation Mincemeat ’s surprisingly poignant conclusion – which I won’t spoil here – the audience is tasked with computing all manner of ethical calculus, a trolley problem to the nth degree. The show is as much a riddle as a musical.

As such, I suspect Operation Mincemeat benefits from repeat viewings – its weaker beginning likely improves with knowledge of its gut-punch ending – and I intend to test that hypothesis thoroughly before the production leaves Toronto in December.

But in those encore encounters with the show, I also have to hope that Mike Walker’s surprisingly crude sound design is tweaked to the needs of the Royal Alexandra Theatre. On opening night, nearly half of Operation Mincemeat ’s lyrics were obscured by microphone feedback and fuzzy speakers; entire songs, delivered quickly and in thick British accents, were all but lost to muddy mixing.

Those perplexing snafus might overpower a weaker piece of theatre. But director Robert Hastie runs a tight ship, and gleefully leans into Operation Mincemeat ’s scrappy sense of spectacle. In the tradition of fellow West End farces (I’m looking at you, The Play That Goes Wrong ), the show embraces low-budget sight gags that elevate rather than cheapen the story. Think big hats, silly sets and impish props (set and costumes are by Ben Stones).

Was Bill’s legacy as a war hero appropriately preserved once MI5’s mission reached completion? I’ll leave that up to you. But Operation Mincemeat offers audiences a madcap whirlwind of a Second World War thriller – with hummable songs and a terrific cast to boot – and, despite the sequin-spangled odds, couldn’t be better calibrated to the intricacies of the history at hand.

stories.title: Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath expelled from UCP
stories.summary: Premier Smith backed the party’s decision to cancel Rath’s membership as it moves to quell separatist rumblings
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday confirmed that her United Conservative Party has expelled separatist leader Jeffrey Rath after he agitated for months to unseat her and turn the party into a vehicle for the independence movement.

Ms. Smith, at an unrelated news conference in Calgary, told reporters that Dustin van Vugt, the Ucp’s executive director, decided on Thursday to cancel Mr. Rath’s membership and voided his registration to the party’s late-November annual general meeting.

Mr. van Vugt informed the Ucp’s 18-person board of his decision on Thursday, Ms. Smith said.

“He believed that there were multiple instances of a breach of the code of conduct that we require of our members, and that it was his decision to pull the membership and cancel his AGM registration,” she said.

“And I’m supportive of that.”

The decision is yet another move by the UCP to quell separatist rumblings within the party since the Oct. 19 referendum, in which 75 per cent of Albertans rejected the prospect of a future vote on independence. Two days after the vote, Ms. Smith asked members to accept the result and said that those wishing to turn the UCP into a separatist party would not be welcome.

Public opinion polls have repeatedly shown a significant chunk of the party’s membership support independence. In the months leading up to the vote, she touted the UCP as a “big tent” party that valued a multitude of opinions and refused to expel one of her MLAs who said he was voting in favour of a binding separation referendum.

This week Ms. Smith said the UCP is now requiring those wishing to serve on its provincial board to pledge that they will respect the result of the referendum on separation. Mr. Rath’s removal appeared to mark another move toward contending with threats from within the party.

“Somebody whose objective and mission it is to turn us into something we are not is not following the objective of our party,” Ms. Smith said on Friday.

“Our objective of the party is to get re-elected, and to make sure that we’re focused on doing that.”

Mr. Rath, in a Friday afternoon interview, was undeterred by the news. He said he plans to ask the party to explain its decision but did not say whether he’d appeal it.

“I wear it as a badge of honour, to be frank,” Mr. Rath said. He said he’s not aware of other party members having their memberships revoked.

“They’re engaged in Stalinist, Soviet-style tactics against me – basically sending me off to the gulag and saying that, you know, we disagree with you and your ideas [and] therefore you’re no longer welcome in the party.”

Mr. Rath, a lawyer from Priddis, Alta., was one of the most polarizing figures in the Alberta independence movement in the referendum campaign. He and Mitch Sylvestre, another prominent separatist and UCP constituency president, have repeatedly threatened to turn the UCP into an independence party by taking control of the party apparatus.

At last year’s UCP AGM, Mr. Rath whipped the crowd into a frenzy when he asked how many party members supported independence. The crowd responded with boos when Ms. Smith said she hoped her progress on federal energy policy was convincing people that Canada can work for Alberta.

With his 2027 ticket cancelled, Mr. Rath suggested he’ll still find a way in, perhaps as an accredited journalist with a media organization.

“There’s all kind of different ways to get in,” he said.

stories.title: B.C.’s non-time change could impact technology and travel
stories.summary: Not getting an extra hour of sleep might not be the only thing that is missing this weekend as the province transitions to permanent Pacific daylight time.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
For the first time, British Columbians will not be falling back this November and won’t have to remember to change their clocks.

But not getting an extra hour of sleep might not be the only thing that is missing this weekend, as the province transitions to permanent Pacific daylight time.

The first few days could present confusion around travel and glitches with technology.

Starting Sunday, Nov. 1, B.C. will only be two hours behind eastern time and one hour ahead of U.S. states in the Pacific Time Zone.

Technology expert Andy Baryar warns of the impact this might have on any scheduled appointments.

“Our phones might say one time, but our calendar, our meeting requests, the meetings we already scheduled, might say another,” he said.

“And so what we need to do and what people need to do is really check to make sure those are synched, because you might have an hour difference, depending on where that meeting was created and when it was created — especially reoccurring meetings.”

Sports fans will notice a difference as well.

The Whitecaps game on Sunday is at 1:30 p.m., but it is listed as 2:30 p.m. in some places and 4:30 p.m. ET, which is off by an hour.

The Whitecaps issued a reminder on its Facebook page.

The Vancouver Canucks will see almost a dozen Saturday games pushed back to 8 p.m. to accommodate TV schedules.

Staff at Vancouver International Airport say they have worked closely with airlines to support the transition and ensure smooth operations for passengers travelling through the airport.

“Any passengers impacted by adjusted flight times will already see those times reflected in their travel information. No further action is required,” the airport said in a statement.

The organization said that with B.C. remaining on daylight saving time year-round, airlines have adjusted their winter flight schedules, particularly for routes connecting Vancouver with destinations that continue to change their clocks seasonally.

The majority of flights arriving from or departing to destinations outside B.C. have seen schedule adjustments of approximately one hour compared with last winter to accommodate the new time zone orientation, the airport stated in a release.

Those new flight times are already reflected in passenger itineraries.

Passengers are reminded to check with their airline if they have any questions.

B.C. is one of several provinces that elected this year not to continue the time changes .

The Maritime provinces as well as Quebec and most parts of Ontario and Nunavut, will adhere to the time old tradition of turning their clocks back while B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Yukon and the Northwest Territories will remain on permanent DST.

This week, Quebec said it intends to end the time changes after this fall .

stories.title: Anand says she called out Russian counterpart invited by U.S. to G20 ministerial
stories.summary: Ottawa - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Russia should not have attended a G20 meeting the U.S. hosted on Friday, but she still used the opportunity to make a point to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Russia should not have attended a G20 meeting the U.S. hosted on Friday, but she still used the opportunity to make a point to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

“I was sitting at a table directly across from Sergei Lavrov and I looked him in the eye,” she told The Canadian Press on Friday.

“I incontrovertibly stated that Russia has committed horrific crimes in its war against Ukraine, including devastating global energy and food supply chains.”

Anand attended a G20 meeting of foreign ministers in Atlanta on Friday. The American hosts took the unconventional step of cancelling the traditional photo of all attendees after European diplomats objected to being pictured with Lavrov.

Anand said her Russian counterpart responded to her comment.

“Lavrov, in return, tried Kremlin talking points, one of which was, ‘We don’t use energy to settle political scores.’ He accused the EU of slavery and piracy for seizing Russian vessels in the shadow fleet,” she said, referring to vessels that obscure their origin to export Russian oil.

U.S. President Donald Trump has pulled back support for Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion. Trump signed a diesel deal that will give millions of dollars to Moscow’s war effort and Ukraine has reported problems with its access to vital American satellite technology.

Anand said she arrived in Atlanta after the “family photo” was set to occur, following meetings in Montreal with EU officials.

“I don’t want to have my picture taken with Sergei Lavrov, in any case,” she said, adding she also brought up Russia’s kidnapping of Ukrainian children and attacks on vessels in the Black Sea.

Lavrov suggested at a news conference that Western countries are not serious about dialogue with Russia.

“All they care about is having me in a photograph, and that’s it,” he said through an interpreter.

Anand said a major concern of nearly all G20 countries is maritime security. Russian strikes on Ukrainian grain vessels in the Black Sea are halting shipments developing countries rely on for food. Iran has drastically reduced shipping in the crucial Strait of Hormuz in response to the U.S. war on Tehran.

“The strength of the G20 is in finding the points of collective agreement,” Anand said.

“No one disagrees with the point that there should be freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, that there is a need to ensure safe passage of ships carrying fertilizer in the Black Sea … except Lavrov.”

She said she encouraged G20 nations to look to Canada for their energy needs.

Anand also said Canada opposes the U.S. excluding South Africa from the G20 meetings it is hosting this year. Washington has made false claims about a genocide targeting white South Africans.

“South Africa should be present,” she said. “Canada shares South Africa’s interest in preserving an effective, inclusive and functioning G20 that is capable of addressing global economic challenges.”

Canada and the European Union wrapped up a major summit in Montreal Friday, a day after the release of Canada’s first national security strategy in decades and ahead of next week’s Commonwealth summit.

“This is diplomacy in a very concentrated period of time, with much activity and wins for Canada on the global stage,” Anand said.

Anand will head to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth summit. Prime Minister Mark Carney will join the summit Monday.

“Canada supports a strong and credible Commonwealth mandate on democracy, including through the Commonwealth ministerial action group,” Anand said, referring to the body that takes up human rights issues.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta football coach faces sentence for making AI sex images
stories.summary: Lethbridge - A girls’ football coach who used artificial intelligence to create sexualized images of some of his players hung his head in court Friday as he listened to the ripple effects of the pain.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Lethbridge - A girls’ football coach who used artificial intelligence to create sexualized images of some of his players hung his head in court Friday as he listened to the ripple effects of the pain.

“It was my face; it was my name. It was me,” one of victims told Justin Tillery at his sentencing hearing.

“The humiliation is real. The fear is real. The betrayal is real. I felt sick. I felt ashamed of something I didn’t do.

“Every day I wonder if my image is still out there. I wonder if someone is looking at it right now.”

It was one of three victim impact statements.

Tillery, 39, was originally charged in 2025 with making, distributing, possessing and accessing child pornography, as well as transmitting an intimate image without consent. He eventually pleaded guilty to making, printing or publishing pornography as well as possessing child pornography.

Special prosecutor Tara Hayes read the agreed statement of facts into the record. She said Tillery and a longtime friend had been sharing the images. They exchanged lewd comments about the girls, prompting Tillery in one text message to say, “We are going to hell with gasoline boots on for sure.”

Hayes urged the judge impose a sentence of two years in prison and three years’ probation.

Tillery’s lawyer, Scott Hadford, asked the judge to consider a sentence to be served in the community. He said Tillery has no criminal record and entered a guilty plea.

“At the end of the day, there’s still a difference in the making of child pornography when it’s AI versus when it’s real,” Hadford said.

The case will be back in court Nov. 6 to choose a date for sentencing.

An expert on online harm said deep fake pornography is becoming more common because of the ease and sophistication of current technology. Kaitlynn Mendes of Western University said all it takes is for someone to have a photo of a person to upload.

“You need no skills. You just need their face, and the tech can make an image. It can make videos,” Mendes said in an interview.

Mendes is a sociology professor at Western University and interim academic director for the Centre for Research and Education on Violence Against Women and Children.

She said emerging research suggests that while the art is fake, the trauma is not. “The impacts are as real as if the image was real,” she said.

“Psychologically, you don’t know who has these images and those people May or May not know that these images are fake.

“So I can imagine this is creating a lot of anxiety for these young people.”

paragraphs: Lethbridge - A girls’ football coach who used artificial intelligence to create sexualized images of some of his players hung his head in court Friday as he listened to the ripple effects of the pain.
“It was my face; it was my name. It was me,” one of victims told Justin Tillery at his sentencing hearing.
“The humiliation is real. The fear is real. The betrayal is real. I felt sick. I felt ashamed of something I didn’t do.
“Every day I wonder if my image is still out there. I wonder if someone is looking at it right now.”
It was one of three victim impact statements.

Tillery, 39, was originally charged in 2025 with making, distributing, possessing and accessing child pornography, as well as transmitting an intimate image without consent. He eventually pleaded guilty to making, printing or publishing pornography as well as possessing child pornography.

Special prosecutor Tara Hayes read the agreed statement of facts into the record. She said Tillery and a longtime friend had been sharing the images. They exchanged lewd comments about the girls, prompting Tillery in one text message to say, “We are going to hell with gasoline boots on for sure.”
Hayes urged the judge impose a sentence of two years in prison and three years’ probation.
Tillery’s lawyer, Scott Hadford, asked the judge to consider a sentence to be served in the community. He said Tillery has no criminal record and entered a guilty plea.
“At the end of the day, there’s still a difference in the making of child pornography when it’s AI versus when it’s real,” Hadford said.
The case will be back in court Nov. 6 to choose a date for sentencing.

stories.title: Museum London hosts final Halloween-themed guided tours
stories.summary: Museum London embraced Halloween festivities with its second annual Haunted Walk event, which showcases London...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
Museum London embraced Halloween festivities throughout October, with its second annual Haunted Histories, culture walk, designed to showcase London’s “spooky history.”

Tour guide Denise Love said she was inspired to start the Haunted Histories last year, after learning about some chilling historical events that took place at different buildings and locations throughout the city’s core.

“I just love scaring people and showing off the interesting history we have here in London,” said Love. “We stop at many places that have some kind of haunted or darker past.”

Each walk takes visitors to about 20 stops, where they hear stories about everything from old murder trials to mysterious disappearances .

Denise Love, haunted walk tour guide (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News)

In addition to Londoners, participants have been coming from out of town to get a taste of Halloween season here in London, Love said.

Haunted Histories is part of the Museum’s continued efforts to show Londoners what the city has to offer.

Denise Love guiding patrons (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News)

stories.title: Hockey’s longest losing streak ends
stories.summary: The Sarnia Legionnaires have snapped their 67-game losing streak after beating the St. Thomas Stars 4-1 Thursd...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
The Sarnia Legionnaires have snapped their 67-game losing streak after beating the St. Thomas Stars 4-1 Thursday night.

The win ended the longest losing streak in organized hockey history. Before Thursday’s game, the Legionnaires went 619 days in the Greater Ontario Hockey League (Gohl) without a win.

People celebrating Sarnia’s first win on Facebook (Credit: Edric Eiermann //Facebook)

“We got the monkey off our back and we’ve got some confidence now,” said Ryan Foster Head coach of the Legionnaires.

Foster said he was proud how his team played including Evan Bannister (forward) and David Healy (goalie).

“Everyone has a role,” he said. “Bannister is scoring right now and we are looking for secondary scoring as well and our goaltending hasn’t been a problem this year.”

Bannister scored a hattrick including the game winning goal and Healy stopped 54 of 55 shots on net including an assist.

Heading into the final minutes the Legionnaires were up 2-1. Then with just over a minute left in the game, Ethan Glavin scored to make it 3-1.

“A lot can happen in one minute especially when you’re playing St. Thomas a offensively talented team,” said Foster.

The players were focused right down to the last minutes of the game, said defender Aiden Israel, who played his second game with the Legionnaires Thursday.

“I was really amped up, but I knew anything could happen in a few minutes of game time and we just had bear down and play smart,” he said, attributing the victory to the team’s determination.

“‘We have to win.’ That was our goal and our mentality,” he said

The venue attracted around 380 spectators and as the buzzer sounded the fans erupted.

Gohl-watchers, including St. Thomas fans, celebrated the victory on Facebook Thursday and Friday.

“I think it’s fantastic, obviously fans have their loyalty to who they support. But at the same time we lost 67 games in a row and a lot of fans are pulling free to get that first win.”

“Against St. Mary’s we were down 6-0 after 22 minutes, than the final 38 minutes we played 0-0 hockey. We get down early a lot and we’re chasing games,” Foster said.

Foster said he always reminds his team that every game starts 0-0 and anything in the past doesn’t matter.

The streak started back on February 20, 2025, losing the final six games of the 2024-25 season, then went 0-50-0-0 in the 2025-26 season and started this season 0-11-0-0 totaling 67 straight regulation loses.

Throughout the 25/26 regular season the Legionnaires lost an average by 5 goals a game.

Thomas Jane is a defenseman for the Legionnaires and is the only returning player from that 25/26 team.

This is Foster’s first season back in Canada to coach after playing and coaching in in Austria and Germany for 27 years. He also played for the Canadian National team program in 1998-99 and travelled all over Europe playing in multiple tournaments.

Here are the Final seconds of the Sarnia Legionnaires win.

stories.title: Female hospital doctors linked to better outcomes for patients, study says
stories.summary: Researchers reviewed data from more than 958,000 adults who were hospitalized for common diagnoses such as pneumonia
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Patients who are cared for by female physicians in hospital are less likely to die or to be readmitted compared with those treated by male physicians, says a newly released study co-authored by two Canadian researchers.

The findings were released on Friday and published in the October edition of Jama Network Open, a peer-reviewed journal published by the American Medical Association.

The research was conducted by Ices, or the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, a not-for-profit Ontario research and analytics institute that uses population-based health information for insights on various health care issues.

The ultimate goal of the work is to improve patient outcomes, said Angela Jerath, the study’s lead author and an Ices scientist.

The study analyzed Ices data on 958,150 adults who were hospitalized in the province for one of seven common medical diagnoses, including pneumonia, between Jan. 1, 2008, and Dec. 31, 2022.

It found that patients who were cared for by female physicians had a 30-day mortality rate of 12.3 per cent compared with 13.7 per cent for those cared for by male physicians.

Greater exposure to female physician care was associated with a 7-per-cent drop in 30-day mortality and the benefit persisted at 90 days and a year.

Additionally, it found a slightly lower hospital readmission rate of 18.6 per cent for those seen by female physicians compared with 18.9 per cent for those seen by male physicians.

Dr. Jerath said a possible explanation for the differences could be that female physicians May engage in more patient-centred communication and that they spend more time with their patients.

She also said female physicians May be more likely to order treatments for their patients that are directed by guidelines, and to consult their colleagues and share their decision-making.

The goal of the study is not to favour one group of physicians over another, but to help identify practices and behaviours to enrich patient care, said Dr. Jerath, who is also an associate professor in the department of anesthesiology and pain medicine at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine.

Dr. Jerath’s co-author, Christopher Wallis, said researching this topic as a male physician gave him an opportunity to be introspective on how he approaches his own surgical practice.

“This is about decision-making,” said Dr. Wallis, an assistant professor in the department of surgery at the University of Toronto.

“This is about how you interact with other human beings. None of this is finite or fixed in stone. We can all learn from each other.”

The findings contribute to a growing body of research on the relationship between physician sex and patient outcomes, Dr. Jerath said.

An additional factor affecting female physicians, which begins early in their careers and continues, is that there are gaps between earnings compared with male counterparts, she said.

Dr. Wallis warned that pay gaps should not be characterized on the basis that women often take on additional duties at home and therefore May work fewer hours in a professional capacity.

He said while this could be a factor, a number of analyses show on a per-hour worked basis, female physicians do not make as much.

“Even when you account in surgery for the number of hours you worked, the number of patients you’ve seen, women still get paid less,” he said.

Research also shows that physicians overall are putting in fewer hours.

In March, 2024, a study published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal found the decline was driven mostly by reductions among married male physicians rather than the fact there are more women in the profession.

Looking to the future, Dr. Jerath said it is important to ask questions about why female physicians May have a different approach and how these insights could be used to improve patient outcomes.

“That is what we are here for,” she said. “We don’t go to med school for any other reason. We all did it for a desire to serve.”

Dr. Jerath said a possible explanation for the differences could be that female physicians May engage in more patient-centred communication and that they spend more time with their patients.
She also said female physicians May be more likely to order treatments for their patients that are directed by guidelines, and to consult their colleagues and share their decision-making.

The goal of the study is not to favour one group of physicians over another, but to help identify practices and behaviours to enrich patient care, said Dr. Jerath, who is also an associate professor in the department of anesthesiology and pain medicine at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine.
Dr. Jerath’s co-author, Christopher Wallis, said researching this topic as a male physician gave him an opportunity to be introspective on how he approaches his own surgical practice.
“This is about decision-making,” said Dr. Wallis, an assistant professor in the department of surgery at the University of Toronto.
“This is about how you interact with other human beings. None of this is finite or fixed in stone. We can all learn from each other.”
The findings contribute to a growing body of research on the relationship between physician sex and patient outcomes, Dr. Jerath said.
An additional factor affecting female physicians, which begins early in their careers and continues, is that there are gaps between earnings compared with male counterparts, she said.
Dr. Wallis warned that pay gaps should not be characterized on the basis that women often take on additional duties at home and therefore May work fewer hours in a professional capacity.
He said while this could be a factor, a number of analyses show on a per-hour worked basis, female physicians do not make as much.
“Even when you account in surgery for the number of hours you worked, the number of patients you’ve seen, women still get paid less,” he said.
Research also shows that physicians overall are putting in fewer hours.

In March, 2024, a study published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal found the decline was driven mostly by reductions among married male physicians rather than the fact there are more women in the profession.
Looking to the future, Dr. Jerath said it is important to ask questions about why female physicians May have a different approach and how these insights could be used to improve patient outcomes.
“That is what we are here for,” she said. “We don’t go to med school for any other reason. We all did it for a desire to serve.”

stories.title: How Canada's new pact with the European Union might affect you
stories.summary: Canada’s new partnership with the European Union is meant to provide benefits to people on both continents. The two jurisdictions wrapped up a summit in Montreal on Friday with various agreements, many of which will take months or years to finalize.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s new partnership with the European Union is meant to provide benefits to people on both continents. The two jurisdictions wrapped up a summit in Montreal on Friday with various agreements, many of which will take months or years to finalize.

Here’s a look at some of the possible benefits for different groups: Youth Canada and the European Union are promising to eventually update their “youth mobility partnership” with the goal of offering young people more opportunities to go abroad.

That would build on existing university exchange programs and working-holiday programs Canada operates with multiple European countries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program that offers training and study opportunities in member nations.

Canada is also hoping to become a full member of the Horizon Europe research partnership program by 2028, which would offer new funding for research and innovation projects undertaken with European peers. Tech workers Prime Minister Mark Carney said the pact with the EU will give Canadian researchers access to European supercomputers that can cut processing times from six months to a single day.

Canada and the EU have signed a digital trade agreement that looks to fold certain sectors into the trade agreement that has governed how goods are exchanged for a decade. The European Commission website defines digital trade as “commerce enabled by electronic means.” It cites banks transferring data, agricultural commodity traders using e-signatures and freight companies tracking their machines through the internet.

Canada is also working on joining the EU’s “instant payment systems” to make it easier to send funds. Both jurisdictions are also exploring opening each other’s markets further to Canadian and European banks, insurers and fintech companies.

Mining firms The European Investment Bank will seek to fund projects to mine critical raw materials in Canada, thanks to negotiations that concluded Friday. Von der Leyen said Thursday that European “industrial demand, technology and investment” can help get such mineral projects off of the ground.

Regulators Canada has signed some sort of updated competition agreement with the EU that looks to crack down on anticompetitive actions by transatlantic businesses, though there were few details provided Friday. The EU’s border agency is also helping its Canadian counterpart tackle migrant smuggling, human trafficking and identity fraud by exchanging information through the European Border Surveillance System.

Both jurisdictions have also agreed to launch formal discussion groups on the Arctic, foreign information manipulation and interference, climate security and transport. A joint statement says on misinformation, both sides have agreed to move “from a reactive stance to a proactive one.” Soldiers in Latvia In June, Canada became the only non-European partner in the EU’s defence procurement program Safe.

Just one project had come out of that arrangement until Friday, when Canada announced a contract worth up to $43 million to provide helmets to Latvian troops. Montreal-based firm Galvion will produce the helmets for Latvia, which has been home to Canada’s largest foreign military presence for years.

Canadian soldiers are in Latvia to prevent a Russian invasion. Ukraine As Washington pulls back support for Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion, Europe has stepped up with more funding. Carney announced Friday that Canada will join an EU loan program for Ukraine.

Ottawa has pledged an initial contribution of 500 million euros, roughly C$775 million. “We will continue to provide comprehensive political, financial, economic, energy, humanitarian, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine and its people,” says the joint statement Canada and the EU inked Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026. Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hilarity, horror, and nostalgia combine at Halloween screening
stories.summary: A screening of a new documentary based on a spooky – yet hilarious – 1970s children’s television show takes place this weekend in London.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A screening of a new documentary based on a spooky – yet hilarious – 1970s children’s television show takes place this weekend in London.

‘Behind the Castle Doors’ plays at Palace Theatre Halloween morning at 11 a.m.

It tells the story of The Hilarious House of Frightenstein (Hhof).

The program has become a cult classic in Canada and the U.S. since its debut on television screens in the 1970s. It ran for 130 episodes.

Hhof began with an introduction from horror movie icon Vincent Price, who also hosted the show.

The program, and its characters including the Count Frightenstein, Igor, and the Wolfman, enamoured Generation X, as Behind the Castle Doors producers Tammy Heisel and Morgan Baker recalled.

“When you watch the show, it’s so over-the-top, it’s so bizarre. But there are these lovable characters,” said Heisel.

In short sketches, the characters helped to take the fear out of fright through laughs and education.

Baker admits that as a youth, monsters that had once scared him suddenly became his TV friends.

“I moved around a lot as a kid across the country, and that show seemed to follow me, you know, from city to city. It was a comfort, a constant almost.”

The Hilarious House of Frightenstein inspired both producers to enter the fields they now teach.

But the opportunity to tell the show’s story is thanks to a chance encounter with one of its producers.

Almost four years later, ‘Behind the Castle Doors’ debuted. A year later, it has won multiple awards on the film festival circuit across Canada.

“The story of the film is basically how the show came to be, the behind-the-scenes stories, things that happened, how the sets were built,” said Heisel.

Those who have never seen the show are drawn to the chance to see familiar characters in a comedic light.

Heisel said die-hards, including a new generation of fans who watch the show on streaming services, keep coming back.

“What we’re finding is the super fans of the original series can’t get enough of this. We’ve had people come back two, three, four times.”

“I think just like on the surface, face value, you know, the show still has legs and can have broad appeal,” added Morgan.

The film screening moved to the Palace Theatre main stage as demand spiked, but some seats are still available online and at the door for those who dare to laugh… and maybe … scream!

More information about Behind the Castle Doors can be found online .

stories.title: London man sentenced to four years in prison for deadly 2020 crash
stories.summary: Nearly six years after a crash claimed the life of a 67-year-old London woman, the man convicted in her death has been sentenced to four years in federal prison.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Nearly six years after a crash claimed the life of a 67-year-old London woman, the man convicted in her death has been sentenced to four years in federal prison.

Bahaa Ali, 32, was sentenced Friday after being found guilty of dangerous driving causing death in the November 2020 collision that killed Joan Clubb.

The sentencing hearing was marked by emotion as Ali’s family watched from the courtroom. His mother began sobbing as Justice Barbara MacFarlane handed down the sentence. Ali was later led out of the courtroom in handcuffs.

The crash happened Nov. 3, 2020, at the intersection of Southdale and White Oak roads.

Clubb was a passenger in a Hyundai Sonata travelling through the intersection when it was struck by Ali’s Mercedes-Benz.

The court heard Ali was travelling at speeds of up to 129 kilometres an hour, more than twice the posted speed limit.

Clubb died in hospital from her injuries. Her sister, Jackie, who was also in the vehicle, survived but suffered serious injuries.

In her sentencing decision, MacFarlane sharply criticized Ali’s driving record, saying it demonstrated an ongoing risk to public safety.

“Mr. Ali chose to drive recklessly at more than twice the speed limit approaching a busy city intersection. Is an offender with a lengthy history of speeding and disobeying traffic laws. One can only surmise he did so to show off his souped-up car without regard for the public using the road,” the judge said.

Ali was found guilty in March following a six-day judge-alone trial.

During the trial, Ali attempted to blame his younger brother, claiming he had been behind the wheel of the Mercedes at the time of the collision. The judge rejected that account.

The defence had argued against a penitentiary sentence, saying it could trigger immigration consequences and put Ali at risk of deportation to Lebanon.

Ali, who has lived in Canada since 2014, is a permanent resident.

In addition to the four-year prison sentence, MacFarlane imposed a six-year driving prohibition, which will run in addition to the prohibition in effect throughout his imprisonment.

In a written statement to the court, Ali apologized, saying he could not change the past but could take responsibility for his actions.

The judge also acknowledged the lasting impact of Clubb’s death on her family. Her husband, Steve Shanahan, had faithfully attended court throughout the proceedings, including the trial, but died this past summer before the sentencing decision.

By Jillian Driessen, Special to Western News,

Explore All News

A new study at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI) and ICES Western is using artificial intelligence and community partnerships to advance equitable care for people experiencing homelessness.

The study led by Stephanie Dixon, a professor of medicine and epidemiology and biostatistics at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, will develop a new frailty score that accounts for the health impacts of experiencing homelessness. Frailty scores are tools used to assess a person’s overall health and risk of complications.

Through the project, Dixon and collaborators will use anonymous health data from more than 35,000 Ontarians who have a history of homelessness. Working alongside community partners, health-care providers and individuals with lived experience, the team will identify factors that can help create a more accurate picture of health risks for individuals who have experienced homelessness.

“Data can tell us a great deal, but it only captures one part of the story,” said Dixon, who is also a research scientist at LHSCRI and ICES Western. “By bringing together data, lived experience and frontline expertise, we hope to build something that helps people see health needs earlier and connect individuals with the care and support they need.”

The long-term goal is to develop a tool that can help physicians and shelter-based care providers identify people who may be at increased risk of poor health outcomes earlier and to deliver more proactive care. The project will also document important gaps in existing health data collection to help researchers better understand where the experiences of people experiencing homelessness are less visible in health care systems.

Professor Stephanie Dixon and collaborators are working on tools to help assess health risks for those with histories of homelessness. (LHSCRI)

The study is supported through the AMS Healthcare Leadership in Compassion and Artificial Intelligence Fellowship, a year-long program that brings together health-care leaders, researchers and innovators to explore how AI can be developed and applied with compassion at its core. Through the fellowship, Dixon is collaborating with an interdisciplinary team, community partners, and individuals with lived experience to develop both the frailty score and a broader framework for compassionate, equity-informed AI in health research.

Existing frailty scores help health-care providers identify people at greater risk of illness, hospitalization or other serious health complications. However, most were developed for older adults living in stable housing and often fail to capture the cumulative impacts of homelessness, including stressors such as trauma, chronic stress, substance use, mental health concerns and barriers to accessing care.

Research suggests that people experiencing homelessness can experience the effects of frailty years earlier than the general population. This can make it difficult to identify who may benefit from additional supports or interventions.

To develop a new frailty score, Dixon is collaborating with community partners and individuals with lived experience to create a model that accounts for the health impacts of experiencing homelessness. The AI-driven tool will incorporate stressors not typically included in existing frailty scores, which often place greater emphasis on a person’s age than their life experiences and health challenges.

“We are using a co-designed approach,” says Dixon, who has worked with ICES Western for nearly 15 years. “Together we can identify commonly missed stressors such as the cumulative effects of adverse childhood experiences, substance use, infectious disease history, and mental health concerns.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

It says the money will go toward the third phase of the North End Wastewater Treatment Plant project, which aims to remove nutrients like phosphorus from the water.

stories.title: Polar bear arrival in Manitoba town prompts safety concerns, conservation opportunity
stories.summary: Hundreds of polar bears are expected to arrive in Churchill, Man. as they partake in their fall trek towards the Hudson Bay.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Work is underway to ensure polar bears can safely coexist with people in Churchill, Man., as the Arctic animals arrive by the hundreds in the coming days.

Polar Bears International (PBI) is a nonprofit dedicated to protecting the future of polar bears and Arctic sea ice. It marks polar bear week during the first seven days of November to align with the time of year that the bears arrive in Churchill near Hudson Bay in anticipation of the waterway freezing.

Once frozen, the bears use the bay to hunt for seals and other prey.

“A couple of things happen, the weather starts to cool off, ice starts to freeze,” Geoff York, vice-president for science and policy at PBI, told Global News in an interview, noting that the land freezes first.

“That cooling weather sort of triggers something in the bears that they know it’s the time to come back towards the coast. And so, we see increased polar bear activity.”

That activity can lead to more polar bear-human interactions than usual in the polar bear capital of the world, he added.

The number of contacts between people and polar bears has risen in recent decades because Hudson Bay takes approximately one month longer to freeze than it has historically, due to climate-related sea ice loss, according to PBI.

To prevent negative interactions between the animals and residents, the nonprofit has put deterrent measures in place.

“One thing we really strive to do is increase tolerance for the people who live, work and recreate around bears, and for polar bears in particular, that means keeping people and bears safe when they have interactions,” York said.

“It’s pretty shocking to see a large bear, and not just one typically, but several.”

This year, the organization is using drones to monitor and herd the animals away from potentially dangerous areas or situations. Researchers are also using the aerial camera to safely monitor and track the polar bears’ activities, York continued.

The drone project is being done in collaboration with the Utah-based Brigham Young University (BYU). Kyle Garrett, a master’s student at BYU who is currently in Churchill, said the noise of the drone prompts the bears to move.

“(It is) a little bit bigger than the average drone but nothing too big. And with the noise that’s caused by the drone we’re able to fly it towards the bears and then use the noise as kind of a scare tactic to push them in the direction we want them to go. Then, if we need to change directions, we just change the position of the drone,” Garrett continued.

Based on the team’s work thus far, Garrett said the drones seemed to be effective as a method of moving the bears.

Work was also done at the town’s waste site, as garbage attracts bears.

Part of that work involves the installation of an electric fence, which PBI has dubbed “Bear-vision.” It involves a camera that is used for early warnings of polar bear detection near the waste facility. In Pbi’s news release, Bear-vision was described as “a doorbell camera that tells you if a polar bear is outside.”

This work is essential for the long-term conservation of the polar bear population, York said. He added that identifying non-lethal deterrents against the bears will ensure more stay alive for longer after human interactions.

“I think for the long-term conservation of any large animal, but especially a large predator, it is incumbent on those of us working in these areas making sure that the people who live with an animal like polar bears can feel safe,” he said.

“It’s through that that we can kind of grow tolerance and make sure we can keep these large predators on the landscape, hopefully for a very long time to come.”

Churchill’s Western Hudson Bay polar bear subpopulation has declined by almost half since 1979 due to climate-driven sea ice loss and fewer females getting pregnant, according to PBI.

“One thing we really strive to do is increase tolerance for the people who live, work and recreate around bears, and for polar bears in particular, that means keeping people and bears safe when they have interactions,” York said.
“It’s pretty shocking to see a large bear, and not just one typically, but several.”

stories.title: Expert witness defends 'advocacy' in youth-led climate trial
stories.summary: Vancouver - A pediatrician testifying at Canada's first youth-led climate trial says doctors in her profession often view advocacy as a form of promoting patients' health, in response to a suggestion she has made "climate advocacy" part of her career.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Zoe Grames-Webb has told Canada’s first youth-led climate trial she still remembers the “completely grey wall of smoke” she woke up to in 2017 while staying at a cabin on British Columbia’s Sunshine Coast.

The wildfire smoke was so thick, it blocked the view of the islands Grames-Webb, then 11 years old, was accustomed to seeing across Howe Sound.

“I was extremely concerned because I was thinking about how thick the smoke would have been to just not (be) able to even see the islands across the water.

“That caused me a lot of stress and that really stood out very strongly. That’s my first memory that stands out very strong to me,” Grames-Webb testified at the Federal Court hearing in Vancouver on Friday.

Grames-Webb, now 20, is one of more than a dozen Canadian youth suing the federal government, arguing federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing Canada’s trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

She also recalled being unable to run or hike outside during the 2020 wildfire season, which overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic.

“When I would go outside ... I would get a quite intense headache. My lungs would feel very full with smoke. I would sometimes get stinging eyes,” she said.

Grames-Webb said being outdoors was also important to her mental health.

“It’s really important to me. So not being able to do those things really added to my stress about the wildfire smoke and kind of further perpetuated that anxiety.”

The trial has so far heard from 10 of the 15 plaintiffs in the case, along with a series of experts in topics including renewable energy, emissions reductions and health.

Dr. Elizabeth Pinsky, an American pediatrician and child psychiatrist, began her testimony Thursday outlining an array of risks children face from climate change, from susceptibility to extreme heat and air pollution to anxiety and depression.

Her cross-examination on Friday included a suggestion from Ottawa’s lawyers that she had made climate advocacy a part of her career.

Pinsky told the court pediatricians in particular have a history of viewing advocacy as a form of promoting patients’ health.

“I think likely the setting in which I practise medicine, there are statements or positions or things that are considered advocacy that in a different political climate might just be considered good sense and caring for children,” she said.

The trial in Federal Court has heard that her testimony marked the fourth time in the last three years that Pinsky has given evidence in youth-led climate change cases, including lawsuits against the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Pinsky is a founding member of Climate Code Blue, a Boston-area climate action group for health professionals, and she is part of another group working to implement the city’s climate plan.

Pinsky, who acknowledged she had not directly treated any of the young plaintiffs in the lawsuit, testified Thursday that babies and very young children have a harder time regulating their internal temperature in a heat wave, while children breath more rapidly than adults, which means they take in more pollution relative to their size.

Pinsky said that as climate change worsens, so too will the health impacts.

“There’s just no question left in the medical literature about whether that’s true.”

She described the knowledge that “the people who should be protecting you and keeping you safe and safeguarding your future are not just failing to do so, but knowingly failing to do so” as a unique harm among children.

In her report to the court, Pinsky said even very low concentrations of wildfire smoke are toxic, and “near-zero exposure” is required to protect public health.

Questioned about mitigating and adapting to those risks, Pinsky said there were treatments for some harms, but the idea that a doctor would not try to prevent diseases because they are treatable didn’t make sense to her.

“We have good and novel chemotherapeutic agents for lung cancer. We do not tell our patients to go ahead and continue to smoke,” she said.

The final witness on Friday was Sarah Newton, a substitute teacher from Smithers, B.C., who described temperatures in her classroom hitting 30 degrees, making the eight-to-12-year-old students uncomfortable and affecting their learning.

Newton, who described herself as a social justice advocate, said students have expressed fears for the natural environment.

“Kids will say they’re worried for the animals, they’re worry for their future, they’re worries for the forest. And that had a profound impact on me, just the volume of that comment coming through,” she told the court.

A lawyer for the federal government asked Pinsky whether participating in a lawsuit would be one way to address climate anxiety.

“It depends on how the lawsuit turns out,” she responded.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

Pinsky told the court pediatricians in particular have a history of viewing advocacy as a form of promoting patients’ health.

“I think likely the setting in which I practise medicine, there are statements or positions or things that are considered advocacy that in a different political climate might just be considered good sense and caring for children,” she said.

The trial in Federal Court has heard that her testimony marked the fourth time in the last three years that Pinsky has given evidence in youth-led climate change cases, including lawsuits against the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
Pinsky is a founding member of Climate Code Blue, a Boston-area climate action group for health professionals, and she is part of another group working to implement the city’s climate plan.

Pinsky, who acknowledged she had not directly treated any of the young plaintiffs in the lawsuit, testified Thursday that babies and very young children have a harder time regulating their internal temperature in a heat wave, while children breath more rapidly than adults, which means they take in more pollution relative to their size.
Pinsky said that as climate change worsens, so too will the health impacts.
“There’s just no question left in the medical literature about whether that’s true.”

She described the knowledge that “the people who should be protecting you and keeping you safe and safeguarding your future are not just failing to do so, but knowingly failing to do so” as a unique harm among children.
In her report to the court, Pinsky said even very low concentrations of wildfire smoke are toxic, and “near-zero exposure” is required to protect public health.

Questioned about mitigating and adapting to those risks, Pinsky said there were treatments for some harms, but the idea that a doctor would not try to prevent diseases because they are treatable didn’t make sense to her.
“We have good and novel chemotherapeutic agents for lung cancer. We do not tell our patients to go ahead and continue to smoke,” she said.

The final witness on Friday was Sarah Newton, a substitute teacher from Smithers, B.C., who described temperatures in her classroom hitting 30 degrees, making the eight-to-12-year-old students uncomfortable and affecting their learning.
Newton, who described herself as a social justice advocate, said students have expressed fears for the natural environment.

“Kids will say they’re worried for the animals, they’re worry for their future, they’re worries for the forest. And that had a profound impact on me, just the volume of that comment coming through,” she told the court.
A lawyer for the federal government asked Pinsky whether participating in a lawsuit would be one way to address climate anxiety.
“It depends on how the lawsuit turns out,” she responded.

stories.title: Ottawa designates B.C. port expansion as project of national interest
stories.summary: The $5.9-billion project is aimed at increasing the port’s container capacity by 50 per cent
stories.author: Jeffrey Jones
stories.content:
Ottawa listed a $5.9-billion West Coast port expansion on Friday as a project of national interest, the second large development to be afforded a fast-track approval process under legislation passed by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney .

Roberts Bank Terminal 2, located in Delta, B.C., is aimed at increasing the port’s container capacity by 50 per cent and supporting up to $100-billion in annual trade, the federal government said in a statement. The expansion is led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority.

With the designation, the three-berth container terminal is expected to get a final investment decision by the middle of next year, the government said.

“Roberts Bank Terminal 2 will add much-needed capacity at our largest port, reduce bottlenecks and strengthen the transportation links Canadian businesses count on,” Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said in a statement.

This is the second major project to be given the coveted designation under the Building Canada Act after the Pacific Link oil pipeline , which was listed at the start of October. The pipeline project would ship one million barrels of Alberta oil a day to the same area of the port expansion south of Vancouver. It is slated to have its approval process completed by Sept. 1, 2027.

Three other developments are awaiting possible listing: the Mackenzie Valley Highway Project in the Northwest Territories, Grays Bay Road and Port Project in Nunavut and a deep nuclear waste storage project in Northwestern Ontario.

All are being evaluated by the Calgary-based Major Projects Office, which the Carney government created as a way to get more developments built to boost and diversify trade. The objective is to bolster Canadian sovereignty against U.S. President Donald Trump ’s trade war, the government has said.

The port expansion is aimed at saving $1-billion a year in shipping costs after investments in rail, logistics facilities and port modernization, the government said. It is also expected to reduce delivery times between Vancouver and Toronto by 17 per cent.

The project has already been through more than a decade of regulatory reviews. It includes a marine land mass and wharf structure, a widened causeway to add roads and rail lines, and an expanded tub basin to support shipping.

It is part of a larger Port of Vancouver Gateway Strategy that would also comprise rail infrastructure, land development for bulk terminals and environmental protections.
