stories.title: Western prof Juan Bello uses archival storytelling to fill history’s gaps
stories.summary: Western University professor Juan Bello uses archival research to highlight untold stories and advance social justice.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
For much of his career as a documentary researcher and producer, Juan Andrés Bello has given voice to others.

“I always think of my work as helping people tell their own stories,” said Bello, a professor in the Faculty of Information and Media Studies (Fims) and expert in archive materials.

In the absence of direct visual records, Bello creatively uses photos, footage, textual records and oral histories to help convey what’s missing. Often, it’s representation.

Western professor Juan Bello (left) and ‘True North: Canadian Myths and Black Power’ producer Leslie Norville at the Focal Awards gala in the U.K. in June 2026, where Bello was recognized with a 2026 Focal Award for his work on the film. (Jed Leicester/Shutterstock/Focal)

This past June, his efforts to fill those gaps were recognized at the Focal International Awards, which celebrate excellence in the use of archival footage across creative and cultural industries.

His work on the documentary True North: Canadian Myths and Black Power, which explores Montreal’s civil rights and anti-racism movement in the 1960s, earned the award for Best Use of Footage in a History Feature. Bello’s imaginative use of archival footage helped provide context, mood and emotion.

The film features a story of students who staged an anti-racism protest at Sir George Williams University, now Concordia University. Many were children of immigrants who arrived in the 1950s.

“There were no records focused on their childhoods, or the discrimination they faced,” Bello said. “We tried to reconstruct and evoke life in Montreal at that time using archival materials to illustrate their emotions.”

His research led him to the National Film Board of Canada collection, where he found footage of life in Québec in that historical period, including wintertime in Montreal, among other relevant material.

“We used footage of a terrible storm in the 1950s to recreate the emotional journey of these kids and to represent their experiences being bullied in a classroom for differences like the colour of their skin or accents. It set the stage, the mood and put people in that time.”

Over the past 20 years, Bello’s independent films and projects have covered a wide range of subjects, from architecture, history and cultural heritage to human rights in both Latin America and Canada.

Bello also worked as one of the lead archival producers for Black Life: Untold Stories, a documentary series about Black Canadians that premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2023 and now streams on CBC Gem.

He called it a groundbreaking project because of the previous lack of representation for Black Canadians.

Part of the challenge was finding an accurate reflection of everyday life.

“When we approached TV networks looking for footage from Jane and Finch in Toronto in the 1970s and 1980s, every single time that neighbourhood was in the news it was in connection with crime,” Bello said. “That’s so unfair and inaccurate in terms of painting a true portrait of life in that community at that time.”

Instead, Bello relied on family photo albums and owners’ willingness to share them.

“It’s about building trust and being respectful,” he said. “Sometimes, people are very generous, sharing materials and giving you access to their photos or home videos, but I think it’s about working with them as partners and collaborators.”

Unlike today, when everyone carries a camera in their pocket, photography was once limited to those with wealth and power. Bello said that can make it harder to find a record of events or daily life. It also demands a critical lens.

“You must always question archive footage and consider the conditions of these records and the intentions of the creators,” he said.

During the Great Depression, Canadian government images promoting a nationwide system of relief camps for single, homeless, unemployed men presented a vastly different story from the reality of the physically demanding labour the men did in exchange for room and board and 20 cents a day.

“When you see images of those men, it looks like they are having a good time at work and at Sunday concerts, but the working conditions were terrible,” Bello said.

In 1935, the harsh state of the camps prompted a mass protest and the On-to-Ottawa Trek, where workers headed to the nation’s capital to demand reasonable work and wages. Bello captured their journey in his documentary Never Forgotten.

A recurring theme throughout Bello’s body of work is his use of storytelling to bring awareness to historical human rights violations and injustices. His 2018 documentary The Chalatenango Massacres reflects the state-sponsored massacres that killed tens of thousands of civilians during the Salvadoran Civil War. The atrocities, long denied by the Salvadoran military and government, are brought to light in testimonies Bello gathered from survivors.

“It was an oral history project, where we followed survivors to the places where the massacres were perpetrated, to hear what they remember about those terrible events,” Bello said.

The film serves as an important archival record, as does his earlier work Queen of the People, about the first democratic elections in his home country of Venezuela in the 1940s.

“When I spoke with the protagonists of these historical events, they were elders already, and have since passed away,” he said. “Now, those interviews are important records of their experiences.”

Bello’s interest in the past also extends to popular culture. He’s helped preserve the cultural memory of television in Latin America as curator of The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950-1999. The travelling exhibition was created in collaboration with Arts and Humanities professor Constanza Burucúa and is currently on view at the University of Miami. A version for Canadian audiences, co-developed with Fims professor Basil Chiasson, is on display in the Fims and Nursing Building and Weldon Library until the end of the year.

The exhibit chronicles the history and cultural influence of the telenovela, serialized fictional dramas that began on radio before moving to television in the 1950s and 1960s and becoming a global phenomenon. Through archival images, stories and memories, Bello explores how television helped shape the political, social and cultural history of Latin America and beyond.

Faculty of Media and Information Studies professor Juan Bello in front a photo wall featured in The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950-1999. Bello curated the travelling exhibit to chronicle the history and cultural influence of serialized fictional TV dramas in Latin America and beyond. The exhibit is on display in the Fims and Nursing Building and Weldon Library until Dec. 2026. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

One powerful example is Ven Conmigo (“Come With Me”), which aired in Mexico from 1975 to 1976 and followed the life of a literacy teacher. The show boosted enrollment in literacy programs in Mexico, prompting India’s national broadcaster to create an adaptation, Hum Log, in the 1980s to advance literacy and support other development goals, including family planning, health and equality for women.

At the opening of the Western exhibit, Bello was struck by comments from a visitor from India. She recalled, in vivid detail, how her family gathered around the television during dinner to watch the show, illustrating the impact it had on their daily and future lives.

“I never had the opportunity before to hear a firsthand account of that experience. It was very meaningful,” Bello said.

The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950–1999 exhibit is on display at Western through December 2026, ON the first and second floors of the Fims & Nursing Building and in the mezzanine level extension of Weldon Library.

The atrocities, long denied by the Salvadoran military and government, are brought to light in testimonies Bello gathered from survivors.
“It was an oral history project, where we followed survivors to the places where the massacres were perpetrated, to hear what they remember about those terrible events,” Bello said.
The film serves as an important archival record, as does his earlier work Queen of the People, about the first democratic elections in his home country of Venezuela in the 1940s.
“When I spoke with the protagonists of these historical events, they were elders already, and have since passed away,” he said. “Now, those interviews are important records of their experiences.”

Bello’s interest in the past also extends to popular culture. He’s helped preserve the cultural memory of television in Latin America as curator of The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950-1999. The travelling exhibition was created in collaboration with Arts and Humanities professor Constanza Burucúa and is currently on view at the University of Miami. A version for Canadian audiences, co-developed with Fims professor Basil Chiasson, is on display in the Fims and Nursing Building and Weldon Library until the end of the year.

The exhibit chronicles the history and cultural influence of the telenovela, serialized fictional dramas that began on radio before moving to television in the 1950s and 1960s and becoming a global phenomenon. Through archival images, stories and memories, Bello explores how television helped shape the political, social and cultural history of Latin America and beyond.

Faculty of Media and Information Studies professor Juan Bello in front a photo wall featured in The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950-1999. Bello curated the travelling exhibit to chronicle the history and cultural influence of serialized fictional TV dramas in Latin America and beyond. The exhibit is on display in the Fims and Nursing Building and Weldon Library until Dec. 2026. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

One powerful example is Ven Conmigo (“Come With Me”), which aired in Mexico from 1975 to 1976 and followed the life of a literacy teacher. The show boosted enrollment in literacy programs in Mexico, prompting India’s national broadcaster to create an adaptation, Hum Log, in the 1980s to advance literacy and support other development goals, including family planning, health and equality for women.

At the opening of the Western exhibit, Bello was struck by comments from a visitor from India. She recalled, in vivid detail, how her family gathered around the television during dinner to watch the show, illustrating the impact it had on their daily and future lives.
“I never had the opportunity before to hear a firsthand account of that experience. It was very meaningful,” Bello said.

The Telenovela Archives: The History of TV Series in Latin America 1950–1999 exhibit is on display at Western through December 2026, ON the first and second floors of the Fims & Nursing Building and in the mezzanine level extension of Weldon Library.

stories.title: Ghost tours are exploding across Canada. Here’s why Halifax’s Citadel Hill has one like no other
stories.summary: Ghost tours are a regular occurrence at the Halifax Citadel National Historic Site, but tour guides are especially busy this week with large crowds, as people celebrate Halloween.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Ghost tours are a regular occurrence at the Halifax Citadel National Historic Site, but tour guides are especially busy this week with large crowds, as people celebrate Halloween.

“I love the spookiness and the coziness,” said Sarah MacLellan who went on her first ghost tour . “I have been bored lately and I want some ‘pep in my step’ so if something jumps out at me, I am down for that.”

“I loved hearing the stories and I loved the history of things that likely and realistically happened here,” added Anastasia Brown who was also a ghost tour first-timer.

In the daytime, the fortress which overlooks Halifax’s downtown core, looks friendly and inviting. But when the sun goes down, the eeriness of this historic site settles in.

“It is very ominous,” MacLellan said.

With 19-century-style candle lit lanterns serving as the guiding lights, the tour took people inside several buildings that date back more than 200 years, up dark stairways, into a cavernous moat framed by steep stone ramparts, through underground tunnels and into darkened rooms to hear some of the many creepy chronicles that have been passed on through generations.

Terrifying people and leaving them unsettled requires a performance art. It’s been said any good story worth telling is also worth stretching.

Tour guide Bryce Walsh does this work on a regular basis, not just on Halloween and one of his favourite tragic ghostly tales involves a soldier named Barry Edwards and his bride who became known as a ghost called “The Grey Lady.”

“As the story goes, he was found dead the morning that he was supposed to be married, to Miss Cassie Allen, who we believe to be ‘The Grey Lady’,” said Walsh.

Ghost tours are growing in popularity, not just in Halifax but also across the country. They offer a mix of history, sightseeing, and spookiness, all rolled up into one.

“Anytime I travel, it’s actually one of the things I want to do because there is some history to it, it is a lot of fun, you get to learn about the place, and get scared,” said visitor, Melissa Brown. “This reminded me a bit of a found footage Halloween movie.”

Walsh said the tours are a creative and often unsettling outing to learn some history, experience some fear and celebrate Halloween in a ghostly setting.

“A part of me thinks that it’s a way to find entertainment in places where people might not be conventionally expecting it,” said Walsh. “People search outside the box and maybe come to places like the Halifax Citadel to do a ghost tour because it is a fun change.”

stories.title: RCMP urges Manitobans to drive safely following increase in fatal collisions
stories.summary: The number of fatal collisions in Manitoba is rising, according to the RCMP, who said it is increasing traffic enforcement as a result.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
More than 70 people have died in collisions in Manitoba this year, according to the RCMP, who are asking people to drive with caution.

The reminder was issued after two 19-year-olds died in separate collisions within the last week, the Manitoba RCMP said in a news release. Thus far in 2026, police have responded to 65 fatal collisions.

Eight people died in collisions this month, contributing to the sum 73 people who have died in collisions this year in the RCMP’s response areas. That figure is 28 per cent higher than the five-year average, according to RCMP. It said 25 of the 73 people who died in collisions this year were under 30 years old.

In Winnipeg, police are pushing for pedestrian safety . In an email to Global News, the Winnipeg Police Service stated that 13 people died in collisions on the city’s roads so far in 2026, compared to a total of 17 people killed last year.

No precise cause for the uptick in events was identified by police, but Greer said various factors played a role in several of the fatalities.

In response, he said the Manitoba RCMP is increasing patrols on the roads in high and low traffic areas.

Lucky Adams lives on Main Street and volunteers with Streets for People of Winnipeg , a group that advocates for a walkable Winnipeg that does not have any traffic fatalities.

They said they first became “acutely aware” of how dangerous cars were when they started biking as their main mode of transportation.

They told Global News that the city seems to care about car traffic, with little regard for non-drivers.

The Manitoba RCMP is reminding drivers to stay sober when getting behind the wheel, keep an eye out for other drivers, pedestrians and wildlife, and stay off their phones while driving.

stories.title: Former Talisman Resort transformed into nature reserve, expanding iconic Bruce Trail with $1M Ontario investment
stories.summary: The former Talisman Mountain Resort is set to become a vital new natural space, the Talisman Forest Nature Reserve, with the Ontario government investing $1 million to transform the site and permanently add a one-kilometre section to the historic Bruce Trail.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The former Talisman Mountain Resort is set to become a vital new natural space, the Talisman Forest Nature Reserve, with the Ontario government investing $1 million to transform the site and permanently add a one-kilometre section to the historic Bruce Trail.

The project, spearheaded by the Bruce Trail Conservancy, aims to revitalize the land once known for its ski slopes and visitor amenities.

The resort closed its doors in 2011 the resort property was acquired by the Conservancy in 2025 and will now serve as a sanctuary for nature and an expanded gateway to Canada’s oldest and longest marked footpath.

This significant land securement project encompasses 123 acres (50 hectares) of ecologically significant land along the Niagara Escarpment, a Unesco World Biosphere Reserve.

The addition of the new one-kilometre trail segment will help close a crucial gap in forest cover along the Beaver Valley. Restoration efforts will include the removal of former ski lift and resort infrastructure, reforestation of ski slopes, invasive species removal, and habitat restoration to benefit species at risk.

The $1 million investment from Ontario, delivered through the Ontario Land Trust Alliance (Olta).

The Talisman Forest Nature Reserve will provide permanent, free public access to a new portion of the Bruce Trail, which stretches nearly 900 kilometres along the Niagara Escarpment.

stories.title: Nova Scotia weighs risks of online gambling as other provinces expand access
stories.summary: Nova Scotia is keeping a close eye on how other provinces are expanding online gambling, but opposition leaders are warning the province should "tread very, very carefully."
stories.author: Skye Bryden-Blom, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government is keeping a close eye on how other provinces are expanding online gambling , but opposition leaders are warning the province should “tread very, very carefully.”

Finance Minister John Lohr told reporters this week that “gaming is in a time of incredible transformation.”

Ontario expanded its online gambling markets in 2022 and Alberta most recently did so in July.

“We’re watching what’s happening in Ontario and Alberta, in particular, very carefully. And obviously, those are conversations that are underway right now,” Lohr said.

The only government-authorized and regulated platform for online gambling in Nova Scotia is currently operated by the Atlantic Lottery Corporation. But Lohr said he’s aware that Nova Scotians are betting on unregulated sites.

“I think anyone can access thousands of gaming sites on their phone through the internet and this is a very significant issue,” he said.

He added he’s worried about potential negative health impacts.

“We don’t feel like we have any handle on it at all as a province. And I don’t know if anybody does. It’s just available on the internet and there are significant harms for people who become addicted to gambling through it,” he said.

A study released last month suggested emergency department visits for gambling disorders had doubled in Ontario since the expansion of online gambling and legalization of single-event sports betting.

Dr. Peter Selby, a senior scientist with the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, said young people are especially at risk of harm.

“The addiction pathways in our brain are geared to consume and lose control. And so what happens is because these games have an element of risk, there’s an excitement to it,” said Selby.

NDP Leader Claudia Chender said she’s concerned and doesn’t want to see government involve itself more in online gambling.

“I think that we should tread very, very carefully before we get more into that business as a government,” she said.

Interim Liberal Leader Iain Rankin said “the first thing that should happen” is a public health risk assessment before expanding gambling services.

“The addiction pathways in our brain are geared to consume and lose control. And so what happens is because these games have an element of risk, there’s an excitement to it,” said Selby.
NDP Leader Claudia Chender said she’s concerned and doesn’t want to see government involve itself more in online gambling.
“I think that we should tread very, very carefully before we get more into that business as a government,” she said.
Interim Liberal Leader Iain Rankin said “the first thing that should happen” is a public health risk assessment before expanding gambling services.

Ontario expanded its online gambling markets in 2022 and Alberta most recently did so in July.
“We’re watching what’s happening in Ontario and Alberta, in particular, very carefully. And obviously, those are conversations that are underway right now,” Lohr said.

The only government-authorized and regulated platform for online gambling in Nova Scotia is currently operated by the Atlantic Lottery Corporation. But Lohr said he’s aware that Nova Scotians are betting on unregulated sites.
“I think anyone can access thousands of gaming sites on their phone through the internet and this is a very significant issue,” he said.
He added he’s worried about potential negative health impacts.

“We don’t feel like we have any handle on it at all as a province. And I don’t know if anybody does. It’s just available on the internet and there are significant harms for people who become addicted to gambling through it,” he said.

stories.title: Pitching in: Charity founded by Bay Street businessmen holds pitchfest to support kids’ mental health
stories.summary: This year’s Capitalize for Kids Investors Conference is expected to raise more than $3-million
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Jeffrey Gallant and Kyle MacDonald

The pitch: Creating Capitalize for Kids

Jeffrey Gallant and Kyle MacDonald became fast friends while studying business at Queen’s University and remained close long after graduating.

They both landed jobs on Bay Street – Mr. MacDonald as an equity analyst and Mr. Gallant as a portfolio manager – and were best man at each others’ wedding.

Mr. Gallant grew up in Ottawa while Mr. MacDonald is from Port Hawkesbury, N.S., but they had shared similar experiences with mental illness.

“Growing up, both myself and Kyle saw firsthand just how deeply depression and suicide can affect people’s lives and communities,” recalled Mr. Gallant. “When a few things transpired to our families, we realized that we needed to do something about that to benefit others.”

They came up with the idea of Capitalize for Kids, a Toronto-based charity that works with youth mental-health agencies to provide pro bono services and innovative funding.

Each fall, the organization holds the Capitalized for Kids Investors Conference where hundreds of representatives from pension funds, hedge funds and other investment firms discuss market insights. Participants pay a fee to attend and proceeds go to the charity.

“They’re all pitching their best investment ideas or where they believe opportunities exist over time, and it just so happens that the net proceeds are really what fuels the impact work at Capitalize for Kids,” Mr. Gallant said. “We’re trying to drive system-wide change by bringing a series of agencies together to work on a concurrent problem to ensure that we can reach the most amount of kids possible.”

The first conference held in 2014 raised $1-million and this year’s event, ON Nov. 18 and 19, is expected to raise more than $3-million.

At first, the money went toward major health care centres including Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children. But over time, the charity began funding community-based mental-health programs and they now work with close to 80 organizations.

Mr. Gallant and Mr. MacDonald, both 37, left their jobs for a year to establish the charity. They’ve since founded their own investment firm and are actively involved with Capitalize for Kids. “It remains a very important passion project for us,” Mr. Gallant said.

stories.title: Can Luke and Kim, both 48, buy a larger home and still retire in a decade?
stories.summary: The couple wants to maintain, or increase, their standard of living and leave an inheritance for their only child
stories.author: Dianne Maley
stories.content:
Both 48 years old, Luke and Kim are looking to buy a bigger house, retire relatively early from their well-paying jobs in the tech field, leave an inheritance for their only child, 14, and maintain and perhaps increase their standard of living throughout their postwork years.

They earn a combined $400,000 a year. Although they have substantial investments , mainly in Vanguard exchange-traded funds, neither has a defined-benefit pension.

They have a house in Toronto valued at $1.2-million with a small mortgage .

“We are considering purchasing a more suitable, larger home in the future,” Luke writes in an e-mail. They’re wondering how much they can “reasonably” spend without compromising their ability to retire at 58 or so and enjoy their desired lifestyle.

Ideally, they want to find the right balance among retiring early, spending more and improving their lifestyle and potentially leaving a meaningful estate, Luke writes.

Their retirement spending goal is $120,000 a year after tax, rising with inflation.

We asked Ross McShane, an advice-only certified financial planner in the Ottawa area, to look at Luke and Kim’s situation.

Luke and Kim are to be congratulated on having accumulated significant wealth at this stage of their lives, Mr. McShane says. “Their primary concern is not simply whether they are on track for retirement, but whether they can loosen the purse strings and enjoy a higher standard of living before and during retirement.”

They have about $4-million of investment assets and generate a substantial annual cash-flow surplus because their lifestyle expenses are relatively modest, the planner says.

They could easily afford to spend more now. “Based on the assumptions used, they are projected to leave a significant estate to their daughter.”

They figure they would have to spend $2.3-million for the house they want, a significant upgrade from their current residence.

Mr. McShane’s projections assume that the new home is purchased in 2028 and that their existing residence is sold. “I have included estimated real estate commissions, land-transfer tax and moving costs,” he says. Additional funds May be required to renovate, furnish or otherwise adapt the new home to their preferences.

A larger property will also carry higher ongoing costs, including property taxes, utilities, insurance, maintenance and repairs. “I have included an additional $18,000 annually for these costs.”

He has also included a $24,000 annual expense contingency because their existing budget does not appear to fully account for occasional large household expenditures and other basic and discretionary expenses.

Private-school costs of $30,000 a year are expected to end in 2030 when their daughter begins university. They have sufficient assets in their registered education savings plan to fund her anticipated postsecondary education costs.

Their projected retirement spending at age 58 consists of after-tax lifestyle spending of $120,000 a year, additional housing costs of $18,000, an annual expense contingency of $24,000 and vehicle-replacement costs every eight years.

Retirement expenses therefore total about $162,000 annually before vehicle-replacement costs, indexed to inflation.

Can Moira, 57, retire in three years and still leave an inheritance for her kids?

“Based on these assumptions, purchasing the larger home does not appear to compromise their current lifestyle or long-term retirement objectives,” Mr. McShane says. Even if the entire net amount required for the purchase is funded from their investment portfolio, at age 58 they are projected to have about $7-million of investment assets in nominal dollars, equivalent to $5.7-million in today’s purchasing power, in addition to the value of their home.

The projections also suggest that they have the flexibility to enjoy other experiences, including travel and spending part of each winter in a warmer climate, the planner says.

They are also projected to leave a significant estate, which May create additional tax and estate-planning opportunities to address over time, he adds. The projections assume an average annual investment return of 5 per cent and annual inflation of 2.1 per cent.

They will need to decide how to fund the difference between the purchase price of the new home and the net proceeds from the sale of their existing residence. They could use their investments, arrange a larger mortgage or adopt a combination of the two approaches.

Their existing mortgage rate is 3.8 per cent. However, new financing could cost 4.5 per cent or more.

Funding the purchase from the sale of securities in their $1.9-million nonregistered portfolio would generate about $175,000 of taxable capital gains, the planner says. The amount reported by each spouse would be based on the accounts and the investments sold.

They could begin realizing some of these gains before purchasing the home, Mr. McShane says. “Spreading the dispositions over more than one tax year May help moderate the resulting tax liability.” Any advance sales should, however, be coordinated with the anticipated timing of the purchase and their overall investment strategy, the planner says.

Can Luther, 52, and Bethany, 49, retire in a few years and still leave a big inheritance?

They also hold approximately $400,000 in their TFSAs . These funds could be withdrawn without tax consequences, with the withdrawn amounts added back to their contribution room at the beginning of the following calendar year. The TFSAs could then be replenished gradually using future cash-flow surpluses or funds transferred from their nonregistered accounts. The trade-off is that they would give up tax-free investment growth until the funds are recontributed.

They are not averse to borrowing part of the required amount.

At a mortgage rate of 4.5 per cent, their nonregistered investments would generally need to earn 6 per cent or more before tax to produce a comparable after-tax result when returns are primarily capital gains.

Another option would be to finance a portion of the purchase and then make substantial annual principal payments using a combination of their cash-flow surpluses and proceeds from the gradual sale of existing investments.

“This approach could spread the realization of capital gains over several tax years rather than concentrating them in the year of purchase,” the planner says. It would also allow a larger portion of the portfolio to remain invested for longer. The potential tax deferral and continued investment growth would have to be weighed against the mortgage interest cost and the risk that investment returns May be lower than anticipated, Mr. McShane says.

Kim has about $400,000 within her corporation. If the corporation has a positive capital dividend account balance, a portion of these funds May potentially be distributed as a tax-free capital dividend, Mr. McShane says.

Their asset allocation is 30 per cent fixed income and 70 per cent stock ETFs. “This balanced-growth allocation is reasonable given their financial position and the fact that they do not expect to rely on their portfolio for retirement income for 10 years.”

With a 27-year age gap, how can Sydney retire early to spend time with his partner?

Once they have a clearer estimate of the amount they will contribute toward the purchase, that portion should be gradually moved into a high-interest savings account, cashable GICs or other suitable short-term investments, Mr. McShane says. This will preserve the required capital and reduce the risk of having to sell investments following a market decline.

Cash-flow surpluses remaining after Rrsp and Tfsa contributions should also go to a high-interest savings account or another suitable short-term investment so the funds will be secure and readily available for the purchase, the planner says.

The People: Luke and Kim, both 48, and their daughter, 14.

The Problem: How much can they afford to spend on a new home without jeopardizing their other financial goals?

The Plan: Go ahead and buy the house they have in mind, taking time to weigh the various options for paying for the purchase.

The Payoff: Knowing they can afford to spend more freely now and in future even after buying a more expensive residence.

(Income, expenses, assets and liabilities provided by the applicants.)

Monthly after-tax income: $22,100.

Assets: His nonregistered portfolio $1,225,055; her nonregistered $682,240; his Tfsa $204,783; her Tfsa $199,654; his Rrsp $565,430; her Rrsp $499,070; his locked-in retirement account $200,665; her defined-contribution pension $52,235; Resp $112,000; house $1.2-million; her corporate account $423,540. Total: $5.3-million.

Monthly outlays: Mortgage $2,000; property tax $350; water, sewer, garbage $60; home insurance $80; electricity $100; heating $100; maintenance $200; transportation $275; groceries $1,000; private school $2,500; clothing $100; gifts, charity $150; vacation, travel $1,500; dining, drinks, entertainment $600; personal care $100; sports, hobbies $100; subscriptions $50; health care $60; health, dental insurance $200; life, disability insurance $100; communications $100; RRSPs and her DC pension $3,985; TFSAs $1,165; contingencies $2,000. Total outlays: $16,875.

Liabilities: Mortgage $40,000.

stories.title: Building tool to help courts spot AI-generated evidence is ‘challenging’: researcher
stories.summary: A team of researchers in Canada are working to make an open-source, free and easy to use tool that the justice system can use to help distinguish what's real from what's fake.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A researcher working to help courts detect evidence that’s been created or altered with artificial intelligence says it’s proving difficult to come up with a tool that’s as effective in the real world as it seems to be in the lab.

Maura Grossman is co-director of a team of researchers in Canada working to make an open-source, free and easy to use tool that courts and others involved in the justice system can use to help distinguish what’s real from what’s fake.

As the two-year project nears its halfway point, she says they’ve built a system that combines state-of-the-art algorithms, which then work as a committee to vote on whether something is AI-generated.

Grossman says the two times she’s tried it in real-life situations, however, the algorithms couldn’t reach enough of a consensus to be helpful. She says it’s a “wicked technical problem” that presents a real challenge as they continue working on the tool over the next year.

Grossman, a computer science professor at the University of Waterloo who also teaches at York University’s Osgoode Hall law school, says the next phase of the project will involve getting input from law enforcement and policymakers.

“I don’t know that I ever thought it was going to be easy, but it’s turned out to be almost daunting how challenging this task is,” she said in an interview Friday.

“We’re still hopeful, we’re still continuing to build, but I think we’ve gotten more modest in terms of thinking of one tool being the answer, as opposed to this is a problem that’s going to need some help from the law, from regulation, from policymakers, from educating people to become better at knowing how to decipher what’s real and what’s not.”

Part of what makes things tricky, she said, is that an image posted to social media, for example, will be compressed and likely stripped of its metadata, becoming very different from the original file by the time it’s presented as evidence.

“It’s not going to have that information that the original copy had, and chances are the original copy is gone three years later by the time you sue me for saying something horrible about you or whatever I did,” she said.

“That’s part of it, and same thing if I email it to you and you email it to six other people, the data just changes through all this transfer.”

The project is one of two inaugural research initiatives funded through the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research’s Canadian AI Safety Institute program, launched by the federal government in 2024 as part of its broader AI safety strategy.

The team includes technologists and legal scholars based in universities in Ontario and British Columbia, but its advisory board is scattered across North America and includes judges as well as organizations supporting self-represented litigants.

When the project was announced last year, Grossman said courts weren’t adequately prepared for AI. The existing commercial tools weren’t transparent or reliable enough, particularly for the judicial context, where the stakes are high, she said then.

She stressed Friday that the team never envisioned its tool as a silver bullet, adding any tool would still require human involvement and discernment.

“You’re going to need somebody to be able to testify why they think what they think and all of that,” she said.

“But there are broader components to this that need to be included in the picture, some of which is policy considerations — like maybe certain things need to prohibited altogether from being created rather than putting all the onus on detecting it after the fact.”

stories.title: Montreal synagogue likely hit with pellet gun bullets, says rabbi: 'Our third incident in less than two years'
stories.summary: "Obviously, this is not what we want to see happening," says Rabbi Lisa Grushcow. "This is our third incident in less than two years."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Montreal synagogue has been hit with what its rabbi believes were bullets of a pellet gun overnight on Thursday.

The incident occurred at Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Westmount. The synagogue’s executive director was about to attend a meeting in the boardroom on Friday and noticed there were “holes in some of the windows” but “nothing penetrated the building,” Rabbi Lisa Grushcow told National Post.

No one was injured and police were notified. The investigation is ongoing.

“Obviously, this is not what we want to see happening,” said Grushcow. “This is our third incident in less than two years.”

In February 2025, a swastika was spray-painted on the side of the building, the Montreal Gazette reported . In June, a man was arrested and charged with arson after an attempt to set the synagogue on fire, according to the publication .

Grushcow clarified that while the motive of this latest incident was not yet known, it is “impossible to ignore the context that we’re in, of rising radicalization and rising antisemitism.”

“All that we know for sure is that this seemed to have been a deliberate act against our synagogue,” she said.

“We’re going to gather tonight and tomorrow morning for Shabbat. We’re going to do what we always do. We’ve got a guest who is a minister in the United Church who’s speaking tomorrow morning because part of what we do is, we build bridges between communities. We will always be on the side of of building and not destroying, and hoping to help be a positive force in this world that we live in.”

Westmount Mayor Michael Stern confirmed to National Post that he was aware of the incident.

“Police are on it, and everybody’s safe,” he said.

Montreal police did not immediately respond to National Post’s request for comment.

stories.title: Ottawa lists B.C. port expansion as project of national interest
stories.summary: The federal government has listed the Port of Vancouver's planned Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion as a project of national interest.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Delta — The planned Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion, which is expected to add 2.4 million containers of capacity at the Port of Vancouver, the largest in the country, has officially been named a project of national interest.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the move provides certainty for a project that’s a key part of Ottawa’s drive to expand and diversify trade, including a goal to double exports to markets other than the United States by 2035.

“When you’re dealing with projects of this scope and size, and cost, time is money. And after 13 years of looking at this from every possible angle, it is time to decide and move on,” MacKinnon told a news conference in Delta, B.C., ON Friday.

The existing port is approaching the limit of its container handling capacity, he said.

Without additional capacity, “congestion at the port could drive shipping costs to more than $800 million a year by 2035,” MacKinnon said.

“That’s a cost that would have to be borne by Canadian businesses and consumers, but that is a cost they should not and cannot afford to bear.”

In his first appearance alongside federal officials since the B.C. Conservatives won a decisive victory in the Oct. 24 election, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said the port expansion is about preparing for the future rather than reacting to it.

“For British Columbia, these benefits are particularly significant. The project will help cement our province’s role as Canada’s leading trade gateway, attracting investment and ensuring our economy remains competitive on the world stage.”

The estimated capital cost for Roberts Bank expansion project is $5.9 billion. A statement from Ottawa said it’s on a “viable path” to a final investment decision by the middle of next year.

The listing as a project of national interest speeds up the timeline for commercial operation by up to four years, to 2035, the federal government said.

The Vancouver Fraser Port Authority is the proponent for the three-berth expansion project set to be built next to an existing container facility.

Ottawa has said the expansion would support roughly 17,000 jobs across Canada’s supply chains, contribute approximately $3 billion annually to the country’s GDP and generate more than $630 million in annual tax revenues.

Tsawwassen First Nation Chief Laura Cassidy said her community has been focused on protecting treaty rights and ensuring the surrounding environment remains healthy and productive for future generations.

The nation’s position on the expansion project “is one of consent, but not unconditional support,” she said.

“We continue to have concerns about the impacts of the project and the long-term health of the Fraser River Estuary and the Salish Sea. At the same time, years of consultation have resulted in a deeper understanding of those impacts and how they can be addressed,” she said.

Cassidy said the nation had previously sought assurances that the Building Canada Act, under which the expansion has been listed, would not be used to cut corners or weaken environmental protections.

Environmental groups have long voiced concern over the potential impacts of the project, which is located in the habitat of endangered southern resident killer whales.

The Wilderness Committee issued a statement Friday saying its listing as a project of national interest was a “path to extinction” for the whales, taken alongside other existing and planned industrial activity in the area.

A statement from another group, the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, said the Port of Vancouver would have been required to obtain a permit under the Species At Risk Act related to the whales, but Friday’s announcement overrides that process.

MacKinnon told the news conference the expansion project “continues the absolutely vital conservation and other work that goes into the final remaining permits.”

The port expansion was not the only infrastructure project discussed at Friday’s news conference.

Doerkson’s Conservatives had promised during the provincial election campaign to scrap the replacement of the Massey Tunnel that runs beneath the Fraser River between Richmond and Delta in favour of a bridge, prompting questions about federal funding for the project, which is already under way.

But MacKinnon said Ottawa supports “crossing that river whatever way the premier tells us to.”

He said the project was not something the federal government would normally be involved in, but the investment was important.

“If the government of British Columbia says it wants to construct a bridge, we’re for a bridge,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

Chuck Chiang, The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Certain units of Harkla Children’s Compression Sensory Swings are being recalled in Canada, United States.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Justin Tang/Canadian Press[](https://www.thestar.com/news/popular-children-s-compression-swing-recalled-due-to-fall-hazard/article_1ae2a179-7483-40ce-ba81-e5046259d227.html)

ByMegan Mills Devoe Staff Reporter

Over 5,000 units of Harkla Compression Sensory swings have been recalled across Canada due to risk of injury caused by a fall.

According to Health Canada, some units of the swing, which is designed to hang from the ceiling, have faulty hardware which can result in the swing collapsing.

“The swing’s ceiling hook can separate from its mounting plate, posing a risk of injury from a fall hazard,” wrote Health Canada in a recall notice published Oct. 29.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

The Zookeeper and The Tin Man: A Halloween Love Story

Image 10Image 11

As of Oct. 23, Harkla states that it has received one report of injury in Canada and 17 reports of injury in the United States.The company said it received four reports of the hook and plate separating in Canada, and 29 reports in the United States.

Compression swings are sometimes used by children with Autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and sensory processing disorder to help regulate their nervous system. Harkla’s swings are designed for children aged 3 and over.

Health Canada stated that this recall affect units of Harkla Children’s Compression Sensory Swings that have a blue fabric seat and come with a four-hole ceiling hook mounting plate for suspension, with a drop length of 18 to 24 inches. Affected units have either LS-COMP-1BLU or LS-COMP-1BLU-SW printed on the side of the product packaging.

According to Health Canada, the products were sold between March 2020 and April 2025.

The health organization has advised customers to stop using the product immediately and to contact Harkla in order to obtain a free repair kit.

Megan Mills Devoe is a staff reporter with the Star. Reach her via email:mmillsdevoe@thestar.ca

stories.title: Former B.C. minister says he's focused on family, but leaves door open to politics
stories.summary: Victoria - Former New Democrat housing minister Ravi Kahlon says his priority is his family after opting not to run in the snap election that toppled his party's government -- but he is not closing the door on politics.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Former British Columbia cabinet minister Ravi Kahlon said the New Democrats must dive deeply and learn from what led to their crushing defeat by the Conservatives in the province’s snap election this month.

Kahlon, who decided not to seek re-election, said appealing to people outside Victoria and Vancouver would be key to the party’s success in the future.

The path to victory is narrow if the NDP counts on those strongholds to win elections, he said in an interview on Friday.

But the snap election itself, called two years into the Ndp’s mandate under outgoing premier David Eby, was also a factor in the government’s demise.

“Overwhelmingly, I heard from people that they just couldn’t get over the fact that the election was called,” Kahlon said.

Kahlon said the NDP must also ask itself how its messages resonate with voters of Chinese, South Asian and Filipino backgrounds.

“Those are communities that we didn’t do as well, and we have to really reflect on what it is that we’re proposing in these communities,” he said.

Kahlon said he hoped that would be a key part of the work the party would do with interim leader Jennifer Whiteside, the former labour minister, at the helm.

As for Kahlon’s future with the party, he said family is his priority for now. He’s been catching up on lost time with his teenage son, teaching him how to drive and coaching his basketball team.

Yet politics and sports have historically given Kahlon what he called his two Ps — purpose and pressure.

“I’ll be searching for those, the two Ps, as I kind of endeavour on what the next steps will look like.”

His Olympic career as a field hockey player for Canada has ended, but Kahlon has not closed the door on politics.

Kahlon did not rule out running for the permanent leadership of the NDP after Eby’s election-night resignation, though he pointed to outgoing deputy premier Niki Sharma and former cabinet minister Josie Osborne as “great” potential candidates.

Port Coquitlam Mayor Brad West could be another “strong voice” to lead the provincial NDP, Kahlon said.

Kahlon, who was first elected in 2017 and also served as jobs minister, said he, like his party, needed time to reflect before determining next steps.

But he has told former caucus colleagues that he is around to help.

“There’s a lot of talent,” he said Friday.

“If I will be involved or not, and at what scope that is, I can’t predict that at this stage. Too much happening, too fresh; we’ll have to see.”

Kahlon had left the game shortly after the opening whistle, announcing he wouldn’t seek re-election in a press release hours after the snap election call.

“The premier called an election and I decided that this was not the time for me to run again and instead spend some time with home base,” he said.

NDP legislators, including Kahlon, had met fewer than 48 hours earlier to discuss next steps after the resignation of former Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Kahlon declined to reveal what he told Eby during that meeting.

“What I told him is what I told him and I’m not going to relive it,” he said.

“The reality is, the premier heard various opinions and he made a decision and it turned out it wasn’t the right one.”

Kahlon’s comments came less than a week after watching the election results from the sidelines, sitting at home with his partner, using a tablet.

“I had Elections BC on my screen and I was just refreshing, refreshing,” he said, adding it was a “weird” way to watch the results after working on seven election campaigns for the NDP and running in three of them.

Being a spectator gave the Oct. 24 election a different flavour.

“You feel a lot of anxiety, because you don’t have control to help change the direction of the game, you’re just watching,” he said.

Kahlon said fear of losing wasn’t a factor in his decision not to run.

“I’ve never been afraid to lose,” he said. “You don’t play field hockey for Canada, and try to compete at the international level if you’re afraid of losing. So, that’s just not my mentality.”

Kahlon said his only regret was not being able to help his colleagues.

“That being said, I probably wouldn’t have been able to make a big significant change in the outcome of that (election),” he said.

“The public mood was the public mood.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Police look for three men in violent Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: Father, two adult daughters were shot after masked suspects forced their way into the home before fleeing in an SUV
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
A real estate executive is decrying an increase in violent robberies in Toronto after he and his family members were shot during a home invasion in the city’s upscale Bridle Path neighbourhood.

Toronto police are investigating what they described as a random home invasion by assailants early Thursday morning.

David Morton, 75, released a statement on Friday thanking the public for its support after the incident left his family traumatized, with some members still in the hospital.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Mr. Morton, chief executive of the MAC Group, said in the statement.

“It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.”

The family includes Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and the couple’s two adult daughters Cristina and Maggie Zohil-Morton.

Toronto has seen an increase in home invasions even as shootings and homicides have declined. Canada’s largest city has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year, according to police statistics.

Police said Friday they are looking for three suspects, who allegedly broke into the home, went up to the second floor and demanded valuables.

During an altercation, police said, the attackers shot the father and his two daughters, while their mother was injured with a hammer.

Mr. Morton’s statement pointed to an increase in home invasions in the city.

“While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto,” he said.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.”

The Bridle Path is one of Canada’s most exclusive neighbourhoods, where large houses are hidden behind high walls and wrought-iron gates. The family’s house on Hyde Park Circle is now surrounded by extra police security.

Years ago, the couple started the MAC Group, which rents out luxury apartments in several countries.

The company’s website has a blog by family members which speaks about their life before the attack.

Mr. Morton writes he spent decades in the hospitality industry before striking out on his own. “My career began with some of the world’s leading hotel brands, including Four Seasons and Westin Hotels, before I went on to build our family of businesses,” he says.

His wife Doriana says she is involved in running the MAC Group and also charities, including ones that help provide furniture to teenagers leaving the child-welfare system. “Relationships remain at the heart of everything I do,” she writes.

Maggie Zohil-Morton graduated from Queen’s and Dalhousie universities. “Maggie’s passion for her hometown of Toronto is evident in her work,” the posting says, adding she is “also a trusted Caribbean expert.”

Cristina Zohil-Morton graduated from the University of Birmingham in England and became a lawyer. She now “offers professional legal guidance to those seeking to relocate to Canada,” the family blog says.

On Friday, members of the Toronto Police Service’s mounted unit paraded through the neighbourhood on horseback. Officers in squad cars and on foot were nearby. Commanders of the force say that this show of law-enforcement will continue for the time being.

“Residents can expect an increased police presence in coming days,” Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said in a statement on X . He said he is ordering “additional resources to address this concerning trend of home invasions.”

With reports from Stephanie Chambers

stories.title: Canada needs a ‘good mix’ of new tech like drones, AI: Nato commander
stories.summary: Next week’s federal budget is expected to have more details about how Canada intends to meet ambitious defence spending targets by 2035.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
As Canada prepares to invest billions into national defence in the coming years, a senior Nato official is advising the alliance’s militaries to include a mix of cutting-edge technology like AI targeting and advanced drones into their plans.

Speaking to Global News from Riga, Latvia, ON Friday, Adm. Pierre Vandier said that it’s not a question of replacing “everything” with drones — but rather incorporating drones and other unmanned systems to protect and enhance existing military capabilities.

“A force that is not protected against drones and (drone) swarms is a force at risk,” Vandier, Nato’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, said in an interview.

Vandier was speaking after observing Nato exercises in Latvia that included a mix of electronic warfare and drones along with “boots on the ground” to simulate a cross-border invasion.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is top of mind for the alliance forces stationed in Latvia, including the roughly 3,000 Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel stationed in the country as part of Operation Reassurance.

That conflict has seen dramatic developments in the use of drones in warfare, including to limit the effectiveness of more traditional military assets — such as tanks and ground forces.

But Vandier said that one of the lessons learned through the Nato exercises is that drone warfare doesn’t make those traditional military systems obsolete — but rather that drones and electronic warfare tactics, including in a “good mix” of other military capabilities, can make a force more effective.

“What we demonstrated was we can extend lethality and extend survivability of existing capabilities … if we bring them with a good mix of new technology,” Vandier said.

Vandier gave the example of an attack helicopter. With the use of both drones and anti-drone defences, the French admiral said that weapons system can execute missions “that were impossible before.”

“What robots are bringing is a risk management system, where you can open the tactical portfolio … and have better use of what you have,” Vandier said.

Since 2022, Nato has been running exercises with the Latvian Ministry of Defence to test electronic warfare, drone and AI technologies in “field-like conditions.” The exercises, known as the Digital Backbone eXperimentation (DIBaX), include the participation of defence companies and academics to test cutting-edge technology in a realistic setting.

According to a Nato official, this year’s exercise included testing of drone swarms, drone-to-drone combat and a cross-border incursion, along with electronic warfare tactics meant to jam or otherwise disable enemy drones.

These are themes that the CAF has been thinking about for years, including deploying anti-drone defences for personnel stationed in Latvia.

Earlier this year, the Department of National Defence launched the Defence Drone Initiative (DDI), an effort to both provide the CAF and the Canadian Coast Guard with new drone technology and to boost the domestic industry.

“Recent conflicts have underscored how rapidly drone technologies are transforming modern warfare and are central to modern military operations … Success increasingly depends on the ability to innovate, adapt and field new capabilities at speed,” the government said in July.

“Canada must be prepared to do the same.”

The push to develop Canada’s drone capabilities also comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to invest billions of new money into national defence, with Canada finally meeting its Nato target of spending two per cent of GDP on the defence this year.

The Carney government has released few details, however, about how it intends to reach the target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence by 2035. A recent analysis by the Parliamentary Budget Office suggested reaching that target would require “core” defence spending to increase from $95.7 billion in 2030 to $163.7 billion in 2035-36.

More details on how the Liberals intend to do that are expected in Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne’s 2026-27 budget, scheduled to be tabled next Thursday.

stories.title: Multiple fire departments respond to large dairy barn blaze near Listowel
stories.summary: Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night that affected dozens of cattle.

North Perth Fire Department crews from the Listowel, Atwood and Monkton stations were dispatched to a working structure fire at a dairy barn on Line 88 at about 9:05 p.m.

Mutual aid assistance was provided by fire departments from Minto, Mapleton and Howick as crews worked to contain the blaze.

Heavy equipment was brought to the scene at approximately 11:15 p.m. to assist firefighters.

Officials said 88 cattle were involved in the fire, although it remains unclear how many animals were possibly lost.

No injuries to firefighters or anyone else at the scene were reported.

While a cause has not been released, officials said the fire is not suspicious in nature.

stories.title: Bennett Jones, Borden Ladner Gervais hit in data breach targeting Bay Street law firms
stories.summary: McCarthy Tétrault and Davies Ward Phillips & Vineberg are also dealing with data breaches that have compromised thousands of files
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki
stories.content:
Bennett Jones LLP and Borden Ladner Gervais LLP have confirmed that they were compromised by data breaches as part of a broader campaign that has successfully infiltrated at least four Bay Street law firms.

David Di Paolo, national managing partner and CEO of BLG, said an unauthorized third party accessed “a portion” of the firm’s Microsoft cloud environment, including files related to clients. The firm engaged Mandiant, a cybersecurity consulting firm and Google subsidiary, to investigate the incident, determine the scope of the breach and support remediation, Mr. Di Paolo said in a statement provided to The Globe and Mail.

Bennett Jones said two of its business services employees’ user accounts were compromised on Oct. 19 as part of what it called a “larger campaign targeting Canadian law firms.”

McCarthy Tétrault LLP and Davies Ward Phillips & Vineberg LLP are also dealing with data breaches that have compromised thousands of files in total, including client information, The Globe reported on Thursday.

All of the firms that were breached have notified law enforcement and are reaching out to affected clients.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security on Wednesday cautioned that multiple Canadian firms have been targeted by cybercriminals impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fraudulent sign-in pages.

The Globe previously reported that at least some of the breaches at law firms involved hackers using Microsoft Teams and posing as internal IT employees to request access to an employee’s computer.

Bennett Jones said the information stolen includes revenue reports from clients and, in some cases, general descriptions of the firm’s mandates for those clients.

However, the firm’s document management system, where legal files are contained, and its accounting system was not breached, Bennett Jones said in a notice on its website.

“We immediately detected the activity and took steps to contain, investigate and assess the affected data in scope,” the firm said in the statement .

The hackers targeted other firms as well, including Stikeman Elliott LLP and Gowling WLG, but didn’t succeed.

Richard McConnell, Gowling’s chief technology and operating officer, said the firm worked with an external cybersecurity firm to investigate attempted attacks, and found no evidence that its systems or client information were compromised.

“We continue to monitor for related activity,” Mr. McConnell said.

Peter Castiel, Montreal-based chair of Stikeman Elliott LLP, said law firms and IT departments across the country are working together to understand how the hackers got access to confidential data, what to do to help clients and how to ensure it doesn’t happen again.

“All the major law firms, and in particular, all the CIOs [chief information officers], are sharing intel and best practices,” Mr. Castiel said.

With a report from Andrew Willis

stories.title: Canada, EU lay out vision for closer ties in ‘dangerous and divided’ world
stories.summary: Canada and the EU are laying out their vision for what a closer relationship looks like in an increasingly “dangerous and divided” where trade has become “weaponized.”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada and the EU are laying out their vision for what a closer relationship looks like as the world becomes increasingly “dangerous and divided” and where trade has become “weaponized.”

While the agreement, signed Friday, only refers to the United States once in reference to its sanctions imposed on the International Criminal Court, Prime Minister Mark Carney has made no secret of his plans to foster relationships with other foreign nations in the wake of increasing trade tensions.

“This is a positive alliance. It’s about creating opportunity, building prosperity, addressing sustainability, and reinforcing sovereignty,” Carney said. “It’s not against anything, it’s for. And those who choose to be for solutions will be pleased with the result.”

The prime minister said the agreement, in which Canada and the European Union agree to pursue “an even closer association” between their respective leaders, industries and people, vows to create opportunities for those on both sides of the ocean.

“Opportunity for our youth, for our artists, for our researchers, for our businesses. It’s about democracy, protecting against foreign interference and social media manipulation while supporting human rights, freedom, and the rule of law. This is about sustainability. Protect our oceans, our forests, and our Arctic, while developing practical, scalable solutions to climate change. And above all, it’s about sovereignty, about being able to live our lives as we wish,” Carney said.

The agreement sets out an alliance for trade, research, raw minerals, energy, security and preparedness, including vows to pursue easier digital money transfers between people in Canada and Europe as well as more opportunities for labour mobility and youth education abroad.

“This is based on partnership, balance, and mutual respect. And like any major bridge, each side has something to offer the other,” Carney said.

Both parties say they will collaborate to work toward connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, low-cost and more seamless border transactions, making it easier to conduct business across the Atlantic and transfer funds between the two economies.

Currently, large sums typically need to be handled by wire transfers which take days to process.

Canada and the EU will also launch negotiations to encourage deeper participation in Erasmus+, the EU flagship program for education, training youth and support to expand opportunities for students, researchers, educators and young people to gain international experience and promote training and lasting institutional partnerships.

Canada and the EU have also agreed to launch discussion on cooperating on skills development and enhancing labour and research mobility, with a focus on reducing barriers for young people and facilitating mobility for highly skilled workers.

“This alliance is built for people. The student in Edmonton who wants to study in Stockholm. The cancer researcher in Saskatoon who needs her answer today, not next spring. The Vancouver startup with new customers in Berlin,” Carney said. “We launch a new alliance for the future that will deliver now and in the future with like-minded nations. We’re just getting started.”

Canada has also signalled its intention to join the Ukraine Support Loan, affirming a commitment to support for Ukraine’s independence and sovereignty through political, financial, humanitarian, military and diplomatic aid.

“We see the world through the same eyes. What matters nowadays is not where a country is on the map, but what it is ready to build with us and what it stands for in the world of fierce geopolitical headwinds. These headwinds won’t stop blowing. This change is permanent and now it is time to act with confidence and with vision to build a new future,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said Friday.

She said Canada’s priorities and visions align with the EU enough that “we can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”

“In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty is no longer the freedom to act alone, but it is the capacity to act together.”

The two leaders have also laid out plans for participation on artificial intelligence, outer space, climate change, as well as European investment in critical raw minerals.

However, the agreement made no mention of whether Canada will align with European regulations on AI, which require the labelling content generated or assisted using AI.

stories.title: Trick-or-treating still popular among Canadians with children: poll
stories.summary: Toronto - A new poll suggests 80 per cent of parents with kids old enough to trick-or-treat will participate in the door-to-door ritual, but only half of respondents plan to dish out candy.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A new poll suggests 80 per cent of parents with kids old enough to trick-or-treat will participate in the door-to-door ritual, but only half of respondents plan to dish out candy.

The online survey from Leger asked 1,513 people aged 18 or older about their Halloween habits between Oct. 24 and 26. Of those, 419 were parents with kids of trick-or-treating age.

stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto police say they are looking for three young men following a violent home invasion and shooting in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood on Thursday.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The head of a corporate real estate firm whose family was attacked during a violent home invasion in Toronto’s affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood says they experienced a “horrific” ordeal and are focused on recovery as police seek three suspects in the case.

In a statement released Friday afternoon, CEO of MAC Group David Morton said three members of his family were recovering in the hospital after being shot during the attack early on Thursday. He said all four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton wrote in the statement.

“It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.”

Police first received reports of three people shot inside a residence on Hyde Park Circle at around 3:40 a.m. Thursday.

Investigators said a father, mother and their two adult daughters were in the home when masked suspects forced their way in through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer. Police said the father and the two daughters were shot.

The male suspects then made their way to the second floor of the home and demanded valuables, police said. They got into an “altercation” with the family and shot their weapons multiple times, investigators said.

All three suspects in the violent attack were wearing dark clothing, are estimated to be about 20 years old and are considered armed and dangerous, police said in an update Friday. They fled in a dark-coloured SUV.

While his family is recovering from the attack, Morton said they are also “deeply concerned” about increasing home invasion violence across Toronto.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives,” he wrote in his statement.

He urged anyone with information about the attack at his home to come forward. “We sincerely hope that the individuals responsible will be identified, apprehended and brought to justice.”

Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith told a news conference Thursday that it was unclear if any belongings were stolen, or if the home was specifically targeted.

“Typically in an affluent neighbourhood come nice things,” she said. “There’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things.”

So far this year, 119 home invasions have been reported in Toronto, up more than 32 per cent from the same time last year, police said in an email.

At a Toronto police board meeting in April, Smith said the city saw a significant increase in home invasions in 2024, connected to the rise in violent car thefts.

This year, some neighbourhoods have become “hot spots” for these offences, she said. That includes areas in the police force’s 32 Division, which covers multiple neighbourhoods across North York, and 53 Division, covering midtown Toronto.

The Bridle Path neighbourhood is located in 33 Division, which also saw an increase in home invasion offences, according to police data.

Violent home invasions have been reported across the Greater Toronto Area in recent years.

In August of 2025, a man was fatally shot in his Vaughan home during a home invasion when he confronted the suspects. The man’s brother said one of the intruders allegedly pointed a gun at the man’s children before shooting him. His family witnessed the shooting.

Earlier that summer, Peel regional police laid 136 charges against 12 people after an investigation into violent home invasions and jewelry store robberies. They said 17 such incidents took place between May and December 2024.

As Toronto police continue to investigate the Bridle Path shooting, they say they will have an increased presence in the neighbourhood.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is,” Smith said on Thursday. “People should be able to feel safe in their homes.”

Morton said many people have reached out with messages of concern and support. “The outpouring of kindness has meant a great deal to us during this incredibly difficult time.”

The family is focused on recovery and asks for privacy, Morton wrote. “Our priority is getting through this together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: London man sentenced to nine years for shooting outside downtown strip club
stories.summary: Kwabena Anhwere, 44, was sentenced Friday by Justice Kelly Tranquilli after pleading guilty to three firearm-related offences stemming from the April 2023 shooting
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London man who fired a handgun outside a downtown strip club more than three years ago has been sentenced to nine years in prison.

Kwabena Anhwere, 44, was sentenced Friday by Justice Kelly Tranquilli after pleading guilty to three firearm-related offences stemming from the April 2023 shooting outside the Solid Gold Club on Dundas Street.

During the sentencing hearing, the court heard how an argument inside the club led to Anhwere being removed by security guards. Surveillance video showed him getting up from the sidewalk with a handgun before running toward the entrance and firing a shot.

The bullet struck the door. No one was injured.

Justice Tranquilli described Anhwere’s actions as a “grave danger to public safety,” noting it was only by coincidence that the incident did not result in a tragedy.

The nine-year sentence reflects a joint submission from the Crown and defence.

Anhwere received credit for time spent in pre-sentence custody and has approximately four-and-a-half years left to serve.

He also received a lifetime firearms prohibition and is subject to mandatory DNA orders.
