stories.title: Textbook terror: University course sinks teeth into the art of the horror film
stories.summary: Calgary - On a chilly pre-Halloween morning this week, Rane Gusdal watches the climactic last moments of her short film with her fellow university students: a video of her entrails being torn out of her stomach.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - On a chilly pre-Halloween morning this week, Rane Gusdal watches the climactic last moments of her short film with her fellow university students: a video of her entrails being torn out of her stomach.

The blood and guts are a crimson mix of bread, Nutella and jam. She screams and flails on screen. She’s hoping they don’t laugh.

“I hope people felt grossed out and scared,” said the 19-year-old film major.

“I was trying to be dead, you know?”

Gusdal’s group is one of several that submit short films for Julia Chan’s course at the University of Calgary on the horror film genre, a style of film that peaks amid the supernatural spirit of Halloween.

As part of their skit, one group member had their drink spiked, turning them into a flesh-hungry monster with white-glossed eyes. They ravaged the group in a dim, concrete-walled hallway.

Gusdal said someone having their drink spiked at a nightclub began as a way to create the monster. As the project progressed, it held a much deeper meaning about the realistic threat of clubgoers being unknowingly drugged.

Over the length of the course, the class discusses how horror stories do more than scare us; they tell us about ourselves, our flaws, our culture, and how to confront our biggest fears.

“Maybe (horror films speak) to the fact that we need some kind of outlet to talk about what we’re afraid of,” said Chan, an assistant arts and film professor.

Chan referenced one scholar, Jeffrey Jerome Cohen, who says that monsters can show people about their culture, what people are afraid of and what their borders are: zombies are metaphors for pandemic and virus fears or something we don’t understand, Frankenstein about unchecked science, and digital and online threats reflect techno-fears.

“The monster itself tells us more about us than it does about the monster,” said Chan.

Her favourite horror film is “The Haunting” from 1963, a black-and-white ghost story about researchers studying the supernatural activity of a haunted mansion.

Between the camera work and the environment, it creates a frightening space, she said.

Earlier in the week, the class watched “Halloween,” the classic 1978 slasher film about the knife-wielding serial killer Michael Myers, to preempt its spooky holiday namesake on Oct. 31.

Horror movies and their supernatural or terrifying elements have become a staple Hollywood tradition for Halloween, which has a storied history drawing from folklore, the ancient Celtic festival Samhain and the Christian festival of All Saints’ Day.

Halloween evening is also believed to be the night that the veil between the living and the dead is thinnest. Pumpkins and costumes have also found their way into the celebration as a way to keep evil spirits at bay.

Every Halloween, Noah Kennedy watches “Scream,” the 1996 slasher movie featuring the iconically masked Ghostface. It sets the tone of the holiday. He first watched it when he was in his early teens.

But, while slashers, monsters and the occult ruled the late 1990s, it’s the psychological and uncanny horrors that toy with the mind that now intrigue 20-year-old Kennedy.

“You turn on a horror movie because you want to get scared, right?”

“It’s the same thing with a lot of films: it’s just feeling those emotions and it feels like really alive.”

Student Shannon Mascarin said she has grown up watching horror movies.

When asked which horror movie was her favourite, she responded, “Which sub-genre?”

She called herself a “latchkey kid,” home alone after school and falling in love with the ghouls.

“Somehow you just fall into those movies. They just find you,” she said.

And, because of that, she’s an avid fan of every Oct. 31.

“I get to wear a costume and I get free candy and all the horror movies are on TV,” she said.

“It’s better than Christmas.”

The blood and guts are a crimson mix of bread, Nutella and jam. She screams and flails on screen. She’s hoping they don’t laugh.
“I hope people felt grossed out and scared,” said the 19-year-old film major.
“I was trying to be dead, you know?”

Gusdal’s group is one of several that submit short films for Julia Chan’s course at the University of Calgary on the horror film genre, a style of film that peaks amid the supernatural spirit of Halloween.
As part of their skit, one group member had their drink spiked, turning them into a flesh-hungry monster with white-glossed eyes. They ravaged the group in a dim, concrete-walled hallway.

Gusdal said someone having their drink spiked at a nightclub began as a way to create the monster. As the project progressed, it held a much deeper meaning about the realistic threat of clubgoers being unknowingly drugged.

stories.title: StatCan to release GDP data for August, early estimate for Q3 today
stories.summary: Ottawa - Statistics Canada is set to release GDP figures for the month of August and its early estimate for September and the third quarter overall this morning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike.

Statistics Canada said Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged for a second straight month in August. That fell short of economists’ calls and the agency’s own early expectations for a gain of 0.2 per cent in the month.

Wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent in August as most subsectors contracted. StatCan said motor vehicle and vehicle parts wholesalers faced their first decline in seven months amid lower vehicle imports and weaker manufacturing activity in the subsector.

Statistics Canada says the economy stalled for a second month in a row in August amid weakness in the public sector and wholesale trade. (Oct. 30, 2026)

StatCan cited a “prolonged summer shutdown at a major auto assembly plant” to explain a 5.8 per cent decline in motor vehicles and parts manufacturing in August.

Tu Nguyen, chief economist at RSM Canada, said what’s notable about the August declines in these sectors is they would only partially capture the impacts of a breakdown in trade talks between Canada and the United States that month.

Both sides have since levied new waves of tariffs and trade restrictions against one another.

Manufacturing and wholesale trade — sectors that are particularly vulnerable to tariff disruptions — will continue to see regular contractions under the re-escalated trade dispute, Nguyen said.

Elsewhere, StatCan said work to prepare the 2026 census was still winding down in August, driving widespread contractions in public administration.

Maintenance work at some nuclear power plants and mining facilities in northern Alberta also dragged on growth that month, StatCan said.

Retail trade, manufacturing as a whole and the transportation and warehousing industries were among those posting gains to offset the declines in August.

StatCan’s early estimates for September suggest real GDP declined 0.1 per cent, driven by losses in manufacturing and mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction.

The agency’s flash estimates still see real GDP expanding 1.3 per cent on an annualized basis in the third quarter, a slowdown from 3.3 per cent growth in the second quarter.

StatCan will provide its official quarterly estimates for the third quarter next month when it reports the September GDP figures.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in a note to clients Friday that some of the weakness last quarter might be overstated, particularly as it relates to census-related slowdowns.

“Still, with the trade tiff still flaring, housing struggling, and recent employment figures concerning, it certainly appears that growth has run into some pretty serious headwinds of late,” he said.

The latest economic data comes two days after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent, the first hike in more than three years.

An increase to the central bank’s key rate will typically take some steam out of the economy, though most analysts still see current monetary policy levels as somewhat stimulative.

Officials at the central bank argued this week that a rate hike was warranted to get ahead of looming inflation risks. Governor Tiff Macklem pointed to signs of resilience in the Canadian economy over the spring in justifying the decision.

The central bank also revised up its expectations for growth on Wednesday. Monetary policymakers are expecting growth in the third quarter ended up at two per cent on an annualized basis, up from 1.5 per cent in its July forecasts.

Many economists weighing in Friday argued the Bank of Canada’s somewhat rosier projections are at risk after StatCan data suggested middling growth in the third quarter.

BMO, which had been in line with the central bank’s call for two per cent growth, trimmed its outlook to 1.5 per cent after Friday’s surprise.

The Bank of Canada is expecting a further slowdown in the fourth quarter will give way to real GDP growth of two per cent in 2027 and 2028.

Nguyen said despite the recent stumbles, there are reasons for optimism in the year ahead. Government spending priorities for a build out of major projects and tax incentives for business investment should give the economy a lift in 2027, she argued.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at Cibc, said in a note that the August data suggested the economy “was already struggling for momentum even before this week’s interest rate hike.”

A slower-than-expected economy could help relieve inflationary pressures and reduce the need for additional rate hikes, he added.

The weak GDP results support a pause from the Bank of Canada at its final rate decision of the year in December, Grantham said, though he noted there’s plenty of additional economic data to come before that meeting.

Financial market odds of an interest rate hike on Dec. 9 stood at 57 per cent as of Friday morning, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

Nguyen said it’s a “coin flip” whether the Bank of Canada hikes in December or its next meeting in January. But given Macklem’s comments this week focused on economic resilience and inflationary fears, she said she leans toward a second quarter-point hike sooner than later.

“A 25-basis-point hike, one month apart, whether in December or in January, I don’t think would change too much in terms of growth trajectory,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Canada-European Union summit in Montreal concludes today with digital trade on agenda
stories.summary: Montreal - A major summit Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting with European Union leaders is set to conclude today with announcements on digital trade and academic exchanges.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Canada and the European Union officially launched an “alliance for the future” on Friday and pledged to spend the next eight months in negotiations on making Canada an associate member — despite objections to that language on both sides of the Atlantic.

“Today we move toward associate membership for Canada and we launch a new alliance for the future,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Friday.

He was speaking at a news conference closing a two-day summit in Montreal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

Canada and the EU have signed agreements to pursue a much closer relationship. Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen describe it as a step on the path to "associate membership" in the EU. (Oct. 30, 2026)

Both jurisdictions released a seven-page joint statement Friday that calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration and cites various current joint projects.

The statement included announcements that officials on both sides of the Atlantic promoted in the days leading up to the Montreal summit.

They include a new digital trade agreement and a deal to allow the European Investment Bank to fund critical raw materials projects in Canada.

Carney said the various agreements signed Friday will make it easier for Canadians to do business with and within the EU.

“Seamless payments will make it easier to sell online in Europe, so a business owner in Manitoba or a lobster harvester in Prince Edward Island will clear customs faster, getting their products to European markets,” Carney said.

“A tech startup in Vancouver will have a smoother path to customers in Berlin. Bottom line, less red tape, more growth, more opportunity.”

Mark Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership, wider alliance against Donald Trump threats. (Oct. 30, 2026)

Carney argued these agreements will help make life more affordable for Canadians.

Carney also announced Canada would join an EU loan program for Ukraine, with Ottawa pledging an initial contribution of 500 million euros, roughly $775 million.

Von der Leyen said the agreements signed Friday will help create “good jobs” and encourage companies to expand.

The joint statement also cites agreements to give Canadian artificial-intelligence researchers access to European supercomputers and to hold more discussions on Arctic and border security.

The statement calls for reforming the World Trade Organization instead of replacing it, and doing more to fight climate change and biodiversity loss.

Carney said he and the other leaders discussed resolving the prospect of Canadian goods being affected by the EU’s anti-deforestation law and its Carbon Border Adjustment Measures, which tariff imports to match European pollution pricing.

A Canadian government official speaking on background said there is more work to do on getting European institutions to recognize what Canada is doing federally and provincially to price emissions. The official said those talks are very advanced.

The agreement also pledges to “explore a next-generation youth mobility partnership” touching on work and academic exchanges.

Von der Leyen said the goal is to have Canada fully join Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program that offers training and study opportunities in member nations.

A Canadian government official said the goal is for Canada to join Erasmus+ midway through 2027. The program is paid for by member states and has a 2021 to 2027 funding pool of about $41 billion.

The official said Canada also wants to become a full member of the Horizon Europe program by 2028. Canada is already a second-tier member of Horizon, which funds research and innovation projects.

Costa said Thursday he wants to see this partnership expand labour mobility between Canada and Europe.

All three leaders discussed the prospect of Canada obtaining “associate member” status in the EU, despite strong pushback from member states, including Germany.

The leaders announced Friday that Carney will next spring join a meeting of von der Leyen’s cabinet — the college of commissioners — and that Costa will host Carney in June at a meeting of the European Council.

Costa said the goal is to announce more details of the partnership at that June meeting.

Culture Minister Marc Miller said Thursday any discussions of labour mobility in industries like film production would need to include the provinces, many of which have their own tax credits that promote local talent.

Miller has been meeting with his European counterparts to discuss setting new regulations on promoting Canadian and European content on streaming services, along with new safeguards for children online.

Culture Minister Marc Miller says he is looking at ways Canada and European partners can find crossover in regulations around online safety for children and the promotion of Canadian and European content on streaming services. Miller is among the Canadian cabinet ministers participating in the Cda-EU Summit in Montreal, where Canada and Europe are preparing to announce a new wide-ranging partnership. (Oct. 30, 2026)

“We’re not talking about the same exact rules potentially, but convergence and allyship with respect to large, transnational companies that in some cases need to be regulated to protect kids or to promote our cultures in the face of overwhelming, monopolistic cultures, one of which is the United States, but others across the world,” Miller said in an interview.

Conservatives have criticized this week’s summit, noting that nine of the 28 countries in the EU have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada known as Ceta. They also want the EU to stop charging a carbon tariff on certain Canadian imports.

“Carney has spent months talking up Canada’s relationship with the European Union. But to date, (he) has failed to eliminate this threat to Canadian businesses, just as he has failed to secure full ratification of Ceta or market access for Canadian pork and beef,” the party said in a news release.

The Bloc Québécois said Carney must fulfil a promise to hold a vote on the new arrangements with the EU.

“This new alliance and this status, about which we know very little, must absolutely be negotiated with Quebec,” the party wrote in French, noting Friday’s announcements touch on provincial jurisdiction.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

stories.title: Money woes, war and Trump — what's motivating U.S. voters ahead of the midterms
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump has been telling supporters to vote like he's on the midterm ballot next Tuesday — but voters are heading to the polls looking for politicians ready to tackle the affordability crisis.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has been telling supporters to vote like he’s on the midterm ballot next Tuesday — but voters are heading to the polls looking for politicians ready to tackle the affordability crisis.

Trump returned to the White House with a massive agenda to realign global trade and a promise to Americans that his tariff policies would reinvigorate domestic manufacturing and reduce the cost of living.

The reality of his second presidency is very different.

Republicans are fighting to hold a slim majority in Congress amid a political backdrop of soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and business uncertainty caused by Trump’s war on Iran and his tariffs.

The biggest issue for voters in nearly every poll is the economy, said Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies.

“People think about the economy all the time,” he said. “It’s one of their most important priorities.”

About eight in 10 registered voters, including a large majority of Republicans and Democrats, believe lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for government, according to a survey by The Associated Press-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research earlier this month.

Seven in 10 want Congress to prioritize ending the war in Iran.

Many of the voters who brought Trump back to Washington to deal with affordability were willing to give the president a grace period on his economic policies, including his plan to hit the world with tariffs.

Halfway through his second term, however, independents, bellwether voters and even some Republicans have lost patience.

Sands said Trump is skilled at getting national attention through his near-nightly rallies and unrelenting posts on social media. That could prove problematic for Republicans facing voter pushback over the president’s inability to deliver a positive message on the cost of living.

Many Republican candidates have been distancing themselves from Trump and his policies, even as the president pushes to make himself the face of the Republican campaign.

An October New York Times/Siena College poll saw Trump’s approval rating sink to 36 per cent. Most respondents gave Trump low numbers on his handling of economic issues.

Trump’s own comments and actions are making it difficult for Republicans to control the message. He has called affordability a “hoax” and insists the United States has entered an economic “golden age.” He boasts about the ballroom and helipad he’s building at the White House while dismissing voters’ concerns about the cost of diesel and gas.

Trump has continued to lob insults at Canada since trade negotiations fell apart in August. He has claimed he holds all the cards in trade talks and that the Canadian government is “willing to give” the U.S. “anything” to secure a deal.

Experts have said that while the tensions between Ottawa and Washington are not necessarily on American voters’ radar nationally, the impacts of the trade war are being felt in key Senate races in Maine and Michigan.

“I think it’s as simple as Trump has had his chance, he’s instituted his policies and we’re not seeing the change at the grocery store register every week,” said Marc Trussler, director of data science for the University of Pennsylvania’s program on opinion research and election studies.

Trussler, who is Canadian, said one of the big shifts in polling since Trump’s 2024 election is over which party voters trust more to handle the economy.

While Republicans were strongly favoured on pocketbook issues before the presidential election, recent polls have seen large shifts toward Democrats, particularly among independents, young people and Hispanic voters.

Trump made historic gains in 2024 with Hispanic and Black male voters and with younger voters. Trussler said polling shows a lot of them are now moving back to Democrats.

Much of that movement is linked to Trump’s handling of the economy — but that’s not the only factor. Voters are also angered by the administration’s controversial handling of immigration and its push for data centres. Some polls also found that preserving democracy is a priority for Americans casting ballots next week.

paragraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump has been telling supporters to vote like he’s on the midterm ballot next Tuesday — but voters are heading to the polls looking for politicians ready to tackle the affordability crisis.

Trump returned to the White House with a massive agenda to realign global trade and a promise to Americans that his tariff policies would reinvigorate domestic manufacturing and reduce the cost of living.
The reality of his second presidency is very different.

Republicans are fighting to hold a slim majority in Congress amid a political backdrop of soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and business uncertainty caused by Trump’s war on Iran and his tariffs.
The biggest issue for voters in nearly every poll is the economy, said Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies.
“People think about the economy all the time,” he said. “It’s one of their most important priorities.”

About eight in 10 registered voters, including a large majority of Republicans and Democrats, believe lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for government, according to a survey by The Associated Press-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research earlier this month.
Seven in 10 want Congress to prioritize ending the war in Iran.

Many of the voters who brought Trump back to Washington to deal with affordability were willing to give the president a grace period on his economic policies, including his plan to hit the world with tariffs.
Halfway through his second term, however, independents, bellwether voters and even some Republicans have lost patience.

Sands said Trump is skilled at getting national attention through his near-nightly rallies and unrelenting posts on social media. That could prove problematic for Republicans facing voter pushback over the president’s inability to deliver a positive message on the cost of living.
Many Republican candidates have been distancing themselves from Trump and his policies, even as the president pushes to make himself the face of the Republican campaign.
An October New York Times/Siena College poll saw Trump’s approval rating sink to 36 per cent. Most respondents gave Trump low numbers on his handling of economic issues.

Trump’s own comments and actions are making it difficult for Republicans to control the message. He has called affordability a “hoax” and insists the United States has entered an economic “golden age.” He boasts about the ballroom and helipad he’s building at the White House while dismissing voters’ concerns about the cost of diesel and gas.

Trump has continued to lob insults at Canada since trade negotiations fell apart in August. He has claimed he holds all the cards in trade talks and that the Canadian government is “willing to give” the U.S. “anything” to secure a deal.

Experts have said that while the tensions between Ottawa and Washington are not necessarily on American voters’ radar nationally, the impacts of the trade war are being felt in key Senate races in Maine and Michigan.

While Republicans were strongly favoured on pocketbook issues before the presidential election, recent polls have seen large shifts toward Democrats, particularly among independents, young people and Hispanic voters.
Trump made historic gains in 2024 with Hispanic and Black male voters and with younger voters. Trussler said polling shows a lot of them are now moving back to Democrats.

Much of that movement is linked to Trump’s handling of the economy — but that’s not the only factor. Voters are also angered by the administration’s controversial handling of immigration and its push for data centres. stories.title: Houston resists calls for legislation as AI data centre backlash grows
stories.summary: Halifax - Julissa Stewart says she panicked when she learned about plans for an 18,600-square-metre AI data centre at an industrial site about 20 minutes away from her home in southern Cape Breton.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Julissa Stewart says she panicked when she learned about plans for an 18,600-square-metre AI data centre at an industrial site about 20 minutes away from her home in southern Cape Breton.

Earlier this month, EverWind Fuels announced it intends to set up a $10-billion AI data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would come online by the end of 2027.

The American AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the centre, which would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase. The company says a 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts.

“I’ve been paying attention to what’s happening with AI data centres in other places in Canada and in the States … then hearing that it’s coming here, so close to where we live, I have serious concerns. Not because I’m against economic development, but because of how this is being rolled out,” Stewart said in a recent interview.

The project by EverWind and Anthropic has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that is playing out across Canada and the United States, as technology companies scramble to find locations for data centres needed to deliver the power for artificial intelligence and other computing infrastructure.

In many cases, it has placed politicians eager for major industrial investments at odds with neighbourhoods filled with suspicion and anxiety about what’s planned in their backyards.

Stewart said she’s been shocked by the speed of EverWind’s plan and lack of consultation with the community.

EverWind’s chief financial officer said Tuesday the company was unable to start community consultation ahead of the Oct. 16 announcement because of a strict non-disclosure agreement with Anthropic. Information sessions hosted by EverWind are scheduled to begin in the Richmond County area next week.

Stewart, who plans to attend, is also skeptical about how Premier Tim Houston appears to have shifted his views about data centres over the past few months.

“The way this has been rolling out has been very upsetting to people,” Stewart said.

On June 18, Houston said it was too soon to turn his government’s attention to the matter, and a discussion about data centres would happen “far out into the future.”

By late September, he softened that stance, opening a door to consider proposals from the sector in a post on social media.

“Then all of a sudden, we’re finding out this is coming to our backyard,” Stewart said.

She said her biggest concern is the lack of environmental assessment for the project and a shortage of regulations. Houston told reporters Wednesday it’s not clear to him if any new legislation is needed.

“Do we want to do a piece of legislation for every business that sets up in Nova Scotia? Probably not. I mean, we’ve got to be realistic about these things. We have guidelines. We have approval processes. And they’ll be followed,” the premier said.

Lora MacEachern, deputy minister of environment and climate change, said Tuesday the data centre doesn’t need to go through an environmental assessment and the industrial approval process is sufficient.

AI data centres are not on the list of projects that would automatically trigger an environmental assessment in Nova Scotia. This list includes quarries, mines, energy generation projects and other industrial facilities.

The premier suggested AI data centres do not need to be on the list.

“We have guidelines that have to be met around water usage … around power rates. The government shouldn’t care what type of company it is, the government should care that the requirements of the province are met, and we’ll make sure that’s the case,” he said.

Stewart said legally binding regulations could help reassure residents about EverWind’s promise to behave responsibly.

“We can’t just rely on a company’s word. It’s not good enough,” Stewart said. “What if this project gets built and it’s not what was advertised?”

Less than two weeks after EverWind’s announcement, a petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org garnered more than 24,000 signatures.

Opposition parties have also called for legislated regulations for AI data centres and for an environmental assessment to be conducted.

NDP Leader Claudia Chender said legally binding regulations are essential given the “long history of large industrial projects in Nova Scotia leaving us with … decades of pollution, huge environmental implications, huge social implications.”

EverWind’s chief financial officer, Matthew Tinari, told a Nova Scotia legislature committee Tuesday that residents deserve clear and factual answers to their questions and the company is committed to addressing concerns.

Tinari said this includes a commitment to prevent rate hikes for residential electricity customers as well as a promise to protect the water supply and minimize water use. He also said the project would follow federal and provincial guidelines for data centres.

“What we’ve heard from community is (that) industry should have binding commitments. So we were proposing to the province some type of agreement like that,” Tinari said.

Houston would not say if his Progressive Conservative government would require a legally binding agreement.

Vaibhav Bahadur, a professor in mechanical engineering at the University of Texas at Austin, specializes in AI data centres in a state that has welcomed massive data centre development. He said “industries don’t like regulations, but in my opinion, you do need to balance what industry wants with environmental concerns and obviously concerns from the general public.”

The University of Texas maintains a database of all data centres in the state. Bahadur says there are about 300 of them running and another 300 or so in various stages of planning or development.

While America is home to far larger data centres than the one EverWind is proposing in Cape Breton, Bahadur said the 95-megawatt facility is significant.

“There’s bound to be concerns when you’re talking about that amount of power going into one facility,” he said in a recent interview.

EverWind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure, which is why the project will not increase power rates for customers.

The company also says the project will include a closed-loop cooling system using recycled water as well as an external cooling system that would require the use of additional water on very hot days.

On average, EverWind estimates the system would use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day from the nearby Landrie Lake in the first phase and an average of 500,000 litres per day when the expansion is complete. Tinari said the peak demand represents 1.5 per cent of the lake’s estimated sustainable daily yield.

Bahadur said based on the location of the planned data centre in Point Tupper, he expects it would use far less water compared to AI data centres in hotter climates, such as Texas.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” says AI companies have learned from the opposition they’ve encountered in the United States over the past couple of years and are trying to head off environmental criticism before it starts.

He said companies are aware of concerns around water use, which is why they’re pivoting from evaporative cooling systems and constant water use in favour of closed-loop systems.

Marx said those closed-loop systems have only seriously been contemplated over the last six to eight months.

“Right now it sounds good because it’s just like, ‘Oh, we’re using less water,’” Marx said in a recent interview.

“But the companies aren’t coming out and being completely transparent about what the trade-offs of that are.”

He said the trade-offs could include the need for using substances such as coolants and the need for more energy to keep the system running.

Bahadur said closed-loop cooling systems have been around for a few years in the United States, and they are a more recent development in Canada. He also agreed that closed-loop systems require more electricity than other cooling options and that there could be broader concerns about pollution, which are not limited to data centres.

The electricity required for a closed-loop system will result in additional water use in Nova Scotia, Bahadur said, because the province still relies on fossil fuels like coal to produce electricity.

“My overall opinion is that under cold climate conditions like in Nova Scotia, water use shouldn’t be much of a concern, especially if the data centre is using state-of-art technologies, and being responsible — which can require regulations in place,” Bahadur said in an email.

Stewart said she’s worried about what May happen to Richmond County’s environment and water supply if the project is not held to high environmental standards that extend into the future.

“I have a six-year-old daughter, and I have concerns about this down the road. If we don’t put proper regulations in place, what is that going to look like for her? … What are the health risks? We don’t have enough information,” she said.

A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries. The report also predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows.

stories.title: ‘I was skin and bones’: London man shares his story on World Stroke Day
stories.summary: Haneef Rasheed suffered from a hemorrhagic stroke caused by a brain AVM, an abnormal tangle of blood vessels.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Spending time with friends and perfecting his jump shot was all Haneef Rasheed worried about at 24 years old.

“My athleticism was a big part of my identity,” said Rasheed. “I was very consumed with basketball.”

That quickly changed.

“All of a sudden I just got this really sharp headache,” said Rasheed. “I didn’t think much of it, I just tried to tough it out and wait for it to go away but it wouldn’t go away.”

Rasheed suffered from a hemorrhagic stroke caused by a brain AVM, an abnormal tangle of blood vessels.

He was given a 30 per cent chance of survival and lost function on the left side of his body.

“I was being fed through a pipe in my stomach and I lost 80 per cent of my muscle,” said Rasheed. “My friends still tell me I was skin and bones.”

Almost ten years later on World Stroke Day, Rasheed is using his story to highlight a key message.

“Stroke and heart disease is not limited to old people,” said Rasheed. “These things can happen to anybody.”

World Stroke Day is observed globally on October 29 to raise awareness on the seriousness of strokes, improve care, and promote prevention.

“About 1.5 million people every year will suffer a stroke below the age of 50,” said Sachin Pandey, Division Head of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology at University Hospital. “So it’s very important to know the signs and symptoms to look out for.”

Pandey said one of the easiest ways to learn the warning signs of a stroke is through the acronym “B.E. F.A.S.T.” created by the World Stroke Organization.

“B” stands for balance loss, “E” for eye or vision changes, “F” for face drooping or twisting, “A” for arm weakness, “S” for speech difficulty, and “T” for time to call 911.

“Any of those symptoms you really should call 911 and get emergency medical care,” said Pandey. “You can lose close to two million brain cells every minute.”

Rasheed said he is grateful to be alive and won’t let anything get in the way of him becoming the person, or athlete he was always meant to be.

stories.title: Sexual assault investigations
stories.summary: London, ON (October 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section have charged a man in relation to two sexual assaults that occurred in the downtown core.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section have charged a man in relation to two sexual assaults that occurred in the downtown core.

On August 17, 2026, a woman was in an alleyway in the 200- block of Dundas Street when she was approached by an acquaintance and sexually assaulted.

In early October, 2026, the suspect male met with the victim again in the 500-block of Richmond Street where he sexually assaulted her.

On Saturday, October 17, 2026, at approximately 12:15 a.m., a woman was outside a business in the 500-block of Dundas Street when she was approached by a man unknown to her.

The two engaged in conversation and walked together toward the 500-block of Queens Avenue.

While in an isolated area on Queens Avenue, the man produced a weapon and sexually assaulted the woman before leaving the area. The victim contacted police and officers searched the area but did not locate the suspect.

A description of the suspect was provided to investigators. With the assistance of video surveillance obtained from businesses in the area, police identified the suspect male.

The suspect was arrested. Investigators determined that he was also responsible for the previous incidents.

As a result of the investigations, Matthew David Coveney, 49, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Two counts of sexual assault;

Sexual assault with a weapon; and

Obtaining sexual services for consideration.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to re-appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims who have not yet come forward. As a result, photographs of the accused are being released.

The London Police Service remains committed to a trauma-informed, victim-centred approach to investigations. We recognize that coming forward to report sexual violence can be difficult, and we are committed to ensuring those affected are treated with dignity, respect and compassion. This is consistent with language used in previous LPS communications seeking additional victims.

If you or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, support is available. Confidential assistance can be accessed at any time. For more information and links to local support agencies, please visit the London Police Service Sexual Assault FAQs

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

content_blocks.text: London, ON (October 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section have charged a man in relation to two sexual assaults that occurred in the downtown core.
content_blocks.html: LONDON, ON (October 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section have charged a man in relation to two sexual assaults that occurred in the downtown core.

content_blocks.text: On August 17, 2026, a woman was in an alleyway in the 200- block of Dundas Street when she was approached by an acquaintance and sexually assaulted.
In early October, 2026, the suspect male met with the victim again in the 500-block of Richmond Street where he sexually assaulted her.
On Saturday, October 17, 2026, at approximately 12:15 a.m., a woman was outside a business in the 500-block of Dundas Street when she was approached by a man unknown to her.
The two engaged in conversation and walked together toward the 500-block of Queens Avenue.

While in an isolated area on Queens Avenue, the man produced a weapon and sexually assaulted the woman before leaving the area. The victim contacted police and officers searched the area but did not locate the suspect.
A description of the suspect was provided to investigators. With the assistance of video surveillance obtained from businesses in the area, police identified the suspect male.
The suspect was arrested. Investigators determined that he was also responsible for the previous incidents.
As a result of the investigations, Matthew David Coveney, 49, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

items: Sexual assault with a weapon; and

content_blocks.text: The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to re-appear in London court today in relation to the charges.
Investigators believe there May be additional victims who have not yet come forward. As a result, photographs of the accused are being released.

The London Police Service remains committed to a trauma-informed, victim-centred approach to investigations. We recognize that coming forward to report sexual violence can be difficult, and we are committed to ensuring those affected are treated with dignity, respect and compassion. This is consistent with language used in previous LPS communications seeking additional victims.

If you or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, support is available. Confidential assistance can be accessed at any time. For more information and links to local support agencies, please visit the London Police Service Sexual Assault FAQs

stories.title: Fanshawe Park Road rehabilitation project moves toward completion
stories.summary: Overnight traffic detours begin November 1 as crews prepare for final pavingAs work progresse
stories.content:
As work progresses on the Fanshawe Park Road Arterial Road Rehabilitation Project , crews will remove the existing top layer of asphalt on Fanshawe Park Road between North Centre Road and Adelaide Street North.

This is one of the final steps before new pavement is installed, with the project expected to wrap up before winter.

Work will take place from 6 p.m. to 7 a.m. Traffic will be detoured in one direction at a time, while traffic travelling in the opposite direction can continue through the area.

Eastbound detour: Sunday, November 1 to Monday, November 2 (two nights).

Westbound detour: Tuesday, November 3 to Wednesday, November 4 (two nights).

During each closure, drivers travelling in the affected direction will be detoured using Adelaide Street, Windermere Road or Sunningdale Road, and Richmond Street. Traffic travelling in the opposite direction can continue through the area.

An additional night May be needed to complete the work.

Milling the existing asphalt can be noisy. Overnight work is necessary to reduce traffic impacts and complete this stage of the project so that the road can be paved before winter weather arrives. Nearby residents are encouraged to keep windows closed during the overnight work, and crews will try to minimize noise and complete the work as quickly as possible.

Sidewalks on both sides of Fanshawe Park Road will generally remain open, although some sections May be temporarily closed and signed detours provided.

Local businesses will remain open during regular hours, with access maintained wherever possible.

Some LTC routes will be affected. Visit the London Transit Commission website for the latest bus schedules and detour information.

Additional traffic detours will be needed for final paving. More details will be shared once those dates are confirmed.

For more information and project updates, visit getinvolved.London.CA/Fanshawe-park-road-rehab .

For more information about construction projects across London, visit Renew London .

stories.title: Winnipeg voters return Gillingham to mayor’s office as challengers struggle to capture public interest
stories.summary: Gillingham acknowledged his slender mandate after winning just under 40 per cent of the vote, according to unofficial results
stories.author: Temur Durrani
stories.content:
Scott Gillingham, a 58-year-old centrist and former Pentecostal pastor with more than a decade’s experience on city council, was re-elected mayor of Winnipeg after being buoyed by a field of competitors who struggled to galvanize public interest.

As municipal elections were held across Manitoba this week, Mr. Gillingham’s victory over his lead challenger, Kevin Klein, owner of the Winnipeg Sun and onetime member of Manitoba’s legislature, signified voters in the provincial capital had embraced his promises of stability.

During his campaign, Mr. Gillingham repeatedly cited his steady partnerships with Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous leaders. And while his lead in pre-election polls dwindled throughout the campaign, the other 11 candidates could not surpass him.

But Mr. Gillingham’s share of the vote Wednesday – just under 40 per cent, according to the city’s unofficial results – is far from the ringing endorsement that incumbents typically enjoy in Winnipeg’s mayoral elections.

In an interview Thursday, he acknowledged his slender mandate from voters, while calling the outcome “major progress” compared with recent elections elsewhere in Canada .

“The polls are always shifting and changing,” Mr. Gillingham told The Globe and Mail. “At the end of the day, I’m humbled that on election night, when the ballots were counted, my support increased by 50 per cent over what it was in 2022.”

Final results in Winnipeg won’t be available until Friday, but early numbers suggest voter turnout was barely higher than the 2022 election, when 37.5 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots, the city said.

In other parts of Manitoba, public apathy manifested at the polls with both lower voting turnouts and uncontested races. Incumbent mayors in hubs such as Portage la Prairie, Steinbach, Selkirk, Niverville and Winkler won automatically because no challengers stepped forward.

In Brandon, the province’s second-largest city , Jeff Fawcett was re-elected mayor after a tight race against his sole competitor, two-term MLA Len Isleifson. By final count, Mr. Fawcett had 5,753 votes, while Mr. Isleifson received 4,845, with 38,300 eligible voters.

Mr. Gillingham called Manitoba’s turnout disappointing, but political observers say it is on par with municipal elections nationwide.

In 2022, Mr. Gillingham was elected with around 27 per cent of the vote. He had twice been previously elected city councillor for St. James, a mostly middle-class residential area that is critical to the local economy because of its proximity to the airport, Winnipeg’s largest mall and other commercial strips.

In this campaign, he received endorsements from across the political spectrum – including the city’s largest union, Cupe Local 500; the Manitoba Métis Federation; and Mark Chipman, chairman of True North Sports + Entertainment , which owns the Winnipeg Jets.

During his first term, Mr. Gillingham was known for practical, collaborative and infrastructure-focused changes. He managed to end a 46-year urban-suburban debate by reopening the city’s iconic intersection of Portage and Main, nicknamed the crossroads of Canada, to foot traffic. And he backed the massive redevelopment of downtown Winnipeg , where multiple landmark properties are undergoing years-long reconstructions.

However, Mr. Gillingham was often criticized for backing off of financial pledges, such as his promise to lower property taxes, along with delays on civic projects, a lack of tangible change on homelessness, and continued high crime rates under his watch.

Although his opponents condemned Mr. Gillingham for those concerns, they did not offer many striking alternatives or new solutions, observed Aaron Moore, a political science professor at the University of Winnipeg.

“It became a very same-same sort of election, with lots of boring ideas from all the leading contenders and not much difference between each of them as personalities or any distinguishable personal brand,” Prof. Moore said.

Both Mr. Klein and funeral director Mike Vogiatzakis, indicated by early polls as a likely third-place finisher, “offered very similar shades of slightly different centre or right-of-centre policies as Scott Gillingham,” Prof. Moore added.

Christopher Adams, an adjunct professor of political science at the University of Manitoba, said the “absence of any real truly progressive or left-leaning mayoral option” likely contributed to the rise of first-time candidate Noah Redden.

In a surprising turn, 27-year-old Mr. Redden, who had a low showing in early polling, placed third in Winnipeg’s mayoral race with 19.8-per-cent support, just behind Mr. Klein’s 20.7 per cent.

Also bucking the city’s historic trend was the downfall of four incumbent councillors, whose position traditionally gives them an advantage.

Prior to election day, five of Winnipeg’s 15 wards had open races, with councillors in those areas choosing not to run again. Now, nine new officeholders are headed to city hall.

Winnipeg city council will also be the closest to gender parity it’s ever been, with eight men and seven women elected.

“There’s clearly an appetite for change in the city,” Prof. Moore said. “I’m not sure Gillingham’s style of politics is cutting it with a sizable contingent of voters any more. And especially with this diverse group coming in as fresh-faced councillors, so many of whom lean further left or right than him, he will certainly need to reflect on that.”

Mr. Gillingham said he looks forward to working with new and returning councillors, and has meetings planned with each of them this week.

But he said he makes no apologies for his centrism. “By nature, inevitably, municipal politicians end up governing from the centre to be pragmatic. We don’t run parties. We’re practical politicians and we just want to get the job done,” he said.

“People haven’t elected me to be radical. They won’t see radical swings from me. That’s not who I am.”

stories.title: Ontario received hundreds of tips, complaints about private career colleges before Osap ban, documents show
stories.summary: Applications for student aid skyrocketed at several GTA career colleges in years leading up to Ontario’s sector-wide ban
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The Ontario government received more than 220 tips and complaints over 2½ years about three private career colleges, some of which alleged that recruiters were filling out financial aid applications and completing online coursework on students’ behalf and using the province’s student aid program as a marketing tool, according to documents filed in court.

As the number of applications for Ontario Student Assistance Plan grants and loans at three Greater Toronto Area campuses of Academy of Learning Career College skyrocketed in recent years, court documents allege thousands of these applications came from a small number of IP addresses, which can reveal an internet user’s approximate location.

Officials in the provincial government’s student financial assistance branch say the usage patterns of the IP addresses point to third parties submitting Osap forms for students, which would be a violation of the program’s rules.

At Academy of Learning’s North York campus, 3,460 Osap applications for 2025-26 – approximately 57 per cent of the total – were submitted from a single IP address. Fifty-two per cent of Osap applications for the Brampton East campus that year came from one IP address, as did 25 per cent of applications for the downtown Toronto location.

The allegations, which are laid out in two Aug. 10 memos confirming the Academy of Learning franchises won’t be eligible for Osap in 2026-27, are the latest revelations in a case that has reverberated across the private career college sector in Ontario.

In early October, Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, announced he was freezing Osap payments to all private postsecondary institutions, blindsiding tens of thousands of students who had been counting on loan disbursements that had already been approved.

Mr. Quinn said the move was necessary to safeguard the integrity of the financial aid program after suspicious activity was flagged at six Greater Toronto Area private career colleges where Osap-funded enrolment in online courses soared in recent years.

In Ontario, postsecondary students can qualify for loans and grants based on financial need, but not if the school they attend is not Osap eligible. To qualify for Osap, students must live in Ontario and be Canadian citizens, permanent residents or protected people such as approved refugees.

In August, the ministry brought in auditor Kpmg to examine the private college sector more broadly. Enough “serious concerns” emerged that the government referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police and decided to implement the sector-wide freeze.

The Academy of Learning franchises in Brampton East, North York and on Bay Street, which are operated by the same group, were among the six GTA schools flagged by the province, all of which were informed in May that they would be cut off from Osap.

The Academy of Learning franchises applied for a judicial review of that decision, kick-starting a legal case that has put details of the allegations against the schools on the public record. (Two locations of Citi College are pursuing a judicial review for similar reasons, but fewer documents have been filed in that case so far.)

The operators of the Academy of Learning franchises have denied wrongdoing. They say they take seriously concerns raised during ministry inspections of their campuses in 2025, and have responded with detailed corrective action plans overseen by a ministry-approved independent compliance monitor.

The new court documents include an Aug. 19 report from the independent compliance monitor, Veronica Bila of accounting firm MNP. The report says Academy of Learning has “implemented the corrective actions committed to” across the three campuses, with one minor exception.

However, MNP struggled to verify the identity of 100 Osap-funded students selected at random from the schools. Forty-four of the students showed international IP activity on Canvas, the schools’ online learning platform, and 50 showed more than 10 IP addresses accessing their Canvas accounts.

The MNP report includes a spreadsheet documenting attempts to reach the 100 students by phone. Only nine completed interviews. Most didn’t answer or hung up.

One note on a student with an IP address in Afghanistan read, “Picked up and constantly beating around the bush, does not understand English well (I feel) did not want to co-operate.”

A note on another with an IP address from Pakistan said, “Picked up, however, said she doesn’t remember much and did not want to answer. Gave me her spouse’s number to call and ask them – tried the number but the number was invalid.”

The new court documents also reveal that the Academy of Learning franchises and the ministry reached a confidential settlement on July 30. Under its terms, the ministry agreed to a fresh review of the schools’ applications for Osap approval for 2026-27, while the schools put their legal case on pause.

Eleven days later, ON Aug. 10, Saba Ferdinands, director of the ministry’s student financial assistance branch, sent two memos to Chamara Perera, chief operating officer of the Academy of Learning franchises, saying their Osap status wouldn’t be renewed.

The memos include line graphs showing mammoth increases in Osap-funded enrolment in a short period. The Bay Street campus went from 1,387 Osap-supported students in 2022-23 to 7,429 in 2024-25 – a 436-per-cent increase in two years. The number of Osap-funded students at the Brampton East campus hit 4,253 in 2024-25, up 455 per cent from 766 students two years earlier. (The North York campus was first approved for Osap in 2024-25.)

The graphs show that Osap-funded enrolment at the schools plummeted the following year.

Academy of Learning did not respond to questions for this story by deadline.

The court documents show the province received more than 200 tips and complaints about the Academy of Learning franchises in recent years.

Mr. Perera, in an Aug. 21 response to the ministry contained in the court filings, said the institutions, “cannot reasonably respond to third party complaints, tips and referrals when the substance of the allegations has not been provided to us.”

None of the allegations have been proven in court.

Mr. Perera also wrote that the large number of Osap applications coming from a few IP addresses could be due to new safeguards that require prospective students to complete in-person interviews and fill out Osap applications at a computer terminal on campus.

However, that explanation wouldn’t account for patterns the ministry detected before those new policies were implemented, the ministry responded in its final rejections of the schools’ applications for Osap status on Sept. 4.

stories.title: Quebec premier’s boycott of Canada-EU summit turns heads
stories.summary: The Canada-EU summit began in Montreal without Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon as his dispute with Ottawa continued to draw attention.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
The Canada-European Union summit got underway in Montreal Thursday without Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, as his decision to stay away continued to draw criticism amid a dispute with Ottawa over Quebec’s role at the international gathering.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was among the high-profile European leaders in Montreal for the two-day summit, delivering remarks in English as meetings began Thursday.

St-Pierre Plamondon chose not to attend after saying he would not accept being reduced to the role of a “spectator” without the opportunity to speak or negotiate on Quebec’s behalf.

Instead, the premier sent Quebec’s chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to represent the province. Paradis defended the premier’s decision Thursday, saying Quebec’s request to speak at the summit was normal and legitimate.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the door remained open for St-Pierre Plamondon to attend.

“If he changes his mind and still wants to come, I’ll be happy to welcome him with open arms,” she said.

The premier had been invited to dinner at the head table alongside von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, but demanded an official opportunity to speak.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Wednesday he would not accept Quebec “falling into line” and being marginalized on the international stage.

“As premier, I will always refuse to see Quebec reduced to the role of spectator when it comes to representing and protecting the economic and political interests of Quebecers,” he wrote.

He also sent a letter to European representatives arguing that the federal government had decided to exclude Quebec from discussions at the summit and questioning whether Quebec would apply any new agreements that are signed.

Former federal foreign affairs adviser Louis Hamann described the dispute as embarrassing for those involved.

“It certainly looks over the last few days that we’ve been living through a bad Halloween horror movie,” Hamann said.

He said the disagreement was putting European officials in the middle of a domestic dispute.

“The Europeans, I mean, imagine being in their shoes. I mean they show up here, they land in Montreal, and they’re essentially walking into a family fight,” he said.

Hamann also warned St-Pierre Plamondon’s letter could have longer-lasting consequences. “That letter was pretty spicy,” he said.

“These words are not going to be forgotten easily. They’re not going to be forgotten in Ottawa, and they’re not gonna be forgotten in Brussels either.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back against the premier’s assertion that Quebec had been excluded, saying there had been four meetings with Quebec officials to discuss the summit.

Carney said he hoped to continue practising what he called co-operative federalism with St-Pierre Plamondon.

“I’ve found that that’s worked in all the other cases, so I’ll continue to practice that and be available to work with Monsieur St-Pierre Plamondon for the interests of Quebec,” Carney said.

Paradis, meanwhile, said he would be at the table to represent Quebec’s interests in discussions with the federal government and European Union.

The premier had previously said he wrote directly to EU representatives to argue that agreements involving Europe and Quebec must go through the Quebec government, particularly when a summit is being held in the province.

He also invited European representatives to hold a bilateral discussion “in a better context” that would allow Quebec to participate rather than be excluded.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard has criticized the premier for staying away, arguing a letter to European representatives is no substitute for attending the summit.

“A letter does not replace a presence at the table,” Milliard said Wednesday. “The prime minister says he wants to meet with European leaders, but refuses to take part in the Canada-EU summit being held on our soil.”

Milliard accused St-Pierre Plamondon of passing up an opportunity to defend Quebec’s interests.

“Diplomacy requires building relationships and seizing opportunities to defend our interests. Not sulking because we don’t have a microphone,” he said. “Our partners will be at the table. The premier of Quebec, for his part, will leave his chair empty.”

Milliard added: “I’ll say it again: being absent means being the loser. What a lack of leadership.”

Hamann also questioned what the dispute could mean for St-Pierre Plamondon’s relationship with the federal government in the weeks and months ahead.

“If he is to react that way, in this case, imagine how he’ll react with all the other things that are coming down the pike,” he said.

The Canada-EU summit continues Friday.

Milliard accused St-Pierre Plamondon of passing up an opportunity to defend Quebec’s interests.

“Diplomacy requires building relationships and seizing opportunities to defend our interests. Not sulking because we don’t have a microphone,” he said. “Our partners will be at the table. The premier of Quebec, for his part, will leave his chair empty.”

“If he is to react that way, in this case, imagine how he’ll react with all the other things that are coming down the pike,” he said.

stories.title: Elderly man sentenced after being found guilty of assaulting Muslim women
stories.summary: In June, 81-year-old James Henkel was found guilty of six charges including, assault with a weapon, assault and mischief.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
In June, 81-year-old James Henkel was found guilty of six charges including, assault with a weapon, assault and mischief.

The court heard that in September 2024, Henkel attacked Muslim women in the area of Berkshire Drive in south London.

Through the victim impact statements, one woman said she and her young child were fearful and she still asks her, “Is the man who hit you put away?”

The woman who says she’s been in Canada for 26 years described herself as a Muslim and Palestinian, and said Henkel yelled at her, “To hear someone say got back to Gaza and die there…that has changed me and I don’t feel comfortable in our neighbourhood anymore.”

The court has heard Henkel brandished a knife. “I can’t take away what my children saw,” the woman said.

The court heard he also grabbed her cellphone and threw it away.

Henkel’s lawyer Edward Berlew said Henkel had suffered a stroke and his family has said that’s when his personality changed. Berlew also said that he has no prior criminal record.

Crown Attorney Jeremy Carnegie said, “This is a hate motivated offence…members of the targeted group were lead to be fearful.”

Carnegie added that if Henkel was younger he would be requesting real jail time.

The court heard that Henkel has moved out of London and now resides in Kitchener with his wife and daughter.

Justice Thomas Stinson sentenced Henkel to 180 days of house arrest with conditions, two years probation along with a ten year ban prohibiting him from possessing weapons.

He is also not allowed to contact the victims in this case.

stories.title: Sentencing hearing for man convicted of manslaughter in fatal stabbing of teen
stories.summary: Treyton Hoffman, 20, of London was found guilty of manslaughter in the fall of 2025 in connection with the killing of 16-year-old Malik McDonell-Mills.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Treyton Hoffman, 20, of London was found guilty of manslaughter in the fall of 2025 in connection with the killing of 16-year-old Malik McDonnell-Mills.

A jury found that Hoffman played a key role in luring the London teen to a spot in the Glen Cairn area in southeast London in August 2023.

Once there, two others would get involved and McDonell-Mills would be stabbed to death.

After several delays, the sentencing hearing for Hoffman was held before Justice Patricia Moore on Thursday at the London Courthouse.

Crown Attorney Shane Wright requested that he receive a 7 year sentence, “He (Hoffman) did have a significant role... he’s the one who orchestrated it and made the ambush possible.”

During his submissions, defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi asked for a conditional sentence or a sentence of time already served, “He (Hoffman) set something up but he didn’t intend death to happen.”

When Hoffman addressed the court he gave a lengthy apology and in part said that he has changed his life, “My whole life it seems I have struggled with mental health. I know I can do better than this and I know I can make better choices in my life.”

The other two who were involved in the stabbing death have both plead guilty to manslaughter under the Young Offenders Act.

Hoffman will learn his fate when Justice Moore hands down her decision on Dec. 2.

stories.title: Summerland landslides raise concerns after wildfire leaves slopes vulnerable
stories.summary: The slides were triggered by heavy rain on Tuesday, with debris spilling into a field on the family’s property.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Three landslides in Summerland’s Garnet Valley sent rocks, water and debris onto property belonging to the Campbell family this week, highlighting the ongoing risks posed by slopes burned in this summer’s Bald Range wildfire.

The slides were triggered by heavy rain on Tuesday, with debris spilling into a field on the family’s property.

“It was a wall of rocks and water coming down into the field there,” said Marty Campbell of Campbell Creek Farm.

The family says the incident is a reminder that the danger did not end when the wildfire was contained.

The Bald Range fire burned vegetation from surrounding slopes, leaving the ground more vulnerable to erosion and increasing concerns about landslides during periods of heavy rainfall.

For Shawn Campbell, the possibility of another slide is a major concern.

“If that mountain behind us gives out and slides right into our houses, that would probably be our biggest fear right now,” he said.

The Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen (Rdos) is monitoring the potential impacts of heavy rainfall, while geotechnical assessments are underway in affected areas.

Erick Thompson, an information officer with the Rdos Emergency Operations Centre, said the regional district is working directly with residents who could be affected.

“The Rdos is certainly looking at the potential for impacts to property because of heavy rainfall events,” Thompson said.

“Sand and sandbags are also being made available directly to residents,” he added.

The landslides come as the B.C. Ministry of Forests releases a report outlining elevated hazards following this summer’s wildfire season.

The report indicates that the likelihood of additional slides varies depending on the terrain, with risks ranked from low to high.

Highway 97 is also identified as an area of concern. The report rates the probability of spatial impact to the highway and private properties on slopes above it as high.

The Ministry of Transportation directed Global News to the Ministry of Forests for comment. With a new provincial government not yet sworn in, communications remain limited while the government operates in caretaker mode.

The risks are not limited to Summerland.

The Central Okanagan Regional District has also warned of elevated hazards associated with the Quilchena fire south of La Casa, including concerns around the Westside Road area.

For residents who endured this summer’s wildfire season, the possibility of landslides and flooding adds another layer of uncertainty.

At Campbell Creek Farm, the fire had burned right up to the family’s doorstep. They stayed to defend their property and managed to save their livestock.

Now, after making it through the wildfire, they are facing another threat.

“The fire burned right to our doorstep. We were able to stay and fight it and save all our cattle and our horses and the chicken, and we thought we were through it,” Shawn Campbell said.

“And now it’s flood watch.”

For the Campbell family, Tuesday’s landslides are a stark reminder that the consequences of a wildfire can continue long after the flames are gone.

stories.title: Loss of Canadian shoppers a $64M hit to Washington State: report
stories.summary: Canadian shopping visits have dropped 71 per cent compared to 2019 — largely driven by the strained political and economic climate between the two countries and a weak Loonie.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Taya Fast
stories.content:
Businesses just over the U.S. border in Whatcom County say the loss of Canadian shoppers continues to hit them hard.

“There’s been a little bit of ups and downs, but right now we’re actually at a little bit more than 20 per cent of a loss of business,” Echo Mae, owner of the Northwest Yarns in Bellingham , told Global News.

“And yeah, that’s directly attributable to Canadians not coming down here.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "And yeah, that's directly attributable to Canadians not coming down here."

The loss of business has meant difficult decisions, including cutting staff hours and shifting away from luxury products.

“A lasting impact, and if this continues, would be that we’d have to shut down the business, and we desperately don’t want to do that,” Mae said.

The drop in business is not unique to Northwest Yarns.

A new report from Western Washington University estimates Whatcom County lost around U.S. $64 million in Canadian spending between 2024 and 2025.

In early 2025, the Donald Trump administration began levying steep trade tariffs against Canada and made threats of taking over the nation — prompting a backlash that included scaling back cross-border travel and spending on American goods.

“The main takeaway from some of our research has been that Canadians who are still crossing the border are doing so less for economic reasons like shopping and purchasing gas, and more to visit family or friends or to recreate,” said Laurie Trautman, the director of the Border Policy Research Institute at the university.

The report shows Canadian shopping visits have dropped 71 per cent compared to 2019 — largely driven by the strained political and economic climate between the two countries and a weak Canadian dollar.

“Business were no longer treating this lack of Canadian visitors as a temporary situation that they sort of had to wait out,” Trautman said.

“They see this as a more medium to potentially longer-term scenario.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "They see this as a more medium to potentially longer-term scenario."

While the loss of Canadian shoppers is significant, the Bellingham Regional Chamber of Commerce says the relationship between Canada and the U.S. goes far beyond retail.

“We’re here and ready to welcome all of you back when you’re ready to be back,” president and CEO Guy Occhiogrosso said.

Mae said that the familiar Canadian shoppers can’t come back soon enough.

“Oh gosh, we miss them so much,” she said. “We miss all of you so much.”

content_blocks.text: The loss of business has meant difficult decisions, including cutting staff hours and shifting away from luxury products.
“A lasting impact, and if this continues, would be that we’d have to shut down the business, and we desperately don’t want to do that,” Mae said.
The drop in business is not unique to Northwest Yarns.
A new report from Western Washington University estimates Whatcom County lost around U.S. $64 million in Canadian spending between 2024 and 2025.

content_blocks.text: In early 2025, the Donald Trump administration began levying steep trade tariffs against Canada and made threats of taking over the nation — prompting a backlash that included scaling back cross-border travel and spending on American goods.

“The main takeaway from some of our research has been that Canadians who are still crossing the border are doing so less for economic reasons like shopping and purchasing gas, and more to visit family or friends or to recreate,” said Laurie Trautman, the director of the Border Policy Research Institute at the university.

The report shows Canadian shopping visits have dropped 71 per cent compared to 2019 — largely driven by the strained political and economic climate between the two countries and a weak Canadian dollar.
