stories.title: Alberta’s Smith faces political test as UCP debate land acknowledgements, transgender policies
stories.summary: Alberta's United Conservative Party is set to debate dozens of policy resolutions as members decide whether Danielle Smith will lead them into next year's provincial election.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Calgary — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith could face another political test as United Conservative Party members prepare to debate dozens of policy resolutions, including proposals to end Indigenous land acknowledgements and restrict transgender access to washrooms and change rooms.

Lori Williams, a political science professor at Mount Royal University, said the resolutions could create challenges for Smith as she tries to respond to grassroot demands while maintaining support among more moderate Albertans ahead of next year’s provincial election.

“If that gap continues to grow, it May be a more difficult thing for the UCP to retain the support of those moderate or more centrist Albertans,” Williams said.

The party’s annual general meeting, scheduled to take place between Nov. 27 to 29 in Calgary, comes on the heels of Alberta’s divisive provincial referendums and controversial legislation targeting diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices in public-sector hiring.

Among the 39 proposed resolutions is a call to end land acknowledgements at government and publicly funded institutions, describing the practice as performative and humiliating.

First Nations advocate Nicole Johnston is pushing back against the proposal.

“To try and use the justification that a land acknowledgment May make Albertans feel like outsiders – that in itself is speaking and pushing to spew more racism,” Johnston said.

“I don’t believe it’s up to the UCP or Danielle Smith to even be commenting or trying to consult or discuss or have discussions about this at all, if this was something that was already here before Alberta became a province.”

Other proposals would restrict access to women’s washrooms and change rooms based on biological sex and amend Alberta’s Human Rights Act to recognize biological sex as a separate protected ground.

Members will also debate voluntary union membership, federal net-zero emissions mandates, carbon policies and challenges to federal land claims.

The resolutions are not government policy, but UCP MLA Dan Williams said the party welcomes input from its members.

“It’s an important part of the process, and in the end, I have to represent the interest, the province of Alberta and the constituents that elected me,” Williams said.

In a statement to CTV News, Smith’s press secretary Ryan Fournier described the UCP as a grassroots party that encourages debate and differing perspectives.

“For successful resolutions, our caucus and cabinet will take those back for discussion and determine how we proceed,” the statement said.

Former UCP cabinet minister Leela Aheer said the convention provides an important opportunity for grassroots members to express their views, even when the issues are controversial.

However, she questioned whether some of the debates are distracting from more immediate concerns.

“I think there’s other priorities of housing and affordability and many other things that the average Albertan is really contending with these days,” Aheer said.

“I just find that some of the stuff can be very distracting from the very, very real issues that the average Albertan is facing every day.”

Williams said the convention could reveal whether moderate conservatives or members further to the right have greater influence within the UCP.

She noted that socially conservative members have historically been more motivated to participate in party conventions, while moderate members have not always attended in comparable numbers.

“The question is whether the more moderate dimension of the party is going to moderate some of those proposals or whether they’re going to pass,” Williams said.

Williams said the resolutions could put additional pressure on Smith.

“They don’t control what the premier or the government does. But to completely ignore them, of course, would have political consequences for the premier and her party,” she said.

While approved resolutions aren’t binding on the government, several from previous conventions have eventually influenced provincial legislation.

With files from CTV News Calgary’s Mark Villani

stories.title: Quebec Premier skips Canada-EU summit in Montreal over Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak
stories.summary: The move is the first in what promises to be a combative relationship with the federal government
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Maura Forrest
stories.content:
By refusing to attend a Canada-European Union summit and declaring that his province was being turned into a “vassal,” Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has fired an opening salvo in what promises to be a combative relationship with the federal government.

The Premier’s comments marked a new tone of conflict between Quebec and Ottawa weeks after the election of the separatist Parti Québécois, which is seeking to abolish the monarchy in the province and hold a referendum on independence.

After days of back-and-forth between the Premier and Prime Minister Mark Carney, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon refused to attend the Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Thursday in protest of Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at the event.

The federal government denied the province’s request to have its leader deliver a speech and hold its own reception, instead offering a seat at the head table for the opening supper and a role greeting visiting dignitaries at the airport.

“The federal government would have us believe that the Premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon in a social-media post on Tuesday.

The PQ government, which has promised to hold a referendum on Quebec independence, was elected with a minority of seats and just 28 per cent of the popular vote on Oct. 5. Though Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said he will not organize a vote on secession before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029, he has already taken steps to demonstrate his continued commitment to sovereignty, including by naming a minister responsible for independence to his cabinet.

This week, the Premier called the federal government’s perceived snub a rupture with the Gérin-Lajoie Doctrine, a policy in which Quebec conducts its own foreign policy on matters touching its areas of jurisdiction, such as education and culture.

Announcing his decision to pull out of the summit on Wednesday, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said on social media that the invitation to sit at the head table was an effective request for Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party.”

Mr. Carney said earlier this week that it was the Premier’s decision to leave an “empty chair.”

“He was invited to the dinner and he refused,” the Prime Minister said.

Asked about the prospect of a more challenging relationship with Quebec under a PQ government, Mr. Carney said Thursday that he would continue to practise “co-operative federalism” with the provinces.

“That means working together on the priorities of Canadians,” he told reporters at a news conference in Montreal. “I’ll continue to practise that and be available to work with Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon for the interests of Quebeckers.”

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard criticized the Premier’s absence from the summit and the provincial government’s choice of replacement, newly appointed chief diplomat and former PQ deputy Pascal Paradis. Sending someone unelected to represent Quebec is insufficient, Mr. Milliard told reporters Thursday.

Every opposition party agreed that Quebec should have been allowed to speak at the summit, however. Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said Ottawa’s refusal constituted “toxic federalism.”

Even Quebec Liberal luminaries such as former deputy premier Nathalie Normandeau and the party’s former parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy called Mr. Carney’s decision “a serious mistake” and an “enormous lack of respect,” respectively, this week.

There are precedents for inviting Quebec premiers to speak at international events held in Quebec, said the public policy scholar Stéphane Paquin, such as the UN biodiversity conference in 2022.

Many of the subjects likely to be discussed between Canada and the EU this week fall under provincial jurisdiction, such as the Erasmus+ program and critical minerals, said Prof. Paquin. Quebec could still refuse to implement aspects of any treaty touching on its constitutional powers, he added.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon seemed to threaten as much this week when he alluded to the “risks” involved in negotiating an international agreement without Quebec’s participation.

“Politically, it would have been easier to let him speak,” Prof. Paquin said.

The Quebec Premier gave another indication of his posture toward the federal government earlier this week, when he chose not to attend a first ministers’ meeting with First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay, Quebec’s Minister for First Nations and Inuit Relations, said in a social-media statement that the Quebec government meets Indigenous nations “on a nation-to-nation” basis and “not at a table organized by Ottawa.”

Sophie Villeneuve, a political analyst and former Parti Québécois staffer, said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon is setting the tone for future discussions with the federal government.

“Few premiers in the last 20 years have taken such a firm and clear position,” she said.

“Paul St-Pierre Plamondon intends to speak out more forcefully and to do so in a different way. We’ll see what kind of results that yields.”

stories.title: Three members of family shot, another injured in Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: Toronto police say masked attackers entered the home around 3 a.m. and demanded ‘nice things’ in latest violent robbery in the city
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
An attack that police said began as a random home invasion in Toronto’s exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood left three family members with gunshot wounds and another with injuries from a hammer.

Toronto police said that shortly after 3 a.m. on Thursday, three masked gunmen stormed into the Hyde Park Circle house through its back entrance while a family of four were inside.

A confrontation erupted in the house as the assailants demanded the family give them money or other valuables.

Police told reporters near the scene Thursday morning the assailants fired their weapons and shot three family members. Each suspect was armed with a handgun, and one also had a hammer.

“There was a demand made for valuables within the home,” Toronto Police Inspector Kristy Smith of the Hold Up Squad told reporters. “The suspects fired their guns, multiple times, and one victim was struck with a hammer. Three members of the family, the father and his two daughters, sustained gunshot wounds.”

The family members are all adults. Two remain in hospital. Police said they do not know what the attackers took and are hoping to recover bullet casings that May help identify the suspects.

Police said they will not publicly identify the victims, two of whom are now said to have “life-altering” injuries.

The Bridle Path is one of Canada’s richest neighbourhoods, where large houses are often hidden behind high walls and wrought-iron gates, and flanked by vehicles belonging to private security companies. Security cameras are almost everywhere. Home invasions in the neighbourhood remain rare.

Authorities said they suspect the motive in the current attack was simply greed. “Typically, in an affluent neighbourhood comes nice things – and there’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things,” Insp. Smith said.

“We can’t go around always being paranoid about having nice things,” she said. “But I would suggest that people be ultra aware if they are being followed and potentially, if they feel like they are being followed, calling 911. ”

Shootings and homicides have dramatically declined in Toronto in 2025 and 2026. But police say one crime category is increasing: The city has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year.

“Across the city we have seen the rise of carjackings decline and the home invasions increase,” Insp. Smith said.

Police have yet to identify any of the suspects in the Bridle Path attack. Insp. Smith said she had no information indicating the family was targeted for any reason other than that they live in one of Canada’s wealthiest neighbourhoods.

The Decibel: Is it legal to defend yourself if someone breaks into your home?

Earlier this year, The Globe and Mail reported that a rash of break-ins and home invasions are affecting another wealthy Toronto neighbourhood – Rosedale, where the rates for these crimes more than doubled between 2015 and 2025.

In that neighbourhood and others, residents have been hiring more security to meet an evolving threat where masked men show up at front entrances in the early morning, bodychecking doors until they give way, or smashing windows in their searches for jewellery and keys to luxury automobiles.

Thieves are also mounting battery-powered trail cameras to remotely monitor homeowners’ comings and goings, police have warned some residents.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow released a statement condemning the latest attack.

“I am deeply troubled by the violent home invasion early this morning in the Bridle Path neighbourhood,” she said.

“This attack has understandably shaken the neighbourhood and many residents across Toronto. This violence is not acceptable in our city. People must be safe in their own homes.”

With reports from Stephanie Chambers, Patrick White and Tavia Grant

stories.title: London man involved in racially charged verbal altercation will not face charges
stories.summary: London Police say a man involved in a verbal altercation with a group of women on the Western University campus will not face charges.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London Police say a man involved in a verbal altercation with a group of women on the Western University campus will not face charges.

Much of the incident was caught on cell phone video. And while racist language can be heard, police say it does not constitute a crime, but rather a hate-incident.

“Hate crime is defined as a crime in the Criminal Code of Canada. It’s a criminal offense. A hate motivated incident is an incident that does not meet the definition of a crime,” explained LPS Acting Insp. Michelle Romano.

In an interview with CTV News Wednesday, the man identified himself only as Tom, and referred to himself a nationalist.

In both the interview and the video-taped altercation, Tom invokes Christianity. That’s something that long time social justice advocate Dean Kevin George of St. Paul’s Anglican Cathedral takes issue with.

“I find it quite offensive when people invoke the name of Christianity to support or prop up their own hatred. The fact is, when people commit to become a Christian, across a whole variety of denominations, the basic promises we make are to seek and serve God and all persons, and love our neighbour as ourselves,” said Dean George

According to the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, the nationalist movement in Canada is the largest it has ever been, and it poses a growing threat to public safety.

“The largest white nationalist group has a political agenda. It is trying to influence politics (…) in order to achieve their main goal, which is racist mass deportations,” said Evan Balgord, executive director of Cahn.

According to the London Police Service, there were 70 hate/bias motivated crimes in 2025, with a total of 53 charges in 24 of these occurrences. There were 98 reported hate/bias motivated incidents

She added that there’s no tolerance for hate crime in London. LPS recently increased its Hate Crime Unit to three full-time investigators, and one outreach officer. It also launched an online hate-crime platform .

stories.title: Fire Marshal’s office investigating cause of Owen Sound house fire
stories.summary: The Fire Marshal’s office has been called in to determine what sparked a house fire in Owen Sound on Wednesday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The Fire Marshal’s office has been called in to determine what sparked a house fire in Owen Sound on Wednesday.

Owen Sound fire crews were called to a home on 3 rd Avenue, around 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday.

No one was home at the time of the fire, which officials believe May have started in the basement.

No one was injured. The home had been turned into apartments, leaving several people without a place to live.

Damage estimates put losses from the fire at more than $100,000.

stories.content:
Toronto - Lawyers representing Elections Ontario told an Ontario Human Rights Tribunal hearing on Thursday that the agency seeks to accommodate all voters with disabilities the best it can, but those accommodations must ensure votes are secure and secret.

The tribunal is hearing final submissions in the complaint accessibility advocate David Lepofsky filed more than seven years ago, following an incident during the 2018 Ontario election.

He has said he tried to vote using Elections Ontario’s accessible voting machine but his ballot fell to the floor as it was coming out of the terminal and a poll worker told him that he inadvertently saw who he voted for.

At the time, Lepofsky also said that a voting affirmation document was not available to him in braille.

Lepofsky argued that Elections Ontario has also failed to ensure he can mark and cast his ballot independently and privately in other elections.

Lawyer Yael Bienenstock, who is representing Elections Ontario, said the agency wants all voters to be able to mark their ballots independently and verify their choice, and noted there are 175 accessible voting machines that people who are blind can use to do so.

“Lepofsky admitted that with AVT, he is able to mark his ballot on his own. He didn’t have to ask anyone else to mark it for him. He has used it to verify his choice before the ballot is printed. And he’s used it to verify his choice after the ballot was printed,” she told the tribunal hearing on Thursday.

“Offering AVT isn’t something that comes with no hardship for Elections Ontario. The evidence is it costs $3,500 to $5,000 per unit.”

Lepofsky argued Elections Ontario did not take sufficient action to ensure accessible voting, including before and after the incident in 2018, and that constitutes a continuing human rights violation.

He said in his closing argument on Thursday that he is seeking an effective, consistent and reliable method for blind people to vote.

Lepofsky said accessible voting machines were available in 159 voting locations while more than 7,000 other locations in Ontario had none.

He asked the tribunal to order Elections Ontario to come up with a plan to do a proper review of accessibility measures, and appoint an official monitor to oversee that process.

“We’ve heard, ‘stay inside the box and don’t change things because that might be a fundamental transformation’ or whatever the label was ... It’s this bureaucratic rigidity in a situation where they needed creativity,” he said.

“I was told they would come up with an action plan with timetables. They still haven’t.”

Lepofsky told the tribunal earlier this month that he has advocated for the rights of blind people for decades and he wants to ensure accessible voting for them.

Elections Ontario says on its website that it’s committed to preventing and removing barriers “so that persons with disabilities can fully participate in the electoral process.”

It says assistive voting technology allows voters to listen to their ballot choices and cast their ballot “secretly and independently,” and that options such as voting by mail or by home visit are also available.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Man gets more than 16 years in prison for Islamic State knife attack on B.C. bus
stories.summary: NEW Westminster - A man has been sentenced to more than 16 years in prison for slashing a bus passenger's throat in Surrey, B.C., in what prosecutors say was a terrorist attack in 2023.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
NEW Westminster - A man has been sentenced to more than 16 years in prison for slashing a bus passenger’s throat in Surrey, B.C., in 2023, in what prosecutors say was a terrorist attack.

The federal prosecution service said in a statement that Abdul Aziz Kawam was sentenced in British Columbia Supreme Court on Thursday to 15 years for attempted murder, as well as 20 months for aggravated assault.

stories.title: Driver charged in Seaforth area crash from March
stories.summary: A crash that injured six people, including three children, has landed a Cambridge driver in hot water.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A crash that injured six people, including three children, has landed a Cambridge driver in hot water.

The crash between two black Suv’s happened on March 19, 2026, at the intersection of Summerhill Road and North Line, between Seaforth and Winthrop.

Six people were injured in the crash. Three adults, and three children, said police.

Injuries ranged from minor, to life-threatening.

A driver of one of the Suv’s has now been charged with four counts of Dangerous Operation of a Vehicle Causing Causing Bodily Harm.

The 56 year old from Cambridge, has been charged and released, facing their next court date in mid-November.

stories.title: Meet the new faces elected to Winnipeg city council
stories.summary: After Wednesday's election, nine new representatives are expected at Winnipeg City Hall.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Winnipeg City Hall will see several fresh faces when the new council assembles , with more than half of the ward representatives taking their first seat in the chambers.

The incumbents for the Winnipeg wards of Old Kildonan, St. James, Transcona and Mynarski were defeated in the civic election Wednesday. The former city councillors in Fort Rouge-East Fort Garry, River Heights-Fort Garry, St. Norbert-Seine River, St. Vital and Waverley West did not seek re-election.

Winnipeg’s nine newly elected city councillors will be led by Mayor Scott Gillingham, who was re-elected Wednesday. The following day, Gillingham said part of his mayoral duties will involve helping the newly elected officials adjust.

He added that he plans to meet the 15 members who will form the newly elected city council to determine priorities and build a cohesive plan.

“I remember getting elected in 2014 as a city councillor. It was like drinking from a firehose,” Gillingham said, recalling the influx of information he received at that time.

Greg McFarlane unseated incumbent Devi Sharma with 56 per cent of the vote in Old Kildonan. Sharma received 36 per cent of the vote. Prior to the election, McFarlane said many residents told him that they felt it was time for change.

“I said, ‘You know what? It’s time.’ And I dropped everything – I quit my job, signed up, knocked on doors,” McFarlane said, adding that he was working as a school trustee and electrician at that time.

“I had key conversations with leaders in the community and listened to what they had to say. And we all came together and we sent a message.”

Shawn Dobson, the incumbent for the Western ward of St. James, finished in last place of the three candidates running. He was ousted by Kelly Ryback, who has lived in the ward for longer than 30 years, and received 43 per cent of votes.

“There’s going to be a lot of work to do, but a lot of learning,” Ryback told Global News. He said part of that learning will involve determining what is in the city’s scope and what is in the hands of the provincial or federal governments.

Before retiring, Ryback said he was “always busy” between work, family and being one of the Winnipeg Blue Bombers’ mascots, Buzz.

The seasoned incumbent for Transcona, Russ Wyatt, was defeated by Lora Meseman. Facing allegations of sexual assault , Wyatt finished second-to-last out of the five councillors running. Meseman secured 31 per cent of the vote .

Natalie Smith defeated the long-serving city councillor for Mynarski, Ross Eadie. It was a nail-biter race, ending with Smith receiving 31 per cent of support while Eadie, who was the city councillor for 16 years, received 29 per cent.

Jeff Palmer was elected to represent the Fort Rouge-East Fort Garry ward. Sherri Rollins served as the area councillor for two terms and opted not to seek re-election this year.

Sara MacArthur will replace John Orlikow, who did not run. MacArthur will sit at city hall for the River Heights-Fort Garry constituency, where she has lived her entire life. She said she has been thinking of running in this race for decades.

“I thought after 17 years of the same city councillor that I could use the skills and this passion for my neighbourhood and be an effective voice,” MacArthur said, noting that Wednesday marked “an election of change.”

St. Norbert-Seine River will have Ray Dubois at the helm. The incumbent councillor, Markus Chambers, was not on the ballot after he said he decided to step away and spend more time with his family.

Chris Sigurdson will represent St. Vital after the new batch of councillors are sworn in. Bryan Mayes, the incumbent, did not run for city council. Instead, Mayes ran, and won, to represent ward 2 in the Louis Riel School Division Wednesday.

After a 12-year stint as a city councillor, Janice Lukes did not run in 2026. The ward she represented, Waverley West, will be in the hands of Jasmine Brar. Speaking with Global News, Brar said that she is still soaking in the news – but excited to get to work.

“It was quite the fight,” Brar said. “Waverley West has spoken. They needed a change. So, the change came. When fresh ideas come to the table and fresh faces come to the table, we do wonders.”

Curtis Brown, the vice president and managing director for Western Canada at Abacus Data, said the newly elected councillors are a manifestation of Winnipeg voters’ displeasure with its last city council, in a conversation with 680 Cjob Wednesday.

“People are not happy with the direction of the city, and they’re looking for people to tackle these big issues that we see,” he said, pointing to crime, homelessness and poor city services as examples of those challenges.

“I think Winnipeg really sent a pretty clear message, even though they didn’t change the person at the top of the council table, they really voted in change in a big way.”

stories.title: Military overstocked on training ammo, left 'gaps' in combat munitions, audit says
stories.summary: Only about half of the ammunition the military acquired for training and exercises was actually put to use, a federal audit examining National Defence’s ammunition stocks has found.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Only about half of the ammunition the military acquired for training and exercises was actually put to use, a federal audit examining National Defence’s ammunition stocks has found.

The audit , released Thursday, also said the military’s strategic stockpile — the reserve it maintains for emergencies and combat — suffers from “significant gaps” between required and actual inventory levels that will take years to fix.

Only 56 per cent of its “regular use” ammunition for training and deployments was used over the past three years, likely because of “overstated” requests for ammo and the cancellation of planned activities like training exercises, the audit said.

National Defence failed to track the reasons for those “limited or cancelled activities,” although it indicated in an analysis in March that key equipment, such as tanks and ships, were “often out of service” when needed.

“Sometimes it’s because of equipment not being available. Other times it’s because of weather conditions. There’s a myriad of reasons why something would get cancelled. What we saw is that they weren’t tracking why,” Auditor General Karen Hogan told a Thursday news conference.

The department also does not centrally track its expenses for ammunition, preventing it from providing detailed dollar amounts broken down across types and groups.

Some of its excess ammunition inventory can still be used in an emergency, Hogan noted, but not all of the military’s training ammunition is lethal.

“They have some weaknesses in the reliability of their information around inventory — not just quantities, but even knowing expiry dates and being able to manage that all well,” Hogan said. “And this is something that my office has flagged for over two decades now when it comes to our financial audits.”

The report said that as of March this year, National Defence “determined that the Canadian Armed Forces’ readiness level to meet North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) commitments was well below target.”

Ammunition was one of the factors contributing to those shortfalls, the report added, singling out the strategic munitions stockpile.

When it comes to procurement, the audit examined 15 contracts and found delivery took an average of almost 19 months after signing with a supplier. Most of the material procured through those contracts was delivered late.

In a media statement, federal Conservative MPs James Bezan, Jeff Kibble and Pierre Paul-Hus said Thursday’s report “confirms a serious lack of action” by the Liberal government on ensuring the military is ready to fight.

“This cannot be allowed to continue,” the statement said. “The Liberals must act immediately to rectify the unacceptable state of Canada’s ammunition stockpiles, both inventory and accounting.”

Defence Minister David McGuinty said the government takes seriously its responsibility to ensure the Canadian Armed Forces has enough ammunition.

“The entire auditor general report on ammunition tells us that we have progress to make, and we’re making it,” he told a Thursday news conference.

“She [Hogan] has made some really important contributions to how we merge our tracking system with respect to the storage of ammunition and distribution of ammunition, and we’re weaving that into the system that’s already being operationalized.”

The federal government has said bolstering domestic ammunition production is one of its top ten priorities under the defence industrial strategy it released this spring.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada still reviewing F-35 purchase after Rcaf received its first jets: minister
stories.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty says the federal government’s planned purchase of 88 F-35 stealth fighters remains under review, even after the military received its first two F-35s in recent days.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Defence Minister David McGuinty says the federal government’s planned purchase of 88 F-35 stealth fighters remains under review, even after the military received its first two F-35s in recent days.

McGuinty told reporters today the federal government will take all the time it needs to consider all factors, including industrial benefits and emerging autonomous air systems that can fly alongside fighter craft.

The Royal Canadian Air Force announced last week on social media it had received its first two jets from Lockheed Martin at Luke Air Force base in Phoenix, Arizona.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the full order for 88 jets under review soon after he came into office, when U.S. President Donald Trump was still in the early stages of his trade war against Canada.

Ottawa has committed financially to purchasing at least the first 16 jets and has ordered spare parts.

Swedish defence manufacturer Saab announced partnerships with several major Canadian aerospace companies this week, as it prepares for the possibility that the Carney government opts to purchase a mixed fighter fleet and build Gripen E fighter jets in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Three products recalled in Canada over fire, fall risks
stories.summary: Health Canada has announced recalls of residential gas boilers, children’s sensory swings and Dreo space heaters over risks including carbon monoxide poisoning, falls and fires.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Three products sold in Canada are being recalled following safety concerns also reported in the United States.

Health Canada issued consumer product recall notices for NTI- and HTP-brand residential gas boilers; Harkla children’s compression sensory swings and Dreo portable space heaters on Thursday. Each of the companies mentioned in the recalls are offering free remedies, including repair kits, boiler upgrades and replacement heaters.

Consumers who own any of the affected products should stop “immediately stop using them,” according to each of the notices, and follow the companies’ instructions to obtain the appropriate remedy.

Gas boilers pose fire, carbon monoxide risks

Certain NTI and HTP residential gas boilers are being recalled because a component inside the units can crack during delayed ignition, allowing unburned gas to accumulate inside the sealed cabinet.

If the gas ignites, the boiler’s front cover can suddenly detach, creating a risk of serious injury or death from impact, fire or carbon monoxide poisoning.

The recall affects NTI boilers in the Ftvn and Tftn series and HTP boilers in the Eftu series. The serial number is printed on the rating plate on the side of the boiler cabinet. Consumers should check the NTI safety recall page ⁠ or the HTP safety notice page ⁠ for the affected models and serial number ranges.

The products were sold from May 2021 to August 2025. About 2,261 affected units were sold in Canada and 4,726 in the United States.

As of Oct. 16, the company had received two incident reports and one injury report in Canada. It had received one incident report and no injury reports in the U.S. The company reported 34 total occurrences of the component breaking overall.

The recall said consumers should “immediately stop using” the recalled boilers and contact Ariston Canada Inc. for a free upgrade kit and help arranging installation by a certified technician.

“Consumers who must continue using the boiler while awaiting repair should have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in their homes,” the recall said.

Consumers can call 1-800-688-2575 for assistance or email email VCexchanger@ariston.com .

Harkla sensory swings recalled over fall hazard

Harkla children’s compression sensory swings are being recalled because the ceiling hook can separate from its mounting plate, potentially causing a child to fall and suffer serious injuries.

The recall covers blue compression sensory swings with a four-hole ceiling mounting plate and a drop length of 18 to 24 inches. The affected products are the Blue Compression Sensory Swing (SKU LS-Comp-1BLU) and Blue Compression Sensory Swing with Swivel (SKU LS-Comp-1BLU-SW).

The swings were sold from March 2020 to April 2025, with 5,534 sold in Canada and 25,541 in the United States.

As of Oct. 23, the company had received four reports of the hook separating from its mounting plate in Canada, including one injury report. In the U.S., it had received 29 reports of separation and 17 injury reports.

“Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and contact Harkla to obtain a repair kit,” the recall said.

The kit includes a replacement ceiling hook mounting plate, a safety strap and updated installation instructions. Consumers are also instructed to dispose of the original hooks according to municipal waste guidelines.

For assistance, call 844-442-7552, Monday to Friday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Pacific time, or email recall@harkla.co .

Dreo space heaters recalled over overheating

Dreo portable oscillating ceramic space heaters are being recalled because they can overheat and ignite, posing fire and burn hazards.

The recall affects model DR-HSH015, which are black heaters measuring about 29 centimetres wide, 33 centimetres tall and supplied with a remote control. The model number and manufacturing date appear on labels on the underside of the unit.

Affected heaters were manufactured from April 2025 through January 2026, with 36,288 units sold in Canada and 338,800 in the U.S. The products were sold from September 2025 to August 2026.

As of Oct. 22, the company had received one incident report and no injury reports in Canada. In the United States, it had received 16 incident reports, including one injury report.

The recall said consumers should “immediately stop using” the recalled heaters and contact Dreo for a free replacement. They can call 833-820-0887, Monday to Friday, from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern time, or email spaceheater@realtimeresults.net .

stories.title: London study explores how AI could help close health care gaps for people experiencing homelessness
stories.summary: Health records May not tell the full story of a person’s health, particularly for people experiencing homelessness. Researchers in London are hoping artificial intelligence can help change that.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Health records May not tell the full story of a person’s health, particularly for people experiencing homelessness. Researchers in London are hoping artificial intelligence can help change that.

The project draws on anonymous health records from more than 35,000 Ontarians with a history of homelessness.

Dixon says the first step is determining whether the information routinely collected by the health care system reflects the realities of people without stable housing.

“Individuals who are assumed housed May interact quite differently with our health care setting than those who are experiencing homelessness,” Dixon said.

The research will look at how health records can be interpreted more effectively before using that information to develop tools for patients and their care providers.

One potential outcome is a new frailty score, which helps health-care professionals assess a person’s overall health and likelihood of developing serious complications.

Current assessment tools May overlook the cumulative effects of homelessness, including trauma, chronic stress, mental health concerns, substance use and difficulties accessing medical care.

By working with community organizations, health care providers and people who have experienced homelessness, researchers hope to identify factors that existing assessments miss.

“Once we have those rules in place, we can build on those to develop tools that will help this particular community as well as the individuals who are caring for them,” she said.

The long-term aim is to help health-care providers identify risks sooner and connect people with appropriate treatment and support.

The project is supported by the AMS Healthcare Leadership in Compassion and Artificial Intelligence Fellowship, which supports research into the responsible and compassionate use of AI in health care.

stories.title: Jennifer Whiteside named BC NDP interim leader
stories.summary: Whiteside steps in after David Eby resigned as party leader last weekend
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
Jennifer Whiteside emerged from a meeting of the decimated BC NDP caucus on Thursday as the party’s interim leader, an outcome she said she was not “necessarily expecting.”

But five hours and a pizza lunch after the meeting convened at the legislature, the outgoing labour minister had secured the unanimous support of the incoming caucus, in the wake of a devastating election loss on the weekend.

“I have to tell you, this is deeply, deeply humbling,” said Whiteside, who was re-elected in the riding of New Westminster-Coquitlam on Saturday.

Whiteside said British Columbians had sent the party an “important message” in the snap election, in which the B.C. Conservatives won a resounding two-thirds majority.

“They have asked that we sit as the official Opposition and we will take on that work with determination, with thoughtfulness, always putting people at the centre of everything that we do,” Whiteside said, surrounded by caucus members after the meeting.

Outgoing labour minister Jennifer Whiteside says it's 'deeply humbling' to be named interim leader of the British Columbia NDP. Whiteside says British Columbians sent an 'important m…

Whiteside has previously served as minister of education, and minister of mental health and addictions.

By accepting the role of interim leader, Whiteside is excluded from seeking the post permanently.

She said Mike Farnworth would serve as house leader, while Niki Sharma would be caucus chair.

Outgoing Premier David Eby , who stepped down as NDP leader on election night, did not attend the meeting.

Whiteside said the caucus needed an interim leader in case premier-designate Lorne Doerkson decided to recall the legislature for a late-year sitting.

“In the event they call a sitting before Christmas, we need to be ready to go. We need to stand up for people in our communities,” she said.

Preliminary election results have the Conservatives winning 63 seats, while the NDP ranks have been reduced to 28, and the Greens have two ridings. But the outcome in a handful of ridings is still pending and official certification of the results isn’t due until Nov. 18.

Before the meeting, fellow former ministers Sharma and Ravi Parmar spoke about the scale of the blunder made in calling the election, and described an emotional meeting on Wednesday where Eby apologized to the outgoing caucus for calling the snap poll two years early.

Sharma and Parmar both left open the possibility they May seek the permanent leadership.

Sharma, who was previously attorney general, said Eby “took full responsibility” at Wednesday’s meeting.

She said of the election call that “clearly it was a mistake, and now our job is to move forward.”

She said the outgoing caucus meeting was an emotional affair, as colleagues bid farewell to each other.

“There’s no sugar-coating it. It was a tough day. We had to say goodbye to MLAs that were excellent, that really served their community well,” she said.

“So we were reflective, and I think there’s a resolve within that reflectiveness to figure out how we do the job that British Columbia has elected us to do now, which is as official Opposition.”

Sharma was noncommittal on the permanent leadership.

“Today is not about my personal ambitions or what I will choose, but it’s about our party and figuring out how we move forward,” she said.

Parmar, the outgoing forests minister, said the party and Eby clearly made the wrong decision to call the election.

“We got it wrong,” he said. “I think we owe an apology to British Columbians for doing so, and in particular to those that are vulnerable, who feel that the Conservative governments will not act in their interests.”

Opinion: Did the B.C. Conservatives’ election win run against the federal tide, or with it?

Parmar, like Sharma, did not tip his hand about the permanent leadership.

“Too early to say,” he said. “I’m looking forward to spending more time at home, spending more time with my constituents.”

Neither Sharma nor Parmar would say if Eby’s decision to call the Oct. 24 election two years early received pushback from caucus, citing confidentiality.

“The premier made a decision, we all stood by him … clearly we made the wrong decision calling the election, and that’s something that we’re all going to live by,” Parmar said before the start of the incoming caucus meeting.

Politics, he added, was a team sport.

Asked to rate the level of frustration at the election call, Parmar said it was “about 10, absolutely.”

“I’m disappointed, I’m frustrated, but that disappointment and frustration can’t last four years, it can only last a few days,” he said.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge victim Maya Gebala leaving hospital after eight months, father says
stories.summary: David Gebala posted a video giving his 13-year-old daughter the news, as Maya responds by punching the air
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
The father of Tumbler Ridge attack victim Maya Gebala says she is being released from BC Children’s Hospital, more than eight months after being shot three times.

David Gebala has posted a video on social media showing him telling his 13-year-old daughter that she is going home, with Maya responding by punching the air.

Maya’s recovery from severe brain injuries in the shootings that left eight victims dead on Feb. 10 has been documented by her parents on social media.

David Gebala says in the post that Maya’s release from hospital is a “milestone no one thought we would reach.”

Gebala says that after the attack, doctors said they didn’t think Maya would even “make it through the night.”

Maya was shot at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School by Jesse Van Rootselaar, who shot herself dead after the attack.

Gebala paid tribute to his daughter’s strength in Thursday’s Facebook post.

“Maya, you are the bravest person I know. You are an inspiration to so many people,” he said.

“Giving up was never an option for me, and it clearly never was for you either.”

He said Maya was going home after 262 days in hospital, listing various milestones along the way.

Gebala said it’s 251 days since she opened an eye, 191 days since tubes were removed to reveal her “beautiful face,” 145 days since she first smiled and 61 days since she first spoke.

Maya has made various trips away from hospital, including going to a Foo Fighters concert to celebrate her 13th birthday last month.

“Thank you to the incredible nurses, doctors and therapists who walked every step of this with us,” Gebala said.

“Thank you to everyone who supported Maya and our family, we could not have done this without each and every one of you.”

stories.title: Canada faces ‘critical gaps’ on military combat ammunition: AG warns
stories.summary: The report found there is a major discrepancy in the supply of munitions for training exercises and munitions to be used in combat.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
It will take several years to bring the Canadian military’s stockpile of ammunition up to where it should be, according to a new report from the auditor general.

With the current gaps, the financial watchdog said Canada is far behind on its commitments made to its Nato allies for collective defence.

In the report, released Thursday, Canada’s Auditor General Karen Hogan said a flawed inventory management system, dysfunctional data analysis and contracts plagued with inefficiencies has resulted in the Department of National Defence (DND) not knowing how much ammunition it has or needs, or how to get more.

“These findings are like the importance of sound planning and acting on known problems before an emergency occurs,” she told reporters Thursday. “Responding to immediate needs is important, but so is being prepared for future challenges.”

“It’s time for National Defence to get all these administrative matters ironed out so that they can make the best use of the funding that they have.”

The auditor general’s office first started sounding the alarm on the inefficiencies two decades ago. In 2024, the government dedicated $9.2 billion over 13 years to support strategic stockpile replenishment.

But Hogan said the current pace at which contracts are being awarded is not sufficient to meet demands.

Public Services and Procurement Canada had four strategic source agreements with Canadian companies to produce ammunition through the Munitions Supply Program, according to the audit. But two of those four agreements had expired over three years ago, Hogan said.

The report found there is a major discrepancy in the supply of munitions for training exercises and munitions to be used in combat.

Five Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) groups accounted for 87 per cent of the total regular-use ammunition assigned by quantity in the 2023-24 to 2025-26 fiscal years, the report said.

Within those groups, only 56 per cent of their assigned regular‑use ammunition was used in the same period.

Hogan said some of the excess inventory can be used in an emergency, but not all training ammunition is lethal.

The auditor general looked at 100 different types of stockpile admission and found it was lacking required types and quantities required to meet targeted operational requirements.

“For national security reasons, I can’t talk to you about the specifics of where there are critical gaps, but there are critical gaps in some of the ammunition,” Hogan said.

In response to the report, Defence Minister David McGuinty said he agrees with the auditor general’s six recommendations and is already acting upon them.

“We’re going to have to make sure we marry that production capacity with the storage, transportation and use of information,” he said. “There’s progress to be made and we intend to fully implement these recommendations.”

stories.title: Fredericton’s emergency shelter space shrinks ahead of winter
stories.summary: As colder weather approaches, those who operate homeless shelters in Fredericton are preparing to work with less this year.
stories.author: Johnny James, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
As colder weather approaches, those who operate homeless shelters in Fredericton are preparing to work with less this year.

Fredericton Homeless Shelters Inc. has run an emergency out-of-the-cold shelter in a building at the exhibition grounds for two winters now. The site allowed for around 33 beds.

However, the building is set to be demolished as part of a redevelopment project.

This week, Fredericton City Council approved another emergency shelter to operate this winter — but it’s at the Small Craft Aquatic Centre on the city’s south side, which is a smaller space.

“The Aquatic Center has been the appointed place right now and it will provide 10 emergency beds for overnight use during the winter months,” said Vanessa Foss, Fredericton Homeless Shelters Inc.’s director of business development.

Foss says the organization also has a men’s shelter with a 27-bed capacity and a women’s shelter with 10 beds “plus emergency couch.”

According to the latest numbers from the Human Development Council, as of September there were 353 people experiencing homelessness in Fredericton .

The data also showed 179 people were chronically homeless, which refers to people who have at least six months of homelessness over the past year or recurrent experiences of homelessness over the past three years.

“The numbers (of unhoused people) have increased quite a bit, so there’s a substantial need for individuals for housing and emergency shelters,” said Foss. “Between housing and shelter, there’s a significant need.”

Foss says work is ongoing to build a permanent shelter, but short-term measures are coming soon.

“We have started up our supported housing, so we have two houses now and then we’ll be opening a third in January. So that is increasing some supported housing elements, but that bigger project will be to come,” Foss said.

Council also approved a new courtyard lot for 12 Neighbours, a tiny home community, which will add 15 new units. The units offer a bridge between emergency out-of-the-cold services and permanent supportive housing.

“One of the things it does is helps us, of course, to deploy solutions more quickly but also house individuals that have some additional complexities that make it difficult for them to succeed even in a supportive, permanent housing context,” said Marcel LeBrun, president of 12 Neighbours, who spoke to council on Monday.

The Aquatic Centre emergency shelter will open in mid-December and is approved to stay open until the end of April.

stories.title: At Windsor’s film festival, a couple wise guys reveal how they uncovered Scorsese’s secrets
stories.summary: Documentary by Australian and British filmmakers is a true passion project, a testament to the immense cultural legacy of Martin Scorsese’s film
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
As far back as Lisa Downs and Ashley Pugh can remember, they wanted to make a documentary about Goodfellas .

Okay, that’s a bit of Scorsese-level hyperbole, but the pair of Australian (Downs) and British (Pugh) filmmakers – who are partners in work and in life – had been inching toward exploring the 1990 crime epic after previously making a series of docs chronicling the productions of more family-friendly big-screen classics: Flight of the Navigator , The NeverEnding Story and Flash Gordon , all of which were childhood favourites of Downs.

“I said to Lisa, ‘Well, you know if we’re going to keep making these kinds of movies, how about we do one about a movie that I love?’” recalls Pugh in an interview. “I first saw Goodfellas when I was 16, and like a lot of movie-obsessed teenagers, I fell in love with it. And we do have a history with the film as a couple. When we first started dating, as a surprise for my birthday, Lisa rented out a cinema so that we could watch the film together on the big screen. I thought after that, well, she’s a keeper.”

It would be fair to say, then, that the pair’s new documentary, As Far Back as I Can Remember ... The Story of Goodfellas is a true passion project, as much a testament to the directors’ romance as it is to the immense cultural legacy of Scorsese’s film, which is rightly considered one of the most influential films of all time. But producing the doc, which will make its Canadian premiere at the Windsor International Film Festival Nov. 2, wasn’t exactly as easy as, say, falling in love.

Determined to make a film that was more than just a standard behind-the-scenes doc that could have been included as a Blu-ray extra, Downs and Pugh spent years researching Goodfellas on a granular level. This involved going so far as to hunt down previously unreleased footage shot by a local film student featuring such cast members as Joe Pesci roaming the set and offering informal interviews – material that had been stored on VHS tapes locked away in an Alaskan safe for the past 35 years.

“We were very wary as to how to treat that footage – because it’s very old, we needed to gently upscale it because we wanted it to look archival without much sharpening – you don’t want it to seem like it’s AI or something,” Pugh says with a laugh.

The documentarians also spent untold hours trying to track down and gain access to as many cast and crew of Goodfellas as possible. Building upon a friendship that the pair had with Christopher Serrone, who played the young version of Ray Liotta’s mobster antihero Henry Hill, Downs and Pugh gradually accumulated a murderer’s row of talent. Eventually, they secured participation from dozens of key members of the Goodfellas team, everyone from actors Samuel L. Jackson and Illeana Douglas to mega-producer Irwin Winkler and screenwriter Nicholas Pileggi. (Alas, Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Pesci remained elusive, while Liotta died in 2022.)

“What we learned from making our previous films is that patience plays a huge part, especially when you have a film with so many people who you’d like to interview. With this movie, every character is iconic, even if they have one line,” says Downs. “Having an in with Chris was a wonderful start, but really we just scour IMDb and start reaching out to people.”

The doc’s biggest coup, though, came about through sheer luck. Learning that there was going to be a fan convention in Woodbridge, N.J., in 2025 called Paisan Con – a celebration of “Italian-American Pop Culture & Heritage” – Downs and Pugh hopped on a plane, brought their cameras along, and walked up cold to actress Lorraine Bracco, hoping that she’d simply say yes on the spot. Surprisingly, Bracco, a doyenne of mafia pop-culture thanks to her performance as Hill’s wife Karen in Goodfellas as well as her Emmy-nominated turn as Dr. Jennifer Melfi in The Sopranos – was all in.

“They were simply delightful, and they had such a love for Goodfellas that I instantly admired them. Their energy was contagious,” recalls Bracco in a separate interview. “Talking with people who love this movie, it’s the best part of being an actor. I’m still amazed that people of all generations, whether they’re my age or my father’s age or your age, come up to me and talk about how much they love this movie. It’s shocking, but it’s also not. Marty is a master filmmaker. So how lucky was I?”

Once Bracco was onboard the doc, an entire new world of Goodfellas was unlocked to Downs and Pugh – not only cast members who had been hard to reach, such as Debbie Mazar, but also crucial behind-the-scenes players such as casting director Ellen Lewis, who plucked everyday New Jersey residents to populate the film, ensuring Scorsese’s vision was that much more authentic.

“Sometimes you get surprised how welcoming people can be in this whole process,” says Downs. “For Nick Pileggi, I got a hold of his phone number through someone and just cold-called him. He was like, ‘Great, just come to the Hamptons and we’ll talk.’”

At the same time that the doc is making its way into the world one screening at a time – in Windsor, Downs and Pugh will be on hand as Bracco receives the festival’s Spotlight Award and participates in a postscreening Q&A – the filmmakers are making three other film-centric documentaries, including one focusing on the legacy of Goodfellas producer Winkler, who also developed such classics as Rocky , Raging Bull and The Right Stuff .

“It’s been a little like a travelling circus taking this movie around,” says Downs. “But the fact that Lorraine can be with us along the journey, we feel blessed.”

Also Playing at Wiff

Given its relatively small region and crowded spot on the fall-season calendar, the Windsor International Film Festival has been punching above its weight over the past few years. Now in its 22nd edition, Wiff will offer 232 features this year across 300 screenings, plus its annual $25,000 Canadian Film prize. Here are a few highlights of this year’s fest, running Oct. 29 through Nov. 8:

Paper Tiger: James Gray’s throwback crime drama starring Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson will open Wiff ahead of its release across the country later in November.

All of a Sudden: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s epic-length drama following the burgeoning relationship between two care workers, a hit at Cannes, plays Wiff before its gradual roll out across the country later this fall.

125, Rue des Malaises: The surprise Québécois hit of the summer, Louis Bélanger’s French-language dramedy following an elderly patriarch who chooses medical aid in dying hasn’t been available outside its home province.

Rose: The second big Sandra Hüller movie of the season – following this week’s release of Fatherland – stars the German actress as a mysterious soldier setting up shop in a 17th-century village.

The Debut: Wiff’s closing-night film was a breakout at Tiff in September, and features a standout performance from Julianne Moore as a suburban housewife who finds her creative side via her local community theatre troupe.

content_blocks.text: Okay, that’s a bit of Scorsese-level hyperbole, but the pair of Australian (Downs) and British (Pugh) filmmakers – who are partners in work and in life – had been inching toward exploring the 1990 crime epic after previously making a series of docs chronicling the productions of more family-friendly big-screen classics: Flight of the Navigator , The NeverEnding Story and Flash Gordon , all of which were childhood favourites of Downs.

content_blocks.text: “I said to Lisa, ‘Well, you know if we’re going to keep making these kinds of movies, how about we do one about a movie that I love?’” recalls Pugh in an interview. “I first saw Goodfellas when I was 16, and like a lot of movie-obsessed teenagers, I fell in love with it. And we do have a history with the film as a couple. When we first started dating, as a surprise for my birthday, Lisa rented out a cinema so that we could watch the film together on the big screen. I thought after that, well, she’s a keeper.”

content_blocks.text: It would be fair to say, then, that the pair’s new documentary, As Far Back as I Can Remember ... The Story of Goodfellas is a true passion project, as much a testament to the directors’ romance as it is to the immense cultural legacy of Scorsese’s film, which is rightly considered one of the most influential films of all time. But producing the doc, which will make its Canadian premiere at the Windsor International Film Festival Nov. 2, wasn’t exactly as easy as, say, falling in love.

The Story of Goodfellas is a true passion project, as much a testament to the directors’ romance as it is to the immense cultural legacy of Scorsese’s film, which is rightly considered one of the most influential films of all time. But producing the doc, which will make its Canadian premiere at the Windsor International Film Festival Nov. 2, wasn’t exactly as easy as, say, falling in love.

content_blocks.text: Determined to make a film that was more than just a standard behind-the-scenes doc that could have been included as a Blu-ray extra, Downs and Pugh spent years researching Goodfellas on a granular level. This involved going so far as to hunt down previously unreleased footage shot by a local film student featuring such cast members as Joe Pesci roaming the set and offering informal interviews – material that had been stored on VHS tapes locked away in an Alaskan safe for the past 35 years.

content_blocks.text: “We were very wary as to how to treat that footage – because it’s very old, we needed to gently upscale it because we wanted it to look archival without much sharpening – you don’t want it to seem like it’s AI or something,” Pugh says with a laugh.

content_blocks.caption: Christopher Serrone, in a scene from 'As Far Back as I Can Remember: The Story of Goodfellas,' played the young version of Ray Liotta’s mobster antihero Henry Hill in 'Goodfellas.' Supplied

content_blocks.text: The documentarians also spent untold hours trying to track down and gain access to as many cast and crew of Goodfellas as possible. Building upon a friendship that the pair had with Christopher Serrone, who played the young version of Ray Liotta’s mobster antihero Henry Hill, Downs and Pugh gradually accumulated a murderer’s row of talent. Eventually, they secured participation from dozens of key members of the Goodfellas team, everyone from actors Samuel L. Jackson and Illeana Douglas to mega-producer Irwin Winkler and screenwriter Nicholas Pileggi. (Alas, Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Pesci remained elusive, while Liotta died in 2022.)

content_blocks.text: “What we learned from making our previous films is that patience plays a huge part, especially when you have a film with so many people who you’d like to interview. With this movie, every character is iconic, even if they have one line,” says Downs. “Having an in with Chris was a wonderful start, but really we just scour IMDb and start reaching out to people.”

content_blocks.text: The doc’s biggest coup, though, came about through sheer luck. Learning that there was going to be a fan convention in Woodbridge, N.J., in 2025 called Paisan Con – a celebration of “Italian-American Pop Culture & Heritage” – Downs and Pugh hopped on a plane, brought their cameras along, and walked up cold to actress Lorraine Bracco, hoping that she’d simply say yes on the spot. Surprisingly, Bracco, a doyenne of mafia pop-culture thanks to her performance as Hill’s wife Karen in Goodfellas as well as her Emmy-nominated turn as Dr. Jennifer Melfi in The Sopranos – was all in.

content_blocks.text: “They were simply delightful, and they had such a love for Goodfellas that I instantly admired them. Their energy was contagious,” recalls Bracco in a separate interview. “Talking with people who love this movie, it’s the best part of being an actor. I’m still amazed that people of all generations, whether they’re my age or my father’s age or your age, come up to me and talk about how much they love this movie. It’s shocking, but it’s also not. Marty is a master filmmaker. So how lucky was I?”

stories.title: Quebec plans to ban religious symbols in schools, Education Minister says
stories.summary: Parti Québécois promised to broaden provincial secularism laws during recent election campaign
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
The president of the National Council of Canadian Muslims is accusing the Quebec government of attempting to take away the rights of children by expanding secularism laws.

“We’re talking about going after the rights of children to have a spirituality and go to school,” said Stephen Brown in an interview.

Quebec’s new education minister, Joël Arseneau, told journalists on Wednesday that he plans to ban schoolchildren from wearing religious symbols. He added that doing so is “non-negotiable.”

The Parti Québécois had promised the ban during the election campaign that resulted in a PQ minority government. In its platform, the party wrote that secularism “embodies the desire of the vast majority of Quebeckers to live in a society where religion is practised in the private sphere.”

But Brown said the government is already breaking its promise to be the “the government of all Quebeckers.”

“What we’re seeing now is anything but that,” said Brown. “It’s ridiculous and a missed opportunity.”

Brown said the government had pledged to reach out to communities and find balanced policy solutions to difficult questions like secularism. He believes that believes preventing children from wearing religious symbols is “blatant discrimination against religious minorities.”

He said the rules would mainly apply to those who wish to wear the kippa, hijab, crucifix and turban.

“We should not live in a country where politicians are able to literally trade away the rights of Canadian citizens in an election or political game,” said Brown. “The Charter rights of Canadian citizens have to be worth more than the paper they’re written on.”

Québec solidaire’s education and secularism critic, Roxane Milot, said the leftist party will vote against the proposed ban.

“Leave the kids alone! The priorities for the education system are clear: address the staff shortage, repair our schools, put an end to the three-tiered school system and reduce the dropout rate,” she said in a news release.

In the same release, Québec solidaire said it is concerning to see the new administration get bogged down by “identity-driven one-upmanship.”

It is unclear when the PQ government intends to table a bill to this effect, though the legislature is scheduled to resume sitting on Nov. 17.

The Quebec government has been strongly criticized for its law banning employees of the public sector, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols.

A legal challenge of that law, known as Bill 21, has made it to the Supreme Court of Canada. Lawyers argued it raised serious concerns involving several Charter rights, including freedom of expression, conscience and religion.

Those legal proceedings are ongoing.

Brown said he is prepared to mount a legal challenge if the PQ’s proposal becomes law.

Jean-Christophe Jasmin, the Quebec director of Christian think tank Cardus, also opposes expanding secularism laws.

In an interview, he said the government’s rationale to ban religious symbols worn by government employees was “presented in the name of freedom of conscience.” The previous Coalition Avenir Québec administration had argued that children are subject to an authority figure, and that that figure must be religiously neutral as to not impose their beliefs on their students.

“I don’t see how that logic applies to children today. Children do not represent the state, they are part of civil society,” said Jasmin. “There is no duty of neutrality on the part of children. The argument doesn’t hold up.”

Brown agreed, saying the scope of secularism laws banning religious symbols has continued to expand since the CAQ took power in 2018.

At first, the government targeted those in positions of authority. It was extended to teachers, daycare workers, all school staff and parents who volunteer in schools.

The CAQ then expanded the scope of the law to the public sphere by banning praying outside, in universities and at workplaces.

“And now of course, we’re going after the rights of children. So where does this end?” said Brown.

Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer who took part in the legal challenge against Bill 21, did not want to comment on Arseneau’s comments but said it was to be expected.

He pointed out that former premier François Legault had openly said in a 2019 radio interview with Radio-Canada that Bill 21 was a concession to “people who are a little racist and don’t want to see religious symbols anywhere in public.”

“It’s never enough,” said Bérard. “It’s a slippery slope.”

stories.title: N.S. university teachers association says premier is using political intimidation
stories.summary: The Association of Nova Scotia University Teachers says it condemns the premier’s response, calling it a threat to academic freedom.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An association representing university teachers in Nova Scotia is accusing Premier Tim Houston of political intimidation after his office complained to a Toronto professor who had commented on a proposed artificial intelligence data centre.

Houston told reporters on Wednesday he’s glad a staffer in his office sent the complaint to the professor, saying his comments about the $10-billion data centre were wrong.

The Association of Nova Scotia University Teachers says it condemns the premier’s response, calling it a threat to academic freedom.

The premier’s office says it disagrees with the characterization and that it has a productive relationship with academic institutions in the province.

The complaint came after Sibo Chen, a communications professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, gave a media interview to CBC News saying that public concerns about the data centre project in Point Tupper, N.S., were valid.

A communications adviser with the premier’s office sent Chen an email describing his comments as slanted and irresponsible, and copied a CBC News reporter and the chair of Chen’s department.

The president of the association of university teachers says the premier’s response raises questions about what consequences Nova Scotia academics could face if they challenge provincial projects.

“Government influence over research grants, board appointments and institutional funding gives that concern real weight,” Mathew Reichertz said. “Faculty should never have to fear that sharing their findings could jeopardize their research support or bring pressure on their employer to discipline them.”

Everwind Fuels announced earlier this month that U.S. AI company Anthropic signed a 20-year lease for the data centre, sparking opposition from members of the public.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org had over 24,000 signatures as of Wednesday afternoon.

stories.title: Maya Gebala is being released from the hospital, father says: 'Never a day I stopped believing'
stories.summary: In an emotional post on social media, he called her an "inspiration" and said she was the "bravest person" he knows.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The father of Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor David Gebala says his daughter Maya, who was severely injured in February, is being released from the hospital.

In an emotional post on social media, he said it has been 262 days since she was airlifted to the BC Children’s Hospital. He recounted in the post on X Thursday that he was told at the time, presumably by doctors, that “we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night.”

He added, “Since then, I’ve watched you fight for every single one of those days.”

Maya has had several emergency surgeries, infections and other struggles during her hospital stay.

“179 days ago, your prosthetic skull was placed. Your fifth surgery, and the one that finally stuck. After that, things slowly began to feel possible again,” wrote David.

Eventually, he said he saw his daughter smile, was able to take her off the hospital grounds briefly, and was even able to celebrate when she turned 13 in September.

“There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here. The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach,” he said.

He called Maya “the bravest person I know” and an inspiration.

“Look at you, my girl. You blew every expectation out of the water,” he concluded, adding that he was grateful for all of the medical professionals who helped her along the way and all of their supporters. “Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear.”

The post also included a video showing Maya, wearing sunglasses and smiling and gesturing happily, as she received the news that she would be released from the hospital.

In February, Jesse Van Rootselaar, a former Tumbler Ridge Secondary School student, killed eight people, including six children, and injured dozens before committing suicide.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

stories.title: Poll suggests long wait times led half of Canadians to avoid going to the hospital
stories.summary: A new poll suggests long wait times lead half of Canadians to avoid seeing a doctor or going to the hospital.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A new poll suggests long wait times lead half of Canadians to avoid seeing a doctor or going to the hospital.

The poll was conducted by Léger and commissioned by right-leaning think-tanks the Montreal Economic Institute, SecondStreet.org and Canadian Constitution Foundation.

The percentage of respondents who said they avoided consulting doctors because of wait times was highest among women, people over 55 and Quebecers.

The poll ran from Oct. 16 to 19, 2026, among an online panel of 1,510 Canadians.

The survey numbers do not indicate whether the people who avoided seeing a doctor had seen a nurse or turned to other services like pharmacists.

It is also unclear whether respondents started avoiding hospitals because of wait times over the past year or at another point in their lives.

Just over a quarter of poll respondents said they have paid for private health care to avoid wait times or unsatisfactory service.

The survey also found that 61 per cent of respondents supported being able to pay out of pocket or use insurance to access private care if they could not get timely care in the public system. However, a quarter of respondents said they opposed the coexistence of public and private health-care systems.

Asked if they believed the health-care system in their area needed change, 84 per cent of respondents said yes.

The polling industry’s professional body, the Canadian Research Insights Council, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

stories.title: Police investigate arson attack on car outside home of Sikh independence activist
stories.summary: Surrey — Police in B.C. are investigating an apparent arson attack outside the home of a Sikh independence activist who was previously warned by officers that his life was under threat.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Surrey — Police in B.C. are investigating an apparent arson attack outside the home of a Sikh independence activist who was previously warned by officers that his life was under threat.

Surrey police say officers found a car engulfed in flames and a bus vandalized after the attack in the Surrey Central neighbourhood, where officers were called to the scene at 11:45 p.m. Wednesday.

Investigators say they believe a suspect fled on foot and no motive has been determined.

The Sikhs For Justice group says in a separate news release that the attack occurred at the home of Narinder Singh Randhawa, who was given a “duty to warn” notice by Surrey police in April and told there was an imminent threat to his life.

Randhawa has organized rallies for the Khalistan movement that seeks the formation of an independent Sikh state in the Punjab region within India.

A former leader of the group, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, was shot dead in Surrey in 2023, in an attack former prime minister Justin Trudeau said was linked to India by credible intelligence.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who visited India earlier this year, has refused to say if he believes the Indian government is involved in acts of foreign interference and transnational repression in Canada.

Randhawa previously told The Canadian Press that police said his activism and participation in protests May be behind threats against his life.

The Sikhs For Justice statement says protesters had rallied in Vancouver on the day of the arson attack.

The group urged police to investigate the attack as an act of terrorism.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published

Chuck Chiang, The Canadian Press
