stories.title: Stelco must recall laid off workers ‘immediately,’ Joly says in new letter
stories.summary: In a letter dated Oct. 29 addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a 'concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.'
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she is prepared to sit down with Stelco representatives on the basis that the laid off workers are “recalled immediately.”

In a letter dated Oct. 29 obtained by Global News and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

Stelco began issuing layoff notices to about 500 employees at the beginning of October following an announcement of its plans to pull back on operations at its Hamilton plant.

The company has said the employees laid off in Hamilton will be offered jobs at their Lake Erie facility but the union representing Stelco workers told Global News only 40 jobs have been offered to the impacted employees.

In a letter sent last week, Joly warned Stelco that if they do not reverse the layoffs within 15 days, the federal government will start legal action against the company that could ultimately lead to the parent company Cleveland-Cliffs being forced to divest of the Canadian steel firm.

Joly said she reviewed an interim compliance report that was provided by Stelco on Oct. 26 but said the report was “far from satisfactory.”

“It does not alter my belief that Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs are not in compliance with their undertakings under the Investment Canada Act as set out in my October 22 section 39 demand,” she said in the most recent letter.

The industry minister said she expects Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs to address her demands “fully and directly” and “provide the underlying data, documents and other evidence necessary to support their assertions.”

With files from Global News’ Mackenzie Gray.

stories.title: Allied Properties Reit cuts distribution by 90% to focus on debt repayment
stories.summary: Second payout cut in 12 months for the Toronto-based office and apartment building owner
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Allied Properties Real Estate Investment Trust AP-UN-T slashed its cash distribution by 90 per cent, its second payout cut in the past 12 months, as the office and apartment building owner puts a priority on paying down debt and selling properties.

Late Wednesday, Toronto-based Allied reduced the monthly distributions it makes to unitholders, who are typically individual investors looking for income, to 0.006 cents per unit, or 7 cents each year.

Last December, Allied cut its distributions by 60 per cent. The price of the Reit’s units has fallen by 78 per cent over the past year. The benchmark S&P/TSX Capped Reit Index is down 1.6 per cent over the same period.

“We recognize that Allied’s performance has been disappointing for our unitholders and that this distribution reduction adds to that disappointment,” said Allied chief executive officer Cecilia Williams in a conference call on Thursday.

“We’re accountable for improving Allied’s financial position, and these decisions are both difficult and necessary steps toward that goal,” Ms. Williams said. The distribution cut will boost Allied’s cash flow by $126-million a year.

On Thursday, the price of Allied units dropped by about 19 per cent to close at $4.32 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Analysts had predicted Allied would cut its payout but were surprised by its scale.

“The 90-per-cent distribution reduction is far greater than our 50-per-cent forecast,” said analyst Mario Saric at Bank of Nova Scotia in a report.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Pammi Bir said in a report the distribution cut “underscores the depths of Allied Properties’ challenges, including elevated leverage.”

Allied owes lenders $4-billion. The Reit owns $8.2-billion in properties and boosted its long-term target for property sales to a range from $750-million to $1.5-billion. Chief financial officer Craig MacIntyre said: “No asset in the portfolio is off limits.”

Allied management won plaudits from one analyst for taking dramatic steps to preserve cash. National Bank Capital Markets analysts Matt Kornack called the distribution cut “a positive move for the Reit” that “should have been done sooner.”

“It will go a long way to aiding in the goal of deleveraging, especially when combined with an accelerated disposition program,” Mr. Kornack said.

Allied’s landmark buildings include The Well, a 3.1-hectare office-and-residential development in downtown Toronto developed in partnership with RioCan Reit. Tech company Shopify Inc. was meant to be a major tenant in the property but opted out of its lease.

On Thursday, Allied executives said they have released Shopify’s space to other commercial tenants.

This year, Allied has sold $321-million of properties and expects to dispose of another $340-million by the end of December. The Reit is on track to exceed its goal of $500-million in asset sales this year.

One of Allied’s problem properties is an office-to-data centre conversion in Vancouver, called 150 West Georgia. Allied lent $268-million to its partner on the project, Westbank Corp., and expected partial repayment of $125-million this year.

On Wednesday, Allied said it no longer expected payment on the 150 West Georgia loan by December “due to construction delays being managed by a third party and ongoing discussions with prospective purchasers.”

Allied hired consulting firm Finnegan Marshall Inc. as its “development monitor and cost consultant” on the Vancouver project. The Riet said it “is actively engaged with its advisers to evaluate and pursue alternatives to maximize recovery of its outstanding loan.”

In February, Allied raised $560-million by selling units to investors for $10 each. As part of the equity offering, Allied sold $160-million of units to the Alberta Investment Management Corp. (AIMCo).

“The 90-per-cent distribution reduction is far greater than our 50-per-cent forecast,” said analyst Mario Saric at Bank of Nova Scotia in a report.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Pammi Bir said in a report the distribution cut “underscores the depths of Allied Properties’ challenges, including elevated leverage.”

Allied owes lenders $4-billion. The Reit owns $8.2-billion in properties and boosted its long-term target for property sales to a range from $750-million to $1.5-billion. Chief financial officer Craig MacIntyre said: “No asset in the portfolio is off limits.”

Allied management won plaudits from one analyst for taking dramatic steps to preserve cash. National Bank Capital Markets analysts Matt Kornack called the distribution cut “a positive move for the Reit” that “should have been done sooner.”
“It will go a long way to aiding in the goal of deleveraging, especially when combined with an accelerated disposition program,” Mr. Kornack said.

Allied’s landmark buildings include The Well, a 3.1-hectare office-and-residential development in downtown Toronto developed in partnership with RioCan Reit. Tech company Shopify Inc. was meant to be a major tenant in the property but opted out of its lease.
On Thursday, Allied executives said they have released Shopify’s space to other commercial tenants.

This year, Allied has sold $321-million of properties and expects to dispose of another $340-million by the end of December. The Reit is on track to exceed its goal of $500-million in asset sales this year.

One of Allied’s problem properties is an office-to-data centre conversion in Vancouver, called 150 West Georgia. Allied lent $268-million to its partner on the project, Westbank Corp., and expected partial repayment of $125-million this year.

On Wednesday, Allied said it no longer expected payment on the 150 West Georgia loan by December “due to construction delays being managed by a third party and ongoing discussions with prospective purchasers.”

Allied hired consulting firm Finnegan Marshall Inc. as its “development monitor and cost consultant” on the Vancouver project. The Riet said it “is actively engaged with its advisers to evaluate and pursue alternatives to maximize recovery of its outstanding loan.”

In February, Allied raised $560-million by selling units to investors for $10 each. As part of the equity offering, Allied sold $160-million of units to the Alberta Investment Management Corp. (AIMCo).

stories.title: Audit finds military using only half of ammunition purchases
stories.summary: The AG has found that the CAF is vastly overestimating how much ammunition it needs for regular use in training and international missions.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal auditor general has found that the Canadian Armed Forces is vastly overestimating how much ammunition it needs for regular use in training and international missions, and it says part of the problem can be chalked up to a lack of usable military equipment and an ongoing shortfall of uniformed personnel.

The audit also found that while the Department of National Defence has started to replenish the military’s strategic ammunition stockpile — the lethal ammunition needed for emergencies and combat operations — critical gaps remain.

Canada has identified a lack of available ammunition and stockpiled ammunition as a reason why it is not meeting the readiness level required of Nato members.

The five Canadian Armed Forces groups that account for 87 per cent of its regular ammunition use — the Army, Navy and Air Force along with the special operations forces command and Canadian joint operations command — are only using 56 per cent of what’s assigned to them, ON average.

The reasons for that were not well tracked. The audit noted that key equipment like tanks and ships are often out of service and unavailable for use in training and exercises, and that a lack of personnel and poor environmental conditions might prevent training from happening.

The audit said that because National Defence doesn’t track the reasons it’s not using its regular ammunition supplies, it has difficulty determining how much it will need each year. Ammunition that’s not used is expensive to store, and risks degrading or expiring on the shelf.

The report comes as the federal government is pouring billions of dollars into national defence in an effort to meet Canada’s Nato commitment to spend the equivalent of two per cent of GDP per year on defence.

In 2024-25, the government awarded some $800 million in contracts to procure ammunition. That number rose to $3 billion in 2025-26.

The audit looked at 15 of those contracts and found it took an average of 19 months between signing a deal and receiving the ammunition. In many cases, the ammunition was delivered late and contracts were extended.

In 2024, the government set aside $9.2 billion over 13 years to restore the strategic ammunition stockpile.

The audit noted that after decades of depleting that stockpile for things like training exercises, National Defence limited access to it in 2021 and tried to establish an inventory baseline. Five years later, the stockpile lacked “required types and quantities of ammunition necessary to meet targeted operational requirements,” the audit found.

The auditor general’s office is calling on the department to establish a formal, regular and documented process for supplying the stockpile.

Also in 2021, National Defence issued a directive to create an ammunition and explosives program meant to address supply and demand gaps and do a comprehensive review of existing processes. The auditor general’s office found the program was not yet established and the comprehensive review had no action plan or timelines attached.

The department has agreed it should develop the program and get it underway.

The auditor general flagged serious issues with data collection and management, and pointed out that it has been raising concerns with the department’s ability to account for the quantity and value of its inventory for more than 20 years.

The department does not have a central tracking system for ammunition expenses and isn’t able to produce a reliable, detailed breakdown of its spending. The auditor’s report says this means National Defence doesn’t have the necessary information to make decisions about its inventory.

In the last two fiscal years, about a third of National Defence locations have not completed their annual ammunition count, and the auditor estimates that meant some $656 million worth of inventory was not counted this year.

stories.title: Studio Red Live is back to showcase Fanshawe College music students
stories.summary: A popular student-fueled Fanshawe TV show is back, as part of a collaboration between the college's TV Film, M...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
A popular student-fueled Fanshawe TV show is back, as part of a collaboration between the college’s TV Film, Musical Industry Arts (MIA) and Multimedia Journalism programs.

Fanshawe TV control room (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM)

Fanshawe’s Studio Red Live aired Tuesday, featuring Fanshawe MIA band You Might Be Sleeping and hosted by journalism student Owen Schuller. The last episode aired nearly a year ago, in November 2025.

“It came up from one of our bosses saying, ‘this show was great. Let’s bring it back,'” said TV Production professor Scott Navarro.

Student camera operator Riley Seferiades said the show provides students an opportunity to get hands-on experience operating and moving heavy broadcast equipment.

“I love music and I’ve done music broadcast in the past, but this is more professional and a great learning experience,” said Seferiades.

This is the first year journalism students have joined the production.

Set up for Studio Red Live. Nico Valeriote, Attila Fay, Toby Rossi, Owen Schuller (Credit: FanshaweTV /YouTube)

“I’m excited to host a live show and watch the music they’re going to perform. I think it’s a great way to collaborate with the different programs,” Schuller said.

You Might Be Sleeping is an indie-rock band that has been together for almost six years, since the members were in high school.

“Our manager Nick McCarthy and coordinator got in contact with each other talking about the show and he recommended us which was awesome,” said bassist, Toby Rossi.

The band also consists if drummer, Attila Fay, and Nico Valeriote, who said the band gets some inspiration from popular 90s music.

Nico Valeriote (Credit: FanshaweTV /YouTube)

“Seeing my dad play guitar inspired me and singing came from guys like Curt Cobain (of Nirvana). I always like guys who play and sing,” Valeriote said.

Studio Red Live is already available on YouTube, and will soon be available on Rogers.

The next live episode airs next Tuesday Nov. 3, 2026 at 6 p.m.

stories.title: Shooting near Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood injures four
stories.summary: Police say they received reports of three people who were shot inside a residence near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East at around 3:43 a.m.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
A father and his two adult daughters were shot during a violent home invasion shooting inside a home in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood, Toronto police said Thursday.

Police said they received reports of three people who were shot inside a residence near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East at around 3:44 a.m.

Two parents and two adult children were transported to the hospital, police said. Two of the family members suffered life-altering injuries and two have non-life-threatening injuries.

Two of the victims remain in hospital.

Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith said the masked suspects were armed with guns and a hammer and forced their way into the home through the rear door.

They demanded valuables from the family, but Smith said it was not clear if any belongings were stolen.

A struggle ensued and the suspects shot their weapons multiple times. One victim was struck with a hammer, Smith said.

Three suspects fled in an SUV, investigators said. No descriptions of the suspects were provided.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is,” Smith said. “People should be able to feel safe in their homes.”

Police said the investigation is ongoing and they will have an increased presence in the neighbourhood. They asked that anyone with more information or dash cam footage contact them.

Police data as of last Friday show 119 home invasions have been reported in Toronto this year, up more than 35 per cent from the same time last year, spokesperson Ashley Visser said in an e-mail.

stories.title: Western alumni and students win top honours in Global Undergraduate Awards
stories.summary: Western ranks third worldwide for undergraduate research recognized through international competition
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
On the morning of her first day of graduate school, Michelle-Lynn Balderston opened an email with some unexpected news: a paper she had written during her final year at Western had been named the best in the world in its category.

Balderston, BA’26, was named Global Winner in the global communication category for the 2026 Global Undergraduate Awards – an international academic competition celebrating exceptional undergraduate research and creative work.

“I was completely shocked,” she said. Receiving the news that morning “definitely provided me with a good dose of motivation and confidence to tackle the new school year.”

Balderston is one of 12 Western students recognized in this year’s awards, which drew 2,373 submissions from 327 universities in 112 countries. For the second consecutive year, Western ranked first in the Americas and second globally for ‘highly commended’ entries. The university also ranked third worldwide and second in the Americas overall.

Balderston’s paper explored how two anti-Apartheid organizations in the Netherlands used posters and collective memories in their activism against South Africa’s apartheid system, bringing together her interests in activism and her Dutch heritage. Read more about Balderston’s research.

Among all the Western winners, research spanned eight of the competition’s 25 award categories, from health and life sciences to the humanities and social sciences.

DiLosa’s research explored whether a bacterial enzyme could be used as a tool to help scientists study an important lipid found in cell membranes. She also modified the enzyme to see whether she could improve its activity.

“When I realized I was a regional winner, I couldn’t believe it. It felt validating to have my hard work recognized globally,” she said. Read more about DiLosa’s research.

Torres Escandon’s fourth-year thesis explored how inflammation is regulated in the brain, research that could help scientists better understand inflammation associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

“It felt like the hours I put into my thesis had come full circle, and like the perfect way to end my undergraduate degree at Western,” she said. Read more about Torres Escandon’s research.

Agakishiev’s research examined why workplace violence against nurses remains prevalent in Canadian health care settings despite existing legal protections. She explores gaps between legal safeguards and their implementation, identifying underreporting, inconsistent enforcement, limited employer accountability, and institutional cultures that normalize violence as key barriers.

“This experience showed me you don’t have to be free of doubt to take a chance on yourself,” she said. Read more about Agakishiev’s research.

Eight Western students also earned ‘highly commended’ honours across a range of disciplines.

The recipients were Jamal al-Ghaziri (literature); Ananya Kalra (psychology); Isaac McKeown and Justin Donovan (medical sciences); Aranya Thavakumar (nursing, midwifery and allied health care); Anum Qaiser and Yi Qu (sociology and social policy); and Ebunoluwa Esomojumi (anthropology and cultural studies), who received the recognition for two separate submissions.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Ottawa launches telecom roadmap to improve competition, consumer choice
stories.summary: The federal government says it is launching a roadmap to boost competition and choice within Canada's telecommunications sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says it is launching a road map to boost competition and choice within Canada’s telecommunications sector.

The plan, announced late Wednesday by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, is meant to break down regional barriers and promote cross-Canada competition in the internet and mobile services sector. It incorporates many policies already unveiled by the federal government and Crtc in recent years, while also outlining a strategy for future actions.

In the road map, the government said it is helping to give consumers more choices and make it easier for providers to access existing networks, or expand the infrastructure they own.

“As the global economy rapidly evolves, Canadians are increasingly relying on telecommunications services in their everyday lives,” said Joly in a statement.

“By improving competition, empowering consumers and supporting the expansion of networks and services, this road map truly puts Canadians first, through actions that will improve choice, transparency, prices and networks.”

The strategy highlights previously introduced regulations, such as those requiring large internet providers to open up their networks to competitors who can resell service to customers in exchange for a fee.

While the rules were initially touted as a way to help smaller companies compete, they also allow large companies to resell internet using their rivals’ networks outside their core regions. Both Telus Corp. and Bell Canada have begun offering fibre service to customers in each other’s dominant territory under the framework.

The policy applies only to existing fibre networks, and any new fibre built by the large telecoms can’t be made available to competitors until 2029.

The government also wants to help consumers take advantage of more affordable plans, noting cellular plan prices are down 49 per cent compared with 2019. It said the government “will spotlight” competitive offers on the market, make it easier to shop around and switch providers, and eliminate unnecessary fees.

Much of that work has been prioritized over the past year by the telecommunications regulator.

In June, the Crtc banned companies from charging fees to activate, change or cancel a plan — a move the government estimates will save consumers $100 million per year — and other new rules require providers to offer self‑serve options to switch or end plans and provide end-of-contract notifications.

Beginning next March, a new policy will also take effect requiring internet providers to disclose certain information via a standardized label when promoting their plans. They must advertise typical speeds associated with a plan during hours of peak usage and list the monthly price after any promotion ends.

Part of the road map appears to respond to industry concerns in recent years, with major players frequently highlighting the need to ensure regulatory policies create incentives for them to invest in new technologies and infrastructure.

The government said it will help companies deploy the latest fibre-optic networks, experiment with new technologies and strengthen access to connectivity in northern, rural and Indigenous communities.

It plans to release more 5G spectrum — the electromagnetic frequencies that enable smartphone communications — over the next three years, which will increase the total spectrum available for wireless services five-fold. Canadians can also expect increased satellite-based cellular and internet services as the technology continues to evolve, the document said.

Last week, a new report from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications Association said the focus of Canada’s telecom policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks, citing that traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are expected to rise. The paper called for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously hinted at an eagerness to help the industry’s infrastructure needs. Last month, while speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, Carney said the government planned to help “finance new nation-building infrastructure, including a sovereign broadband backbone that connects Canadians from coast to coast to coast with more direct and secure links to Europe and Asia.”

Last year’s federal budget also announced a new “dig once” policy approach, which is meant to encourage telecom companies to co-ordinate when installing fibre optic lines as part of the development of major projects such as energy transmission, railways, pipelines, and roads and highways.

The road map released this week said that strategy could result in significant savings for companies, with studies having shown that 75 to 90 per cent of the cost of a fibre project comes from construction and labour activity rather than the fibre itself.

Meanwhile, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada is consulting on changes to speed up wireless tower approvals, the road map noted.

It said the Crtc will also speed up how it handles disputes between providers, using tools such as mediation and administrative penalties to ensure companies meet their obligations.

The Canadian Telecommunications Association said Ottawa’s priority should be building on progress that has already seen prices come down for consumers “by ensuring that Canada’s telecommunications policies support both competition and the substantial private investment needed.”

“Measures that make it easier to invest and deploy advanced networks, including making more spectrum available for wireless services, implementing ‘dig once’ policies, streamlining wireless tower approvals, and reducing red tape and unnecessary regulatory burdens, are particularly important,” said spokesperson Nick Kyonka in a statement.

“Policies that balance competition with the need for sustainable investment are essential to delivering lasting benefits for consumers and supporting Canada’s broader economic ambitions.”

The government plans to monitor progress of its various goals through indicators such as prices, switching behaviour, network speeds, coverage and consumer complaints.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Two people charged after human remains found in Calgary home: police
stories.summary: Calgary police said its officers were called around 8:15 a.m. Tuesday to a home in the 200 block of Skyview Ranch Road N.E. for a welfare check.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Two people are facing charges after Calgary police reportedly found human remains inside a home.

Calgary police said its officers were called around 8:15 a.m. Tuesday to a home in the 200 block of Skyview Ranch Road N.E. for a welfare check.

The remains were found during a search of the home, police said. A 49-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman have each been charged with indignity to a dead body.

Police are in the process confirming the identity of the remains and how they died.

An autopsy is scheduled for Thursday, and the victim’s name will be released once officially identified by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Auditor general reports to detail greenhouse gases, coal and pesticides
stories.summary: The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies' progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies’ progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and working toward a ban on the export of thermal coal.

The latest batch of reports from Auditor General Karen Hogan will also evaluate efforts to reduce health and environmental risks from pesticides, manage the Canadian Dental Care Plan and oversee the national emergency stockpile.

Other audits will examine the activities of Canada’s anti-money laundering centre, the Canadian Armed Forces’ management of ammunition and the federal border agency’s collection of customs duties and taxes.

Another report will assess whether several agencies managed procurement and contracts of selected call centre systems with regard to economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

Hogan plans to hold a media conference to discuss the reports after they are tabled in the House of Commons.

Liberal cabinet ministers and opposition MPs are also expected to comment on the auditor’s findings.

stories.title: Hamilton Stelco workers to get $1,100 profit-sharing cheques, as Cliffs asserts business isn’t profitable
stories.summary: Union president questions why workers were laid off given that bonus amounts are substantially higher than a year ago
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Stelco Inc. workers in Hamilton are set to receive profit-sharing cheques of more than $1,000 apiece for the latest quarter, even as U.S. parent Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N asserts the plant’s galvanized-steel business isn’t making money.

On Sept. 28, Stelco said it was cutting hundreds of jobs in Canada in large part because its steel business in Hamilton wasn’t profitable. So far, 175 people have been laid off.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, told The Globe and Mail that employees at Stelco’s Hamilton plant are set to receive around $1,100 each for the fiscal quarter ending Sept. 30 with the final amount dependent on the exact number of hours worked.

The Ohio-based steelmaker has repeatedly argued that the layoffs are necessary because it can’t make money in Canadian galvanized steel, which Stelco manufactures in Hamilton.

Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Wells questioned why workers were laid off given that they are not only receiving bonus cheques, but the amounts are substantially higher than a year ago. In the comparable third quarter of 2025, the average profit-sharing cheque for each Hamilton worker was only around $85, he said.

Since then, Stelco’s Hamilton employees have been consistently receiving bonuses, Mr. Wells said, with workers earning on average $3,400 apiece in the fourth quarter of 2025, $1,300 in the first quarter of 2026 and $900 in the second quarter.

After the layoffs were announced, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Cliffs had “betrayed” its work force. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has repeatedly demanded the company comply with legally binding commitments made after Cliffs acquired the Canadian steelmaker in 2024, or face being sued, or forced to divest the business.

Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves has said repeatedly that fierce competition from overseas imports and the inability to sell into the U.S., owing to the 50-per-cent tariffs, has made its Canadian galvanized-steel business uneconomic.

But concerns have already been raised that Cliffs coated-steel business May be stronger than it is claiming. Earlier this month, Jim Ritchie, owner of Cascadia Metals Ltd., a former buyer of coated steel from Stelco, told The Globe that the galvanized market is booming .

“Cleveland-Cliffs comes out and says it’s not economical to make galvanized steel in Canada. What a joke,” he said.

Last week, Cliffs requested a meeting with Ms. Joly to discuss ways to potentially bring workers back. On Wednesday, Mr. Goncalves said they could be back on the job by Christmas if demand from Canadian steel customers is high enough.

On Thursday, Ms. Joly in a new letter to Stelco president Paul Simon said Cliffs must come up with a “concrete and credible plan” to immediately bring back the laid-off workers.

Mr. Goncalves said on Wednesday that his plan “will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco.”

By laying off workers in Canada, Ms. Joly has alleged the company violated a commitment around maintaining certain employment levels when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

Cliffs has repeatedly said that it is not offside with its commitments and has provided data showing its employment levels are above the minimum threshold.

But in her latest letter to Cliffs, Ms. Joly said that the company’s compliance claims fall short, saying that in several instances there isn’t enough hard evidence.

“Assertions of compliance are not a substitute for the information and evidence necessary to establish compliance,” she wrote.

Ms. Joly has said multiple times that Cliffs could face financial penalties or be forced to divest Stelco for non-compliance with its Investment Canada Act commitments.

Mr. Goncalves said in an e-mail to The Globe on Wednesday that before his company acquired Stelco, the Canadian steelmaker “was flooding the U.S. hot rolled steel market,” doubling down on comments he made during a U.S. congressional hearing in January when he called Canada a “problematic” trade partner.

“Since we acquired Stelco in 2024 – before President Trump was back in office – we blocked Stelco from selling steel into the U.S. market,” he said in the congressional hearing.

Mr. Carney was asked on Thursday during a media scrum in Montreal that given everything that is now known about Cliffs, whether it was a mistake to allow it to buy Stelco.

“The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition,” he said.

With a report from Stephanie Levitz

stories.title: National security strategy release expected to focus on economic safegaurds
stories.summary: The Liberal government plans to release a national security strategy today that maps out plans to safeguard Canada's economy.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Liberal government plans to release a national security strategy today that maps out plans to safeguard Canada’s economy.

The long-awaited strategy is also expected to discuss the handling of traditional security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism.

David Morrison, diplomatic and international affairs adviser to Prime Minister Mark Carney, recently told a House of Commons committee the strategy looks to bolster Canada’s defences against an array of security threats.

Privy Council Office spokesperson Mélany Gauvin said recently the strategy would increase Canada’s focus on economic security.

In 2004, the Liberal government led by Paul Martin released Securing an Open Society, the most recent overarching national security policy.

The new policy is likely to address shifting global alliances, Arctic security and Canada’s intelligence needs in a volatile world.

stories.title: Doug Ford ‘all in’ on ending seasonal time changes if Quebec, eastern U.S. agree
stories.summary: The discussion about ending seasonal time changes has been revived for Ontario as several provinces and territories all opted to keep daylight time this year.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he will be “all in” on ending seasonal time changes only if Quebec and parts of the United States are fully on board.

“I’m easy going. This argument has been going on for decades,” he said. “If Quebec and New York and the eastern corridor of the U.S. wants to do it, I’m all in,” he said.

Quebec Premier Paul St- Pierre Plamondon announced last month that the province is planning to scrap the twice-annual time switch, but the government hasn’t decided yet if it will keep daylight time or standard time for the entire year.

“(Plamondon) was going to do it, then he pulled back,” said Ford. He said he’s ready to get on the same page once Plamandon is ready.

“At the end of the day, it’s pitch black out there. So I am very open to discussions with the premier of Quebec.”

Ontario has made regulatory changes to the Time Act and allowed regions west of the 90th meridian to align with Manitoba and keep daylight time. Manitoba decided in September to make daylight time permanent.

The discussion about ending seasonal time changes has been revived for Ontario as Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia all opted this year to keep daylight time in perpetuity. Saskatchewan does not adjust its clocks.

By Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press

EDMONTON - Two more soldiers injured in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have been discharged from hospital.

The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario, so they can receive treatment closer to their families.

The update comes a little more than two weeks after a fierce wind whipped a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright onto troops in a training exercise.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

The Oct. 17 blaze killed four and left 39 wounded, many with serious burns.

Officials previously said 13 were in critical condition.

“Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” said a news release.

“Ongoing support and services remain available to injured personnel, their families, and all CAF members as they continue to navigate the effects of this tragedy.”

Three separate investigations are looking into the fire.

stories.title: Ford says Osap auditors will clear low-risk career colleges first; no timeline given
stories.summary: Career college students say they don't know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their Osap funding that had been previously approved.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says an audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, but he was not clear on a timeline.

Ford’s government paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions while Kpmg is conducting an audit looking at serious concerns with the integrity of the system.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said that pause will last until the government puts a new and strengthened approval process in place for career colleges looking for Osap eligibility, and he expects that to be done in the new year.

In the meantime, career college students say they don’t know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their Osap funding that had been previously approved.

Career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions have been calling on the government to take more targeted action against schools they refer to as “bad actors,” while not making innocent students pay the price.

Ford says his government has asked Kpmg to prioritize low-risk colleges to get money flowing again as soon as possible, but he did not give a specific idea of timing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: ‘We’re in tough times’: Doug Ford shuts the door on new funding deal for Toronto
stories.summary: The initial three-year, $1.2 billion new deal was ironed out in November 2023 after Olivia Chow was first elected mayor.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford is shutting down any talk of a new funding deal for the City of Toronto, suggesting Ontario’s $16.9 billion deficit has left the province facing “tough times” with less room to support municipal budgets.

The initial three-year, $1.2 billion new deal was ironed out in November 2023 after Olivia Chow was first elected mayor.

As part of the agreement, the province agreed to fund new transit vehicles, upload both the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, and gave the city $353 million for operation and maintenance until the upload is complete.

As the city crafts its latest budget, hopes for a revised funding deal remained high.

Under repeated questioning from Global News, however, the finance minister, municipal affairs minister and premier said the government doesn’t have plans for a new deal 2.0.

“There’s no 2.0, to answer your question directly,” Ford said during a news conference at Queen’s Park on Wednesday.

“Keep in mind with collaboration with the federal and the provincial government, we’ve given Toronto $9 billion — with a ‘B’. They have to be responsible for their own budget.”

While the premier said he was willing to look at “certain priorities” such as crime reduction and public safety on subways, he also suggested the province might be tapped out of cash to help municipal governments.

“You can’t always rely on the province. We’re in tough times right now, really tough times. So we’re going to be prudent fiscal managers, respecting the taxpayer,” Ford said.

The comments come after the Ford government tabled the fall economic statement, which included $36 billion in deficits over the next three years and once again delayed the province’s path to balancing the budget.

Critics say the government overleveraged on capital construction during its early years, leaving the province with little capacity to help.

“You know, we have cost overruns at the Ottawa Hospital, the Ontario Line, the Eglinton Crosstown, the Scarborough subway. We’re spending billions of dollars on things that we build, but the stuff that happens inside, it’s not working,” said interim Liberal leader John Fraser.

“What’s the point in building a hospital or a school if the stuff happens inside isn’t working for people? And this government needs to start to focus on that.”

“If the municipalities don’t get a new fiscal deal, we’re likely going to see double-digit property tax increases. I’ve been telling mayors they should call it the Doug Ford property tax increase,” Schreiner said.

“Homelessness is also only going to get worse. Municipalities cannot solve this crisis. They don’t have the fiscal resources to do it. We need the province to step up.”

stories.title: Doug Ford says he did ‘cartwheels’ after seeing U.S. midterm election results
stories.summary: As soon as the newly elected U.S. officials are sworn in at the end of January, Ford said he’s directing his ministers to head down to Washington, D.C.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford said he was doing “cartwheels” and was “as happy as possible” when he saw the results of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections , which saw the Democratic Party flip the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, in a clear rebuke of Donald Trump’s presidency.

“Trump wants to blame everyone but himself,” said Ford. “The cheese has slipped off the cracker with this guy.”

But Ford cautioned that Ontario is “under no illusions that the trade war is done.” “It’s not even close to being done because (Trump) still has the power…the January tariffs are still on the table,” he said.

As soon as the newly elected U.S. officials are sworn in at the end of January, Ford said he’s directing his ministers to head down to Washington, D.C. and connect with senators, congresspeople and governors about the importance of Ontario as a trading partner and the damage done by the trade war with the U.S.

“We’re going to be down there, communicating, building those relationships,” he said. “We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board.”

As the midterm results flowed in Tuesday night, the sheer scale of the Democrat’s win quickly became apparent. Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina. Seven seats were flipped in total.

Democrats also triumphed in the House of Representatives, clearing the number of seats needed to take control of the chamber. Historic wins were seen in several governor races, with Keisha Lance Bottoms being elected as Georgia’s first Black female governor.

It was a clear indication of Americans’ disapproval of Trump’s policies, which have led to higher prices at the pump and grocery stores.

New officials in office is a huge opportunity for Ontario, said Ford, particularly as the trade war with Canada became ballot box issues in Michigan and Maine, where the province is a key trading partner.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive senator-elect who won the Michigan race, is someone Ford said he’s willing to work with.

“He wants jobs, he wants prosperity. He wants economic growth in Michigan….we’re going to continue building that great relationship,” he said.

But Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser said Ford needs to temper his excitement as “the reality is we’re not out of the woods.”

“Trump is still the president. The representatives that were elected last night won’t take office until January. What we need is a plan,” he said.

Fraser urged Ford to take a more “disciplined” approach and follow the tone set by Prime Minister Mark Carney. “I would not get excited and say ‘Trump lost’, how’s that going to do any good?” said Fraser. “You’re getting out of the gate.”

When it comes to ironing out a trade deal with the president, Ford said it’s ultimately up to Prime Minister Mark Carney and shook his head when asked if Trump can be relied upon in negotiations.

“I can’t trust [Trump] as far as I could throw him…maybe the Prime Minister feels differently, but he has shown, over and over again, that he can’t be trusted,” said Ford.

On Tuesday, Carney said “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. had begun following his call with Trump last weekend. He said both sides have made progress on the issue of restricting Canada’s ability to negotiate deals with other countries.

In August, Carney called off formal trade talks with the U.S., after rejecting what he described as a “bad deal.” Canada launched retaliatory counter-tariffs in September that ranged from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods.

stories.title: Spy watchdog flags privacy risk from military’s online intelligence activities
stories.summary: A national spy watchdog report says the military's policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn't sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A national spy watchdog report says the military’s policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn’t sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.

The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency found the Defence Department and the Canadian Armed Forces have the legal authority to collect publicly available information from the internet for intelligence purposes, but the watchdog noted shortcomings on privacy protection and oversight.

The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it’s collected and analyzed by government organizations.

It says Canadians should be able to trust that intelligence collection has a clear, lawful purpose and that their privacy rights are respected.

The watchdog found the military does not systematically record the link between open-source collection activities on the internet and the approved operation or defence activity.

It also says policies and record-keeping do not adequately address all privacy risks or demonstrate that collection involving Canadians is necessary.

stories.title: Canadian woman accused of joining Isis was ‘brainwashed,’ former friend testifies
stories.summary: At Canada's first trial of a woman accused of living under Isis in Syria, a witness described Ammara Amjad's descent into extremism.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A witness testifying at the trial of a Canadian woman accused of joining Isis in Syria has described watching her close friend become “brainwashed.”

Naveed Deol said she and Ammara Amjad were once like sisters. But Amjad’s extremist rhetoric eventually became so preachy that they parted ways.

“It just wasn’t the same person,” Deol testified.

Captured in Syria during the 2019 defeat of Isis , Amjad is currently on trial in Brampton, Ont., for participating in the activities of a terrorist group.

She is the first Canadian woman to face criminal prosecution for allegedly living under the Islamic State in Syria as the terror group committed atrocities.

The Crown wrapped up its case against the Pakistan-born 32-year-old mother of two on Wednesday, following testimony from the RCMP officer who extracted Amjad’s messages from her mother’s phone.

Appearing as a Crown witness on Tuesday, Deol described her former friend’s sudden transformation — a change she blamed on Amjad’s first husband, Canadian extremist Bilal Khan .

Deol said she first met Amjad when their families lived in Montreal. She later moved in with the Amjads in Brampton while she completed her studies.

Far from an extremist in her teens, Amjad came from a happy Pakistani-Canadian family, would drink alcohol and remove her hijab once she had left home, Deol said.

But in 2015, when the two met at a Boston Pizza, Amjad said Khan had been sending her reading materials, people were suffering and she wanted to help.

Then Amjad asked Deol to take her to the airport. She said she was flying to Turkey to meet Khan, who was already in the Middle East, she explained.

Deol said she felt Amjad, then a 19-year old Walmart worker who had never showed any interest in politics or current affairs, was having an “existential crisis.”

Although Amjad was vague about specifics, Deol suspected she was heading for Syria to join an extremist group and refused to take her friend to the airport.

“I was concerned for her safety,” Deol said, adding she feared Khan was misleading a naive teenager. “I felt that he had brainwashed her.”

On March 17, 2015, Amjad applied to renew her Canadian passport, writing that she was travelling on March 19. She allegedly crossed from Turkey into Isis controlled Syria.

Although she never gave away her location, she messaged Deol upon arriving to say that she had married Khan, a suspected Isis fighter, and “was happy.”

“Bilal left today,” according to a message Amjad sent to Deol on WhatsApp. “I don’t know when he’s going to be back or even if he will be back.”

When Khan was killed in November 2015, Amjad took it in stride, Deol said. “She always knew that he was going to die and she was prepared for it.”

Amjad later gave birth to their child, but the baby only lived a day. Again, she was fatalistic. “I’m happy. Whatever happens, happens for a reason,” she said.

Deol, who said she was not religious, said Amjad would accuse her of being “blinded” and not knowing anything, and that she needed to think about the afterlife

Over time, they lost touch. Deol said she was busy with her own life and had grown tired of the way Amjad spoke to her about religion.

By the time they reconnected, Amjad had been taken prisoner by U.S.-backed Kurdish fighters and was being held at a camp for Isis families in northeast Syria.

“I just don’t know you anymore,” she told Amjad.

She said she felt guilty that she hadn’t warned Amjad’s parents that their daughter was talking about going to Turkey. But she decided to let her friend go.

She tried to message her once more, when the RCMP visited her in 2020 and said they were trying to bring her home from Syria, but Amjad never responded.

Amjad spent four years in detention camps for Isis suspects until the Canadian government brought her home from Syria in April 2023. She was charged with terrorism in October 2023.

Dozens of Canadian extremists left B.C., Alberta, Ontario and Quebec to join Isis after the terror group emerged from Al Qaeda and seized parts of Syria and Iraq.

While many died, several were captured during the 2019 rout of Isis. Canada has repatriated nine women from Syria, at significant expense . Two have pleaded guilty, but a half-dozen others have not been charged .

The Crown’s case hinges largely on Amjad’s own messages, which are mostly in Urdu, while the defence has challenged the accuracy of the RCMP’s translations.

“It just wasn’t the same person,” Deol testified.

She is the first Canadian woman to face criminal prosecution for allegedly living under the Islamic State in Syria as the terror group committed atrocities.

stories.title: Amazon breaks ground on 200,000-square metre fulfilment warehouse in the Halifax area
stories.summary: Dartmouth - American e-commerce giant Amazon held a ground-breaking ceremony in the Halifax area today for a massive new warehouse that will use robots and more than 1,000 full-time employees to fulfil orders.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
DARTMOUTH - American e-commerce giant Amazon held a groundbreaking ceremony in the Halifax area Wednesday for a massive new warehouse that will use robots and more than 1,000 full-time employees to fulfil orders.

The online retailer said the warehouse in Dartmouth, N.S., will cover more than 200,000-square metres in the Burnside industrial park. It’s slated to open in 2029.

Brooks Barnett, head of economic development for Amazon Canada, declined to say how much the project will cost.

He said Halifax’s port, growing customer base and openness to investment were reasons Amazon chose the area for the new facility.

Barnett said the new site should offer more products and speed up deliveries for customers in the region, but he would not commit to same-day delivery.

“The second you click ‘buy,’ a robot in this building will be moving to satisfy your order,” Barnett said, adding that the facility will complement Amazon’s existing Dartmouth delivery facility.

Barnett said employee wages will start at $26 per hour. Benefits will include health, dental and a retirement savings plan.

He declined to say if the new site will replace a warehouse in Quebec that the company shuttered in January 2025 after employees there formed a union.

“All I’ll say is that we respect our employees’ right to have their voice heard and to make whatever decisions they want around unionization. But today we’re really talking about a new investment here in this region,” he said.

About 240 Amazon workers at the company’s warehouse in Laval, Que., unionized in May 2024, becoming the first of the tech company’s Canadian warehouses to do so.

The company had challenged the union drive before the province’s labour tribunal, but their case was rejected in October 2024. The tribunal’s ruling was upheld by Quebec Superior Court last month.

Amazon also faced anti-union allegations at a now-closed warehouse in the Montreal borough of Lachine. In August 2024, the labour tribunal ordered Amazon to stop interfering in union affairs and pay the union $30,000.

In January 2026, Amazon Canada announced it would close all seven of its Quebec warehouses within two months, eliminating 1,700 permanent jobs and 250 temporary ones.

At the time, the company said the move was aimed at cutting costs and improving service, and it insisted the closures had nothing to do with unionization.

Amazon isn’t the only major U.S. tech firm growing its operations in Nova Scotia. Artificial intelligence firm Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease to set up in a proposed $10-billion data centre in Cape Breton, slated to open late next year.

Meanwhile, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said there’s no government money in the Amazon project. While the province does have economic development programs that the Jeff Bezos-led company can apply for, Houston said Amazon is driving the investment on its own.

“This is a company investing in our province, like the data centre as well. That’s not government money either,” the premier told reporters Wednesday. “So these are good statements from international companies about the prospects that they see for Nova Scotia.”

Barnett declined to comment on how Democrats taking control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections could impact Amazon’s business, which has sought close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, a Republican, in his second term.

In his first term, Trump accused Bezos of using The Washington Post, which he owns, to persuade politicians not to tax Amazon. Trump also criticized the Post and Bezos over coverage of his campaign and presidency.

In 2019, Amazon sued after the Pentagon awarded a $10-billion cloud computing contract to Microsoft, alleging Trump’s interference harmed Amazon’s chances of winning.

Both sides have been friendlier since Trump won the 2024 election. In December 2024, Amazon said it planned to donate US$1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund. The company also and said it would stream the event on Prime Video, a separate in-kind donation worth another US$1 million.

The following month, Amazon acquired the licensing rights for a documentary about First Lady Melania Trump. In March 2025, it began streaming the first seven seasons of Trump’s reality show “The Apprentice.”

In November 2025, Amazon was among the 37 donors the government said were helping to pay for Trump’s US$300-million White House ballroom.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— With files from Michael MacDonald and The Associated Press.

stories.title: Ford says Osap auditors will clear low-risk career colleges first; no timeline given
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford says an audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, but he was not clear on a timeline.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - An audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at Ontario career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, Premier Doug Ford said Wednesday, but he was not clear on a timeline.

Ford’s government paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions while KPMG is conducting an audit looking at serious concerns with the integrity of the system.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said the audit’s preliminary findings include concerns about inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment, and unusually high concentrations of OSAP from the same geographic locations. He has referred those preliminary findings to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Quinn has said he paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions while that audit is ongoing because concerns are systemic and he wants to ensure the integrity of the system.

But colleges, students and critics say it is too blunt of an instrument and is making students pay the price even at schools where no concerns have been raised. Many students say they don’t know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their OSAP funding that had been previously approved.

Ford said Wednesday that his government has asked KPMG to look at the most reliable colleges first, but he did not give a specific idea of timing.

“We’ve asked KPMG to prioritize low-risk colleges,” he said. “Let’s get them back up and moving as quickly as possible, and that’s our goal.”

Bianca Giacoboni, a spokesperson for Quinn, later said the ministry is “working as quickly as possible to restore integrity to the private post-secondary OSAP system” and renew institutions’ access to OSAP.

Tatiana Bramnik, a vice-president at APlus Institute, said students at her dental hygienist career college are already having to withdraw and she is facing the prospect of having to consider layoffs with OSAP-funded students unable to pay their tuition.

Quinn should not have enacted a blanket OSAP pause in the first place, Bramnik said.

“This is a crisis they created, and now they don’t know how to deal with it,” she said.

Bramnik and her business partner came to Canada 33 years ago as immigrants from the former Soviet Union and many of their students are immigrants, she said, people who were professionals in their home country and want the accelerated education a career college can provide so they can start working and support their families.

“Dental hygiene is a good opportunity, still in high demand, and very well paid, so it’s a chance,” she said. “It’s a chance to have a normal life, to be able to live your life fully and give this to your children.”

Career Colleges Ontario said in a statement that it is hopeful that OSAP will be restored “without delay” for students at compliant institutions.

“Our position has been consistent: concerns about some institutions should not result in students at compliant colleges losing access to the financial assistance they rely on,” the association wrote in a statement.

“For many students, OSAP helps cover not only tuition, but also rent, food, transportation, books and other essential living costs. Restoring access for students at compliant institutions is urgent.”

Quinn has said the OSAP pause will last until the government puts a new and strengthened approval process in place for career colleges, and he expects that to be done in the new year.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said students at institutions who have always followed the rules should never have been caught up in this in the first place.

“Students did all the right things,” she said. “They are pursuing careers in professions that we desperately need in Ontario, and they are being punished for this minister’s incompetence.”

Quinn has also said the government is reaching out to banks to try to secure third-party loans for students while OSAP is paused, but he has not given any updates on that in the month since making the announcement.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said students can’t wait until the new year.

“People live paycheque to paycheque,” he said. “The premier doesn’t understand that.”

Ford also said the KPMG report will “eventually” be released, but he doesn’t want to jeopardize a potential OPP investigation. That is counter to what Quinn said Tuesday, when he said the audit would not be made public.

Quinn’s office said later that day that they will “consider” releasing information from the audit if it doesn’t compromise a potential police investigation, a potential future auditor general investigation, “or the ministry’s efforts to obtain evidence, recover funds and hold bad actors accountable.”

The government is in panic mode, Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner suggested.

“I think the government knows they have completely mismanaged the OSAP file, and they don’t know what to do about it,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Man seriously injured in Hamilton assault involving cadets selling poppies
stories.summary: A 59-year-old man suffered life-altering injuries after intervening in an incident involving air cadets selling poppies over the weekend, Hamilton police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 59-year-old man suffered life-altering injuries after intervening in an incident involving air cadets selling poppies over the weekend, Hamilton police say.

The man was supervising the cadets outside a restaurant at 1223 Barton St. E. Sunday afternoon when two youths allegedly approached and blew an air horn directly into their ears, police said in a news release.

He then followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them.

“A struggle ensued and an adult female who was not initially involved in the altercation jumped in to assist the youths,” police said.

Police allege the woman assaulted the man, who fell to the ground. One of the youths then hit the victim several times before leaving the restaurant. The woman also left the scene before police arrived.

“Upon arrival, officers located the adult male victim inside the restaurant suffering from serious injuries. Hamilton Paramedic Services attended and transported the victim to a local hospital for treatment. His injuries are considered life-altering,” police said.

“A short time later, officers located the two youths at a nearby retail store after receiving reports of a new, unrelated disturbance.”

A 12-year-old boy was arrested and charged with assault level one as well as aggravated assault. A 48-year-old woman was arrested Tuesday and charged with aggravated assault.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: 'A victory across the world,' Ontario Premier Doug Ford says after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he was "doing cartwheels" after the Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was “doing cartwheels” after the Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.

Ford cautioned the trade war is not over, but said he is buoyed by the rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump by the American electorate.

“I was doing cartwheels down the street,” Ford said at Queen’s Park on Wednesday.

“But it’s very simple, the American people spoke on a couple issues: cost of living, cost of gas, the war in Iran, but most important is tariffs, because that’s all tied into the cost of living.”

On Tuesday, Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina while also taking over House seats.

Trump has begun backpedalling following the losses, shifting blame elsewhere but also pledging to work with the Democrats in a rare moment of bipartisanship.

Ford called out Trump for lambasting some of his supporters after the loss, including Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

“The cheese has slipped off the cracker with this guy totally,” Ford said of Trump. “Like there is no cracker, there’s no more cheese, and I think the Republican Party are going to start moving forward without him.”

Ford and Trump traded barbs in late August after Trump said he would implement stiff tariffs on the auto sector on Jan. 1. Ford told Trump to “kiss my ass” in response, which enraged Trump, who responded by saying Ford was the less charismatic and less intelligent brother to the late Rob Ford, the former mayor of Toronto.

stories.title: AFN chief says no one besides Carney, Kinew talked about abolishing Indian Act
stories.summary: The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
stories.content:
Ottawa — The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, called for the act to be abolished during the historic gathering of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

The prime minister said he was “very open to” the idea but later said it could be reformed rather than abolished.

The Indian Act, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do.

Both Kinew and Carney said the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room, but AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says that’s not true.

Woodhouse Nepinak says the chiefs were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, and those conversations “went to the wayside” after Kinew and Carney made their remarks.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: McGill confirms convicted murderer no longer enrolled as a law student
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal's McGill University says a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 is no longer a student.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Montreal’s McGill University says a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 is no longer a student.

McGill’s provost, Angela Campbell, informed students and staff about the news in a statement sent on Monday.

“McGill’s principal obligation is our duty of care to everyone who learns, works and lives on our campuses,” Campbell wrote.

Campbell sent the message after news from October about Jeffrey George Ewart’s enrolment in law classes while on parole sparked concern about student safety and debate over whether or not he should be allowed to attend.

Ewert, now in his 60s, was sentenced to two life sentences after he sexually assaulted and strangled two women in British Columbia in separate 1984 incidents that left one victim dead and the other severely disabled.

Campbell’s note did not identify Ewart by name, but said a person on day parole who was admitted to its law faculty this fall is no longer enrolled.

“Each student and colleague deserves a learning and research environment that is safe, respectful, inclusive, and conducive to their flourishing and success’” Campbell said.

Campbell said the university has launched an independent review of admissions processes and protocols that will take several months to complete.

“The goal of this review is to make sure existing procedures are sufficiently rigorous, set clearly defined responsibilities, and reflect our values, our academic mission, and our duty of care,” she wrote.

Campbell said the school is also committed to “dignity and second chances.”

“We believe in rehabilitation and in education’s power to transform lives,” the statement read. “Accordingly, past convictions do not, on their own, bar anyone from studying here.”

Campbell also acknowledged that students have been under strain due to media attention generated by the case, and that “differing views about recent events have created tensions within our community.”

The statement did not say whether Ewert’s enrolment was revoked by the school or whether he withdrew. The Canadian Press could not immediately reach his lawyer for comment.

Correctional Service Canada confirmed that it had issued a warrant to suspend Ewert’s conditional release and said he has returned to custody while the situation is being reviewed.

The agency said it can move to return someone to custody “when there are reasonable grounds to believe that the offender has breached a condition of release or that the risk they present can no longer be safely managed in the community.”

The agency said it can either cancel the suspension within 30 days or refer the case to the Parole Board of Canada for a post-suspension review.

McGill said it could not comment on specific cases for privacy reasons. However, it said that while criminal background checks are not typically part of Canadian universities’ admissions processes, the school “would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus.”

McGill said its procedures also include consulting relevant government bodies and its own policies to remove the individual from campus and to review its admission processes to ensure the situation isn’t repeated.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Head of UN relief praises Canada, calls for accountability in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan
stories.summary: The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide. “Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa. “I really hope […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide.

“Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line.”

Fletcher leads the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. For two years he has visited the front lines in Ukraine and Gaza while urging the world not to forget about ongoing crises in Sudan, Afghanistan and Mali.

His term started just weeks before the U.S. made deep cuts to foreign aid — though Fletcher praised the United States for restoring some of that funding over the past year.

Pointing to the conflicts in Sudan and Gaza, Fletcher said the funding shortfall is being compounded by wars that are spreading hunger and blocking humanitarian relief.

Roughly 19 million people in Sudan are living with acute hunger and Fletcher warns their plight could be made worse by changing weather patterns and the U.S. war in Iran blocking supply routes.

Sudan’s warring parties in the now three-year-old civil war have banned aid workers from certain areas based on how they perceive the local population’s loyalties.

Fletcher said he worries about normalizing practices the Israeli government has implemented in Gaza, such as barring journalists from the territory and drastically restricting aid flows.

“It’s sort of infectious, in the way that it undermines international law elsewhere, and creates or adds to this climate of impunity that we’re seeing across all the crises we work in,” he said.

Fletcher has faced sustained criticism from supporters of Israel who say the UN is downplaying groups like Hamas diverting aid or embedding themselves among civilians.

Fletcher said it’s important not to bow to that pressure, which he said comes from people who don’t want the world to see the extent of suffering inside Gaza.

“We’re being told, ‘Well, you’ll get more access if you change your reporting, or if you reduce your criticism, or your advocacy, or, if you spend less time talking about international law,’ and so on,” he said. “We just have to be consistent here.”

Technology is also making wars easier to fight. Fletcher said drones are being used more frequently against civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon.

“The way in which humans are using their ingenuity to find new ways to kill civilians is terrifying,” he said. “We need the member states to be holding themselves and each other to account.”

Fletcher praised Canada for its advocacy and its foreign aid funding, which he said “is saving millions of lives every year from Sudan to Afghanistan, to Gaza, to Ukraine, to Haiti and beyond.”

“We’re in a world right now where we’re underfunded, we’re overstretched, we’re literally under attack — a thousand dead humanitarians in three years,” he said.

“And at each point at which I’ve felt particularly exposed and where we as humanitarians feel exposed, we do look behind us and we find that Canada does have our back. And that means a huge amount.”

Fletcher met Tuesday with Randeep Sarai, Canada’s secretary of state for international development, who announced the renewal of $6 million in federal funding to help co-ordinate global emergency responses.

But Canada has changed its approach to foreign aid since Prime Minister Mark Carney took office. It cut funding for global health programs, is pushing for more private-sector investments in aid programs and spinoffs for Canadian companies, and dropped the “feminist” label from its foreign policy.

The aid sector has criticized this shift. They argue it prioritizes domestic growth over aid intended to address the issues which drive migration and conflict, and does not support the world’s most vulnerable people.

Ottawa has insisted it can fight poverty abroad while boosting Canadian companies at home.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports reforms but is urging Ottawa not to cut development and humanitarian funding further.

Coalition head Kate Higgins said during a Monday reception for Fletcher that the government’s recent national security strategy called for “strong international partnerships and a disciplined foreign policy.”

“Canada can give practical expression to that ambition through sustained humanitarian funding, principled diplomacy, and consistent leadership in upholding international humanitarian law,” she said.

Next July, Canada will chair a donor support group which consults with other rich countries on how the UN uses its humanitarian funding.

Fletcher said that’s an opportunity for a “reimagination” of what humanitarian aid looks like in an era when governments aren’t meeting the needs.

“I’d like to reach out beyond just traditional humanitarian development partners, actually towards technology companies, to the private sector, to really get their sense of how we can together deal with these crises,” he said.

Fletcher said UN agencies and large organizations have a crucial role to play in addressing complex problems like the hunger crisis in Darfur.

But he said places with internet connectivity and a functioning market might benefit more from cash transfers to individuals, or from health care programs where private companies can help while making a profit.
